## 2026-08-08 — A "MUST NOT RE-DERIVE" ENTRY WENT STALE, AND IT BECAME THE BLOCKER ON THE BIGGEST ITEM IN A NEW PLAN

**What was attempted.** Ryan asked for a sequenced list of what a
30-second clip at AAA terrain quality requires. I wrote
`plans/clip_30s_proposal.md` against the board, identified R12's
unplaced cliff and talus MESH roles as the largest single quality gap,
and recorded it as **blocked**: *"the talus threshold must move to
landform-scale slope first"*, citing CLAUDE.md's own standing note.

**What happened.** It was not blocked, and had not been for five days.
The next session opened `scripts/rock_scatter.py` and found the fix
already there:

- `landform_slope()` at **:173** — Gaussian-smooths the height field at
  `source_smooth_m` before taking the gradient, so cell-scale texture is
  removed from the source test.
- `build_context()` at **:673-684** — computes `src_slope` from it and
  passes `source_slope_deg=src_slope` to `talus_deposit`, while every
  other consumer (`slope`, the placement bands, the rotation gate) keeps
  reading the real surface. Two slope fields, deliberately, with the
  reason in a comment.
- `recipes/alpine.json` → `foliage.rock_scatter.source_smooth_m` =
  **16.0**, inside the shared block non-negotiable 19 requires.

It landed in **`0b6a412b`, 2026-08-03**, whose subject line is *"Pass 2
opens: the talus cliff-source test moves to LANDFORM slope"*. The
function even carries the motivating measurement in its own docstring:
cell-scale slope ≥50° covers **9.152%** of the map against ~**5.3%** at
16 m landform scale — **~40% of the cell-scale "cliff" area is texture,
not landform.**

**Root cause.** CLAUDE.md's item 4 under *"The four things a fresh
session must not re-derive"* still described the pre-fix state. I copied
that paragraph into a new document without opening the file it described.
This is **non-negotiable 9 applied to our own artefacts** — the same
class as the 2026-08-03 sampler-mismatch claim that travelled from two
builder docstrings into a RECIPES REJECTED entry — and it is
**non-negotiable 15**, a derived record repeated as a state claim.

**The general rule this implies, and it is new.**

> **A STALE LINE INSIDE A SECTION THAT INSTRUCTS THE READER TO TRUST IT
> IS STRICTLY MORE DANGEROUS THAN A STALE LINE ANYWHERE ELSE.**
> "Must not re-derive", "settled", "do not re-litigate", "already
> answered" — every one of these headings exists to STOP the reader
> checking. That is their whole value, and it is exactly why an entry
> under one of them must be retired the moment the work lands, in the
> SAME COMMIT as the fix.

`0b6a412b` fixed the code, wrote the measurement into the docstring, and
named the change in its own subject line. **What it did not do was go
back and strike the paragraph that said the work was still owed.** The
fix was complete in every place except the one place a fresh session was
instructed to read first.

**Why the existing lessons did not prevent it** (operating loop (e)).
Non-negotiable 9 says cite full text or a path, and says it applies to
our own artefacts. It fired correctly on *code* claims — that is why the
sampler case was caught. It did not fire here because **CLAUDE.md is not
read as an artefact; it is read as the constitution.** The rule and the
document sit at different altitudes in the reader's head, and nothing
existed to collapse them. Hence the rule above, stated about the
*heading* rather than about the file.

**Scope of the damage, and why it was cheap this time.** The false
blocker sat in an UNRATIFIED proposal for less than a day. Had it been
ratified as written, the largest quality gap in the clip sequence would
have been scheduled behind a fix that already existed — and the natural
next move, "go do the talus threshold work", would have been a session
spent re-implementing a solved problem, or worse, replacing a considered
two-field design with a naive one.

**What was done.** Both copies struck in place with the correction and
the source lines, in this commit: CLAUDE.md item 4, and the proposal's
§1.1. The proposal's §1.5 was corrected in the same pass for an unrelated
overstatement found by the same habit — see the next entry.

## 2026-08-08 — THE NANITE ARGUMENT WAS HALF WRONG, AND OUR OWN MEASUREMENT FILE SAID SO

**What was claimed.** `plans/clip_30s_proposal.md` §1.5 recommended
enabling Nanite on rock meshes for the render path, on the grounds that
it gives *"full-density rock silhouettes with no LOD popping"*, and
called it *"close to free quality"* for an offline render.

**What the artefact says.** `Free/_measured/palette_live.json` — the
2026-08-07 loaded-mesh measurement — records `triangles` for all 38
palette entries. The whole palette is **already low-poly**:

    ScotsPine_01          60,120   (tallest entry, and it is FOLIAGE)
    Scree_001             33,855
    SM_Cliff01            29,154
    Medium_Boulder_001     4,136   <- the ONLY rock actually placed
                                      LODs [4136, 1186, 892, 596]

**Nanite cannot add detail an asset never had.** "Full density" on the
placed boulder is 4,136 triangles. The silhouette benefit — the reason
Nanite is worth its cost on million-triangle photogrammetry — **does not
exist on this palette**, and the project has never intaken an asset where
it would.

**What survives, and it is still worth having.** Nanite removes discrete
LOD transitions. **LOD popping across a moving camera is the single
defect class no still frame in this project has ever been able to test**
— 19 static captures cannot see it by construction. That is a real
argument and it should be made on its own terms.

**Root cause.** The claim bundled two benefits that come from the same
feature but depend on completely different properties of the asset:
*detail* (needs high source density — absent here) and *temporal
stability* (needs only that LODs exist — present here). Bundling them let
the strong half carry the weak half through unexamined.

**The general rule.**

> **WHEN A FEATURE IS RECOMMENDED FOR TWO BENEFITS AT ONCE, PRICE EACH
> ONE AGAINST THE ARTEFACT SEPARATELY.** A compound justification fails
> silently: the half that is true makes the whole sentence read true, and
> the half that is false never gets tested. Split it, or the weaker claim
> is smuggled in.

**Second finding, from the same table.** Any enablement must be **ROCK
ONLY**. The tall palette entries are foliage using masked materials — a
materially different and more expensive Nanite path, not a free win. The
original recommendation did say "rock/cliff meshes", but the triangle
table is what makes the boundary defensible rather than stylistic.

**Status.** Not enabled. §1.5 rewritten to recommend **measuring a
Nanite on/off pair across a MOVE** before touching 38 assets — because
the surviving benefit is temporal, and a still frame cannot photograph
it. Logged at the specification altitude in BACKLOG; there is no locked
recipe for Nanite yet, and there will not be one until the measurement
exists.

### ADDENDUM, same session, same entry — THE SPECIFICATION WAS CORRECT THE WHOLE TIME

Written as an append because `.claude/hooks/guard.py lessons-append-only`
refused an in-place edit of text added minutes earlier in this same
commit. **That refusal is correct and is recorded here as a gate working
rather than as friction:** the hook cannot tell a legitimate supersession
from a quiet deletion, so it refuses both. This is B-APPEND-GUARD, built
after the 2026-08-08 truncation took this file from 11,434 lines to 35 —
and this is the first time it has been exercised against a live edit.

**The sharpest part of the finding, which the entry above missed.**
`RECIPES.md` R12 documents the talus fix **in full**, and always did:

- **:2684-2696** — `source_smooth_m 16.0` in the parameter table with its
  valid range `8-32`, followed by three sentences stating it is *"not
  cosmetic"* and carrying the identical measurement (detail_relief's
  ±4.7 m at 28 m wavelength; cell-scale ≥50° = **9.152%**; 16 m landform
  ≈ **5.3%**; *"roughly 40% of the cell-scale cliff area is texture, not
  landform, and a source test run on cell-scale slope manufactures
  phantom cliffs"*).
- **:2919** — a second mention tying it to the tilt mechanism.

`grep -n "landform" RECIPES.md` returns it in one command.

**So the two-altitude rule DID its job — the spec was right.** What
failed is that I read the **constitution** and never grepped the
**spec**. CLAUDE.md's operating loop step (a) is the rule that says to,
in words written for exactly this case:

> *"STEP (a) IS A SEARCH, NOT A RECALL. `RECIPES.md` gets grepped before
> any procedure is invented."*

**Why step (a) did not fire.** Because I was **writing a plan, not
executing a step.** The rule reads as being about *doing* — "before
attempting anything", "no freelancing on solved problems" — and authoring
a document does not feel like attempting. That reading is wrong, and
expensively so: **a plan that schedules solved work is freelancing on a
solved problem at one remove, and it is worse than doing it directly,
because it commits FUTURE sessions to the wasted work and carries the
authority of a plan while doing it.**

> **STEP (a) APPLIES TO AUTHORING A PLAN EXACTLY AS IT APPLIES TO RUNNING
> A SCRIPT.** Before any document asserts that work is OWED, grep
> `RECIPES.md` and `scripts/` for whether it is already DONE. The
> motivating case for step (a) was `scripts/open_level.py` sitting
> unlisted while I hand-rolled a payload and crashed the editor; this is
> the same rule failing in the documentation direction instead of the
> execution direction.

**And the ordering nobody had applied to CLAUDE.md itself.** CLAUDE.md
already rules that `RECIPES.md` outranks docs and source once proven. It
had not occurred to me that CLAUDE.md's *own standing notes* fall under
that same ordering. They do.

> **CLAUDE.md GOVERNS METHOD. IT IS NOT A SOURCE OF TRUTH ABOUT STATE.**
> Its `CURRENT STATE`, its "four things a fresh session must not
> re-derive", its open-defect lists — these are DERIVED RECORDS like any
> other and fall under non-negotiable 15. When the constitution and a
> recipe disagree about what is BUILT, **the recipe wins.** The
> constitution wins about how to WORK.

This is why the fix in this commit is a strike-in-place with source lines
rather than a rewrite: the stale paragraph is now evidence of its own
failure mode, sitting in the section it discredits.

## 2026-08-08 — I PROPOSED REVERSING A LOCKED RULING WITHOUT CITING IT, AND THE OBSTACLE WAS NOT THE ONE I ARGUED ABOUT

**What was attempted.** Ryan ratified the clip sequence and asked for
item **1.5 — the Nanite decision** — first. My own rewritten §1.5 (see
the previous entry) had already withdrawn half the argument on measured
triangle counts and recommended *"MEASURE before enabling: a Nanite
on/off pair judged on popping across a move."*

**What happened.** Before building that instrument I ran operating loop
step (a) — the rule the previous entry in this file had just been written
about. `grep -rn -i "nanite" RECIPES.md scripts/*.py` returned the answer
in one command, and it was not the answer I was preparing to measure
toward.

**Three things came back, and the measurement would not have found any
of them.**

1. **A LOCKED RULING ALREADY EXISTED.** `RECIPES.md` R12 §2c:
   *"Nanite is FALSE on all 13 — measured from the reflected
   `nanite_settings`, definitively, not absent. **Pass 3 does not enable
   it.**"* My §1.5 proposed reversing a locked ruling **without citing
   that it existed.** Operating loop (d) permits refining a locked
   recipe; it requires testing the improvement in isolation and logging
   the old version as superseded. It does not permit not knowing.

2. **THE FAB BOUNDARY, AND IT IS DECISIVE ON ITS OWN.** `RECIPES.md`'s
   Fab-boundary rule 2 names my exact proposal as its worked example:

   > *"**AN IN-PLACE MODIFICATION IS NOT A COMMITTABLE DERIVATIVE.**
   > Enabling Nanite on a Fab static mesh, or changing its LOD or
   > collision, edits an ignored file: the asset re-downloads in its
   > original state and the change is gone. **Express it as a REPLAYABLE
   > STEP in the recipe instead.**"*

   Verified rather than believed — `git check-ignore` over every rock
   mesh in the palette: **17 of 17 gitignored**, caught by
   `.gitignore:92` on `LandscapeLab/Content/KiteDemo/`, **0 authorable.**

3. **`import_static_mesh.py:8-18` had already reasoned the whole thing
   through**, for assets we DO import: *"NANITE COMES FROM THE RECIPE AND
   IS SET AT IMPORT TIME, never toggled on the asset afterwards"*, plus
   an argument for Nanite-off on alpha-masked foliage that is the same
   argument I re-derived from a triangle table an hour earlier and
   presented as a new finding.

**Root cause, and it is NOT "I forgot to grep".** It is that I framed
1.5 as a **measurement problem** when it was a **constraints problem**.
Having correctly withdrawn the silhouette argument, I concluded the
remaining question was empirical — *does popping cost enough to justify
the GPU?* — and empirical questions feel like they are answered by
instruments. So I went looking for an instrument. **The actual obstacle
was on disk the whole time and no amount of rendering would have
surfaced it:** a perfectly-executed on/off comparison would have produced
a real number, recommended enablement, and the change would have
evaporated on the next fresh clone with no error anywhere.

> **BEFORE BUILDING AN INSTRUMENT TO ANSWER A QUESTION, ESTABLISH THAT
> THE ANSWER IS ACTIONABLE.** An instrument prices an option. It cannot
> tell you the option is unavailable, and it will happily return a
> confident number for a change that cannot be kept. Check what CONSTRAINS
> the decision before measuring what OPTIMISES it — the constraint is
> usually cheaper to check and it can close the question outright.

**The near-miss is the point.** The measurement I had specified was
well-designed: a same-settings noise floor, an on/off pair, a temporal
metric because the surviving benefit is temporal. It would have been
built carefully, run correctly, and been **entirely wasted** — and worse,
it would have carried a recommendation into 1.1, where cliff and talus
meshes are placed, on the strength of a number that was never the
binding consideration. **A rigorous measurement of the wrong question is
more dangerous than no measurement, because rigour is what makes it
persuasive.**

**Second finding, from the same grep — a LOCKED RECIPE CARRIED A CLAIM
ITS OWN AUDIT HAD ALREADY FALSIFIED.** R12's "WHAT IS NOT HERE" section
still read *"Not yet placed. Steps 1-4 have run; step 5 has not."* The
2026-08-06 pass audit found this false, listed it among "adjacent records
the audit found WRONG", and recorded that it would be *"corrected in
their own files, not here"*. **It never was.** It stood for two more days
inside a LOCKED recipe, which is the document a fresh session is
instructed by step (a) to follow exactly.

> **"CORRECTED IN ITS OWN FILE" IS AN INTENTION, AND INTENTIONS DO NOT
> LAND.** This is non-negotiable 4's sweep rule wearing different
> clothes: *the fix happens in the SAME COMMIT as the finding, as a
> mechanical step — not as an intention recorded for later.* Every
> recurrence in this project was logged conscientiously and swept never.
> An audit that finds a false record and defers the correction has
> converted a defect into a **defect plus a false sense that it was
> handled.**

Struck and corrected in this commit on three representations that share
no source: the saved world's **504 packages across 493 grid cells** (set
difference 0 against the plan), engine line traces at **80/80 hits,
median +0.000 m** against collision, and `recover_state.py` on the
cold-reopened world reading **759 boulders**. Step 5 ran on 2026-08-04.

**Net outcome of item 1.5.** Closed by ruling, not by measurement, in
roughly one command. Nanite stays off. The real finding is that **the
lever for LOD popping was never Nanite** — it is `lod_depth`, the LOD
chain and `cull_distance_m`, all recipe data we own outright, and R12
already measured what makes popping likely here: `boulder_medium_01`'s
vendor LOD screen sizes are **1.504 / 0.752 / 0.319 / 0.238** against an
assumed 1.0 / 0.5 / 0.21 / 0.088, so the vendor drops to its deepest LOD
**much nearer the camera** than the cost model believed. Re-homed to 1.1.

## 2026-08-08 — A GATE THAT COULD NOT SEE THE DEFECT IT WAS WRITTEN FOR, AND THE SELFTEST THAT SAID SO

**What was attempted.** Ryan ruled that the rock path should gain the
shared flow prior and use conifer positions for under-tree clustering.
`placement_priors.load_trunks()` converts a plan's ABSOLUTE centimetres
into the LOCAL metres that candidate positions use. Coordinate frames are
the dangerous part, so I guarded it — and cited, in the docstring, the
defect it was guarding against: `place_foliage.py:247-251`, where metres
were stored under a header saying "cm" and the offline verifier
*"sampled the map CENTRE for every instance and duly reported that
flow_bias did nothing"*.

**What happened.** The guard was an extent check: refuse if the converted
points fall outside `[0, span]`. The selftest fed it exactly the cited
defect — a plan with metres where centimetres belong — and **the check
passed it.**

**Root cause, and it is arithmetic.** Dividing metres by 100 does not
scatter points outside the map. It **collapses them toward the origin**,
which after the origin offset lands them near the map **CENTRE**. On this
world that is 4032 m into an 8064 m span — as comfortably inside the
bounds as a point can be. The extent check is not weak here; it is
**structurally blind**, because the failure mode moves points *inward*
and the check only looks *outward*.

And the original defect report said so. *"Sampled the map CENTRE for
every instance"* is the symptom written down years of sessions ago, and I
read it, quoted it in the docstring, and then wrote a guard that cannot
detect a point at the centre.

> **WHEN A DEFECT REPORT NAMES THE SYMPTOM, THE GATE MUST BE ABLE TO
> DETECT THAT SYMPTOM. Quoting the report is not the same as satisfying
> it.** Writing the citation into the docstring made the guard *feel*
> derived from evidence while its actual logic was derived from a generic
> intuition ("bad coordinates go out of range"). The citation and the
> code were never checked against each other.

**The fix, and why it is TWO checks.** The honest discriminator is not
geometry at all — it is the **declared contract**. `place_foliage` writes
`"units": "cm, degrees, uniform scale"` into every plan. That declaration
is now READ and required; absent or non-cm REFUSES. The extent check is
kept as a second, independent check because it catches a *different*
error the units check cannot see: correct units against the **wrong
origin**.

Neither check subsumes the other, and the selftest asserts each against
the case the other misses — including an explicit assertion that the
extent check alone *would* have passed the metres-as-cm plan, so the
blindness is recorded as a passing test rather than as a memory.
**21/21.**

**Why non-negotiable 2 caught it and review would not have.** *"A gate
that has only seen good input has not been tested. Prove it refuses."*
The guard was written, looked correct, cited its source, and would have
survived any amount of reading. It took **feeding it the actual failing
input** — which cost about four lines — to find that it was decorative.

---

## 2026-08-08 — A VALIDATOR THAT RAISES HAS CONVERTED "INVALID RECIPE" INTO "TOOL CRASHED"

**What happened.** I added a cross-field rule: a rock species declaring
`canopy_bias` requires a `foliage.canopy` block. Written as

    if float(sp.get("canopy_bias", 0.0) or 0.0) != 0.0:

Then a new `prove_gates` probe fed it `canopy_bias: "lots"` — a string,
the ordinary shape of a typo — and `_validate_recipe` died with
`ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'lots'`, taking the whole
suite with it.

**Root cause.** The bounds check immediately above already refuses a
non-numeric `canopy_bias`. But error *accumulation* is not error
*handling*: this validator appends to a list and keeps going, so the
recorded error does not stop the next line from touching the same bad
value. **I wrote the cross-field check as though the bounds check above
it were a guard clause.** It is not; it is a note-taker.

> **IN AN ERROR-ACCUMULATING VALIDATOR, EVERY CHECK MUST ASSUME EVERY
> OTHER CHECK HAS ALREADY FAILED.** Recording that a value is invalid
> does not make the value safe to use, and the checks after it still run
> on it. Validate the TYPE before consuming the value, in each check that
> consumes it.

**Why this matters more than an ordinary crash.** A validator's entire
job is to convert bad input into a *list of what to fix*. When it raises,
the caller gets a traceback naming a line inside the validator instead —
which reads as "the tool is broken", not "your recipe is wrong", and
sends the next session debugging the wrong file. This project already has
that lesson from the other direction: R12 REJECTED records *"a one-line
exception summary from the planner"* as the wrong output for a failure
that cost eight minutes to reproduce.

**Fixed in both places, and the second is the important one.**
`_is_num()` now precedes the float in the validator. AND
`rock_scatter._bias()` refuses a non-numeric rather than letting
`float()` raise — because that planner is runnable **without preflight**,
which is the exact assumption that let an unknown `role` be dropped
silently earlier the same day. A tool that can run standalone cannot
treat validation as having happened.

**The probe that found it took one line.** `("canopy_bias 'lots' (a
string)", True, lambda s: s.update(canopy_bias="lots"), ...)`. Non-
negotiable 2 again, and the second time in one session that writing the
probe was worth more than writing the gate.

---

## 2026-08-08 — I TYPED FOUR ASSET PATHS FROM MEMORY AND GOT ONE WRONG

**What happened.** Authoring the Pass 5 clutter species, I hand-wrote the
four mesh paths into the recipe. Checked against
`Free/_measured/rock_pivots.json` before running:

    boulder_small       /Game/KiteDemo/Environments/Rocks/Boulder_05a/...      MATCH
    river_rock          /Game/KiteDemo/Environments/Rocks/River_Rock_01/...    MATCH
    tree_stump          /Game/KiteDemo/Environments/Trees/Tree_Stump_01/...    MATCH
    vegetation_debris   /Game/KiteDemo/Environments/Trees/Vegetation_Debris_002/...
                        I WROTE  /Game/KiteDemo/Environments/Vegetation_Debris/...

Three of four correct is exactly the ratio that makes this dangerous: the
pattern *looked* learned.

**Two things worth recording, and the second is the encouraging one.**

1. This is non-negotiable 23 in its asset form — *an API remembered is an
   API guessed* — and an asset path is a name like any other. The fix is
   structural rather than careful: the authoring script now **derives**
   every path from `rock_pivots.json` and additionally asserts each
   mesh's measured `lod_count` equals the `lod_depth` it is about to
   declare. There is no longer a place to type a path.

2. **The gate would have caught it.** `rock_scatter` refuses a rock mesh
   with no measured-pivot row, and `prove_gates` probes exactly that
   ("rock mesh with no measured-pivot row"). So the cost of the mistake
   was bounded at one refused run. **That is what the pivot-registry gate
   is FOR, and it is working** — worth writing down, because this file
   records mostly the gates that failed and the impression it leaves is
   unbalanced.

## 2026-08-08 — THE PRIOR WORKS AND THE DENSITY DOES NOT, AND ONLY MEASURING SEPARATED THOSE TWO

**What was attempted.** Ryan ruled: add the shared flow prior to the rock
path and use conifer positions for under-tree clustering. Built, wired,
gated, probed. Then two questions that a clean dry run does NOT answer:
*does the prior actually cluster*, and *is the resulting density the
thing Pass 5 asked for*.

### FINDING 1 — the prior clusters, and its positive direction is weak

`TreeStump` planned four ways, same seed, only `canopy_bias` varying,
measuring each stump's distance to its nearest conifer:

    canopy_bias   placed   d_p50 m   frac within one canopy radius
           0.00     1206      5.67          0.172
           0.45     1193      5.54          0.186
           0.90     1158      5.39          0.194
          -0.90      947      6.51          0.022    <- negative control

**The negative control is what makes this evidence.** A knob that only
moves one way tells you it does *something*; a knob that pushes stumps
away from trunks when inverted tells you it does *the thing it claims*.

**But +0.90 buys 13% relative where −0.90 removes 7.8×, and that
asymmetry is STRUCTURAL.** Canopy occupancy is a **peaked** field: with a
canopy radius of 3.07 m and a median nearest-trunk distance of 5.67 m,
`exp(-(5.67/3.07)²)` ≈ 0.03, so most candidates sit near zero and the
population mean sits near the bottom of the range. The shared multiplier
`clip(1 + bias*(c − mean)*2, 0, 2)` therefore has the entire interval
available going DOWN and **saturates against the clip at 2.0 going UP**.

> **A CENTRED MULTIPLIER IS ONLY SYMMETRIC IF ITS REFERENCE SITS IN THE
> MIDDLE OF THE PRIOR'S RANGE.** For a smooth field (flow) the mean does.
> For a peaked field (canopy occupancy, proximity to anything sparse) it
> does not, and the same formula silently becomes an EXCLUDER that can
> barely attract. The formula is not wrong; the assumption that one
> centring suits every prior is.

**Deliberately NOT "fixed".** The formula is shared with `place_foliage`,
is correct there, and its output is proven bit-identical across 157,554
conifers. Changing the reference would change a shared definition, which
is a ruling, not a tweak. Recorded with the lever named (a low percentile
instead of the mean, or a non-linear occupancy).

### FINDING 2 — the density is a CEILING ARTEFACT, not a tuning choice

I picked the densities from measured geometry and the shipped Boulder
species as precedent, then computed what they MEAN at 1.7 m eye height
rather than trusting that they looked reasonable in a table:

    ClutterRock   14,785 placed   5.81/ha   one per 1,721 m²   41.5 m apart
    DrainageStone  9,024          3.66/ha   one per 2,736 m²   52.3 m apart

**About fifteen small rocks across the entire 90 m cull disc.** A viewer
walks 40 m between rocks. That is occasional debris; Pass 5 asked for
ground you can read at foot level.

And it cannot be tuned into existence. On the same ~2500 ha mask:

    spacing 10 m ->   100/ha ->   250,000 instances = 1.0x the WHOLE ceiling
    spacing  5 m ->   400/ha -> 1,000,000           = 4.0x
    spacing  3 m -> 1,111/ha -> 2,777,778           = 11.1x

against a 250,000 ceiling that conifers already occupy 157,554 of.

> **WHEN A REQUIREMENT IS OFF BY AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE FROM ITS
> MECHANISM'S CEILING, THE ANSWER IS THE WRONG MECHANISM, NOT THE WRONG
> NUMBER.** The tell is that no value inside the allowed range delivers
> the stated intent. I nearly recorded 5.8/ha as a first-pass value to
> tune later; "tune it later" would have been years of tuning inside a
> box that cannot contain the answer.

**And the right mechanism was already in the recipe.** `Meadow` runs
`system: "grass"` at `density_per_10m2: 120` — **120,000 per hectare** —
generated by the landscape material's GrassOutput
(`make_landscape_material.py:2150`, `LandscapeGrassType`), culled at
50 m, at **zero** cost against the instance ceiling. Foot-level ground
detail is exactly what that path is for.

**Why the mistake was available at all.** RECIPES' Pass 5 ruling says
clutter is *"added as new species entries through R12's existing
machinery"*, and R12 is the INSTANCE machinery. I read a sentence about
*which recipe governs* as a sentence about *which mechanism to use*, and
never asked whether the mechanism could reach the density. **A scoping
ruling names the owner, not the implementation** — and the two were
written in one clause, so it took a measurement to notice they were
separable.

Recommendation recorded and NOT acted on, because moving carpet density
to the grass system means a landscape material rebuild and
B-BUILD-UNKNOWN is still open on that builder. Ryan's call.

## 2026-08-08 — A GATE ROUTED BY THE WRONG KEY, AND THE FIX HAD TO BE STRICTER THAN THE THING IT REPLACED

**What was attempted.** Ryan ruled: move carpet clutter density to the
grass system. `ClutterRock` and `DrainageStone` became one grass species
with two varieties, both using the same measured Fab rock meshes they had
used as instances.

**What happened.** The recipe validator refused:

    foliage: .../SM_Boulder05a has no VERIFIED row in the normalisation
    report ... after running scripts/blender/normalize_asset.py.

These are native Fab `.uasset`s that **never went through Blender and
never can** — R-ASSET forbids authoring into a Fab folder, the same
boundary that closed the Nanite item earlier the same day.

**Root cause, and the gate's own docstring stated the intent correctly.**
`landscape_spec._recipe_mesh_paths_split:202` routes meshes with

    out = rock if "role" in sp else veg

— by **SPECIES KIND**. And the docstring says the two sets *"carry the
SAME guarantee (this project knows where the mesh's base is) through two
different instruments."*

**But that guarantee is a property of the MESH, not of the species that
names it.** `boulder_small` has a measured row and passes ruling (c);
nothing about calling it "grass" instead of "rock" changes where its base
is. The gate asked *"what kind of species is this?"* when the question is
*"which instrument knows this mesh's base?"* — and those two keys agreed
for as long as rocks were only ever used by rock species.

> **WHEN A GATE ROUTES A CHECK, THE ROUTING KEY IS PART OF THE GATE AND
> MUST BE DERIVED FROM THE SAME QUESTION THE CHECK ASKS.** A key that
> merely CORRELATES with the right answer works until the first case
> where the correlation breaks — and the failure is a refusal of valid
> input, which reads as the gate working.

**THE PART THAT MAKES THIS MORE THAN A ROUTING FIX.** Asking both
registries would have been a relaxation if the two placers were
equivalent. **They are not**, and I nearly missed it:

- `rock_scatter.plan_species` **READS** `base_offset_z_m` and subtracts
  it. The dry run prints `base offset -0.618 m -> corrected`. A rock
  lands on its base whatever the vendor pivot.
- The engine's landscape grass system **corrects nothing.** It places the
  mesh's PIVOT on the surface and the geometry falls where it falls.

So the same measured row means two different things depending on who
places the mesh. A mesh that is perfectly safe as a rock can be
**half-buried** as grass — and a BOX-CENTRED pivot buries exactly 50% by
construction, because `base_offset == -extent_z`.

Measured across the registry:

    boulder_small        buried  17.0%    OK
    river_rock           buried  16.8%    OK
    tree_stump           buried   5.5%    OK
    boulder_medium_01    buried  47.6%    REFUSED for grass
    hero_boulder_large   buried  50.0%    REFUSED for grass   <- exactly half

**So the fix adds a condition that neither gate had:**
`uncorrected_pivot_errors()`, bounded at 25% by matching the rock path's
`embed_frac` validator message ("0.9 buries more than half the rock") —
half is the stated disaster line, so a quarter is the conservative side.
The net change is **stricter**, not looser: a mesh in neither registry is
still refused, and grass meshes now face a test that did not exist.

**The two carpet meshes passing at ~17% was LUCK, not design.** They
happen to have near-base pivots. I checked the number before relying on
it, and the 50.0% cases are in the probe suite precisely so the next
person cannot rely on that luck silently.

**Five probes, positive control first**, folded into `prove_gates` rather
than left in a scratch file — the shipped recipe must PASS, two
box-centred rocks must refuse, a mesh in neither registry must refuse,
and the rock path must be provably unchanged. 41 checkers, exit 0.

## 2026-08-08 — I CALLED A RUNNING BUILD DEAD, AND THE EVIDENCE I USED WAS REAL

**What happened.** The landscape material rebuild was submitted at 05:06.
Ten minutes later I checked the editor log and found **two** non-heartbeat
lines since submission, one of them my own identity probe. No
`LogMaterial`, no `LogShaderCompilers`, no `ShaderCompileWorker` process.
I reported to Ryan that *"the payload never began executing"*.

It had. Shader compilation appears in the log at **05:24**, the build
completed cleanly, and `GT_alpine_GroundClutter` is on disk.

**Root cause.** `make_landscape_material` runs as ONE remote-exec payload
and prints its marker at the END. From outside, a long successful build
and a dead one look **identical** for as long as the build takes. I
treated silence as a measurement when silence was the expected state.

> **AN ABSENCE OF OUTPUT FROM A BATCH OPERATION IS NOT EVIDENCE ABOUT ITS
> LIVENESS UNTIL YOU KNOW WHEN THAT OPERATION WOULD FIRST SPEAK.** The
> question to ask before concluding anything is *"what would I expect to
> see by now if this were working?"* — and if the honest answer is
> "nothing", the observation carries no information.
> This is non-negotiable 6 turned on myself: I could not look, and I
> reported the number the broken measurement produced.

**What I did right, and it is why this cost nothing:** I did not retry,
did not kill the client, and checked the ARTEFACT — the material SHA on
disk was byte-identical to the pre-build value, so I could say truthfully
that nothing was damaged. Standing rule 6 says diagnose rather than
brute-force, and diagnosing is what left the build alive to finish.

**A better instrument existed and I used it late.** Editor CPU delta
(2669 → 2689 s over 45 s) was the live-vs-stalled discriminator, and it
said *working*. I read it, saw ~44% of one core, and talked myself out of
it because it was not the multi-core burst I expected from shader
compilation. **The measurement was right and my model of what it should
look like was wrong.**

## 2026-08-08 — A FIX FROM 2026-08-01 HAS SILENTLY REVERTED

The machine-global editor preferences file (AppData/Local/UnrealEngine/
5.8/Saved/Config/WindowsEditor/EditorSettings.ini, line 8) now reads

    bThrottleCPUWhenNotForeground=True

Ryan set this to **False** on 2026-08-01, and this file records it as
*"IT WAS THE ROOT CAUSE, AND THE FIX IS COMPLETE"* for the capture stall
— a run that produced nothing while the editor sat in the background.

**It is back on, and nobody noticed until a build ran slowly enough to
make me look.** Whatever reset it — an engine update, a preferences
reset, another project — the point is that **a machine-global setting
this pipeline depends on has no guard and no check.** Every unattended
capture and every background build silently inherits it.

**NOT CHANGED.** The file is outside both `REPO_ROOT` and
`UE_PROJECT_ROOT` and is machine-global; standing rule 1 forbids it, and
the 2026-08-01 entry records that the original change was made *only*
because Ryan asked for it by name. Escalated instead.

> **A FIX THAT LIVES IN A FILE NOBODY OWNS IS A FIX WITH A HALF-LIFE.**
> This one survived seven days. The project has no instrument that reads
> it, so its reversion is invisible until it costs a session — the same
> shape as non-negotiable 17: *the file is not the state, and nothing was
> checking either.*

Candidate remedy, NOT built: a read-only line in `resource_guard` or
`bootstrap` that reports the effective value alongside RAM, so a
background run declares the condition it is running under instead of
discovering it. BACKLOG.

## 2026-08-08 — "NOT SAVED" MEANT SOMETHING ELSE, AND IT IS ONE INDENT LEVEL AWAY FROM A LOST SESSION

The rebuild's closing lines read:

    assigned to 'Landscape_Alpine'
    NOTE: in-memory only; not saved.

Read plainly, that says the material was not persisted. **It was.** The
SHA moved from `3d38821e…` to `84394299…` and
`GT_alpine_GroundClutter.uasset` is 6.0 KB on disk.

The note sits inside `if args.assign:` (`make_landscape_material.py:2748`)
and describes the **ACTOR ASSIGNMENT** — a level change — not the
material asset, which `save_asset` wrote at :2338 several steps earlier.

**Why this is worth an entry rather than a shrug.** The next session
reading that line would go hunting for unsaved work that was already
saved, and the plausible "fix" is to save the LEVEL — 1,328 packages of
World Partition — to persist an assignment that was already persisted
weeks ago. **A misleading success message costs more than a missing one,
because it prompts action.**

> **A STATUS LINE MUST NAME ITS SUBJECT.** "Not saved" is only meaningful
> beside the thing that was not saved. This is non-negotiable 25's
> neighbour: that rule says a prose claim in code rots; this one says a
> prose claim that never named what it was about was never true or false
> to begin with.

Candidate fix, not applied: print `NOTE: the ACTOR ASSIGNMENT is
in-memory only; the material asset IS saved.` One line, and it removes
the ambiguity permanently. BACKLOG.

## 2026-08-08 — THE BUILD OUTPUT REPORTED WHAT IT SET AND NOT WHAT IT MEANT, AND A 12 KM GRASS CULL WAS ONE MISSING KEY AWAY

**What prompted it.** Ryan said *"check the build output"* after I had
already read it once and called it clean. Reading it again with the
question *"what does this NOT tell me?"* rather than *"is anything
wrong?"* produced the finding.

**What the output says about the new grass type:**

    GroundClutter  ->  /Game/Foliage/GT_alpine_GroundClutter
        SM_Boulder05a                       0.900 /10m2
        SM_River_Rock_01                    0.600 /10m2
        2 variety(ies), densities sum to 1.5 against a species total of 1.5

**Densities get a genuine read-back** — the builder sums what the ENGINE
kept on the asset and compares it against the species total, which is a
different instrument from the list it wrote. **The CULL DISTANCE appears
nowhere.** It is set and never mentioned, so nothing in the report
distinguishes "cull 70 m applied" from "cull silently defaulted".

**What was behind it.**
`make_landscape_material.py:2441` read

    "cull_cm": float(sp.get("cull_distance_m", 12000.0)) * 100.0,

and `import_heightmap` validated the key only `if "cull_distance_m" in
sp`. So a grass species could omit it, validate clean, and receive a
**twelve kilometre** cull. At this recipe's locked 12 tufts/m² that is
`π·12000²·12` ≈ **5.4 billion instances**.

**AND THE LESSON WAS ALREADY IN THAT FILE, FORTY LINES ABOVE.** The
comment on the instanced cull reads:

> *"…every instanced species was left on the engine default of 0, which
> `FoliageType.h:292` documents as '0 disables', so 28,302
> 505k-triangle trees were submitted every frame across an 8 km map
> until the GPU missed the Windows TDR deadline and returned
> `DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_HUNG`."*

The same file, the same validator function, the same field name, the same
failure mode — and the grass branch beside it was never given the rule.

> **A LESSON APPLIED TO ONE BRANCH OF A FUNCTION IS NOT APPLIED.** Non-
> negotiable 4 says sweep the defect class the moment you find it; this
> is the sweep failing at the smallest possible radius — not "grep the
> repo", but "read the other half of the `if`". The instanced path got
> the fix and its post-mortem comment; the grass path got neither, and
> the comment's presence made the area *look* audited.

**And the shape of the defect is the one CLAUDE.md's casualty list already
names:** *"`CullDistance` 0 means 'disabled', not 'unlimited', and cost a
GPU hang."* A magnitude that reads as a harmless default — `12000.0`, or
`0` — meaning something catastrophic.

**The fix is non-negotiable 3, not a bigger gate.** `cull_distance_m` is
now REQUIRED for `system: "grass"` and bounded `(0, 250]`, so the
12 km value is no longer expressible rather than merely refused. Enforced
in BOTH places, because the builder is runnable without preflight — the
same assumption that let an unknown rock `role` be dropped silently
earlier the same day, and the second time in one session that "the
validator will have run" turned out to be an assumption rather than a
fact.

**Proven 9 ways**, positive control first: 4 validator probes (key
removed, 12000, 0, a string), 5 builder probes (including a bool, since a
bool IS an int in Python and this suite has been bitten by that before).
The shipped recipe still resolves to Meadow 5000 cm and GroundClutter
7000 cm — **which is also the answer to the original question: the 70 m I
wrote did reach the payload.**

**What this says about reading output.** My first pass asked "is anything
wrong here?" and everything present was correct, so it passed. The second
pass asked "what would I need to see to believe the thing I am about to
claim?" — and the answer was a number that was not there. **An output
review that only examines what was printed cannot find an omission.**

  — the project DEFAULT is set, but the PPV is `AEM_MANUAL` and the
  interaction needs a live read.
- **Whether the existing HLOD is current** — the asset exists; whether
  it was rebuilt after any placement is not knowable from the filename.

### TOP 5 BY VISUAL IMPACT PER EFFORT

1. **RVT mesh blending on rock/cliff** — 13,515 rock instances just
   landed with visible hard intersection lines. First step: a design
   review, because non-negotiable 27 already held an RVT design once for
   carrying 20 uncited API names on a GPU that has hung.
2. **Wind on conifers** — 157,554 rigid trees is the biggest motion tell
   in a 30 s shot. First step: add a wind node to `make_foliage_material`
   behind a recipe-declared amplitude, and judge on a MOVE, not a still.
3. **Cliff species band 200–1700 m → restrict to the Rock layer weight**
   — pure recipe data, no new system, fixes rock-on-snow. First step:
   change `mask.kind` from `slope` to `layer`+Rock and re-run the dry run.
4. **VSM tuning + rebuild HLOD** — both are "already on, never touched",
   and both directly serve the new geometry. First step: read the live
   VSM cvars before changing anything.
5. **Valley fog volume** — measured proof that global height fog cannot
   reach high cameras (0.389 at 8 km from 300 m vs 0.022 from 1200 m).

### CONFLICTS WITH KNOWN PROJECT ISSUES

- **Nothing here touches the heightmap.** The retracted collision split
  is not a constraint, and no recommendation re-composites terrain. The
  two genuine terrain defects (the polished falloff spots) are still
  best handled by routing the camera, since fixing them invalidates
  157,554 conifer and 759 boulder placements.
- **RVT allocates GPU memory** on a machine that has returned
  `DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_HUNG` once. Design review first, not optional.
- **Disk is ~26 GB against a recorded 50 GB floor.** HLOD rebuild and
  RVT both consume disk; check headroom before either.
- **Lumen must not be enabled project-wide.** The exposure solve
  (−1.786) was made under Lumen-off and the entire historical evidence
  base is Lumen-off; enabling it globally silently shifts every
  comparison. It belongs in the MRQ render config at **−1.897 EV**.

## 2026-08-09 — THE GAEA REBUILD IS AUTOMATED, AND THE Z SCALE WAS ONE ARITHMETIC STEP FROM BEING 2.7x WRONG

Ryan ruled on the two items R-GAEA left open and asked for the headless
rebuild path. Three things worth keeping came out of it.

### 1. A NORMALIZATION THAT DESTROYS THE THING YOU LATER NEED

`ue5_import_alpinelab.py` shipped with `TODO_Z_SCALE_PLACEHOLDER = 100.0`
and a note that solving it was not trivial. It was solvable, and the
solution is instructive about WHY it looked hard.

The Gaea project declares its elevation range:

    C:\Users\ryanb\AppData\Roaming\QuadSpinner\Gaea\2.0\Autosaves\
      AlpineLabe_v1_2026-08-09_19-12-59.terrain      (JSON)
        /Assets/$values[0]/Terrain/Height = 2500.0     metres

Reading that and typing `2500 / 512 * 100 = 488.3` into the import dialog
gives a landscape **2.7x too tall**. It would look like a dramatic alpine
range and nothing would flag it, because there is no instrument in this
project that measures a mountain against reality.

The 2500 is the PROJECT's full range. This BUILD occupied only 496-24763
of 65535 before the export was stretched to full range, so the real span
is `2500 * (24763-496)/65535 = 925.73 m` and Z is **180.81**.

**The general shape: a normalization step destroys the very quantity a
later step needs, and it does so silently, leaving a file that looks
complete.** The number was still recoverable here only because the
un-normalized `Snow_Out.png` happened to be kept in `_archive/`. Had it
been deleted as "superseded", the vertical scale of this terrain would
have been unrecoverable from the package.

So `rebuild_terrain.py` records the source range into
`height_normalization.json` BEFORE it stretches, alongside the derived Z
and both sha256s. And `derive_z_scale()` returns `None` when the project
range cannot be read — an unknown vertical scale is reported as unknown,
never defaulted to UE's 100, which would read as a decision.

### 2. AN ACCEPTANCE TEST THAT FAILED ON A CORRECT RESULT

The proof that automated normalization reproduces tonight's manual
process compared **sha256**, because that is what this project does
everywhere — non-negotiable 20 hashes adopted artefacts against their
source, and it is right to.

It FAILED. `9d21f165...` against `11bb09f7...`, and the file sizes were
26 MB against 14 MB — an 88% difference, which is an absurd magnitude for
"the same image".

**An absurd magnitude is a question about the instrument** (the
2026-08-08 audit's own near-miss, where `git show` returned an LFS
pointer and reported 100% of bytes differing). Decoding both PNGs and
differencing the arrays gives **16,777,216 of 16,777,216 samples
identical, max |diff| 0**. `write_png16_grey` emits filter-0 rows; the
reference uses adaptive PNG filters. Same samples, different encoding.

**The rule this yields: hashing is correct for a file COPIED and wrong
for a file RE-ENCODED.** A hash test on a re-encoded artefact tests the
encoder. The sha INEQUALITY is now kept in the proof as the positive
control for the pixel test — if both ever passed, the test would be
comparing a file with itself.

Nearly-shipped consequence: I would have concluded the automation did not
match the manual process, and gone looking for a difference in the
arithmetic that was not there.

### 3. A REJECTED ENTRY THAT BANNED THE OPERATION INSTEAD OF THE DEFECT

R1 REJECTED said **CROP, NEVER RESAMPLE**. The intake resampled, on
instruction, and R-GAEA section 7 recorded the conflict rather than
resolving it.

Ryan ruled: narrow the entry, do not grandfather the intake. The recorded
failure is height resampled while the masks are NOT — a defect of
INDEPENDENCE, which an entry phrased as a ban on resampling cannot
express. Whole-package resampling in one verified operation is permitted;
independent or differently-filtered resampling is not.

**And the permission is enforced rather than intended.** `verify_build.py`
now collects the dimensions of the heightmap and every mask and exits 4
if more than one distinct size is present — non-negotiable 24, because a
rule that lives only in a REJECTED entry is a rule the next session has
to remember. Proven on `002/UE5_Ready`: all 6 files at 4033x4033.

The register claim behind the permission is tested too, and offline:
`check_registration()` takes the brightest 1% of the flow mask and asks
where those pixels sit in the heightmap's percentile ranks. Water runs
downhill, so a registered mask must sit below the median. Measured
**37.7** against a random control at **50.1** — the control is what makes
the low median evidence rather than an artefact of the statistic.

### WHAT IS NOT DONE

`rebuild_terrain.py` has **never built anything**. Its preflight, its
normalization and its refusals are proven (12/12, offline); the Gaea
subprocess call is not. It also cannot run yet: every `AlpineLabe_v1
.terrain` on this machine is an AUTOSAVE, and the script refuses to build
the canonical terrain from a file Gaea rotates and overwrites. Saving the
project once from Gaea is the unblock, and it is Ryan's to do.

## 2026-08-09 — THE LANDSCAPE IMPORT FAILED SILENTLY, AND THE FILENAME WAS THE CAUSE

Ryan ran the manual landscape import from `IMPORT` step 4 of R-GAEA. The
dialog asked *"Use 'AlpineLab_v<v>_Height_normalized.png' Tiled Image?"*,
and after it, **no Landscape actor existed**. No modal error, nothing in
the log worth reading. The mask textures imported fine, so the session
looked mostly successful.

### ROOT CAUSE, AT SOURCE LINES

`Engine/Source/Editor/LandscapeEditor/Private/LandscapeTiledImage.cpp`:

    :14-19   Tokens = { u, v, x, y }
    :22-24   GetTokenRegex(prefix) -> prefix + "(-?[0-9]+)"
    :190     CheckTiledNamePath -- replaces every token match in the
             BASE FILENAME with a glob, then looks for matching files
    :86-104  only <u>/<x> assign the tile X coordinate;
             only <v>/<y> assign Y
    :105     if (X >= 0 && Y >= 0)  -- the guard that decides whether a
             tile is recorded at all
    :149-155 TileFilenames.Num() == 0  ->  Error "No files found"

`LandscapeEditorUtils.cpp:80` is the prompt, and YES sets
`Filename = TiledFileNamePattern`.

So: `AlpineLab_v1_Height_normalized` contains `v1`, which matches
`v(-?[0-9]+)`. The pattern becomes `AlpineLab_v<v>_Height_normalized
.png`, the glob finds one file, and the prompt fires. Answering YES then
sets **Y = 1-1 = 0 and leaves X = -1**, because the name has no `u` or
`x` token. The `X >= 0 && Y >= 0` guard adds no tiles, the tile list is
empty, and Load returns "No files found" -- which the dialog does almost
nothing with. **The import cannot succeed and does not say so.**

### WHAT I GOT WRONG ON THE WAY, AND IT MATTERS

Ryan described the trigger as *"the `_v1_` pattern"* and *"digit-adjacent
underscores"*, and I wrote a `_\d+_` regex to detect it. **That regex is
wrong and would have called the canonical filename SAFE** -- `_v1_` is
underscore-letter-digit-underscore, not underscore-digit-underscore. My
own detector printed "clean" for the exact file that had just failed.

That mismatch is the only reason I opened the engine source instead of
shipping the fix. **An instrument that disagrees with a known-bad case is
information, not noise** -- the same shape as the 2026-08-08 near-miss
where `git show` reported 100% of bytes differing. The real rule is
broader and stranger than the reported one: **any `u`, `v`, `x` or `y`
followed by digits, anywhere in the base filename, with no underscore
required.** `Terrain_x0_y0` trips it (correctly, it is tiled).
`Alpine_v2` trips it. `Everest_y2024` trips it.

### THE FIX, AND WHY IT IS A COPY AND NOT A RENAME

`AlpineLabHeight.png` -- byte-identical (sha256 verified), no digits at
all, so no token can match. `rebuild_terrain.py` now writes BOTH names on
every build, and `verify_build.py` declares the alias, asserts it is
byte-identical to its canonical, and REFUSES on mismatch.

Renaming would have been simpler and wrong. The canonical name is the
provenance record that R-GAEA, the recipes and the sidecar all refer to;
the alias is a convenience for one dialog. **Non-negotiable 3 applies
here in its literal form: prefer an input that cannot express the
catastrophic value over a gate that rejects it.** The prompt cannot be
answered wrongly if it is never asked.

`verify_build.py` also now prints, for every file in the package, which
tiled tokens it matches -- so the next person hits a warning in a build
report instead of a dialog at 11pm.

### THE OTHER HALF: A VERIFIER THAT COULD NOT TELL FAILURE FROM SUCCESS

`ue5_import_alpinelab.py` had checked the landscape and then imported the
masks REGARDLESS. On this failure it would have reported "landscape
verified: NO, masks imported: 5 of 5" -- a partial success over a level
with no terrain. Masks are terrain-registered data; without a landscape
they register to nothing.

It now REFUSES at the landscape check and imports nothing, printing the
tiled-prompt cause directly in the failure banner. It also gained two
checks it should have had from the start:

- **component count** vs the expected 4096 (64 x 64). A dialog set to
  127 quads imports a perfectly valid landscape of the wrong terrain.
- **height span** vs the 925.7 m that Z 180.81 predicts for a full-range
  heightmap. This is a DIFFERENT REPRESENTATION of the Z scale than
  reading `scale.z` back: `scale.z` is what the dialog wrote, the span is
  what the geometry came out as. Non-negotiable 8 -- a read-back that
  reads the field the setter wrote proves only that the value landed.

And it now SKIPS masks that already exist rather than re-importing over
live assets, reporting what is there instead of asserting it is right.

## 2026-08-09 — I READ FIVE CAPTURE OUTCOMES OFF 196 BYTES OF TAIL, AND REPORTED ONE OF THEM BACKWARDS

The AlpineLab_v1 mountain frames landed and are good. The story I told
about how they landed was wrong, and the mechanism is the plainest
non-negotiable in the file.

### WHAT I CLAIMED

Commit `7db2d79f` records a controlled comparison: five capture attempts,
one variable, conclusion that WINDOW FOCUS is what makes a HighResShot
complete on this machine. The discriminating row was

    21:09  multiplier 2  SUCCEEDED  1.6 GB free, editor forced foreground

### WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED

That run reported **NO NEW OR REWRITTEN FILE**. So did the three before
it. `HighresScreenshot00003.png` appeared at 21:09:40 anyway, and it is
**856x561** -- the viewport's own size, which is what `HighResShot 1`
produces, not the 1712x1122 a `HighResShot 2` would. The likeliest
origin is the 21:02 `HighResShot 1` completing late once focus let a
backlog drain. **Which request produced it is genuinely unknown.**

### ROOT CAUSE

Every one of those runs was invoked as

    python scripts/highres_shot.py ... | tail -4

`highres_shot.py` prints its verdict as a BANNER FOLLOWED BY A LONG
DIAGNOSTIC. `tail -4` therefore kept the diagnostic and threw away the
verdict. The saved task outputs are 196, 196, 257 and 319 bytes. I read
five outcomes off the last four lines of a message whose FIRST line said
the opposite, and then built a five-row causal table on top of them.

**Non-negotiable 14: never truncate the output of an operation you
cannot repeat.** A HighResShot on a throttled editor at 1.6 GB free is
that operation exactly -- each attempt cost minutes of wall clock and
could not simply be re-run. I truncated all five.

The one run I could read in full (581 bytes, the 20:50 success) is the
only capture outcome of the night that rests on the tool's own verdict
rather than on my inference from a directory listing.

### THE SECOND, COMPOUNDING ERROR

Having discarded the verdicts, I fell back on the file system -- and
attributed a new file to the request I had just made. That is the SAME
defect I had caught and written up ninety minutes earlier in the same
session, when `HighresScreenshot00001.png` turned out to be a four-hour
old frame of a different world. I identified the trap ("a file is there
is not my shot landed"), wrote it into a commit message, and then walked
into it from the other direction: not a stale file read as fresh, but a
fresh file read as MINE.

`highres_shot.py` already solves both: it snapshots `{path: mtime}`
before the command and reports only genuinely new or rewritten files.
The tool was right and available in both cases. I overrode it with a
directory listing twice.

### WHAT CHANGES

- Capture runs go to a FILE, or are read whole. `tail` on a tool that
  prints a verdict then an essay is a truncation of the answer.
- Focus before a capture stays worth doing. It is a PLAUSIBLE
  contributor to the stall class, alongside memory. **It is not
  demonstrated**, and the record now says so.
- The frames themselves are unaffected: the camera was parked at 20:55
  with position and aim read back to 0.00 cm and 0.000 deg, and every
  request after that time renders that same view.

### THE UNCOMFORTABLE PART

The wrong claim was not a guess I flagged as a guess. It was presented
as a measurement, with a table, in a commit message, as the kind of
controlled comparison this project treats as evidence. A fabricated
control is worse than no control, because it ends the investigation.

## 2026-08-10 — THE OVERNIGHT ALPINELAB SESSION: FOUR DEFECTS, AND THE ONE THAT MADE THE GROUND A CHECKERBOARD

Ryan went to bed asking for a fully rendered 4K environment. The terrain
ended the night with 30,589 instances on it, a compiling material and
3840x2160 frames. Everything below is what went wrong on the way, because
that is the part worth keeping.

### 1. I BROKE THE MATERIAL BY FIXING THE TEXTURES

The five 4033-square masks were imported UNCOMPRESSED
(`TC_VECTOR_DISPLACEMENTMAP`), inherited from `import_layer_textures.py`
whose reasoning is sound: a block compressor destroys thin drainage
lines. On this machine it was fatal for a different reason -- the editor
logged, for tens of minutes at four cores:

    BEWARE: AssetCompile memory estimate is greater than available, but
    we're running it [TextureDerivedData] anyway!
    RequiredMemory = 4609 MiB, MemoryLimit = 994 MiB

with free RAM pinned near 0.9 GB. So I recompressed them to
`TC_GRAYSCALE` (BC4).

**That changed what sampler type the engine requires**, from
`LINEAR_COLOR` to `LINEAR_GRAYSCALE`. The material's five mask samplers
still declared the old type. `VerifySamplerType` errors on EVERY
mismatch, so the WHOLE MATERIAL failed to compile, and the landscape fell
back to UE's default material -- which is why every ground frame came
back as a grey CHECKERBOARD.

**The trap is already in CLAUDE.md, and I reached it from the direction
nobody was watching.** Non-negotiable 9's motivating case is exactly
"VerifySamplerType errors on EVERY mismatch". Every prior instance was a
sampler typed wrongly by hand. This was a sampler typed CORRECTLY and
then invalidated by changing the texture underneath it. A sampler audit
had passed on these same nodes hours earlier, when the compression still
matched -- so the audit was right, and then quietly stopped being right.

**The instrument that found it in one call:**
`MaterialEditingLibrary.recompile_material` RETURNS the error list. The
editor log only says *"Failed to compile Material for platform
PCD3D_SM6, Default Material will be used in game"*, which names the
symptom and not one of the five offending nodes.

**General rule: changing a texture's COMPRESSION is a change to every
material that samples it.** The sampler type is a contract between the
two, and only one side was edited.

### 2. MODE_EXEC_FILE MEANS THE COMMAND IS A FILENAME

Payloads had been sent as inline source with
`exec_mode=MODE_EXEC_FILE` and it worked, so it looked like the
established pattern. It fails for longer commands, and the failure is
almost unreadable:

    Could not load Python file
    'C:/Program Files/Epic Games/UE_5.8/Engine/Binaries/Win64/<the
     entire payload, with newlines rendered as /n>'

-- the engine resolving the source text as a path relative to its own
binaries directory. **The scatter placed nothing three times before this
was understood**, and the first two theories were both wrong (transport
size limit; busy editor).

What settled it was a bisect: 6,000 bytes of filler went through, so it
was not length; prefixes of the real payload failed at a REPRODUCIBLE
boundary, which ruled out load. Both builders now write the payload to a
file under `Saved/` and send the PATH.

### 3. AN API I REMEMBERED, AGAIN

`Actor.add_component_by_class` does not exist in 5.8's reflected
surface. I used it to attach a HierarchicalInstancedStaticMeshComponent;
the editor raised AttributeError and the stub confirmed the absence.
Non-negotiable 23, and `place_foliage.py` had the correct path
(`FoliageType_InstancedStaticMesh` + `InstancedFoliageActor.add_
instances`) the whole time. **Step (a) is a search, not a recall** --
and I searched the stub only after the failure, not before the call.

### 4. THE FOG WAS TUNED FOR A TERRAIN THAT STARTS AT ZERO

`ExponentialHeightFog` attenuates by height above its OWN actor, which
the Basic template puts at -68 m. This terrain spans -462 m to +462 m,
so a valley camera sat 240 m BELOW the datum, at the thickest part of
the curve. The first ground frame was a blue wash with ghost trees, and
it read as a render failure rather than a fog setting.

Datum moved to -460 m, density 0.0436 -> 0.008, falloff 0.2 -> 0.08.
**A fog default is a statement about where the ground is.** A terrain
whose datum is its MIDDLE breaks that assumption by half its height.

### 5. A READ-BACK THAT COULD NOT MATCH REPORTED A CATASTROPHE

The scatter's own verification compared `static_mesh.get_path_name()`
against the recipe's package path. `get_path_name()` returns
`/Game/X/SM_Foo.SM_Foo` -- the OBJECT path -- so the comparison was
false for every mesh and the tool reported **0 placed for all six
species** while the engine actually held 30,589. A separate probe found
them immediately.

Non-negotiable 6 says a failed measurement must report that it could not
measure. This one reported a NUMBER, and the number was zero, which is
indistinguishable from the disaster it was describing.

### WHAT IS NOT WORKING, AND IS THE FIRST THING TO LOOK AT

**Grass does not spawn.** `GT_AlpineLab_Ground` exists with three
varieties at 14/18/22 instances per 10 m2, read back from the asset; a
`LandscapeGrassOutput` is in the graph; the material compiles with zero
errors; `grass.FlushCache` was run with the camera parked, followed by a
dwell and a fresh capture. No grass in the frame. The most likely
suspect is the wire from the weight expression to the output's named
input pin -- the pin is named by the GrassInput's `name`, and a failed
lookup there would leave a graph that compiles and produces nothing.
Unverified; do not treat this paragraph as a diagnosis.


### ADDENDUM, same night — THE GRASS: FIVE HYPOTHESES ELIMINATED, ONE TEST NAMED

I kept going on the grass after the handoff was written, and did not
solve it. What follows is worth more than the failure: the next session
should not re-test any of this.

**RULED OUT, each by a measurement:**

| Hypothesis | Instrument | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Grass type missing or empty | asset read-back | EXISTS, 3 varieties at 14 / 18 / 22 per 10 m2 |
| Grass output node absent | `get_material_expressions` | 1 node, name `AlpineLabGround`, bound to the right asset |
| The weight wire never landed | `audit_material_connectivity` | **90 of 90 expressions reachable, 0 orphaned** |
| Scalability zeroing density | cvar reads | `grass.DensityScale` 1.0, `grass.Enable` 1.0, `sg.FoliageQuality` 1.0, `enable_density_scaling` true |
| Cache not flushed | `grass.FlushCache` x2, then `set_grass_enabled(True, flush_grass_maps=True)` | still nothing |

The connectivity result is the interesting one. It was my leading
theory in the handoff -- "the likeliest suspect is the wire into the
named input pin" -- and it is WRONG. The auditor walks backwards from
every output INCLUDING custom outputs, and the two Subtract nodes and
the Multiply that compute the grass weight are all reachable, which they
could only be through the grass output. **The wire landed.**

**THE NEXT TEST, and it is one edit:** wire a `Constant 1.0` straight
into the grass output in place of the computed weight, rebuild, flush,
capture. Grass appears -> the weight expression evaluates to zero in
that area and the fault is arithmetic. Nothing appears -> the fault is
in the plumbing between a connected grass output and the landscape, and
the next suspects are a full landscape Build (grass maps are built as
part of it, and this landscape has never had one) and the grass meshes'
own materials.

**Two API notes banked on the way:**
`Material` has no `expression_collection` property in 5.8 -- I guessed
that name and the editor said so; the accessor is
`MaterialEditingLibrary.get_material_expressions`, which
`audit_material_connectivity.py:156` already used.
`get_grass_types_bp` is NOT on `Landscape`, though `set_grass_enabled`
is. That accessor would have answered "does the landscape resolve any
grass type from its material" directly, and finding where it actually
lives is worth five minutes next session.

### THE INSTRUCTION THAT WOULD HAVE DESTROYED THE MIGRATION

The brief said to robocopy each source to `<Drive>\Migration\` with
`/MIR`. **`/MIR` mirrors: it deletes anything at the destination that is
not in the current source.** Three sources into one destination root
means the second copy deletes the first and the third deletes the
second, and **robocopy reports success every time** -- the deletions are
what mirroring is FOR. `scripts/migrate_to_drive.ps1` gives each source
its own subfolder, where `/MIR` does the useful thing instead: a re-run
converges rather than accumulating.

Ryan's plan was to skip ProjectTitan's 61 GB and re-hydrate it from
OneDrive on the new machine, conditional on sync being demonstrably

642 files under `ProjectTitan\Binaries\Win64` carry reparse points, and
Windows exposes no "fully uploaded" flag a script can read. All 208,726
files are local (0 marked Offline), which proves they are DOWNLOADED and
says nothing about whether they are UPLOADED -- the direction that
matters here.

By his own rule -- "if sync status is at all murky, add it to the drive
anyway" -- ProjectTitan is IN the copy set. **Reading an absence as a
negative is non-negotiable 17's mechanism**, and "no offline files" is
exactly that kind of absence.

destination (a copy onto the source is not a backup). It needs the drive
connected and its letter.

The entry above concludes "ProjectTitan is IN the copy set" on the
strength of Ryan's murky-sync rule. Ryan then asked the question I
should have asked first: **is it part of the landscape pipeline at
all?** It is not, and the answer was cheap:

- `ProjectTitan.uproject` declares **`"Category": "Samples"`** — an Epic
  sample, not authored work.
- `VaultCache\Titan_5.8` holds **61.14 GB / 208,727 files** against the
  project's 61.11 GB / 208,726. The launcher can restore it.
- **`BACKLOG.md:244` had already classified it**, on 2026-08-03:
  *"Project Titan — selective migration | Large community art project.
  Very large on disk; audit what is actually wanted before creating it
  at all."*
- Nothing in this repo references Titan; nothing in Titan references
  this pipeline. The one apparent cross-match,
  `...\LI_GreatStairway\A\1F\XH9GAEA8PCP8AX49BDZE4M.uasset`, is a
  World Partition GUID filename that happens to contain the letters
  G-A-E-A. **A substring is not a reference**, and reporting it as a hit
  without opening it would have been the same class of error as trusting
  a name over an artefact.

**The migration set drops from 92.9 GB to 31.8 GB.**

**What this is really an instance of.** I spent the OneDrive
investigation answering "can we safely NOT copy it", which is a question
about transport, and never asked "does it belong in the set", which is a
question about scope. Both are legitimate, but scope decides transport
and not the reverse — and the scope answer was already written down in
our own BACKLOG four days earlier, in an entry that says *audit before
creating it at all*. **Step (a) applies to a migration exactly as it
applies to a script: the answer may already be in the repo.**

The OneDrive finding still stands on its own terms and is worth keeping:
the sync engine is **not running**, so any plan that treats OneDrive as
a transfer mechanism for anything is currently unfounded.

## 2026-08-10 — the migration to the 5080 machine, and the check that was briefed wrong

**Hard rule 4 note, capture of record:** `alpine__*__20260811T052640Z__9be22845-dirty_5080baseline.png`,
19/19 stations, 1920x1080, `verify_frames` VERDICT: every frame present
with real tonal structure. First render on the RTX 5080 machine.

**THE BRIEF SAID `git fsck` WAS THE INDEPENDENT CONTENT VERIFICATION FOR
A 9.2 GB HISTORY "INCLUDING 8.8 GB OF LFS". IT IS NOT, AND THE DIFFERENCE
COST TWO FILES.** `git fsck` validates the git OBJECT DATABASE — 391 MB
packed in this repo. The 8.9 GB lives in `.git/lfs`, which it never
opens, because git tracks an LFS file as a 130-byte POINTER and **a
pointer is intact whether or not the object it names still exists.**
`git lfs fsck` looked like the fix and is scoped to HEAD — 2,263 of
18,241 files — and it returned "OK" in **3 seconds**. That was the tell:
8.9 GB cannot be read in 3 s, so whatever it checked, it was not the
bytes.

Re-hashing every object in the store against its own filename — the LFS
layout names each object by its SHA-256, so the expected value is
self-describing — gave 18,430 objects, 0 mismatches. Then the question
that actually mattered: is anything MISSING? Corruption and absence are
different failures and only the first was being checked. **2 of 18,241
referenced oids were absent, both `__ExternalActors__` of `/Game/Alpine`**,
and `origin/main` is 60 commits behind so GitHub did not hold them.

**ROOT CAUSE, and it is a rule not an accident:** an editor was running
from `C:/Migration/LandscapeLab_repo/LandscapeLab 5.8/` and the repo was
moved out from under it 16 minutes later. A process holding files open is
the same mechanism this file already records for 2026-08-08 — "unable to
unlink old ... Invalid argument", where two bulk checkouts reported exit
0 while writing nothing. **The migration script verified COUNTS and
BYTES and still missed it, because 2 files in 23,050 is inside the noise
of any count-based check.** Only per-object identity found it.
General rule: *a bulk file operation verifies that no process holds the
tree open BEFORE it runs, and verifies the DESTINATION afterwards rather
than trusting its own exit code.*

**NON-NEGOTIABLE 17 FIRED ON MY OWN EDIT, WHICH IS THE HONEST PART.** I
set `bThrottleCPUWhenNotForeground=False` in
`DefaultEditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini` per the ratified BACKLOG item,
and wrote it into the handoff tagged UNVERIFIED because an ini records an
OVERRIDE, not the state in effect. It then measured **2.03 CPU-seconds
per 20 s wall backgrounded against 36.06 foregrounded — 17.8x**, against
the OmniBook's ~21x. The setting did not deliver the behaviour. Had I
claimed it, the next session would have trusted a dead switch.
`bAllowSlateThrottling` is still True and is the untested suspect.
**Operationally: force the editor foreground before any capture.**

**A VISUAL CLAIM I HAD TO CORRECT MID-SESSION.** I ranked "no global
illumination" as the largest AAA gap after opening the
`CLIFFS_TALUS_LUMEN2` frames — but that tag, and the 2026-08-09 handoff,
say Lumen was **ON** for those. The GI-off reading came from the LIVE
cvars, and render state dies with the process, so the two observations
belong to different worlds. The frames' bare canopy and smooth terrain
are NOT explained by missing GI. What survives, because it was measured
offline instead of judged from a render: the twig atlas is **24.02%
opaque and effectively binary** (25.06% at clip 0.1 vs 23.56% at 0.5), so
the opacity threshold is not the lever; needle albedo where opaque is
**mean RGB 85/81/49**, green BELOW red. The canopy is substantially the
ASSET. `fir_tree_01` is a sparse young fir.

**AND ONE THING NOBODY HAD LOOKED AT.** The 2026-08-09 handoff ranked
"look at a ground frame" as item 1 and said no frame yet showed the new
rocks. The capture had completed. Opening `cliff_face` shows the rock
instances on the slope — cliffs and talus are on pixels now, not only in
a count. **The frames had been sitting on disk for a day.**

## 2026-08-12 — the screen-percentage A/B, and picking the wrong instrument for the claim

**Hard rule 4 note:** `alpine__*__20260812T000119Z__b4dde6cf_5080sp100.png`,
19/19, `verify_frames` clean. ScreenPercentage 100 + Lumen on.

**I HYPOTHESISED THAT 70% SCREEN PERCENTAGE WAS EATING THE CONIFER
NEEDLES — thin alpha-tested cards aliasing away at 0.7 scale — and the
measurement does not support it.** mae against the SP70 set is 4.1x the
noise floor on all 19 stations, which looks like confirmation until you
ask what mae measures: **how far pixels MOVED**. A resolution change
shifts edges whether detail was gained or lost, so mae cannot separate
"sharper" from "differently blurry". It is the wrong instrument for a
sharpness claim and I nearly reported it as one.

Mean gradient magnitude asks the actual question. SP100 buys **+1.3%**
edge energy on average and **six of nineteen stations LOSE** it
(`cliff_face` -2.7%, `sweep_2000` -1.5%). **The discriminating row is
`player_eye`: the LARGEST mae of all nineteen at 13.4x, and +0.1% edge
energy.** Its pixels moved more than anywhere else and got no sharper —
that mae is resampling and TAA jitter. Two stations did gain properly,
`forest_floor` +11.9% and `ridge_wide` +11.8%, which also rules out the
alternative explanation that the capture path ignores the cvar entirely.

**The general shape, and it is non-negotiable 8 wearing new clothes:** a
metric that MOVES is not a metric that AGREES WITH YOUR CLAIM. Both
numbers here are arithmetically correct and only one is about the
question. Ranked by measured effect the levers are **Lumen 38.2x** and
then ScreenPercentage at 4.1x that is mostly not sharpness at all.

**A HEALTHY RUN I KILLED.** `capture.py` takes `--timeout` as its
DISCOVERY WINDOW, so `--timeout 900` sits at the identity gate for 15
minutes before writing a frame. Both successful captures used 600 and
produced their first frame near the 10-minute mark. I read "still at the
identity gate" as a stall twice, and the second time force-killed a run
that was very likely about to succeed — then built a theory
(half-open connection from the killed client) on top of the symptom I had
manufactured. **The connection-stealing finding stands on its own
evidence** — that capture ran far past its window with zero frames while
the editor served my other calls normally — **but "stuck at the gate" is
not evidence of anything on its own, and I treated it as such.**
