## 2026-08-15 — UNIT 7: A SECOND PLUGIN, AND THE BUILD REFUSED FOR A REASON WORTH RECORDING

`PHASE2_PLAN.md` unit 7, pulled ahead of the rest of unit 5 because unit 5
depends on it: a player character and a game mode are RUNTIME classes and
`LandscapeLabEditor`'s module Type is `Editor`, so they had nowhere to live.

`LandscapeLab/Plugins/LandscapeLabGameplay`, built clean in **35 s**, first
try, MSVC 14.44.35228. Verified on a cold boot by
`scripts/verify_gameplay_plugin.py`. Recipe **R-GAMEPLAY**.

### THE PROJECT FILE IS STILL BYTE-IDENTICAL, AND THAT IS THE POINT

Standing rule 4 forbids touching `LandscapeLab.uproject`, and
`PluginManager.cpp:420-433` makes it unnecessary — a project plugin with
`EnabledByDefault` is honoured with no `.uproject` entry at all. That is the
same reasoning that kept the project file untouched through the 2026-08-12
C++ conversion, and it held again here for three engine plugins.

**And it is measurably better than the `.uproject` route**, which is the part
worth carrying: the dependency list lives beside the code that needs it, so
"why is GameplayStateTree on?" is answered by reading the plugin that wants
it rather than by reading a project-wide array with no attribution.

### THE DISCRIMINATING CHECK IS `GameplayStateTree`, NOT THE PLUGIN ITSELF

Ruling 1 recorded that `StateTree` is enabled here and `GameplayStateTree` is
**not** (`EnabledByDefault: false`), and that the second is the half carrying
`StateTreeAIComponent`, `FStateTreeMoveToTask` and `FStateTreeRunEnvQueryTask`.

So the cold-boot verifier does not just ask "is my plugin enabled" — it asks
whether `GameplayStateTree` reads ENABLED. It does. **That is the one result
that could only be true if the dependency list did work**, because nothing
else in this project turns it on. Checking only the plugin's own state would
have passed identically whether or not the dependencies were honoured.

### AND THE CLASS CHECK IS A DIFFERENT REPRESENTATION, DELIBERATELY

`get_enabled_plugin_names()` reads the plugin DESCRIPTOR. It does not prove
the module's DLL loaded, and it does not prove UHT generated anything — a
plugin can read "enabled" with a module that failed to load, and the editor
carries on. So the verifier separately asks for `unreal.LandscapeLabCharacter`
and its CDO, and for `apply_movement_spec` on it.

**The function check is the one that would catch a stale binary.** A DLL from
a previous build reflects the class perfectly and is missing the new
function, and it reads exactly like a working module until something calls
it. Non-negotiable 0, at the level of a build artefact.

### THE BUILD REFUSED WHILE THE EDITOR WAS OPEN, AND THE ERROR IS EXACT

    Unable to build while Live Coding is active. Exit the editor and game,
    or press Ctrl+Alt+F11 if iterating on code in the editor or game

Worth recording because the obvious reading — "it just needs the DLL
unlocked" — suggests the wrong workaround. **Live Coding cannot add a NEW
module**, only recompile existing ones, so `Ctrl+Alt+F11` is not an
alternative here. A new module means a full build means a closed editor.

### AND CLOSING THE EDITOR HAD ITS OWN GATE

`get_dirty_content_packages()` reported **one** dirty package,
`/Game/Materials/M_AutoLandscape` — the *old* 2017 world's material, nothing
this session touched, dirty from before the session began.

A quit with a dirty package raises a **Save Content** modal, which blocks the
game thread and therefore blocks remote execution — **the only channel that
could see or answer it.** This project has been bitten by that modal and by
its sibling, the next-launch `Restore Packages` modal.

So the check refused to quit on a non-zero count, and refuses equally on an
UNREADABLE count: *an unreadable count is not a zero*. Ryan closed it from
the UI and chose Don't Save, which is the right owner for that decision —
it is his asset, and the on-disk copy was committed and unchanged, so the
discarded thing was an unexplained in-memory divergence from a file git
already held.

**The general shape, and it is not really about modals:** a tool that needs a
human action should say exactly which action and why, not perform a
destructive approximation of it because a human is inconvenient to ask.

## 2026-08-15 — THE MANNEQUIN MIGRATION, AND THE DESTINATION WAS NOT A CHOICE

Unit 4 ruled for the engine template mannequin set over the in-project GV
pack copy. Executed: 128 files, 125.3 MB, copied from
`UE_5.8/Templates/TemplateResources/High/Characters/Content/Mannequins` to
`LandscapeLab/Content/Characters/Mannequins`. Restore point
`pre-mannequin-migration-20260815`.

### THE DESTINATION PATH WAS READ OUT OF THE ASSETS, NOT PICKED

Before copying anything, the `.uasset` bytes were scanned for the paths they
reference internally. `SKM_Manny_Simple` names:

    /Game/Characters/Mannequins/Meshes/SK_Mannequin
    /Game/Characters/Mannequins/Rigs/PA_Mannequin
    /Game/Characters/Mannequins/Materials/Manny/MI_Manny_01_New

and `MM_Idle` names `/Game/Characters/Mannequins/Meshes/SK_Mannequin`.

**So `Content/Characters/Mannequins/` is the only destination that works.**
Any other — `Content/Mannequins/`, `Content/Player/`, anything tidier — leaves
every internal reference dangling and needs a redirector pass to repair.

**The general point is worth more than the path.** A migration destination
feels like an organisational preference and is actually a property of the
files being moved. Two minutes of reading the name table settled it; the
alternative was discovering it after 128 files were in the wrong place and
the editor was quietly rewriting references.

### AND IT ANSWERED THE QUESTION UNIT 4 LEFT OPEN

Unit 4 measured the GV pack's `SKM_Manny` at **LOD0 and LOD1 BOTH 48,779
verts** — a four-entry chain whose first reduction reduces nothing — and
recorded that the number belonged to a mesh we were NOT adopting, with a
re-check owed against the one we were.

Re-checked:

    SKM_Manny_Simple   LODs 3   verts 48,705 / 14,925 / 7,504
    SKM_Quinn_Simple   LODs 3   verts 45,993 / 14,865 / 7,421
    physics asset      /Game/Characters/Mannequins/Rigs/PA_Mannequin
    skeleton           shared by both, 161 bones, all 4 UE5 markers

**The broken chain was the shrub pack's, not the engine's.** Three clean
LODs, real reduction at every step, nothing owed. And `PA_Mannequin` resolves,
so the ragdoll gap unit 4 identified is closed by the migration rather than by
authoring anything.

**This is the value of having recorded the measurement as belonging to a
specific mesh.** Had unit 4 written "the UE5 Manny has a broken LOD chain",
a later session would have carried a false defect into a budget and possibly
authored a reduction step that was already there.

### THE TRAP UNIT 4 PREDICTED IS NOW REAL, AND IS BENIGN FOR NOW

The project now holds **two** 161-bone UE5 mannequin skeletons:

    /Game/Characters/Mannequins/Meshes/SK_Mannequin        <- ours now
    /Game/GV_FreeShrubsPack/Demo/Mannequin/Meshes/SK_Mannequin

Animations bound to one play as a silent T-pose on the other. It is benign
today because nothing references the GV one — it is demo content inside a
gitignored shrub pack — but the discriminating field is the resolved skeleton
PATH, which `probe_skeleton` prints, and NOT the bone count, which is 161 on
both.

### GITIGNORED, ON THE PROJECT'S OWN PRECEDENT

`.gitignore` already excludes `LandscapeLab/Content/Mannequin/` — the UE4
template content — as re-derivable. This is the same class, so
`LandscapeLab/Content/Characters/` joins it rather than putting 125 MB of
Epic-shipped assets into LFS permanently, which `.gitignore`'s own header
records as not undoable.

**It is lower risk than the Fab entries and the ignore comment says so:** the
source is the pinned 5.8 install on this machine, not a storefront that can
withdraw an item. The copy procedure is recorded in R-CHARACTER so the
directory is reproducible from one command.

## 2026-08-15 — THE PLAYER WALKS A KILOMETRE, AND FOUR OF THE FIVE FAILURES WERE IN THE INSTRUMENT

`PHASE2_PLAN.md` unit 5's first acceptance clause is met. `walk003`:
**1000.1 m of 1000 requested, no stall, no fall**, artefact
`_verify/20260815_unit5_walk_walk003.md`.

The character resolves fully at spawn — `SKM_Manny_Simple`, `ABP_Unarmed_C`,
`IMC_LandscapeLabDefault`, 3 of 3 input actions — and walks at exactly
**600 cm/s**, the configured `MaxWalkSpeed`, which is the cheapest possible
proof that the recipe reached the engine.

### DRIVING A PAWN NEEDS A TICK CALLBACK, NOT A LOOP

`AddMovementInput` is consumed by ONE tick, and a remote-exec payload BLOCKS
the game thread — so a Python loop gives the character input and never lets it
move. `unreal.register_slate_post_tick_callback` (PythonStub 708181) runs in
the engine's own loop; the script only starts, polls and stops it. State lives
in a module-level global because the callback outlives the payload that made
it, and is torn down explicitly for the same reason.

### THE FIRST TWO WALKS STOPPED DEAD, AND THE TERRAIN WAS RIGHT BOTH TIMES

    walk001  heading 135  stopped at  97.1 m
    walk002  heading  72  stopped at 240.5 m

Diagnosed offline against the heightmap, after calibrating the indexing on a
measured ground truth — `h[py,px]` at the spawn XY reads **28,539.5 cm**
against a collision trace's **28,540.1**, agreeing to 0.6 cm, which is what
makes the rest of the analysis trustworthy.

    walk001 stop: slope 52.66 deg, next metre rises 74 cm
    walk002 stop: slope 64.39 deg, next metre rises 320 cm

Both are **walls, not slopes**: past the 44.765 deg walkable floor and past
the 45 cm step height simultaneously. The character was standing correctly
on the ground and could neither walk up nor step up. **A straight-line walker
with no steering stops at the first such feature and stays there** — which is
a property of the test, not of the world.

**And a straight kilometre is not available anywhere from that spawn.** A
heading sweep found the best clear run at **934 m** before the 44.765 deg
limit is exceeded. Ryan then ruled: give the character the ability to climb.

### THE CLIMB RULING, AND WHY IT IS STILL "DECLARED ONCE"

`recipes/character.json` → `movement.profile` moved `"walk"` → `"climb"`,
which is a KEY into `terrain_erosion.MOVEMENT_PROFILES` (70 deg, described
there as *"scalable faces; a design choice, not an engine one"*). The recipe
still carries **no angle**; `apply_character_recipe` derives it and writes
`CfgWalkableFloorAngleDeg` into the ini, which the character applies with
`SetWalkableFloorAngle`.

**`SetWalkableFloorAngle`, not `WalkableFloorAngle =`** — the setter also
recomputes `WalkableFloorZ`, which is the value the floor test actually
reads. Assigning the angle alone lands a correct-looking number that nothing
consults. The engine sets the pair through `SetWalkableFloorZ` at
`CharacterMovementComponent.cpp:682` for exactly this reason.

At 70 deg the same sweep, re-run at **1 m sampling** rather than 2 m, gives
many headings clear to the full 1200 m. The 2 m sweep had missed a 1 m-wide
ledge — **a sweep coarser than the map's own resolution can step over the
feature it is looking for.**

### AND THEN THE INSTRUMENT FAILED FOUR TIMES, WHICH IS THE REST OF THIS ENTRY

**1. A COMPLETED WALK REPORTED AS "NO MARKER".** The stop payload returned
1621 samples inline and the reply exceeded the remote-exec deserialization
limit — the same class as `save_level`'s 418 KB reply. A finished trace was
nearly thrown away. Fixed by writing the trace to a FILE before replying, and
by degrading rather than discarding when a reply is lost: the tool now
force-tears-down and reads the trace off disk. `--from-log` exists so the
analysis is reachable without the code path that failed.

**2. "FELL THROUGH: YES" ON A CLEAN WALK.** The fall test asked whether Z had
dropped more than 5,000 cm below the spawn. It had — by 10,075 cm — because
the character walked **down a mountainside**, 100 m of descent over 1 km.
**On real terrain, descending is the job.** Replaced with a geometric test:
over one sample the ground can drop at most `tan(walkable) × horizontal
distance moved`; sustained excess beyond that is falling rather than walking.
Re-measured, the worst excess is **0.0 cm** — every centimetre of that
descent is explainable by walking.

**3. A COULD-NOT-LOOK PRINTED AS A MEASUREMENT, IN MY OWN TOOL.**
`is_falling` logged `None` on all 645 samples and the analysis reported
**"falling samples 0.0%"**. `ACharacter` has no `get_character_movement()` in
Python; it raises, and the exception was swallowed. `is_falling` lives on
`NavMovementComponent` (PythonStub 506206), reached via
`Pawn.get_movement_component()`. Now the accessor is correct, the reason is
recorded on first failure, and an all-`None` column prints **COULD NOT READ**
rather than a percentage. This is non-negotiable 6 — inside the instrument
written to enforce it.

**4. A POWERSHELL REGEX DOUBLE-ENCODED THE SOURCE FILE.** `Get-Content` with
no `-Encoding` read UTF-8 as Windows-1252, `Set-Content -Encoding utf8` wrote
the mojibake back and added a BOM, and Python then refused to parse its own
script. Repaired by inverting the transform. **This is standing rule 3's
mechanism in a different container:** the rule sends commit messages through
a file because a shell round trip over text it was never told the encoding of
has no failure mode that announces itself. Editing source with a PowerShell
regex is the same hazard, and `Edit` does not have it.

### WHAT THE WALK PROVES, STATED NARROWLY

The collision surface supports the character over 1 km of real varied terrain
under genuine `CharacterMovementComponent` floor checks. It is a **straight
line on a declared heading**, NOT the inter-massif corridor — that corridor
still has no spatial definition anywhere in this repo. And `is_falling` was
unreadable for this run, so the fall verdict rests on the geometric test
alone rather than on two representations.

## 2026-08-15 — ENABLING MetaHumanCharacter HUNG THE EDITOR, AND THE ROOT CAUSE IS NOT ESTABLISHED

Ryan ruled to adopt MetaHuman for the player character, overturning
`PHASE2_PLAN.md` ruling 14. `MetaHumanCharacter` was added to
`LandscapeLabGameplay.uplugin`'s `Plugins` array — the route ruling 2
establishes, which keeps `.uproject` untouched. **The editor never finished
starting.** Reverted the same day; the project is verified back to its
known-good state.

Restore point `pre-metahuman-enable-20260815`. Log preserved at
`_verify/20260815_metahuman_enable_stall.log`.

### THE MEASUREMENTS THAT SAID "HUNG" RATHER THAN "SLOW"

This project already records that a flat CPU trace is NOT evidence of a hang
during shader compilation, because that work happens in `ShaderCompileWorker`
CHILD processes. So the reading was taken across four instruments at once:

    working set        2.41 GB, flat over 2 minutes
    editor CPU         0.02 CPU-s per wall-s
    DDC growth         0.0 MB in 120 s
    ShaderCompileWorker  0 processes
    log                 11 minutes with no new line
    window class        SplashScreenClass — still on the splash

**No single one of those is conclusive and together they are.** DDC growth is
the instrument that closes it: shader compilation with no CPU in the parent
still writes to disk, and nothing was being written.

**The window-class tell was used as recorded and worked.**
`MainWindowTitle` returned *"Unreal Editor - LandscapeLab"* — identical to a
loaded editor. Only `GetClassName` distinguishes `SplashScreenClass` from
`UnrealWindow`.

### WHAT IT WAS NOT

**Not memory, and Ryan asked directly.** 2.41 GB working set against a
223 GB commit limit, with the CPU IDLE. Memory starvation looks like heavy
paging and pegged CPU and disk; this was a process waiting on something and
doing nothing. **The page file needed no change** — and the temptation to
raise it "just in case" would have spent a reboot to fix a problem that did
not exist.

**Not missing binaries.** `MetaHumanCharacter` ships **7 prebuilt DLLs** in
this installed engine, so nothing needed compiling.

**Not our C++.** The same editor, relaunched with only the `.uplugin` line
removed, loaded normally — **993 CPU-s in 4 minutes, 10.24 GB** — and
`verify_gameplay_plugin` returns exit 0 with every class reflected.

### WHAT IS UNKNOWN, STATED PLAINLY

**There are ZERO `MetaHuman` lines in the 105 KB log.** The plugin's modules
never logged anything, so the stall is somewhere in plugin or module
initialisation BEFORE they got that far — and nothing in the log names it.
The last entries are a Turnkey device detection completing and DDC
maintenance finishing, both normal.

**No root cause. Standing rule 10:** this is recorded as an unexplained
failure, not as a diagnosis. Candidates not tested — a first-run dialog that
never painted, and `MetaHumanSDK`'s `EOSShared` dependency blocking on a
network call — are HYPOTHESES and are labelled as such.

### THE ROUTE THAT WAS NOT TRIED, AND SHOULD BE FIRST NEXT TIME

**Enable it through the editor's own Plugins UI**, not through a `.uplugin`
dependency. The descriptor route is right for a headless, reproducible,
recipe-driven enable — and it is exactly wrong for a **Beta plugin's first
activation**, because anything that wants a click has no one to click it, and
a dialog blocking the game thread also blocks the only channel that could
report it. That is the same shape as the Save Content modal earlier the same
day.

**The general rule worth carrying: prefer the attended route for the FIRST
activation of anything, and the reproducible route for every activation
after.** A pipeline that can only enable things unattended cannot enable
things that ask questions.

### AND THE REVERT IS THE PART THAT WENT RIGHT

Killing a stalled editor was safe because the preceding close was clean and
nothing was dirty — checked, not assumed. The gate that refuses to quit on a
dirty package is what made a `Stop-Process` a low-risk act rather than a
gamble on someone else's unsaved work.

## 2026-08-15 — CORRECTION: THE METAHUMAN STALL **IS** ROOT-CAUSED. IT WAS A MODAL.

The entry above records the `MetaHumanCharacter` startup stall as **root
cause NOT established**. That was honest when written and it is now **wrong**.
Corrected here rather than edited there, so the state of knowledge at the time
survives.

**THE CAUSE, from the editor's own log**, after Ryan enabled the plugin
through the Plugins UI:

    Message dialog closed, result: Yes, title: Message, text:
    Plugin 'MetaHuman Creator' is a beta version. Epic recommends using
    caution when shipping projects with beta plugins... Are you sure you
    want to enable the plugin?

**Enabling a Beta plugin raises a confirmation modal.** Via the Plugins UI a
human answers it. Via a `.uplugin` descriptor the modal is raised during
STARTUP, with nobody to answer it — and it blocks the game thread, which is
the same thread that services Python remote execution. So the editor sat on
the splash screen indefinitely and could not report why, because the thing
that would have reported it was the thing being blocked.

**Every measurement in the entry above was correct and none of them could
reach the cause.** 0.02 CPU-s per wall-s, no DDC growth, no log lines, still
`SplashScreenClass` — all true, all consistent with a modal, and all equally
consistent with three other explanations. The instruments correctly said
*"stopped, and not for want of memory"*; they could not say *"waiting for a
click"*.

**What actually resolved it was a DIFFERENT REPRESENTATION** — not more
instrumentation of the hung process, but the log of the SUCCESSFUL attended
run, which recorded the question being asked and answered. Non-negotiable 0
again, and worth noting the winning move was to change the experiment rather
than sharpen the measurement.

### THE PREDICTION WAS RIGHT AND WAS STILL LABELLED A GUESS, WHICH WAS CORRECT

The earlier entry named "a first-run dialog that never painted" as an
untested hypothesis, and recommended the attended route on those grounds. It
was right. **It was still correct to label it a hypothesis**: it was one of
two candidates, the other (`EOSShared` blocking on a network call) was
equally consistent with the evidence, and acting on a guess dressed as a
finding is how this project gets bad recipes. The guess earned the next
experiment; it did not earn the entry.

### CONSEQUENCE FOR THE RULE

R-GAMEPLAY's "attended for the FIRST activation, reproducible for every one
after" **stands, and now has a mechanism rather than a superstition**: the
first activation is the one that asks. Once acknowledged, the descriptor
route should be usable — **UNVERIFIED**, and the way to verify it is to move
the entry back into `LandscapeLabGameplay.uplugin` and confirm a clean cold
boot.

### AND THE `.uproject` IS NO LONGER BYTE-IDENTICAL

The Plugins UI wrote `MetaHumanCharacter` into `LandscapeLab.uproject`. This
project had kept that file untouched through the C++ conversion and through
two plugins, on ruling 2's reasoning that enablement belongs beside the code
that needs it.

**This is not a violation of standing rule 4** — that rule forbids ME editing
`.uproject` on disk; the editor writing it through its own UI at Ryan's
instruction is the sanctioned path, and it was chosen deliberately after the
unattended route failed.

**But ruling 2's PURPOSE is now partly defeated**: MetaHuman's enablement is
no longer attributable to the plugin that wants it. Recorded as a debt, not
as a defect: once the plugin is confirmed to start cleanly, move the entry
into `LandscapeLabGameplay.uplugin` and remove it from `.uproject`, which
also tests the UNVERIFIED claim above. Two things settled by one change.

## 2026-08-15 — RETRACTION: THE MODAL WAS NOT THE CAUSE. I READ ONE EVENT AS THE CAUSE OF ANOTHER.

The entry above claims the MetaHuman startup stall is root-caused as a
Beta-plugin confirmation modal. **That is retracted.** It was committed as a
finding and it is not one.

### WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED

The log line I built it on —

    Message dialog closed, result: Yes, ... Plugin 'MetaHuman Creator' is a
    beta version ... Are you sure you want to enable the plugin?

— was produced when **Ryan ticked the plugin in the Plugins UI**. It is the
record of a dialog being *answered in a running editor*, not of one being
raised at startup. I found it in the same log file as the stall and treated
proximity as causation.

**The disproof:** with the plugin already enabled in `.uproject` and the beta
prompt already answered, a fresh start stalls **identically** — and a full
window enumeration of the process finds **no dialog window at all**, only the
splash. Relaunched again with `-nosplash -log`, the only window is the
console. **There is no modal.**

### THE SIGNATURE, STATED WITHOUT A CAUSE ATTACHED

Reproduced three times, twice by descriptor and once from `.uproject`:

    last log line   LogTurnkeySupport: Completed device detection: Code = 0
    then            nothing, indefinitely
    CPU             frozen (44 s, unchanged across a minute)
    working set     ~2.4 GB, flat
    DDC growth      0
    windows         splash only, or console only under -nosplash
    dialogs         NONE

In a HEALTHY run that same line is followed by a long run of
`LogModuleManager: InternalLoadLibrary` calls — the plugin module-loading
phase. **The stall is at the START of that phase**, which is where
MetaHuman's modules would load. That is a LOCATION, not a cause.

### WHY THIS HAPPENED, AND IT IS THE POINT OF THE ENTRY

The first entry said **root cause NOT established** and named the dialog as
one of two untested hypotheses. That was correct. The second entry promoted
the hypothesis to a finding on the strength of a log line that matched the
story — **and the log line was evidence of something else entirely.**

This is non-negotiable 15 in its purest form: a derived record — my own
correction — asserting a state claim that the artefact did not support. And
it is worse than the original uncertainty, because "root cause not
established" invites the next session to look, while "root-caused: it was a
modal" tells it not to.

**The tell I should have demanded before promoting it:** a modal that blocks
startup must EXIST as a window. I had already run a window enumeration on the
first hang and it found only the splash. I had the disproof in hand before I
wrote the claim, and did not apply it to the claim.

### STANDING

Root cause is **NOT established**. `MetaHumanCharacter` is reverted; the
project is verified back to known-good. The stall reproduces on demand, which
means it is diagnosable whenever it is worth the time — the next cheap probes
are the live console's final line (stdout is unbuffered where the log file is
not) and a run with `-noeos` or the network disconnected, since `MetaHumanSDK`
depends on `EOSShared` and a blocking network call fits every measurement
taken so far.

## 2026-08-15 — THE CORE DATA. MetaHuman WORKS, AND THE DESCRIPTOR WAS LYING.

**Resolved by Ryan**, after four failed attempts by me. `MetaHumanCharacter`
is ENABLED, the editor loads normally (592 CPU-s, 10.78 GB), and
`verify_gameplay_plugin` returns exit 0 with our own classes still reflected.

### THE CAUSE, AND IT IS EXACT

The editor's Plugins UI told Ryan it **needed the Core Data first**. Enabling
that alongside added **`MetaHumanCoreTech`** to `.uproject`. Verified:

    MetaHumanCharacter.uplugin declares 20 plugin dependencies.
    MetaHumanCoreTech IS NOT ONE OF THEM.
    It does not start without it.

Every route I tried enabled exactly what the descriptor **DECLARES** — the
`.uplugin` dependency array, then the `.uproject` array. Both faithfully
reproduced an **incomplete declaration**, and the editor blocked at module
load with no CPU, no dialog and no log line, four times.

**A plugin descriptor is a DERIVED RECORD.** It states what somebody wrote
down about the plugin's needs, not what the plugin needs. This project has a
non-negotiable for exactly this class (15) and three recorded instances of
its cousin (17: a config records what was overridden, never what is in
effect). This is a fourth, in a file nobody thought of as a config: **an
`.uplugin`'s `Plugins` array is a claim, and Epic's own claim was wrong.**

### THE ANSWER WAS IN THE DOCUMENT RYAN GAVE ME, AND I SKIPPED IT

His Gemini plan, step 1, reads verbatim:

> "navigate to Edit → Plugins, enable the MetaHuman Creator plugin, **and
> ensure the Core Data is active**."

I reviewed that plan critically and at length. I caught the inverted
`ForcedLOD` advice, flagged the 8K memory risk, and correctly identified that
the clothing pipeline was the bulk of the work. **And I read straight past
the one clause that was load-bearing**, because it was a short phrase in a
step I had already judged to be the easy part.

**The failure is in where I aimed the scepticism.** I audited the claims the
plan made about things I already knew about (LODs, texture budgets) and gave
no attention at all to a bare instruction about a thing I did not know about.
Prior familiarity decided what got checked, which is precisely backwards —
the unfamiliar clause is the one carrying information I do not have.

### WHAT THE FOUR FAILED ATTEMPTS WERE ACTUALLY WORTH

Not nothing, and this matters for how the record reads. Each eliminated a
real candidate by measurement rather than by argument: memory (2.4 GB against
a 223 GB limit, CPU idle), missing binaries (7 DLLs present), our own C++
(identical editor minus one line loads fine), a modal (no dialog window
exists, twice enumerated), antivirus (engine folder excluded, no change), and
a crash (the exit was `ConsoleCtrl`, i.e. Ryan closing the console).

**The diagnosis was sound and the hypothesis space was wrong.** Every
candidate I generated was about the ENVIRONMENT — memory, security, our code.
None was about the plugin's own declaration being incomplete, because I had
read that declaration and treated it as ground truth. **I verified the
descriptor's contents and never questioned its completeness.**

### AND I RETRACTED A CORRECT INSTINCT ON THE WAY

The second entry claimed a modal was the cause; the third retracted it as
unsupported. The retraction was RIGHT — there was no modal, and the log line
I built it on was Ryan's own click. But note what the retraction cost: it
left "root cause not established", which is honest and inert. The thing that
actually moved this was Ryan reading a UI message I never saw.

**Operationally: when a headless route fails four times, the attended route
is not a fallback, it is the diagnostic.** The Plugins UI knew the answer the
whole time and said so in one sentence. Nothing I could measure from outside
the process would have produced "you need the Core Data".

### THE RULE

**Enable a plugin the way the editor enables it, at least once, before
encoding it anywhere.** The descriptor route is for REPRODUCING an
enablement that is already known to work — never for discovering one. R-GAMEPLAY's
"attended for the first activation, reproducible after" stands, now with a
second and better mechanism behind it than the modal I guessed at.

**OWED:** `MetaHumanCharacter` and `MetaHumanCoreTech` are in `.uproject`,
not in `LandscapeLabGameplay.uplugin` where ruling 2 wants them. Now that
BOTH names are known, the descriptor route should work — moving them is the
tidy end state and the test of that claim. **Not done tonight:** MetaHuman
finally works, and another restart to prove a point about attribution is not
worth risking it.

## 2026-08-16 — THE HERO BECOMES PLAYABLE, and five tools lied on the way

Ryan went to bed asking for one thing: *"my hero available to run around in the
environment."* He got it. What follows is what it cost, and five of the six
findings are instruments that reported success while doing nothing.

### TRELLIS RUNS ON BLACKWELL, WHICH THE PLAN SAID THE DOCUMENTED PATH COULD NOT DO

472,734 vertices, 945,456 faces, watertight, 64 s end to end from Ryan's
portrait. TRELLIS ships PyTorch 2.4.0+cu118, which has no sm_120 support at all,
so the install deviated to torch 2.11+cu128 and every extension had to meet a
toolchain years newer than it expects.

**The install was PIECEWISE on purpose, and that is the only reason four
blockers were each attributable to one cause.** A `setup.sh` run would have
produced one failure and no information.

1. **`open3d` absent.** `trellis/pipelines/__init__` imports the TEXT-to-3D
   pipeline at package import, so an image-only job pays for it anyway.

2. **`ATTN_BACKEND=sdpa` WAS SILENTLY IGNORED, and this is the trap.**
   `trellis/modules/attention/__init__.py` accepts `xformers`, `flash_attn`,
   `sdpa`, `naive`. `trellis/modules/sparse/__init__.py` accepts ONLY
   `xformers` or `flash_attn` and leaves its default in place otherwise. So the
   same environment variable is honoured in one module and dropped in the other,
   and the run printed `[SPARSE] Backend: spconv, Attention: flash_attn` while
   the environment plainly said `sdpa` — with flash_attn not installed.
   **A configuration value that is accepted by one reader and ignored by
   another is worse than one that is rejected everywhere**, because the log
   line that would tell you is the one nobody reads on a working run.

3. **`kaolin` was NOT needed, and installing it would have been the wrong
   fix.** The library path imports exactly one symbol —
   `from kaolin.utils.testing import check_tensor`, used in six assertions with
   `throw=False`. Every other kaolin reference in the package is under
   `examples/` and is never imported. kaolin publishes no wheel for torch
   2.11+cu128, so building it would have been a large risk for one shape check.
   `scripts/trellis/kaolin_check_tensor_shim.py` IMPLEMENTS the contract
   instead.
   **It is implemented and not stubbed, deliberately.** `def check_tensor(*a,
   **k): return True` would satisfy the import and silently disable all six
   assertions — non-negotiable 2's un-failable gate, which reads as coverage
   while being its absence. The shim's selftest asserts it REFUSES wrong rank,
   wrong dimension, wrong dtype and non-tensors, and the installer refuses to
   shadow a real kaolin if one ever appears.

4. **xformers has no sm_120 kernel for float32.** The dispatcher named all
   three candidates: `fa3F` and `cutlassF-pt` require capability <= (9, 0), and
   `fa2F` supports only fp16/bf16. DINOv2's conditioning runs fp32.
   The fix was NOT to patch TRELLIS. `dinov2/layers/attention.py:21` reads
   `XFORMERS_ENABLED = os.environ.get("XFORMERS_DISABLED") is None`, so
   `XFORMERS_DISABLED=1` routes DINOv2 to its own attention while leaving
   TRELLIS's sparse attention — which imports xformers directly and never
   consults that variable — on xformers where it must stay.

xformers was installed `--no-deps` on purpose, so a resolver could not swap out
the torch that had passed the sm_120 gate. Verified after: still 2.11.0+cu128,
still capability (12, 0), and `memory_efficient_attention` executes a real fp16
kernel on this card.

### FOUR WAYS TO MANGLE A PAYLOAD ON THE WAY INTO WSL, ALL MEASURED

Every one produced a WRONG READING rather than an error:

  * PowerShell 5.1 split a single-quoted argument at the first space; bash died
    on an unterminated `if`.
  * Git Bash rewrote `/usr/lib/wsl/lib/nvidia-smi` into
    `C:/Program Files/Git/usr/lib/...` — the msys path-conversion hazard this
    repo already hooks for `/Game/...`.
  * **`wsl.exe` RE-PARSES the command line**, so a heredoc's quoted delimiter
    `<<"EOF"` arrived as `<<EOF` and the body expanded after all. That one wrote
    an EXPANDED Windows PATH snapshot into `/etc/profile.d/cuda.sh`, and the
    file then looked correct while doing the wrong thing — non-negotiable 17, in
    a file I had written myself minutes earlier.
  * `$(...)` inside a payload returned empty unpredictably. `command -v nvcc`
    printed nothing in the same shell where `type -a nvcc` resolved it
    correctly, and I was one sentence from recording "CUDA is not on PATH".

`scripts/wsl_exec.sh` base64-encodes the script. The alphabet is
`[A-Za-z0-9+/=]` — no spaces, quotes, dollars or slashes — so no layer has
anything to mangle. It also strips CR, because a script authored on Windows
carries CRLF and bash then fails naming the wrong thing.

**And a detach that reported success and left nothing behind.** `setsid nohup`
inside a `wsl.exe` call printed `STARTED ... log ...`, exited 0, and produced no
log, no `/opt/trellis` and no process: **WSL tears down the whole session
process tree when the initiating `wsl.exe` exits.** Backgrounding the CALLER is
what holds the session open, which is why the CUDA and PyTorch installs
completed and that one did not. Kept in the tool as a NAMED TRAP rather than
deleted.

### I REPORTED "NO HEAD" AND THE MEASUREMENT OVERTURNED IT

From the first PIE frame I wrote that the face mesh was not rendering. **That
was wrong.** The camera was ~1 m from the body and the head was simply out of
frame. What settled it was not another look but a different question: the
FaceMesh's `head` bone read 150 cm above its root with a correct
root/pelvis/spine hierarchy, and lifting the pawn above the canopy then showed a
complete head and face.

Three photographs said "something is wrong" and none could say what. The eye is
a poor instrument through a 219,659-instance forest — non-negotiable 16 again,
and it cost three wasted frames before I asked the geometry instead of the
pixels.

### `Rotator(ROLL, PITCH, YAW)` RECURRED IN A COMMITTED TOOL

`place_player_start.py:118,122` called `_unreal.Rotator(0.0, __YAW__, 0.0)`.
The signature is `(ROLL, PITCH, YAW)`, so `--yaw 135` set **pitch** to 135,
which the engine normalises to exactly `(roll 180, pitch 45, yaw 180)` — the
value measured off the live actor.

CLAUDE.md already records this casualty by name from 2026-08-12. **It recurred
because the tool READ BACK LOCATION AND NEVER ROTATION.** It printed
"drift 0.000 cm" and returned 0 over a scrambled rotation, for as long as
nobody looked.

The consequence was not cosmetic. The PlayerController inherits the
PlayerStart's rotation and the third-person boom follows it, so a 45 degree
pitch aimed the arm into the ground behind the player: the camera sat **88.1 cm
BELOW** the pawn, **125.5 cm** back on a 400 cm arm, looking up at him from the
floor. After the fix: **381.8 cm back, 138.4 cm above**. Same config, same
probe, one correct rotation.

**I first blamed the forest and shrank the collision probe.** That was not
wasted — the probe size deserves to be config — but it was treating a symptom,
and three more frames would not have found the cause. Reading the control
rotation did, immediately.

**The rule: a value that is never read back is a value nothing defends.** The
tool now asserts rotation and refuses with exit 5 when it disagrees.

### A SAVE REPORTED True AND WROTE NOTHING — the most dangerous shape yet

`EditorLoadingAndSavingUtils.save_dirty_packages(True, True)` returned True. The
PlayerStart move never reached disk. **Caught by the filesystem**, not by any
tool: nothing under `__ExternalActors__` and no `.umap` had changed in ninety
minutes.

A Python actor edit does not reliably flag the external actor package dirty, so
"save every DIRTY package" saved an empty set and truthfully reported success at
having done so. And every check agreed with it:

  * the location read-back said drift 0.000 cm;
  * a second run listed the actor at its new coordinates;
  * PIE spawned the pawn there.

**All three were correct and all three read EDITOR MEMORY** — precisely where
the unsaved change lived. Non-negotiable 0: agreement among instruments that
share a source is one measurement, not three. Only the file on disk was a
different representation, and only it could see the defect.

The project already carries this rule from the 2026-08-09 `save_level`
incident — *"verify a save from the ARTEFACT, never from the tool's report"* —
written when a save SUCCEEDED and reported failure. **This is the same rule
earning its keep against the inversion, which is far more dangerous: a false
failure gets investigated, a false success gets built upon.**

Fixed by removing the dependency rather than adding a retry: the tool reaches
the actor's own package, saves THAT package explicitly, PRINTS ITS NAME so the
caller knows which file's mtime to check, and refuses if the save returns false.

### METAHUMAN: WHAT PYTHON CAN AND CANNOT DO IN 5.8

**Can:** `try_add_object_to_edit`, `get_preview_collection`,
`spawn_meta_human_actor`, `conform_to_target_meshes`,
`fit_state_to_target_vertices`, `track_face_landmarks_from_image`,
`request_auto_rigging`, `get_body_constraints` / `set_body_constraints`. All ten
probed present and reachable.

**Cannot: ASSEMBLE.** There is no unpack and no build anywhere in the 5.8 stub.
The reachable route is duplicating `spawn_meta_human_actor`'s preview meshes
into real packages, which works — and their materials then point at
`/Engine/Transient` dynamic instances that are null on reload.

**And the skin cannot be recovered from them.** MetaHuman sets skin as parameter
OVERRIDES on the dynamic instance, and the getter hard-refuses that type:

    GetMaterialInstanceTextureParameterValue
    TypeError: Cannot nativize 'MaterialInstanceDynamic' as 'Object'
               (allowed Class type: 'MaterialInstanceConstant')

Measured against all 80 texture parameters of the face material. **The names
enumerate; the values are unreachable.** So a Python-built MetaHuman is
untextured white BY CONSTRUCTION, and `build_hero_assets` says so in its
docstring and on every run rather than shipping a mystery.

**A NULL RESULT I DID NOT TRUST, AND SHOULD NOT HAVE.** The body carries a
`Masculine/Feminine` constraint, range -2.0 to +2.0. Setting it to -2.0 and
+2.0 produced BYTE-IDENTICAL body bounds `[53.53, 19.74, 71.22]` on all four
trials including the baseline. A plus-or-minus-2.0 swing changing nothing to two
decimals means the constraint almost certainly never reached the mesh — not that
the slider does nothing. **Reported as an unusable instrument rather than as a
finding**, and the zero dirty packages afterwards corroborate that nothing was
written. The body is still the female medium template and that is Ryan's
one-slider fix, not a mystery.

### THE THROUGH-LINE

Six findings tonight. **Five were tools reporting success while doing nothing** —
an ignored environment variable, a detach that left no process, a rotation never
read back, a save that wrote no bytes, and a shim that would have disabled the
assertions it was standing in for. Not one was caught by a gate. Every one was
caught by asking a DIFFERENT REPRESENTATION: the log line instead of the
environment, the process table instead of the exit code, the control rotation
instead of another frame, the filesystem instead of the editor, and — for the
shim — writing the test before trusting the substitute.

## 2026-08-16 (later) — THE FACE CONFORM CRASHED THE EDITOR, and the route is now known

Logged BEFORE any retry, per the operating loop's step (b).

### WHAT WAS ATTEMPTED

`conform_to_target_meshes(character, target_mesh_key, params)` with the TRELLIS
head as the target: `TargetPartsType.HEAD_ONLY`, `head_vertices` and
`head_vertex_indices` taken from
`MetaHumanCharacterEditorSubsystem.get_mesh_data_for_conforming(SM_HeroHead_TRELLIS)`,
`auto_solve=True`, and NO `curve_tracking_points`, `camera_view_info` or
`image_size`.

### WHAT HAPPENED

    CrashType     Assert
    ErrorMessage  Assertion failed: IsValid()
                  [Templates/SharedPointer.h] [Line: 1133]
    CallStack     UnrealEditor_Core
                  UnrealEditor_Core
                  UnrealEditor_MetaHumanCharacterEditor   x4
                  UnrealEditor_CoreUObject
                  UnrealEditor_PythonScriptPlugin ...

The editor died. `ue_exec` surfaced it as `ConnectionResetError: [WinError
10054]`, which is what a crashed editor looks like from the client side and is
NOT itself diagnostic — the crash log is.

**NOTHING WAS DAMAGED.** `git status` clean, and `MHC_AlpineHero.uasset` still
carries its pre-session mtime. The conform mutates in memory and nothing was
saved. Restore point `pre-hero-face-conform-20260816` was tagged first and was
not needed.

### ROOT CAUSE, AS FAR AS IT IS ESTABLISHED

A `TSharedPtr` was dereferenced unset inside `MetaHumanCharacterEditor`. The
call reached engine code — this is not a Python type error and not a bad
argument the binding could reject — so something the solver requires was absent
rather than wrong.

**The strong candidate is the face-tracking context.** `ConformTargetParams`
carries `curve_tracking_points`, `camera_view_info` and `image_size` alongside
the mesh, and all three were left at their defaults. `auto_solve=True` was
assumed to make them optional. **That assumption is the thing that failed**, and
it was an assumption — nothing in the reflected surface says auto_solve
substitutes for landmarks.

**STATED AS A LOCATION, NOT A CAUSE.** Without symbols I cannot say which
pointer. What is established: the call is reachable, the argument types are
accepted, and it dies inside the solver rather than at the boundary.

### WHAT THIS BUYS THE NEXT ATTEMPT

The expensive unknown is now settled, and it is the one that mattered:

**`get_mesh_data_for_conforming` IS the bridge, and arbitrary topology IS
supported.** It returns `(vertices, triangle_indices)` from a StaticMesh or
SkeletalMesh — "the same data that the interactive conform tool uses
internally" — and those map one-to-one onto `ConformTargetMesh.head_vertices`
and `.head_vertex_indices`. **The indices are TRIANGLES, not archetype
correspondence.** I had earlier read `head_vertex_indices` as implying archetype
topology and concluded a raw TRELLIS mesh was not a drop-in. That reading was
wrong and is corrected here.

Measured on both meshes:

    SM_HeroHead_TRELLIS   472,734 verts   extent (0.696, 0.921, 0.998)
    SKM_HeroFace          33,845 verts    extent (34.99, 24.28, 37.32) cm
                          bbox Z 134.7 .. 172.0  -- CHARACTER space, Z up

Same axis convention, so no rotation is needed — only scale and translation.
**Scale from HEIGHT, not width or depth:** the TRELLIS reconstruction includes
the armour collar, and the bbox ratios disagree accordingly — 50.3 on width,
26.4 on depth, 37.4 on height. Only height measures the same thing on both.

### THREE THINGS THE NEXT ATTEMPT SHOULD DO DIFFERENTLY

1. **Supply the tracking inputs.** Render the target mesh from a known camera
   into a TextureRenderTarget2D, read it as BGRA, run
   `track_face_landmarks_from_image`, and pass the returned curves together
   with the `MinimalViewInfo` that produced them and the image size. The
   docstring for the tracker says exactly this: *"Use with a front-facing
   portrait of the target mesh — typically a SceneCapture2D render."*
2. **DECIMATE FIRST.** 472,734 vertices is not precision this solve needs, and
   building that array crosses the Python binding once per element — the call
   took over ten minutes before it died. `scripts/trellis/decimate_head.py`
   produces ~40k triangles via open3d and records the bbox change so the
   silhouette is checked, not assumed.
3. **CROP THE COLLAR OUT OF THE MESH**, not just out of the input image. It is
   the reason the three scale estimates disagree by 2x, and it is geometry the
   solver has no use for.

### THE RULE

**A crash inside engine code from a reflected call is an ARGUMENT that was
absent, not an argument that was wrong** — the binding rejects wrong types at
the boundary and it did not. When a struct offers several fields and only some
are populated, the unpopulated ones are the suspects, and a flag named
`auto_solve` is not evidence that the others are optional.

And: **an editor crash is a measurement.** It cost seven minutes of restart and
established more about this API than three careful probes had.

## 2026-08-16 (later still) — THE FACE TRACKER WORKS, AND THE INPUT IS THE HARD PART

The conform's blocking unknown from the previous entry is answered:
**`track_face_landmarks_from_image` returns real landmarks for a TRELLIS
reconstruction rendered inside Unreal.** 16 curves — `crv_eyelid_upper_l/r`,
`crv_eyelid_lower_l/r`, `crv_lip_upper_inner_l/r`, `crv_lip_lower_outer_l/r`,
`crv_lip_philtrum_l/r` and more. Frame:
`_verify/20260816_headtrack_plus_y.png` in the run that succeeded.

**And it settled the orientation by MEASUREMENT.** I had written earlier that
the two meshes shared an axis convention so no rotation was needed. Extents
cannot say which way a nose points, and that claim was unsupported. Capturing
from four directions and asking the tracker is the discriminator: it returned
16 curves from `+Y` and NOTHING from the other three. **The head faces +Y.**

### THE PIPELINE THAT WORKS

    crop the collar off      scripts/trellis/crop_and_decimate_head.py
    decimate to ~40k tris    472,734 verts crosses the binding one at a time
    import as a StaticMesh   AssetImportTask, automated
    spawn at Z 250,000       far above terrain, sky background only
    scale 24 cm / Z extent
    PointLight at the camera 200,000, travelling with it
    SceneCapture2D          FOV 35, 70 cm out, SCS_FINAL_COLOR_LDR
    read_render_target      returns Array[Color], which is exactly what
                            track_face_landmarks_from_image takes

### FOUR WAYS I BROKE IT AFTERWARDS, ALL VISIBLE ONLY IN THE FRAME

Having got 16 curves, I tried to improve the input and lost them four times.
Every diagnosis came from EXPORTING THE FRAME and looking; not one was
diagnosable from the tracker's return value, which is `None` for all of them.

1. **No material** — the mesh imports with none, so it renders with the
   engine's default CHECKERBOARD. Against a low sun at Z 45,000 it was a black
   silhouette. Nothing to track.
2. **Lower crop to keep the chin** — the automatic neck cut had removed the jaw
   (visible the moment it was rendered: the mesh ends below the mouth). Cutting
   lower kept the chin AND changed the Z extent, so a Z-based scale shrank the
   FACE in frame: 37.5 to 32.0.
3. **More triangles** — 160,000 instead of 40,000 produced WORSE geometry, not
   better: faceted planes with holes at the eyes and ears. More triangles made
   it worse, which is the opposite of the expected direction and is why it has
   to be looked at rather than reasoned about.
4. **A white material and a dimmer light** — replaced the checkerboard's
   mid-grey with near-uniform blown-out white. The successful render's TONAL
   RANGE, which came from a material I had thought was a defect, was part of
   why the tracker could see anything.

**The through-line: the tracker's failure signal is a single `None` for every
distinct cause.** Exporting the render turned one undifferentiated failure into
four separate diagnosable ones, and that instrument was added only after the
second failure. It should have been there first.

### WHAT IS STILL NOT DONE

`conform_to_target_meshes` has **never run with landmarks**. The one time it
ran it crashed on the missing tracking context; every run since has skipped it
because the tracker found nothing to pass. The call is assembled and correct as
far as the argument types go — world-space vertices consistent with the camera,
triangle indices, curves, `MinimalViewInfo`, `IntPoint(1024, 1024)` — and it
sits behind a `if _best is None: skip` that has been taking the skip.

**Reproducing the successful render is the whole remaining task**, and its
settings are recorded above.

### A LEAK CAUGHT BY RE-ENUMERATING

The probe payload destroyed `HeadTrackProbe` and `HeadTrackLight` between runs
and NOT `HeadTrackCapture`. Eight capture actors had accumulated in the editor
world, one per iteration. Found by listing the actors again after the cleanup
rather than trusting `destroy_actor` — the same shape as every other finding
tonight. Level now holds none of them and nothing is dirty.

### CORRECTION, same session — THE SUCCESSFUL FRAME NO LONGER EXISTS

The entry above cites `_verify/20260816_headtrack_plus_y.png` as the frame from
the run that succeeded. **That file does not hold that frame.** Every probe run
exported to the SAME filename, so four later runs overwrote it, and what
survives is the FAILED faceted render — now kept and relabelled
`_verify/20260816_headtrack_plus_y_FAILED_faceted.png` so the name cannot
mislead.

The 16 tracked curves are still a real measurement: they are in the run log,
with their names. But **the image evidence for the success is GONE**, and the
image evidence that survives is of a failure.

This is the two-phases-one-filename defect this project already recorded in
`save_level`, arriving in a new form: there it cost a reply, here it cost the
artefact. **A probe that writes to a fixed name destroys its own best
evidence**, and it destroys it precisely when the probe starts working and you
begin iterating on top of the success.

**The rule: a probe's output filename carries the run's identity** — a tag, a
counter, anything — for the same reason `capture.py` takes `--tag` and for the
same reason `ue_exec` gives every caller its own stage filename. I applied that
rule to the payload staging tonight and not to the frames the payload wrote.

### AND THEN I COULD NOT REPRODUCE IT — ten runs, every hypothesis refuted

The 16 curves happened once. **Ten subsequent runs returned `None`**, and every
hypothesis I formed was tested single-variable and refuted:

| tested | result |
|---|---|
| the white material blowing out the face | disabled it; checkerboard returned, still `None` |
| missing smooth normals in the OBJ | added them — **MADE IT WORSE**, and was my own regression |
| normals again, removed | reverted to no-normals, still `None` |
| triangle budget 40k vs 160k | 160k produced faceted geometry WITH HOLES |
| crop height (chin included) | changed the Z extent and so the scale; still `None` |
| light intensity 200k vs 40k | blown out either way |
| scale basis, Z extent vs width | 37.5 vs 23.3; still `None` |
| re-import vs delete-then-fresh-import | fresh import, still `None` |

**THE NORMALS ONE IS THE INSTRUCTIVE FAILURE.** I saw faceting, reasoned that
Unreal must be computing per-face normals for a normal-less OBJ, and "fixed" it
by writing open3d's vertex normals. It is the other way round: Unreal SMOOTHS a
normal-less OBJ, and honours supplied normals — which after decimation are
effectively per-face because the decimator splits vertices. **My fix caused the
symptom I was trying to cure**, and I only established the direction by
reverting it and comparing.

### THE REAL DEFECT IS THAT THE SUCCESS WAS NOT REPRODUCIBLE, AND I MADE THAT WORSE

Every probe run exported its frame to the SAME filename. The successful frame
was overwritten four runs later, so the one artefact that could have told me
what was different is gone, and what survives is a failure wearing the same
name. I relabelled them `_FAILED_faceted` and `_UNREPRODUCED` rather than let
the names mislead.

**A success you cannot reproduce is not a capability, it is an anecdote.** The
16 curve names are in the run log and I believe the measurement; I cannot
demonstrate it on demand, and those are different claims. Recorded as the
second, not the first.

**What the next attempt should do FIRST, before any tuning:** make the probe
write `<tag>_<run>.png` and keep every frame, so two runs can be diffed. I
applied exactly that rule to payload staging in `ue_exec` earlier the same
night — every caller gets its own stage filename, and the docstring explains
why — and did not apply it to the frames the payloads wrote. The rule was
already in my hands.

### THE POSITIVE CONTROL I SHOULD HAVE RUN FIRST

After ten runs of `None` I finally asked the question that was available from the
start: **can this tracker succeed at all, through this pixel path?**

Fed it Ryan's actual PHOTOGRAPH — `hero_face_bald_headcrop.png`, imported as a
Texture2D, drawn into a render target with `Canvas.draw_texture`, and read back
with the SAME `read_render_target` call every mesh capture uses:

    landmarks         16 curves
    centre mean RGB   105.0 / 66.5 / 56.2   -- red-dominant
    verdict           TRACKER AND PIXEL PATH ARE SOUND

Two things settled at once. The instrument works, so every `None` is a statement
about the SUBJECT. And the channel order is right — skin came back red-dominant,
which is what `BGRA8` in the docstring made worth checking explicitly rather
than assuming.

**This should have been the second thing I did, not the twelfth.** I spent ten
runs varying the subject while never establishing that the instrument could say
"yes" — which is non-negotiable 2 turned around: a gate that has only ever
refused has not been shown capable of accepting, and until it has, every refusal
is uninterpretable.

### AND IT IMMEDIATELY EARNED ITS KEEP

With the tracker exonerated, the render is the whole problem, and the control
also hands over the TARGET NUMBER: a face that tracks measures 105/66/56 in the
centre. Measuring the mesh renders against it:

    photo (tracked)     105.0 /  66.5 /  56.2   red-dominant
    mesh render         177.9 / 172.3 / 166.9   near-neutral, bright

Not a near miss. The renders are bright and colourless where a face is dark and
warm — and the reason is now visible rather than inferred: **the skin material
never applied.** The imported OBJ carries ZERO material slots, so
`set_material(0, mat)` on the component has no slot to override and does nothing,
silently. Every render has been the engine's default checkerboard throughout,
including the one that worked.

That is the fourth silent no-op of this session, and the same shape as the rest:
a call that returns without complaint and changes nothing.

**The next attempt sets the material on the MESH ASSET** (giving it a slot),
not as a component override, and tunes light against 105/66/56 rather than by
eye. It should also fix the faceting, which is still unexplained: the render
that tracked had a ROUND crown and the current ones are angular, from the same
40,000-triangle budget and the same 20,189 vertices.

**Nothing about the conform has changed.** It has still never run with landmarks.

### THE MATERIAL BOUND AND THE RENDER DID NOT MOVE — where I stopped

Acting on the control's diagnosis, the material was set on the MESH ASSET rather
than as a component override, and **it took**: 1 material slot,
`M_HeroHeadSkin` bound, verified by reading the property back off the asset
rather than trusting the setter.

The render did not change. At all:

    run          plus_y            minus_y           plus_x            minus_x
    component    177.9/172.3/166.9 155.6/157.3/162.0 143.4/147.8/154.1 151.8/153.2/156.3
    mesh asset   177.9/172.3/166.9 155.6/157.3/162.0 143.4/147.8/154.1 151.8/153.2/156.3

**Byte-identical across a real change.** That is the same signature as the
body-constraint experiment earlier tonight — a setter that lands and a result
that does not move — and by the rule I applied there, it is an unusable
instrument reading rather than a finding about materials. Something between the
bound material and `capture_scene()` is not being refreshed, and I did not
establish what.

### WHY I STOPPED HERE RATHER THAN CONTINUE

Twelve runs. The last four each tested a specific, well-founded hypothesis and
none moved the result. The honest position:

* the tracker WORKS — proven on a photograph, 16 curves, through this pixel path
* the mesh render does not present a face to it, and I cannot say why
* the conform has NEVER RUN with landmarks
* the one success was never reproduced and its frame was destroyed

**What is banked is real and is not this.** The hero is playable, walks a
kilometre, spawns in a clearing, and survives a cold boot; TRELLIS runs on
Blackwell and produced the head; and four silent no-ops in existing tools were
found and fixed. Continuing to iterate on a render at 05:00 with a clean tree and
a working deliverable is how a good state becomes a bad one.

### THE COUNT THAT IS THE REAL LESSON OF THE NIGHT

**Silent no-ops found tonight: five.** A save that returned True and wrote
nothing. A rotation set on the wrong axis and never read back. An environment
variable honoured by one module and dropped by another. A detach that printed
STARTED and left no process. A material set on a component with no slot to
receive it. Add the sixth I could not close — a bound material that does not
reach the renderer — and the pattern is not incidental to this session, it IS
this session.

Every one was found by asking a DIFFERENT REPRESENTATION: the filesystem instead
of the tool's return, the control rotation instead of another frame, the log
line instead of the environment, the process table instead of the exit code, the
asset instead of the component. **None was found by a gate**, and none announced
itself.

### CORRECTION 2026-08-16 — I CALLED A GOOD INSTRUMENT BLIND

Earlier this session I set the `Masculine/Feminine` body constraint to -2.0 and
+2.0 in a script, read the preview body's bounds, got `[53.53, 19.74, 71.22]`
byte-identical on all four trials including the baseline, and concluded the
BOUNDS READ was an unusable instrument.

**The instrument is fine.** Ryan set the same constraint through the UI, and the
same read moved:

    before  [53.53, 19.74, 71.22]
    after   [55.32, 20.71, 73.15]

with the constraints reading Masculine/Feminine -2.0, Muscularity 2.0, Fat
-1.26, Height 178.196, all active.

**What was wrong was the SCOPE of my conclusion, not the observation.** The
observation — identical numbers across a ±2.0 swing — was correct and remains
correct: my scripted `set_body_constraints` never reached the mesh. From that I
generalised to a claim about the READ, and those are different things.

**A null result from an instrument that CAN respond is evidence about the
INPUT.** I had no evidence the read was incapable of responding, because I had
never seen it respond — the same gap the tracker positive control closed a few
hours later, and I made the identical mistake twice in one night in opposite
directions:

  * the tracker: ten `None`s, and I kept blaming the subject without ever
    proving the instrument could say yes;
  * the body bounds: one null, and I blamed the instrument without ever proving
    it could say no.

**Both are the same missing step — a control.** One run of a known-good input
would have settled either in minutes. The rule is not "distrust instruments",
it is: *before a null result is allowed to mean anything, show the instrument
responding to something.*

I was right to refuse to report the body change as a finding. I was wrong to
convert that refusal into a verdict on the instrument, and the record said so
for several hours.

# 2026-08-16 (evening) — THE HERO'S FACE IS SCULPTED, AND THE UNITS LIED FIRST

Ryan: *"add in the hero features to the face to create the hero look based on
the image"*, then mid-session: *"the image starting with qv94 should be the
final product look of the hero"* — the HAIRED portrait is the product target.

## A SCULPT THAT REPORTED SUCCESS AND MOVED NOTHING

`MetaHumanCharacterEditorSubsystem` exposes the sculpt directly:
`get_face_landmarks` returns 79 control points, `translate_face_landmarks`
moves them, `commit_face_state` persists. The first application asked for
moves up to `3.48e-03` and the landmarks moved `6.08e-06` — 0.17% — while the
facial rig did not move at all.

**Root cause: `get_face_landmarks` REPORTS in one space and
`translate_face_landmarks` ACCEPTS another.** A ladder of five deltas on one
landmark settles it, and the consistency is what makes it a calibration
rather than a coincidence:

    requested   landmark moved   requested/moved   rig moved
      0.001       1.343e-06          744.85          0.0
      0.01        1.342e-05          745.32          0.0
      0.1         1.342e-04          744.99          0.0
      1.0         1.342e-03          745.11          0.0
     10.0         5.876e-03         1701.97          0.0

**745.0 delta units per landmark unit**, linear across three decades, then
**saturating** at 10.0 — the face model constrains large single moves.

Two structural consequences: a one-shot delta CANNOT land on target, so the
applier iterates `(target - current) * 745` clamped into the linear regime and
prints the residual per pass; and the spec carries absolute TARGETS rather
than offsets, so re-running is a no-op instead of sculpting the face twice
(pipeline rule 3).

This is *"a value can arrive and still mean something else"* from the
resolution protocol, landing exactly as written. The magnitude was derived
correctly from a premise about units that was never checked.

## THE GATE CAUGHT IT — AND THE GATE'S OWN INSTRUMENT WAS ALSO WRONG

The applier refuses to commit when landmarks move and the mesh does not,
because that is the signature the body `Masculine/Feminine` slider produced
earlier the same day. It fired on the first run and produced the numbers that
led to the calibration.

**But its instrument was wrong in the dangerous direction.** It read facial
rig joints via `get_socket_location`, which returns reference-pose positions
and reads `0.0` even after a *successful* sculpt, even after
`assemble_for_preview`. A gate that reports "no movement" on a working sculpt
is a false refusal that would have blocked the correct result.

What settled it was a third representation: **the asset's bytes on disk**,
`104,960,609 B sha 95024DC2` → `104,977,162 B sha DF57585B`. Fixed in the same
pass: the gate had treated an unreadable mesh measurement as a PASS. "I could
not look" is not "yes" (non-negotiable 6).

## `request_auto_rigging(blocking=True)` TAKES THE EDITOR DOWN

    Requesting Auto-Rigging ... Blocking: true
    Assertion failed: IsValid() [SharedPointer.h] [Line: 1133]

**The same assertion, file and line as the recorded `conform_to_target_meshes`
crash**, from a different entry point on the same subsystem. Two instances
make it a property of driving `MetaHumanCharacterEditor` SYNCHRONOUSLY from
remote Python, not a property of either call. `blocking=False` runs clean and
finishes in **24.8 s** — and Ryan's own successful run at 18:35 logged
`Blocking: false`, so the working configuration was in the log the whole time.

Nothing was lost: the sculpt was saved before the crash and the restore point
was not needed. Context at `_verify/20260816_autorig_crash/`.

## THE RIG WAS ALREADY GONE, AND THE LOG NAMES WHAT TOOK IT

`build_meta_human` refused: *"Character is not rigged."* The log answers
whether my sculpt caused that:

    18:35:40  Requesting Auto-Rigging ... finished in 50.496 seconds
    19:34:08  Face and body texture selection are locked while the character
              is rigged. Unrig to modify them.

The character WAS rigged, and the texture workflow REQUIRES unrigging — which
is what removed it, before this session, matching the 40 MB the editor's own
write dropped from the asset at 13:52. **The ordering constraint is worth more
than the incident: sculpt → textures → rig → build.**

## `build_meta_human` IS REFLECTED; THE UNPACK IS NOT

CURRENT STATE said *"MetaHuman's Assemble is NOT REFLECTED — no unpack, no
build anywhere in the 5.8 stub"*. **Half false, and the half that is true is
the important half.** `build_meta_human` and `can_build_meta_human` ARE
reflected, with `MetaHumanCharacterEditorBuildParameters`; the earlier reading
was almost certainly taken off a stub generated BEFORE the MetaHuman plugins
were enabled. **The Python stub is a DERIVED RECORD, regenerated per editor
start, only as current as its last regeneration** — non-negotiable 15 in a
file nobody treats as a config.

But calling it logs **"MetaHuman Character assembly succeeded"** and writes
nothing to disk: everything lands in `/Engine/Transient.MHC_..._Collection:`.
There is **no reflected unpack function anywhere in the 5.8 stub**, with any
`absolute_build_path`. So Python can sculpt, rig and assemble; only the editor
UI can unpack to `/Game/Hero/Generated/SKM_HeroFace`. That is the same shape
as the "Save Face Textures" finding: a door that exists only in the UI.

## A CLAIM I MADE FROM A PHOTOGRAPH, AND THE MEASUREMENT REFUTED IT

Seeing the bald and haired references side by side I reported them as
different face shapes — the haired one *"leaner, hollower cheeks, tapered V
jaw"*. Tracked with the same instrument and normalised to interpupillary
units they agree to within ~3%:

    eye_to_mouth  1.002     eye widths  1.011 / 1.003
    mouth width   0.971     nasolabial  1.034

`hero/reference/README.md`'s "the SAME face" is SUPPORTED; my reading was the
eye being fooled by hair and beard framing the face. **Non-negotiable 16 — the
eye is a poor photometer — extends to geometry: it is a poor proportioner
too.** Stated narrowly, because the instrument has a scope: the tracker
returns eyelids, lips, philtrum and nasolabial folds ONLY, so jaw and
cheekbone contour are unmeasured on the haired image, not agreed.

## ANATOMY ASSUMED IS ANATOMY GUESSED

The 79 landmarks arrive unlabelled and `get_preset_body_key_points` names only
`P1`…`P102` against BODY vertex indices. Naming them from extremes (most
anterior = nose tip, lowest = chin) produced a nose-to-chin of **13.7 cm**
against a scale three axis ratios agreed on. The arithmetic was right; the
premise was invented.

What worked was LOOKING. X is lateral by a bilateral-symmetry test (median
mirror residual 0.7% of span, against 13.7% and 4.0%), and Z is up — so an
orthographic X–Z plot IS a front view, and the mid-sagittal chain reads
directly: 7 forehead, 59 glabella, 6 nose bridge, 64 nose tip, 65 subnasale,
5/50/4 lips, 62 chin crease, 8 chin, 12 under-chin, 13/14/15 the POSTERIOR
midline, 60 the crown.

**And the landmarks are a CONTROL CAGE, not surface points**: nose-tip-to-chin
implies 222 cm/unit, forehead-to-chin 315, tip-to-subnasale over 400. Three
irreconcilable answers is the data refusing the premise, so every move is
expressed as a fraction of head extent rather than in centimetres.

## SYMMETRY BELONGS IN THE STRUCTURE, NOT IN THE TUNING

Region predicates have edges, and the first plan caught nose wing 45 without
its mirror 67, and jaw points 3 and 30 without 43 and 63 — a crooked face from
a symmetric intent. Tuning predicates until the edges line up would need
re-tuning on every future edit. Mirror-pairing the delta field makes symmetry
structural: all 79 pair, worst residual asymmetry **0.000e+00**.

## FOUR WHITE FRAMES, AND THE INSTRUMENT THAT REPLACED THE RENDERER

Every engine capture of this character came back pure white — mean RGB
255/255/255, nonwhite fraction 0.0000, four times, across two camera designs
and an actor scaled 2000x. The cause: the preview mesh is ~0.12 units tall,
its components sit at world origin and **do not follow `set_actor_location`**,
so the subject is inside the near clip plane. `get_actor_bounds` reports a
subject 250,000 units tall because it spans from world origin to wherever the
actor root was moved — two readings of the same actor that cannot both be
about the same head.

The fix was to stop asking the renderer. `get_mesh_data_for_conforming` returns
the face mesh's 33,845 vertices and 64,094 triangles; rasterised offline they
give a clear, shaded portrait — and, unlike 79 landmarks, they ARE a
silhouette, so the width-at-height comparison against the photograph finally
became sound. It shows the hero still 2–18% wider than the sculpted mesh,
largest at the jaw (1.13–1.22) and closed at the ear line (1.00–1.02), which
drove a second, purely measured widening pass.

## AN OPERATIONAL TRAP THAT COST ~8 MINUTES

`ue_exec.py --timeout N` passes N into `_select_verified_node`, so **N is a
fixed discovery window, not a deadline**: `--timeout 240` bought 240 s of
sitting followed by 3 s of work. Same shape as the recorded `capture.py
--timeout` lesson. Use 12–15.

Also: `save_asset` immediately before `build_meta_human` wedged the editor —
log frozen at `InternalPromptForCheckoutAndSave started...` →
`FlushAsyncLoading`, game thread at 0.05 CPU per wall-second, an untitled
modal up. The autorig step had already saved it; the second save bought
nothing and cost the editor.
