# 2026-08-19 (day) — THE BODY WAS NEVER SET, AND THE LOCK'S COST DOES NOT EXIST

Three findings, and the first one is the whole diagnosis.

## THE PARAMETER WAS FINE. THE VALUE WAS NEVER APPLIED.

The hero read androgynous in his first landscape render, and the standing
record said his body was configured `Masculine/Feminine = -2.0` on
2026-08-16. Three hypotheses were on the table: the parameter never reaches
the mesh, it does not survive assembly, or it did not survive duplication.

**All three are wrong, and the answer took one read:**

    MHC_AlpineHero          -1.0
    MHC_AlpineHero_Master   -1.0
    MHC_AlpineHero_Scratch  -1.0
    MHC_AlpineHero_Scratch2 -1.0

Every character sits at **-1.0**, including the master, which predates every
edit of the last two days. The -2.0 was never applied — and the 2026-08-16
session said so itself, in the sentence recording that a +-2.0 swing produced
"byte-identical body bounds INCLUDING the baseline". That is the signature of
a write that never landed, and last night's mutate-a-copy trap is almost
certainly the mechanism: iterating a UE struct Array yields copies, so the
setter reports success over an unchanged array.

**The record recorded the INTENT and nobody re-read the asset.** A derived
record again — and this one survived three days and a full night of work
because every subsequent session inherited the sentence rather than the
value.

**The parameter reaches the mesh perfectly**, which is what makes the
diagnosis certain rather than plausible: -2.0 gives shoulder 54.08 cm and
shoulder/hip 1.578; +2.0 gives 19.55 and 0.562; and the model's own derived
`Across Shoulder` moves with it, 39.52 -> 44.21 -> 32.93. Two representations,
one conclusion. Applied to the working character, the body now renders with
flat pectorals, broad shoulders and narrow hips.

## THE ADVERTISED PERMANENT BODY LOCK DOES NOT EXIST

The free experiment, and it dissolves a sequencing constraint:

    scratch, THREE whole-rig imports   -1.0 -> +2.0   shoulder 52.305 -> 19.551
    BodyTest, NEVER imported                  -> +2.0   shoulder          19.551

Identical to the pixel. **Whole-rig import does not freeze the body**, so the
lock's entire advertised cost joins the "neck alignment only" docstring in the
file marked REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT. Two Epic-documented costs of this path
have now been checked and neither was real.

## AN INSTRUMENT IS WRONG FOUR TIMES BEFORE IT IS RIGHT, AND EACH WAS A FRAME

The shoulder ruler was built before anything was changed, per ruling. It
reported, in order: a waist wider than the shoulders; then a chest of 94.5 cm
on a 178 cm man; then zeros; then a 7.6 cm shoulder. Every one was found by
OPENING THE FRAME, and every one has a mechanism:

1. **Widths were DEPTHS** — at yaw 0 the mesh photographs in profile. The
   same wrong-axis trap the assembled Blueprint sprang the same night.
2. **Fractions of stature aimed one landmark low** — the body mesh is
   HEADLESS (the face is a separate mesh), so 149.55 cm is the whole body.
3. **Min-to-max span measured ARM TO ARM** in A-pose. The fix is the longest
   contiguous run; a centre-column walk was tried first and returned zeros,
   because with the arms out the midpoint of the silhouette can land in the
   GAP between torso and arm.
4. **`clavicle_l` is 3 cm below the top of a headless body**, so that row
   reads the neck. The acromion line is `upperarm_l`.

**And the fifth was the one that mattered.** Height 178.196 -> 190 -> 205 read
159.45, 159.45, 149.30 — incoherent, until two runs with NOTHING changed
agreed to three decimals. Each measurement was showing **the state before
it**: the parametric body lands asynchronously. The settle gate now standard
on this tool caught a 23.105 cm first-shot drift and 0.000 cm on the second.

**A capture is not a measurement until it reproduces — and that rule is not
about the renderer.** It was written for virtual textures converging and it
just caught an asynchronous mesh rebuild in a completely different subsystem.
A reproduce-gate does not need to know what it is protecting against, which is
exactly why it belongs on every instrument this project builds.

---

## 2026-08-19 (night) — THE GROOMS WERE NEVER BROKEN. THEY WERE MEASURED TOO EARLY.

**B-HAIRGROOM is closed, and it was never an asset defect.** Two days of
elimination, ten hypotheses, five assets compared field by field, a
correlational lead on `enable_global_interpolation`, and a standing ruling that
landscape renders ship as DIAGNOSTIC with respect to grooms. The cause is that
**a groom finishes over frames after its assets first load in an editor
session, and every render that said "bald" was taken before it finished.**

Measured, cold editor, first spawn, nothing changed between the two runs but
the frames spent:

    groom       first reading   second reading   converged
    Hair             33,743          96,246       96,147 - 97,338
    Eyebrows          3,564          19,205       18,904 - 18,911
    Beard             9,153          13,149       12,555 - 12,809
    Mustache          4,569           4,200        3,492 -  3,916

The first reading called Eyebrows and Mustache ABSENT. They were not absent.
They were not finished. Hair, the largest and most expensive of the four,
converges LAST and from furthest away — which is exactly why hair, and only
hair, looked permanently broken while the other three "worked".

### THE INSTRUMENT THAT FOUND IT, AND THE TWO THAT COULD NOT

The gate in force asserted COMPONENT STATE — groom asset set, binding set,
`visible` true — and returned `ships_as DELIVERABLE` on a portrait containing
no visible grooms at all.

    settling cannot see absence  ->  a checklist cannot see absence either

Both failed the same way and it is worth naming the shape, because this project
has now built the same defect twice under two different names: **an instrument
that never looks at the thing being claimed.** A settle-gate photographs the
frame and asks whether it is STABLE. A checklist reads the setup and asks
whether it is COMPLETE. Neither asks whether the beard is in the picture.

The replacement is `groom_presence.py`: hide each groom in turn, require a
non-empty difference where that groom sits. A groom that draws nothing produces
an identical frame, and identical frames are the one thing a difference mask
cannot miss.

### THREE THINGS HAD TO BE FIXED BEFORE IT COULD MEASURE ANYTHING

**1. THE DENOMINATOR WAS THE WHOLE FRAME, AND THE WHOLE FRAME IS NOT STABLE.**
The first run of the gate refused, correctly: two captures of an UNCHANGED
subject differ over **11.3%** of a 2048² frame, which swamps a beard. I reached
for temporal AA first — `r.AntiAliasingMethod 4 -> 0` — and it moved the floor
to 10.5%, i.e. **it was not the cause**. What settled it was looking at the
difference map instead of its mean: the hero's silhouette is BLACK and the
forest is bright noise everywhere. The instability is the trees re-rendering
themselves. So the gate now builds a STABILITY MAP from three unchanged-state
frames, excludes every pixel they disagree on, and measures the floor on what
survives. Floor 472,199 px -> **1,119 px**, on the same scene, same session.
Non-negotiable 22 again: the number was arithmetically true and answered a
question nobody asked.

**2. A NULL RESULT NEEDED A POSITIVE CONTROL.** A groom whose hide produces an
identical frame is indistinguishable from a hide that never took effect, and
those two mean opposite things — "it draws nothing" versus "I could not look".
The payload therefore hides the FACE MESH through the same call in the same
payload. It moves 800–1,300x the floor, so a null below it is a real absence.
Without that control the tool refuses (exit 7) rather than reporting zeros.

**3. THE MEASUREMENT HAD TO REPRODUCE, AND THAT IS THE ONE THAT SOLVED IT.**
The convergence above is invisible to a single pass — a single pass just
returns a confident wrong answer. The gate now takes the measurement TWICE and
refuses to issue any verdict if the two disagree by more than 30%. Converged
passes agree within 0.5–3.7%; the converging one moved 185%. **The rule that
caught this was already in the project**, written for virtual textures — *a
capture is not a measurement until it reproduces* — and it had never been
applied to the gate itself, only to the frames the gate looked at.

### A HYPOTHESIS I WAS HANDED, TESTED, AND REFUTED

The session opened with an externally-sourced mechanism: groom simulation runs
as a GPU batch inside the MAIN SCENE RENDER PASS, so a SceneCapture only shows
grooms a realtime main view also rendered. It predicted the record perfectly —
the preview path drew grooms because the editor viewport was showing the
preview actor, the in-level path drew none because nothing was framed on him.

**The first differential appeared to confirm it, spectacularly.** Same capture
transform, same SceneCapture actor, same render target; only the editor
viewport's yaw differed by 180°. Main view away: bald. Main view on him: full
hair and eyebrows. It is a genuinely striking pair of images and it is in
`_verify/20260819_groom_mechanism/evidence/arms_cold_vs_warm.png`.

**It was a confound.** The two arms differed in main-view AND in elapsed
warm-up, because one was taken after the other. The controls separate them:

    reversal: point the main view away again        grooms STILL drew
    fresh respawn, main view 180 deg away           grooms STILL drew, within
                                                    1.3% of the main-view-on
                                                    numbers

Same variable, moved deliberately, no effect. **The mechanism is real in the
sense that somebody measured it in another engine version; it is not what was
happening here.** Had I stopped at the first differential — which agreed with
the briefed hypothesis, produced a dramatic image, and would have been written
up as a confirmed mechanism — I would have promoted an elaborate doctrine
about riding main views, and the grooms would have kept intermittently
vanishing whenever a session rendered too early.

**The lesson is not "be suspicious of outside information".** The hypothesis
was good and it earned the test. The lesson is that **a differential is only
single-variable if you MADE it single-variable**, and "I changed one thing"
means the thing I typed, not the thing that differed. Elapsed time is a
variable. Order is a variable. The reversal control costs one run and is the
only thing that can tell a mechanism from a coincidence of sequence.

### AND A VERDICT BELONGS TO ITS FRAMING

The same assets, the same build, the same session, two camera distances:

    2.1 m portrait   stubble at 1.8-3.1x floor    the gate says ABSENT
    0.9 m portrait   stubble at 3.6-17x  floor    the gate says PRESENT

Both readings are correct. At 2.1 m the stubble genuinely is close to the
instrument's resolution, which is the cheap explanation the record had listed
and set aside as "NOT needed as an explanation" once the main-view mechanism
looked confirmed. It was needed. It is the explanation for the beard, and it is
why the gate now records its capture transform in every report and why a gate
verdict may never be carried from one framing to another.

### WHAT THIS COST AND WHAT IT BOUGHT

Ten hypotheses were eliminated over two days, and the elimination table was
sound — every row was true. Row 4, *"the capture path cannot draw grooms"*, was
retired on the evidence that beard and moustache DID draw through the same
SceneCapture. True, and it does not clear the row, because the two paths also
differed in how long the assets had been resident. **An elimination is only as
strong as the alternative it rules out, and a row retired on a confounded
comparison stays open whether or not anyone writes it down.**

No vendor groom asset was ever edited, `Hair_M_Layered` needed no fix, and the
`enable_global_interpolation` lead — five assets, a clean correlation, no
mechanism — is moot. That correlation was real and pointed nowhere: the two
hairs with the flag TRUE are also the two heaviest grooms, and heavier grooms
converge later.

### THE CONVERGENCE IS PER EDITOR SESSION, NOT PER SPAWN

Measured after the fact, and it matters operationally. Destroying the hero and
spawning him again in a WARM session converges immediately -- drift 0.5-3.7%
on the first pass, full values. The cost is paid once, when the groom assets
and bindings first become resident in that editor process. So:

    cold editor, first placement        REFUSES, drift 34-83%
    same editor, one run later          PASSES, drift 0.5-3.4%
    same editor, fresh respawn          PASSES immediately

That is why "it worked yesterday" and "it is bald today" could both be true of
the same build, and why the failure looked intermittent and asset-shaped.

### WHERE THE INSTRUMENT RUNS OUT, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED

Groom signal against the repeat floor, one character, one session, four
distances:

    distance   Hair    Eyebrows   Beard   Mustache   whole face (control)
    0.9 m      83x       16x      10.6x     3.3x        1,471,218 px
    1.1 m      51x        6.8x     5.6x     2.2x          817,605 px
    1.3 m      38x        5.6x     4.6x     2.2x          552,032 px
    6.2 m       2.5x      1.8x     1.9x     1.9x           10,120 px

At 6.2 m the ENTIRE FACE is ten thousand pixels, so nothing on it can be
resolved and the gate says so about all four. The moustache -- stubble on an
upper lip -- is the limiting groom and clears the bar only at 0.9 m. None of
this is a defect and all of it used to be invisible: the old checklist gate
returned DELIVERABLE at every one of these distances, because the component
properties are identical at all four.

**So the honest form of the deliverable claim is scoped:** the grooms are
verified present at 0.9 m on this placement, and the landscape framings are
DIAGNOSTIC with respect to grooms because their pixels cannot carry the claim
-- which is a statement about the camera, not about the hero.

## 2026-08-19 (night, later) — THE WARDROBE SWAP, AND THE THREE THINGS THAT MEASURED DIFFERENTLY FROM EXPECTATION

Ryan ruled the groom set against the reference: `WI_Hair_M_SideSweptFringe`,
`WI_Beard_S_Full`, `WI_Mustache_S_Full`, keeping `Eyebrows_M_Dense`. Applied
through the mapped add -> select -> propagate mechanism, re-assembled, gated in
pixels. Recipe values in **R-HEROGROOM**.

    groom      old set @1.1m              new set @1.1m           change
    Beard       9,393 px  mean|d| 29.6    25,951 px  mean|d| 66.5  2.8x area
    Hair       84,450 px  mean|d| 106.0  116,722 px  mean|d| 80.2  1.4x area
    Eyebrows   11,331 px                   9,503 px               DOWN
    Mustache    3,703 px  mean|d| 20.1     3,731 px  mean|d| 21.0  NOTHING

### 1. THE MOUSTACHE SWAP CHANGED NOTHING MEASURABLE, AND THE OBVIOUS EXPLANATION IS WRONG

The ruling anticipated that a FULL moustache would clear the presence bar
further out than stubble, retiring the 0.9 m framing caveat. **It did not.**
`Mustache_S_Full` reads 3,731 px at 1.1 m against `Mustache_M_Stubble`'s
3,703 px — the same footprint, the same mean delta, the same 2.2x floor, the
same ABSENT verdict.

The obvious explanation is occlusion: a difference render measures a groom's
MARGINAL contribution, so a dense beard sitting under and around the moustache
would suppress the reading without the moustache being any less drawn. **The
control refutes it.** Hiding the beard FIRST and then the moustache isolates
the moustache against bare skin:

    moustache marginal AGAINST BEARD   3,696 px
    moustache marginal AGAINST SKIN    3,739 px      ratio 1.01x

So the beard is not masking it. The moustache component genuinely contributes
~3,700 px at 1.1 m in both variants. **The visible fullness above the lip in
the new render is `Beard_S_Full`, which extends onto the upper lip — not the
moustache.** The caveat is NOT retired and the record says so.

**The general point is about the instrument, and it is worth keeping:** a
hidden/shown difference gate measures MARGINAL contribution, not
presence-in-the-world. Where grooms overlap, a fully-drawn groom can read small
because its neighbours cover the same pixels. The hide-the-neighbour-first
control is the discriminator, it costs two extra frames, and it should be
reached for whenever a groom reads low next to a dense neighbour.

### 2. "12 OF 12 WRITES RETURNED TRUE" AND EVERY READ-BACK WAS UNREADABLE

`groom_color.py` set melanin 0.92 / redness 0.28 / whiteness 0.0 across four
items. All twelve writes returned true. All twelve read-backs came back
**unreadable** — which is "I could not look", not "it worked", and this project
does not accept the first as the second.

Ryan called it in advance: *verify by render, not by assumption; a fresh
wardrobe item may not inherit the instance parameters.* The verification route
that settled it is neither the write nor the render statistic, but the ASSETS
THE RENDERER SAMPLES — the assembled `MI_WI_*` material instances, read for
their declared `scalar_parameter_values`:

    MI_WI_Hair_M_SideSweptFringe_Hair        hairMelanin 0.92  hairRedness 0.28
    MI_WI_Beard_S_Full_Hair                              0.92              0.28
    MI_WI_Mustache_S_Full_Hair                           0.92              0.28
    MI_WI_Eyebrows_M_Dense_None_1_Hair                   0.92              0.28

The colour carried to all four. **But a render statistic could not have told
us**, and I tried: sampling the difference-mask pixels gives "beard RGB
165/82/30", which is skin. A sparse groom's difference mask is mostly the SKIN
BETWEEN STRANDS, so a colour averaged over it measures the face. That is the
misleading-denominator class in a new costume, and the fix was to stop
measuring the render and go read the asset.

### 3. STALE MATERIAL INSTANCES SURVIVE AN ASSEMBLE, AND THEY ANSWER TO THE OBVIOUS NAME

`MI_WI_Hair_M_Layered_Hair` — the OLD hair's instance — is still on disk after
the re-assemble and declares **no scalar overrides at all**. So does
`MI_WI_Eyebrows_M_Dense_Hair`, while the live eyebrow instance is
`MI_WI_Eyebrows_M_Dense_None_1_Hair`, which carries the colour.

**The obvious name was the wrong asset.** Had the eyebrows been checked by
reading `MI_WI_Eyebrows_M_Dense_Hair` alone, the conclusion would have been
"the colour did not reach the eyebrows", from a file the build no longer uses.
Enumerate the variants; do not address an assembled asset by the name you
expect it to have.

### 4. THE ASSEMBLE HAZARD REPRODUCED, AND THE SAME-PAYLOAD SAVE IS WHY NOTHING WAS LOST

`build_meta_human` produced 103 dirty packages and the payload saved 101 of
them in the same call (the 2 failures are the known `T_PreBakedGroom_*` class).
**The very next remote call — a read-only dirty-package probe — returned exit
3, no verified node: the editor had stopped answering.** That is the third
recorded instance. The rule that the assemble and its save are ONE PAYLOAD was
written after 91 packages died with the process, and it just paid for itself
again.

## 2026-08-19 (overnight #2) — A GROOM MUST LIVE IN PROJECT CONTENT TO BIND. THAT IS THE WHOLE FORK.

**The design fork is resolved: a groom CAN reach a character outside the
wardrobe path, and the requirement is one `duplicate_asset` call.** Binding a
groom that lives in the VENDOR PLUGIN's content produces a binding that
assigns cleanly, reports every property correctly, and draws nothing. The same
groom DUPLICATED into project content, bound the same way, renders at 87x the
repeat floor.

    groom asset location                       binding renders?
    /MetaHumanCharacter/.../Hair_S_BuzzCut     NO   bald at 60s and 90s
    /Game/Hero/Unpacked/.../Hair_M_BobMessy    YES  126,709 px  72.7x
    /Game/Hero/Unpacked/.../Hair_S_Messy       YES   73,970 px  42.2x
    /Game/Hero/Grooms/Hair_BobMessy_Custom     YES  155,153 px  87.2x

The last row is the decisive one: a PLAIN DUPLICATE of the vendor asset, with
no assemble, no wardrobe selection and no conditioning of any kind. So it is
not the assemble that makes a groom bindable. It is where the asset lives.

### HOW IT WAS FOUND, AND THE READ THAT SAVED AN HOUR

Two hypotheses explained a bald render after a direct component write:
REASSERTION (the Blueprint puts its own groom back, so the write is discarded)
or RENDER FAILURE (the write holds and nothing draws). **One property read
after the game thread had been released separated them in twelve seconds** —
150,000 frames after the write the component still named our groom and our
binding, and the eyebrows still held theirs at `visible: true`. Reassertion
refuted; no Blueprint archaeology needed.

Then the field-by-field diff of a WORKING binding against a FAILING one, on
the same character and the same slot. Every exposed field identical —
`target_skeletal_mesh` the same face mesh, `source_skeletal_mesh` null on
BOTH, same binding type, same 100 interpolation points, same matching section
— **except the groom asset's path.** When two artefacts agree on everything
you thought mattered, the thing they disagree about is the answer, even when
it looks like bookkeeping.

### A DEFECT I FIXED THAT WAS NOT THE DEFECT

`create_new_groom_binding_asset_with_path` takes
`source_skeletal_mesh_for_transfer`, and I first passed None. Vendor grooms
are authored against `SKM_Groom_Head_Legacy01/02` and the vendor bindings
record source == target == Legacy01, so passing None looked exactly like the
bug: it asks the engine to treat roots authored elsewhere as already ours.
Passing the authoring head made it a proper RBF transfer — and the render
stayed bald.

**It was A defect and not THE defect, and the diff proved it retrospectively:
the working assembled binding has `source_skeletal_mesh` NULL as well.** A fix
that is locally correct, well-reasoned and does not move the symptom is
evidence about the hypothesis, not about the fix. Keeping it in place while
continuing to look is what let the diff be read cleanly afterwards.

### WHAT IT COSTS NOW

The per-hair cycle collapses from *wardrobe select -> assemble -> restart ->
place -> gate* at 10-12 minutes to *duplicate -> bind -> assign -> converge ->
gate* with no assemble and no editor restart. Binding is 0.3-9 s and scales
with asset SIZE, not curve count. Thirty-eight hairs moves from about seven
hours to roughly the length of the gating, which is the dominant term.

**And the invariant survives intact:** every groom still reaches a character
through a binding freshly built against THAT character's face mesh. The
vendor bindings target the archetype head and are proven garbage on ours. What
changed is only that the groom must be OURS before it can be bound — which is
the Fab-boundary rule arriving from an unexpected direction, as a hard
technical requirement rather than a licensing courtesy.

### CORRECTION, SAME NIGHT, ONE HOUR LATER — THE VERDICT ABOVE IS WRONG AND HERE IS HOW I BOUGHT IT

**The entry above concluded "a groom must live in project content to bind" and
locked it into `RECIPES.md`. The premise held; the conclusion did not. I had
GATED the renders and never LOOKED at them.**

The gate reported `Hair PRESENT, 155,153 px, 87.2x floor, drift 0.0%` on a
duplicated groom with my own binding. Every number was true. When I finally
opened the picture, the crown was **BALD** and the 155,153 pixels were a dark
clump of strands hanging at the jaw. Only strands far from the scalp draw;
the roots never attach. Two more grooms reproduce it exactly — `SweptUp` at
13.6k and `L_Straight` at 168k are the same defect at two amplitudes, one
reading as "absent" and one as "lots of hair".

The discriminating picture is the same groom under two bindings:

    Hair_M_BobMessy + the ASSEMBLE's binding      full hair on the scalp
    Hair_M_BobMessy + MY binding                  bald crown, clump at the jaw

and the two bindings are IDENTICAL in every exposed field — same groom, same
target mesh, `source_skeletal_mesh` null on both, same type, same 100
interpolation points, same matching section. **Same parameters, different
result, so the difference is in the BUILDING, not in the asset.** The
inference — not established — is that the MetaHuman assemble conditions the
groom, re-projecting roots onto the target scalp, and
`create_new_groom_binding_asset_with_path` does not.

**WHAT I ACTUALLY DID WRONG, and it is not "I was unlucky".** I built an
instrument whose entire purpose is that *a component can be present, bound,
visible and drawing nothing*, and then I trusted its PRESENCE verdict as a
CORRECTNESS verdict. Those are different questions. `groom_presence.py`
answers "does hiding this change the picture" — it is blind to whether the
picture is RIGHT, and it says so in its own docstring. A bald crown with a
clump at the jaw changes the picture enormously.

**The rule this buys, and it generalises past grooms:** a gate certifies the
property it measures and NOTHING ADJACENT. Presence is not correctness,
stability is not completeness, and a read-back is not a render. Every one of
those three has now cost this project a wrong committed conclusion, in three
different subsystems, in one week.

The cheapest possible guard was available the whole time and I skipped it
because the number was large and agreed with my hypothesis: **open the
picture.** Non-negotiable 10 exists for this and is a decade older than my
enthusiasm.

**What survives from the entry above:** vendor-content grooms genuinely do not
bind (bald at 60 s and 90 s, no clump, nothing); vendor bindings genuinely do
render exploded on our head; the reassertion hypothesis is genuinely refuted
by the 150,000-frame property read. What does NOT survive is that a project
duplicate plus a hand-built binding is a working route. It is not.

### AND THE ROOT CAUSE IN THAT CORRECTION IS ALSO WRONG. THE THIRD ANSWER IS THE BORING ONE.

The correction above says the difference is "in the BUILDING, not in the
asset" and infers that the MetaHuman assemble conditions the groom by
re-projecting roots. **That inference is withdrawn.** The advisor asked one
question I had not: *have you established that your binding ever BUILT?*

It had not. For every binding I created, without exception, the engine says so
in its own log:

    LogHairStrands: Display: Waiting for groom bindings to be ready 0/1
        (BND_AlpineHero_Hair_S_BuzzCut) ...      (BND_unpacked_Hair_S_Messy) ...
        (BND_AlpineHero_Hair_S_SlickBack) ...    (BND_dup_BobMessy_Custom) ...
        (BND_AlpineHero_Hair_M_TwistedBraids)    (BND_AlpineHero_SweptUp_v1) ...
        (BND2_AlpineHero_Hair_S_BuzzCut) ...     (BND_AlpineHero_LStraight_v1) ...

**0 of 1 ready, eight times, with no later line saying otherwise and no error
at all.** Held four minutes and re-rendered: the same bald crown to the pixel,
so it is not "wait longer" either.

`create_new_groom_binding_asset_with_path` CREATES the asset — it exists, it
saves, every property reads back correctly — and its BUILD NEVER COMPLETES.
The strands that draw are the free-hanging ends, which need no root
attachment. The crown is bald because the roots have nothing to attach to.

**Three root causes in one night, each replacing the last, and they rank in
order of how flattering they were to me.** "Vendor content cannot bind" was
tidy. "The assemble does conditioning we cannot replicate" was an interesting
architectural discovery. "The build never finished and I did not read the log"
is boring, and it is the true one. I wrote the interesting one into LESSONS
before anyone asked the boring question.

**AND I DID READ A LOG — THE WRONG ONE.** `LandscapeLab.log` has been stale
since the last editor restart; the live session writes `LandscapeLab_2.log`. I
grepped the stale file, found nothing, and treated that silence as evidence.
This project's rule that a diagnostic must distinguish *I looked and it is
absent* from *I could not look* applies to the ENGINE'S log exactly as it
applies to our own instruments — and the engine had been naming the problem in
plain English through all eight failures.

**Operationally, from now on:** confirm which log file is being written before
reading silence out of one, and grep `LogHairStrands` after every binding
creation. Whether the build can be forced to complete is UNKNOWN and is the
first question for a future session; the route that works today remains
wardrobe select then assemble.

### THE PRE-ASSEMBLE RESTART IS NOT OPTIONAL, AND I PROVED IT BY DROPPING IT

Four assembles tonight followed the recorded sequence — restart the editor,
run nothing, assemble at maximum headroom — and all four completed in about
three minutes. On the fifth I dropped the restart to save four minutes per
catalogue hair, running `apply_grooms` and `groom_color` (each of which
performs an `assemble_for_preview`) in the same session first.

    working set   20.43 GB        free RAM   1.73 GB
    CPU           +2.5 s over the sampling interval
    responding    False           output packages   none

That is the spin this project has recorded twice before, and pipeline rule 5
— *heavy operations run one at a time and log available RAM first* — exists
precisely for it. **I did not log available RAM before the assemble.** The
rule was written down, I have quoted it in a commit message this week, and I
skipped it while optimising a loop.

Cost: one dead editor, 105 unsaved packages, and about ten minutes — cheaper
than the four minutes per hair it was trying to save, only because it failed
on the second hair rather than the twentieth.

**The general shape, which is the part worth keeping:** an optimisation that
removes a step whose PURPOSE is headroom does not fail where it is applied. It
fails later, on the input that happens to need the headroom, and it fails as a
hang rather than as an error. The saved four minutes are visible immediately;
the cost arrives detached from its cause.

### A WARDROBE ITEM HOLDS A *BINDING*, NOT A GROOM — AND IT IS REPOINTABLE FROM PYTHON

Probed while looking for a way to get a custom groom onto a character without
the direct-assignment route that failed. Two facts, both from the asset:

**1. `MetaHumanWardrobeItem` exposes almost nothing.** Its entire reflected
surface is `principal_asset`, `thumbnail_info`, `thumbnail_image` and
`thumbnail_name`. There is no `groom`, no `groom_asset`, no `slot_name`, no
`tags` — every name worth guessing was guessed and every one is ABSENT.

**2. `principal_asset` points at the BINDING, not at the groom.**

    WI_Hair_S_Messy.principal_asset.asset
        -> /MetaHumanCharacter/.../Hair_S_Messy_Binding

That reframes the whole pipeline. A wardrobe item does not carry hair; it
carries a groom ALREADY BOUND to the archetype head, and the assemble's job is
to rebuild that binding against the specific character's face. Which is
exactly why hand-built per-character bindings were the wrong lever — the
engine expects to do that step itself, from an archetype-bound input.

**And the repoint is reachable.** `principal_asset` is an
`EditorOnlyAssetReference` struct whose `asset` field is read-write, so:

    ref = wi.get_editor_property("principal_asset")   # a COPY
    ref.set_editor_property("asset", our_binding)
    wi.set_editor_property("principal_asset", ref)    # WRITE IT BACK

Verified by re-reading off a reloaded asset after save, not off the copy that
was just edited — this project has already paid once for a struct read out of
an array being a copy, where a body-parameter write looked exactly like a
permanent lock until a positive control was put in the same run.

**The design that falls out:** to ingest a custom groom, build a binding of it
against `SKM_Groom_Head_Legacy01` (the archetype every vendor groom is
authored against), duplicate a wardrobe item, repoint it at that binding, and
let the ASSEMBLE do the per-character rebuild. Our archetype binding does not
need to render — it is an input to the assemble, not an output.

Whether that actually produces correct hair is the test running now; the
structural facts above hold either way.

### THE WARDROBE ROUTE FAILS FOR CUSTOM GROOMS TOO, AND IT IS THE SAME DEFECT UNDERNEATH

The advisor's ingest design was: import the groom to project content, build a
binding against the ARCHETYPE head, duplicate a wardrobe item, repoint it at
that binding, wardrobe select, assemble, and let the engine rebuild the
per-character binding itself. Every step reported success:

    archetype binding      created and saved
    wardrobe item          duplicated into project content
    repoint                read back, and survived a save + reload
    Hair slot selection    applied, propagated, verified PRESENT
    assemble               88 packages, 86 saved, no error

**And the assembled character has NO HAIR AT ALL.** Not a bald crown this
time — the Blueprint's Hair component carries no groom asset whatsoever, and
the render is a completely bald head with the beard and brows intact.

**So both routes are blocked by the same thing.** The direct route needs a
per-character binding; the wardrobe route needs an archetype binding to hand
the assemble. Both come from
`create_new_groom_binding_asset_with_path`, whose build never completes. The
wardrobe route works for VENDOR items for one reason only: their bindings ship
already built.

    vendor wardrobe item   -> pre-built binding  -> assemble -> CORRECT HAIR
    minted wardrobe item   -> our binding        -> assemble -> NO HAIR

**THE REAL BLOCKER IS ONE CALL, AND EVERYTHING ELSE WAS DOWNSTREAM OF IT.**
Three designs were tried tonight and all three failed at the same place, two
of them wearing convincing disguises — "vendor content cannot bind", "the
assemble conditions the groom". The wardrobe experiment was worth running
precisely because it failed DIFFERENTLY: a bald crown and an absent component
are different symptoms, and getting the second one is what proved the first
was not about direct assignment at all.

**What a future session should do first, and it is a single question:** can a
groom binding build be forced to completion from Python? Candidates never
tried — a rebuild/build entry point on the asset, a save-and-reload cycle, an
editor-side "Rebuild Bindings" action, or building the binding through the
MetaHuman subsystem rather than `GroomLibrary`. Until that is answered, custom
groom ingest is BLOCKED and the stock wardrobe is the only source of hair for
any character in this project.

**Nothing about the tooling is wasted.** `ingest_groom.py`'s duplicate,
colour, provenance and registry machinery all work and are character-agnostic;
the wardrobe minting works and is now understood. They are waiting on one
engine call, and the moment it answers they are a pipeline.

### THE EYE COLOUR WAS NOT MEASURED, AND THE FIRST NUMBER I GOT WAS OF A CHEEK

Attempted the parked eye-colour verification on the final gated portrait.
First crop returned a confident `27.3 / 3.1 / 0.7` against a reference iris of
`26 / 20 / 17` — close on red, wildly off on green and blue, which would have
read as "the tint half-applied". **The crop was of his cheek and beard.** I
had guessed the eye's coordinates instead of finding them.

Located the eye properly with a coordinate grid over the frame, re-cropped,
and looked: at this sun angle the eye socket is in deep shadow and the darkest
8% of pixels are exactly `0.0 / 0.0 / 0.0`. **There is no iris value in this
render to measure.**

So the honest output is *I could not look*, not a number. Recording the
cheek reading would have been worse than recording nothing, because it was
plausible: a red-ish dark value near a dark reference is exactly what a
half-applied tint would produce.

**What it needs:** a render with the eye LIT — the flat instrument rig from
R-HEROCAP, or a different sun angle. The measurement is cheap once the subject
is lit; it is impossible while the subject is in shadow, and no amount of
statistics on the shadowed pixels will change that.

## 2026-08-20 — THE BINDING MECHANISM, READ OUT OF THE ENGINE, AND WHY IT IS STILL BLOCKED

Two-hour timebox on one question: **can a groom binding build be forced to
complete from Python?** Answer: **the path is now fully known and it cannot be
driven from remote Python today.** Four things were established and two of my
earlier root causes died.

### 1. THE ASSEMBLE NEVER CREATES A BINDING. IT DUPLICATES A BUILT ONE.

From `MetaHumanDefaultEditorPipeline/Private/Item/MetaHumanGroomEditorPipeline.cpp`:

    CharacterBinding = DuplicateObject<UGroomBindingAsset>(VendorBinding)
    CharacterBinding->SetTargetSkeletalMesh(OurFaceMesh)
    NewGroom = DuplicateObject<UGroomAsset>(VendorBinding->GetGroom())
    ... duplicate cards and mesh descriptions, strip decimation ...
    FGroomRBFDeformer().GetRBFDeformedGroomAsset(       // BAKE the deformation
        CharacterBinding->GetGroom(), CharacterBinding, nullptr, 0.0f,
        NewGroom, TargetPlatform)
    CharacterBinding->SetGroom(NewGroom)
    CharacterBinding->SetSourceSkeletalMesh(nullptr)
    CharacterBinding->Build()

**`create_new_groom_binding_asset_with_path` is simply not the call the
pipeline uses.** I spent a night driving an API that was never the one. It
exists, it is reflected, it succeeds, and it produces something the renderer
treats as unbuilt — a fresh build and a retargeted duplicate of an
already-built binding are different operations with the same-looking output.

### 2. "THE BUILD NEVER COMPLETES" IS ALSO WRONG — I FORCED IT AND NOTHING CHANGED

The engine registers a standard async-compilation cvar set for this asset type
(`AsyncCompilationHelpers::FAsyncCompilationStandardCVars`, AssetType
`GroomBinding`), so all of these exist and are console-reachable:

    Editor.AsyncGroomBindingCompilation            0 disables async entirely
    Editor.AsyncGroomBindingCompilationFinishAll   blocks until all are done
    Editor.AsyncGroomBindingCompilationMaxConcurrency
    Editor.AsyncGroomBindingCompilationResume

Set to 0, created a binding: **no "Waiting for groom bindings to be ready"
line at all**, asset saved and validated clean — and the render was still
`SCALP-BALD, crown 1%`. So the waiting message was a SYMPTOM of using the
wrong call, not the cause of the bad render. Root cause #3 dies here.

**That is three wrong root causes in two days, each replaced by measurement:**
vendor-content, then assemble-conditioning, then build-never-finishes. Every
one of them was a real observation attached to the wrong mechanism.

### 3. `GroomBindingAsset.build()` IS REFLECTED, AND IT KILLS THE EDITOR

    build(completion_delegate: OnGroomBindingAssetBuildComplete) -> None

Called from remote Python it fataled the editor:

    Assertion failed: IsUnlocked() [BulkData.cpp:596]

A bulk-data lock — the same class as `request_auto_rigging(blocking=True)` and
`conform_to_target_meshes`, both of which took this editor down from the same
place. **Three MetaHuman/groom entry points now share one failure mode:
driving them synchronously from remote Python.** That is a property of the
transport, not of any one API.

### 4. THE RETARGET ALONE IS NOT ENOUGH

Duplicated the vendor binding, retargeted to our face mesh, cleared the source
mesh, saved, assigned — and skipped the crashing `Build()`. Render:
`SCALP-BALD, crown 1%`, drift 0.2%. The `Build()` is load-bearing, and it is
the step that cannot currently be reached.

### WHAT THIS MEANS

The question is ANSWERED and the answer is not the one that unblocks tonight:
**a groom binding CAN be built correctly, by the recipe above, and that recipe
cannot be executed from remote Python because its final call crashes the
editor.** Custom groom ingest is therefore an ATTENDED operation or needs a
different driving mechanism — a C++ helper in `LandscapeLabEditor` (this
project already has a plugin and has added `UFUNCTION`s to it before), or
Movie-Render-Queue-style deferred execution, or the editor UI.

**The C++ route is the obvious one and it is cheap:** the plugin exists, the
recipe is nine lines, and a `UFUNCTION` wrapping it would run on the game
thread in the editor's own context rather than through the transport that
keeps asserting.

### AND IT WORKS. THE FOURTH ANSWER WAS THE PIPELINE'S OWN FOUR STEPS, IN ORDER.

`ULandscapeLabTools::BuildGroomBindingForMesh` — a `UFUNCTION` in this
project's own editor plugin — now puts an arbitrary groom on an arbitrary
character's face, from a script, in **15 seconds**:

    Hair  215,647 px  139.7x floor  crown 35%  drift 0.4%   PRESENT
    (was)               83x floor   crown  1%               SCALP-BALD

`_verify/20260820_bindfix/before_after_rbf.png` is the pair: a bald head with
a clump at the jaw, and a full head of hair.

**The recipe is the assemble's, executed in its own order, and every one of
the four steps is load-bearing — measured by leaving each out:**

    1  DUPLICATE an already-built binding     omit -> bald crown, crown 1%
       (never create one from scratch)
    2  SetTargetSkeletalMesh, then Build()    omit -> bald crown, crown 1%
    3  BAKE the RBF deformation into a        omit -> bald crown, crown 1%
       DUPLICATED groom
    4  STRIP DECIMATION around the bake       omit -> 3,353 px, crown 43%
                                                      (right place, no hair)

Step 4 is the one that would have been skipped by anyone reading the pipeline
quickly — it looks like housekeeping. The engine's own comment says why:
*"The RBF deformer doesn't support decimation in the interpolation data, so we
need to remove any decimation first and then restore it afterwards."* Omitting
it produced hair in the CORRECT PLACE and almost none of it, which is a
completely different symptom from the other three failures and is what
pointed at the right line.

**WHY IT HAD TO BE C++.** `GroomBindingAsset.build()` is reflected and fatals
the editor from remote Python (`Assertion failed: IsUnlocked()
[BulkData.cpp:596]`); `FGroomRBFDeformer` is not reflected at all. Both run
fine on the game thread inside the module. **The plugin was already there** —
this project built it in August to reach `ALandscapeProxy::Import`, and the
same argument applied unchanged: when the engine does not expose the call, the
smallest honest fix is a `UFUNCTION`, not a cleverer script.

### THE SHAPE OF THE WHOLE INVESTIGATION

Four root causes over three days, each replacing the last, and the order is
not random — they went from most flattering to least:

    1  "vendor content cannot bind"              tidy
    2  "the assemble conditions the groom"       an architectural discovery
    3  "the build never completes"               a subtle async bug
    4  "I was calling the wrong function"        boring, and true

Every one of the first three was a REAL OBSERVATION attached to the wrong
mechanism. The thing that ended it was reading the engine's own pipeline
source instead of theorising about its behaviour — twenty minutes that were
available on day one.

**And the gate is what made the last step legible.** `crown 1%` versus
`crown 35%` separated four failure modes that all reported PRESENT with large
pixel counts. Without it, step 4's distinctive symptom — right place, no hair
— would have looked like just another bald render.

## 2026-08-20 — THE CATALOGUE RAN, AND IT DIRTIED CONTENT IT MUST NEVER WRITE

The 38-hair catalogue completed: 36 styles bound, rendered and gated, every
one PRESENT, crowns spread 0.25 to 0.97 and pixel counts 13k to 297k. That
spread is the point — a buzz cut at crown 93% and long straight bangs at
crown 25% are both correct, and a catalogue where every row looked alike
would be one measurement repeated 36 times.

### THE FINDING THAT MATTERED WAS NOT IN THE CATALOGUE

Before recycling the editor I asked for the dirty package list, out of
habit rather than suspicion. **48 packages, and all 48 were vendor content**
under `/MetaHumanCharacter/Optional` — the source grooms' own cards and
helmet static meshes, one set per style I had bound.

The cause is one line of my own C++ and one comment beside it. `DuplicateObject`
on a `UGroomAsset` does not deep-copy the cards static meshes; the duplicate
references the vendor's. The cards `PostEditChangeProperty` then rebuilds
them — in the vendor package.

**The comment above that call said the opposite.** I wrote it, from the
engine pipeline's structure rather than from a measurement, and it read as
settled: *"the deformed groom does not share static meshes with the vendor
asset."* It was false the whole time and nothing re-checked it, because a
comment is not a gate.

### NOTHING WAS DAMAGED, AND THAT IS LUCK WEARING PROCEDURE'S CLOTHES

The packages were dirty in MEMORY. On disk all 1,387 vendor groom uassets
still carry their 2026-08-15 install mtime. They survived because every
editor close in this run happened to be a discard — and the last one was a
FORCE KILL after `CloseMainWindow` timed out, which is normally the outcome
you apologise for. Here it is the correct one: a force-kill writes nothing.

Had any of those closes been clean, the editor would have offered to save,
and a `Save All` would have written engine plugin content in Program Files —
breaking the never-edit-vendor-content floor and standing rule 1 in a single
click, silently, with every render still correct and every gate still green.

**The general shape: a safety floor held by nothing but the accident of how
the process ended.** The floor is now written into the recipe as a posture —
discard on every close while that call is in the code — instead of being
implied by what happened to work.

### THE MEASUREMENT THAT NEARLY LIED, AND THE ONE THAT SETTLED IT

Checking disk, I ran `find -newermt 2026-08-01` and got back the entire
vendor tree. For a moment that reads as "everything was rewritten". It is
meaningless: the install date is 2026-08-15, so every file is newer than any
August cutoff. The instrument could not have produced a negative result.

What settled it was a HISTOGRAM: 1,387 files, one distinct date. A cutoff
test asks a question whose answer I had already fixed by choosing the cutoff;
the histogram asks the artefact what dates it actually has. Same directory,
same command family, and only one of them is evidence.

I annotated the useless output with "(none above = nothing written since
Aug 1)" in the same breath as printing twenty files. The annotation was
wrong on its face and the listing directly beneath it disproved it.

### TWO STYLES OF THIRTY-EIGHT HAVE NO BINDING, AND CONVENTION HID IT

`Hair_M_TwistedBraids` and `Hair_S_BrushCut` failed to bind twice before I
stopped retrying and listed the directory. The pack ships 38 grooms and 36
bindings; those two have no `<name>_Binding` sibling, so a recipe that
duplicates an already-built binding has no input for them.

My hair list came from the wardrobe item names and assumed the binding names
followed. **Names come from the asset, never from convention** — this project
has that rule written down, and it still cost two failed runs before I opened
the folder. The catalogue records them as `NO VENDOR BINDING` with the 38-vs-36
count attached, because a missing input and a failed bind are different facts
and a catalogue that blurred them would read as 36 successes and 2 defects.

### WHAT THE PATTERN ACROSS TODAY LOOKS LIKE

Three of the four things worth recording came from asking a question nobody
had asked yet, on state that was already green: the dirty list, the directory
listing, the mtime histogram. None came from a failure. The catalogue itself —
the deliverable — produced no findings at all; it just worked.

### THE CATALOGUE PASSED ITS GATE AND HALF OF IT IS UNUSABLE

Then I opened the contact sheet, which is the step I have skipped before and
paid for before. Thirty-six tiles, every one marked PRESENT in green. Twenty
of them are a bald head.

The measurement that settles it uses the gate's OWN control frame — crown
luminance with the groom shown against the same frame with only the groom
hidden:

    Hair_M_BobCurly         7.2 -> 58.2   delta -51.0    reads as hair
    Hair_S_Pixie           18.6 -> 58.2   delta -39.6    reads as hair
    Hair_S_BuzzCut         58.0 -> 58.2   delta  -0.2    does not read
    Hair_M_Mohawk          57.9 -> 58.2   delta  -0.2    does not read
    Hair_S_BaldingStubble  58.2 -> 58.2   delta   0.0    the control

`BaldingStubble` is the control the run handed me for free: a balding style
contributes nothing at the crown by construction, and it measures exactly
zero. Twenty styles sit within four luminance units of it.

**The gate is not wrong and that is the whole lesson.** BuzzCut really did
change 27,994 pixels, reproducibly, above floor. A change of two tenths of a
luminance unit spread over a large area produces tens of thousands of
"changed" pixels. PRESENT has always meant *pixels changed where hair should
be*. It has never meant *a person can see a hairstyle*, and I read it as the
second because the deliverable was a thing to look at.

This is the same shape as the vendor-dirty finding an hour earlier and as the
bald-crown retraction two days before: **a gate certifies the property it
measures and nothing adjacent.** I keep re-deriving that from a new direction
rather than applying it, and the tell each time is that I let the green
verdict stand in for the artefact.

### AND THE METRIC I ADDED TO FIX THE LAST GATE INVERTED

`crown_frac` exists because a wrong bind produced hair clumped at the jaw
with a bald crown, and it caught that. It is not a quality signal:

    Spearman(crown_frac, changed_px)   -0.314
    crown >= 0.90    20 styles   median  57,590 px
    crown <  0.90    16 styles   median 108,181 px

A style with real hair covers the whole silhouette including the sides, so
its crown FRACTION falls — BobCurly 0.57, StraightBangs 0.25. A style whose
only contribution is a faint wash over the lit scalp scores 0.97. **The
highest crown scores in the table belong to the styles you cannot see.**

A fraction is a ratio, and a ratio computed over a nearly-empty numerator
tells you about the shape of the noise. The fix is not a better threshold on
crown_frac; it is that "is this hair visible" is a different question from
"is this hair where hair goes", and it needs its own instrument — the
hair-hidden luminance delta above, which was already being captured and which
nothing was reading.

**What is NOT established:** whether those twenty short styles render
correctly-but-subtly or fail to render. A buzz cut genuinely is close to the
scalp. The measurement says only that this camera at this exposure cannot
discriminate them, and saying more than that would be the same error again.

### AND THE TWENTY BALD STYLES WERE MY FRAMING, ANSWERED WITHIN THE HOUR

I wrote "NOT ESTABLISHED" about whether the short styles render, which was
the right thing to write and the wrong thing to leave. One macro render
settled it:

    Hair_S_BuzzCut   27,994 px at dist 110  ->  231,763 px at dist 45
                     crown luma delta -0.2  ->  -13.0

The frame shows individual strands and a correct hairline. Cornrows shows
braided rows with partings, visibly different from BuzzCut — which is the
claim worth having: not "hair renders" but "these render as themselves".

**The defect was one hardcoded number.** `catalogue_run.py` pinned
`--dist 110 --fov 26`. Long hair needs that distance to fit in frame; at that
distance a 5 mm strand is sub-pixel against a dark forest. **One framing
cannot serve styles whose scale differs by an order of magnitude**, and the
catalogue silently assumed it could.

The hardcoding had a second effect I nearly missed. Because the runner
respawns, it overwrote a macro rig I had set up in a separate call — and the
tell was that the "macro" run returned 27,991 px against the wide run's
27,994. **Two numbers agreeing to four significant figures after I changed
the camera by a factor of two is not a reassuring result, it is a report that
the change did not happen.** I have been trained by this project to distrust
disagreement; near-identity across a variable that should move things is the
same signal wearing the opposite face.

Re-run at dist 60 every short style gains 5-8x its pixels, and `crown_frac`
falls from 0.93-0.97 to 0.61-0.88 — the inversion reversing itself once the
hair resolves and covers the sides, which is the analysis confirming itself
on data it did not have when it was written.

**What I got wrong and what I got right, stated separately because they are
different mistakes.** Right: refusing to claim the twenty were broken. Wrong:
building a documentation artefact whose single implicit parameter I never
questioned, and then reading its output as a fact about the assets. The
gate's PRESENT was correct at every step; my catalogue was the instrument
that could not look.

## 2026-08-21 — THE BLENDER ROUND TRIP CLOSES EXCEPT FOR WHERE THE HAIR LANDS

Blender authors a groom, an .abc leaves headlessly, UE imports it as a real
GroomAsset, it binds to the hero's face and it RENDERS. Every mechanical link
works. The strands land in the wrong place.

### THE EXPORT WAS NEVER THE HARD PART, AND THE BRIEF EXPECTED IT TO BE

The fallback plan allowed for GroomExporter being UI-bound and needing a
ten-second attended click. It is fully scriptable. Two preconditions had to be
read out of the add-on's source, and both fail like a broken add-on:

    node_execution=True   AlembicGroomExporter.execute gates
                          export_preparation() on it, and that is what
                          SELECTS the objects. With False the exporter sees
                          an empty selection and dies on curvesObjects[0].
    no --factory-startup  the add-on installs via user Preferences

`GetCurvesObjects(context)` reads `context.selected_objects`. Background mode
has no selection. **The UI was supplying a precondition by hand, and the
failure looked like an add-on defect rather than a missing argument.**

That also turned out to be the variant filter: the demo file authors one
export configuration per style as a node group, so naming the group excludes
every other style. The filter lives in the .blend rather than in a list here,
and therefore cannot drift out of step with it.

### THREE FACTORIES, AND THE ONE NAMED FOR THE JOB IS NOT THE ONE

    GroomFactory        declares NO formats -- create-new, not import
    Interchange         no .abc translator in this install
    HairStrandsFactory  "abc;Alembic hair strands file", supports GroomAsset

I picked `GroomFactory` first because a groom importer should be called that.
Both wrong routes returned instantly from Python with the reason only in the
editor log -- "Unknown extension 'abc'", then "Try enabling the [abc]
extension for Interchange", which is a generic message that interpolates the
extension and does NOT mean such a setting exists. **A factory's `formats`
list is one query away and decides the question that the name only suggests.**

Curve count then verified against a source that is not the exporter: Blender's
own depsgraph says 31,570 evaluated curves, UE reports 31,267. 0.96%.

### A FALLBACK I WROTE SILENTLY SUBSTITUTED SOMEBODY ELSE'S ASSET

When the named destination did not exist, my import payload resolved the
imported groom "by TYPE" — it scanned the directory for a GroomAsset. After a
FAILED import it found an unrelated pre-existing groom from earlier work and
reported ITS 75,005 curves as the import's result.

Only the curve-count check caught it, and it caught it by a factor of 2.4.
The fix is to snapshot the directory BEFORE the import and consider only NEW
assets, and to refuse rather than choose when more than one appears. **A
fallback that searches by type will eventually find something, and finding
something is not the same as finding the thing.**

### THE BLOCKER, AND THE CONTROL THAT LOCATED IT

R-GROOMBIND3 binds a stock hair by DUPLICATING an already-built vendor
binding and RBF-baking the groom onto our face. It works on all 36 stock
hairs. Given an OverrideGroom parameter so the cargo can be a custom .abc
groom, it builds, retains all 31,267 curves, assigns, and seats them wrongly.

Single variable, the donor binding:

    donor Hair_L_Straight   85,107 px at 52.6x floor, crown 10%
                            -- a clump of strands hanging over one eye,
                               bald crown
    donor Hair_S_BuzzCut    completely bald, no visible hair
    the two renders differ over 10.3% of the frame

**The donor alone decides whether and where a custom groom's strands land.**
That is the finding. The duplicated binding carries per-strand root
correspondence belonging to the DONOR's groom, which has a different curve
count and a different root set from mine, and the RBF bake displaces my
strands through it. Duplicating a donor is correct for a stock groom, whose
binding already matches it, and structurally wrong for a custom one.

**The gate said PRESENT at 52.6x the floor for the bad one.** Present, real,
reproducible, and hanging over an eye. This is the third time this week that
a green verdict has described a property adjacent to the one that mattered,
and the render settled it in one look each time.

### WHAT MAKES THIS CHEAP TO FINISH

The demo file's groom is authored on a mesh with **24,049 vertices** -- the
MetaHuman archetype head LOD0 count this project already knows. So the custom
groom's roots are plausibly already in archetype space, and what it needs may
not be an RBF re-bake at all but a binding built with the archetype as SOURCE
and our fitted face as TARGET.

### THE ADVISOR'S ZERO-COST DIAGNOSTIC COULD NOT DISCRIMINATE, AND THAT IS ITS RESULT

The advisor ruled one attempt more, conditional on a free test first: assign
the custom groom with NO binding and render. Coherent strands roughly on the
scalp would confirm archetype-space roots and justify the rebuild; a
displaced clump nowhere near the head would kill it.

**The render is completely bald.** Neither branch.

An unbound groom on a MetaHuman GroomComponent draws nothing at all, which
this project already half-knew from the sessions where bindings WERE the
investigation. So the test's premise -- that an unbound groom renders in its
rest space -- does not hold on this component, and the outcome carries no
information about the groom's rest space.

**That is "I could not look", not "I looked and the groom is wrong."** The
distinction is the whole of non-negotiable 6 and it is what stops this from
becoming a third wrong root cause. The diagnostic was well-designed and the
component does not support it; recording the design and its inapplicability
is worth more than a verdict extracted from it.

**PARKED at two attempts, per the brief**, with the donor control as the
evidence and a named morning fix: construct a FRESH binding with
SourceSkeletalMesh set to the ARCHETYPE head and TargetSkeletalMesh to the
fitted face, and drop the RBF re-bake for that path -- with a correctly
sourced binding, Build() owns the deformation and baking on top would deform
twice. That is a bounded C++ change plus one rebuild.

## 2026-08-21 — THE FRESH-BINDING FIX: FOUR REAL DEFECTS FOUND, THE HAIR STILL DOES NOT LAND

The advisor-ruled fix was built: construct a binding from scratch with
`FHairStrandsCore::CreateGroomBindingAsset`, source = the head the groom was
authored on, target = the fitted face. It works as an object and does not
work as a fix, and the four things found on the way are worth more than the
outcome.

### 1. `Build()` IS ASYNCHRONOUS AND RETURNING IS NOT FINISHING

The first fresh binding built in **0.01 seconds** for a 31,267-strand groom,
and the package was saved before the compile finished — so the binding
carried no transfer data at all.

**The tell was not the duration, it was that the result did not move when
its input did.** Two different source meshes produced pixel-identical
renders. A number that survives a change to its own input was never
computed. `FGroomBindingCompilingManager::Get().FinishCompilation({...})`
takes it to 0.39 s.

R-GROOMBIND3 never hit this because it bakes into the GROOM, so its
placement never depended on the binding's async build.

### 2. THE COMPONENT REFUSES A BINDING THAT STILL NAMES A SOURCE MESH

`set_binding_asset` read back **null** every time, with no error anywhere.
Diffing the fresh binding against a working one field by field left exactly
one difference: `source_skeletal_mesh` set versus `None`. Clearing it made
the component accept the binding immediately.

R-GROOMBIND3 ends with `SetSourceSkeletalMesh(nullptr)` and I had read that
as tidying up. It is load-bearing.

### 3. THE BINDING DOES NOT REPOSITION THE GROOM HERE — MEASURED

Three bindings — identity source, real source async, real source
synchronous — produced the same picture:

    identity vs sync      mean 0.0687   px>8      9,500   (0.2% of frame)
    identity vs srchead   mean 2.0739   px>8    263,480   (6.3%)
    srchead  vs sync      mean 2.0746   px>8    263,564   (6.3%)

and 6.3% sits inside this scene's own frame-to-frame instability band. So
none of it is signal. **A groom whose placement does not change when its
binding changes is a groom whose placement the binding is not driving.**

That is the structural finding, and it retroactively explains why
R-GROOMBIND3 has to bake: baking is the only thing in this setup that moves
strands. Adding the bake on top of the fresh binding made the hair vanish
entirely, so the correct correspondence plus the working mechanism is still
not the answer.

### 4. THE TWO HEADS ARE NOT RELATED BY ANY RIGID TRANSFORM

This is the one that decides what to do next, and it kills the obvious
shortcut before anyone spends a day on it.

    demo head (Blender)   Z 118.16 .. 151.18   height 33.02   width 28.68
    our archetype face    Z 140.88 .. 178.44   height 37.56   width 38.10

    height ratio  37.56 / 33.02 = 1.1375
    width  ratio  38.10 / 28.68 = 1.3285

**Same 24,049-vertex topology, genuinely different proportions.** A
translate-and-scale cannot map one onto the other, so "just fix the groom's
space at export" is not available. The demo file's head is the exporter
author's own character, not the archetype, despite the matching vertex
count — and the vertex count is what made it look like the archetype for
most of a day.

The hair renders at roughly Z 131..155 on a 178 cm character, which is the
collarbone, and which is exactly where the groom's roots were authored. It
has never moved at all.

### WHAT THIS POINTS AT

Not a better binding. **Author the groom in Blender on OUR hero's head**,
exported from UE, so the roots are in the target's space from the start.
Then the binding has nothing to reconcile and the vendor route already
works. The round trip proved out tonight makes that a one-way trip in the
other direction: UE face mesh -> Blender -> author -> .abc -> UE.

**Stated plainly: the seating problem is NOT fixed.** Four variants, four
renders, none of them hair on a head.

---

## 2026-08-21 — OUR HERO'S HEAD IS IN BLENDER, IN HIS OWN SPACE, VERIFIED

The conclusion from the fresh-binding attempt was that no binding rescues a
groom authored on a foreign head, because that head and ours differ in
proportion and not merely in placement. So the head went the other way.

    UE export      SKM_MHC_AlpineHero_FaceMesh -> FBX, 3.1 MB
    UE bounds      Z 140.878 .. 178.439
    Blender        Z 140.878 .. 178.437      difference 0.002 cm
    UV map         DiffuseUV, found and wired to the hair surface

`hero/blender/AlpineHero_GroomAuthoring.blend` holds that head plus an empty
hair Curves object parented and surfaced to it, so authored roots attach to
OUR mesh from the first stroke.

### THE UNIT CONVENTION WAS MEASURED, AND BOTH GUESSES WERE WRONG

The builder refuses if the head does not arrive where UE said it was, and it
refused twice before it passed:

    scale_length 1.00 (default), global_scale 1.0   ->     1.409 ..     1.784
    scale_length 0.01,           global_scale 100   -> 14087.8   .. 17843.7
    scale_length 0.01,           global_scale 1.0   ->   140.878 ..   178.437

**The demo .blend runs in CENTIMETRES** — `scale_length` 0.01, measured, not
assumed — which is why its head reads 118..151 rather than 1.18..1.51 and why
grooms exported from it arrive in UE at centimetre magnitudes. Our authoring
file inherited the default metric-metres startup, and my correction then
applied the factor twice.

**The refusal is the only reason either of those was caught.** Both wrong
files contained a head that looked entirely correct; nothing but a number
compared against the source could tell them apart.

### THE ROUND-TRIP PROOF IS INCONCLUSIVE, AND THE LIMIT IS MY TEST

A mechanical test groom — 1,982 straight strands rooted on the scalp band,
6 cm long — exports, imports with the curve count matching exactly (1,982),
binds and assigns. It renders nothing: the gate reads ABSENT at 2.1x the
floor.

Setting a strand radius did change the file (the two .abc hashes differ) and
did not change the render. **I first read the equal BYTE SIZE as proof the
radius never landed, and the hashes refuted it** — same point count and
layout, different floats, identical length. Size is not content, and I know
that.

What this does not establish is anything about the pipeline. A Curves object
built through the API is not an authored groom: it carries none of the guide
structure, width curves or attribute set that GroomExporter expects and that
a real groom has. Chasing it further would be testing the test.

**So: the head is delivered and verified; the loop is unproven.** The next
move is to author something real on that file rather than to keep
synthesising strands, and if that also fails to render, the width/attribute
surface is where to look first.

## 2026-08-21 — REAL HAIR AUTHORED ON THE HERO'S OWN HEAD. UE STILL WILL NOT DRAW IT.

The groom is real now in every sense I can measure: 12,000 strands rooted on
his own scalp, shaped by declared parameters, deterministic under a seed,
carrying root UVs and radius, with the exporter told which attribute is
which, and with the demo file's Geometry Nodes stack producing guide flags.
It exports at 6.3 MB, imports as a GroomAsset with exactly 12,000 curves,
UE derives 1,200 guides from it, it binds and assigns.

**It renders nothing.** The beard and eyebrows render in the same frame, so
grooms work on this character; only mine does not.

### WHAT A WORKING GROOM CARRIES — read, not guessed

Dumped off the demo's groom, and this is the shopping list:

    authored    position, surface_uv_coordinate                    FLOAT2
    evaluated   position id surface_normal surface_uv_coordinate    FLOAT_VECTOR
                rest_position groom_guide_id groom_guide_weights
                groom_guide_closest resolution groom_color
                groom_is_guide radius groom_AO

and the object's `GroomProperty` NAMES which attribute is which:
`att_groom_root_uv -> surface_uv_coordinate`, `att_groom_width -> radius`,
`att_groom_guide -> groom_is_guide`.

My first test groom had `position` and `radius` and no GroomProperty at all,
so the exporter did not know where its width or its roots were. **A groom
that imports with the correct curve count can still be missing everything
that makes it a groom.**

### THE EXPORTER'S FLOAT2 PATH IS BROKEN, AND THE DEMO ONLY SURVIVES IT BY LUCK

Writing the root UV as FLOAT2 -- the type the demo AUTHORS -- kills the
export:

    could not broadcast input array from shape (24000,) into shape (12000,2)

`getAttributeArray`'s FLOAT2 branch builds a flat 2N array and copies it into
an (N,2) view without reshaping. The demo never trips it because its Geometry
Nodes stack converts the attribute to **FLOAT_VECTOR** before the exporter
sees it -- measured on both sides of that stack. Writing FLOAT_VECTOR under a
custom name takes the working branch.

**The authored type and the exported type are different, and only the second
one matters.**

### WIDTH IS NOT THE REASON, AND THE TEST COULD HAVE SAID OTHERWISE

At `radius_root_cm` 0.5 -- five millimetres, absurd, strands like spaghetti --
the render is still bald. A negative result from an instrument that would
plainly have shown a positive.

### A STAGE RAN AGAINST AN EMPTY PLACEHOLDER

The Geometry Nodes stage reported `hair_curves: 0`. The authoring script
deliberately does not save, so the 12,000 strands lived only in that process,
and the template it opened contains an EMPTY hair object by design. The stage
dutifully stacked nodes onto nothing and exported 1,982 bytes.

It was caught only because the report prints the curve count it operated on.
**A stage that does not say what it acted on cannot tell you it acted on
nothing** -- and an empty placeholder is the most convincing nothing there is,
because it has the right name and the right type.

### WHAT IS STILL MISSING, NAMED

Against the working groom, ours lacks `groom_guide_weights`,
`groom_guide_closest`, `groom_color`, `groom_AO`, `rest_position` and
`surface_normal`. The appended `GE_Set Guides Distances and Weights` group is
present as a modifier and produced no weights, so it wants wiring I did not
give it.

**Stated plainly: the hair is authored and UE will not draw it.** The next
move is the guide weights, and if those do not do it, the honest conclusion
is that the demo's full node stack is not optional and the right route is to
author inside a copy of that stack rather than to reconstruct it piece by
piece.

## 2026-08-21 — COPY-AND-REPOINT GIVES THE WHOLE GROOM AND WILL NOT MOVE IT

Appending the demo's working hair object into our authoring file and pointing
it at our head produces, for the first time, a COMPLETE groom:

    position id surface_normal surface_uv_coordinate UVMap rest_position
    groom_guide_id groom_guide_weights groom_guide_closest resolution
    groom_color groom_is_guide radius groom_AO

31,570 interpolated curves from 303 authored ones -- exactly the attribute set
a groom that renders carries, and everything my from-scratch authoring lacked.
**The stack is the thing that makes a groom, and it is not reconstructible
attribute by attribute.**

### AND THE POSITION IS NOT REPOINTABLE

Read back from a FRESH FILE LOAD, not from the call that wrote them:

    curves data.surface              SKM_MHC_AlpineHero_FaceMesh.001
    parent                           SKM_MHC_AlpineHero_FaceMesh.001
    Attach.Surface Object            SKM_MHC_AlpineHero_FaceMesh.001
    voxelyze.Object                  SKM_MHC_AlpineHero_FaceMesh.001
    evaluated Z                      131.059 .. 154.735
    our head Z                       140.878 .. 178.437

Every pointer names our head. The groom evaluates exactly where it always
did, on the demo's skull.

Then I moved the authored curves themselves -- all 3,636 points, mapped by
the two heads' bounding boxes per axis, `fit_scale [1.3272, 1.3793, 1.1375]`,
which independently reproduces the height and width ratios measured earlier
from the meshes. **The evaluated result did not move by a single unit.**

So the stack does not derive its output position from the authored points OR
from the surface pointer. It regenerates from baked state -- `rest_position`
is in the evaluated set and is the obvious candidate -- tied to the head it
was authored against.

### WHAT THAT MEANS, STATED CAREFULLY

The two things I know: this route yields a complete groom, and nothing I can
do to it headlessly moves it onto a different skull. What I have NOT
established is whether an interactive Blender session would rebind it on a
surface change; the modifiers may well recompute on a UI-driven update that a
background depsgraph evaluation does not trigger.

**So the honest statement is not "this route is dead", it is "this route does
not survive being repointed from a script."** That distinction matters
because it points at an attended step rather than at a different pipeline,
and this project has a precedent: enabling MetaHuman needed one attended
click that four headless routes could not reproduce, and the attended run was
the DIAGNOSTIC rather than the fallback.

### THREE ROUTES, THREE HONEST FAILURES, AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME FAILURE

    fresh binding      binding built and correct; bindings do not position
                       grooms in this setup at all
    author from scratch complete control of position; missing the attribute
                       set the stack generates, renders nothing
    copy and repoint    complete attribute set; position welded to the
                       original head

Each one has exactly what the other lacks. That is not three dead ends; it is
a fairly precise statement of what the remaining work is -- get the demo's
stack to regenerate against a new surface, which is one attended experiment
rather than more scripting.

## 2026-08-21 — THE GROOM WAS FROZEN BY A DISK BAKE, AND UNFREEZING IT DESTROYS IT

The operator route was run as briefed and it works headlessly:
`bpy.ops.curves.snap_curves_to_surface` polls true and returns FINISHED under
a `temp_override` with no window, in both attach modes, and it MOVES the
authored roots:

    before            authored Z 131.352 .. 154.204
    NEAREST                     135.743 .. 156.007
    DEFORM                      131.352 .. 162.001

**And the evaluated output did not move by a thousandth.** 131.059..154.646
before and after both modes, measured from real point positions.

### THE CAUSE: A DISK BAKE POINTING AT SOMEBODY ELSE'S CACHE

    "Curly hair _ modded to custom head"   [GroomExporter Curly Hair]
        bake_target     DISK
        bake_directory  //../../../Documents/blendcache_Groom_Metahuman_Test_52/...
        bakes           1   bake_id 1309841462, STILL

Its 31,570 curves were being READ OFF THE DEMO AUTHOR'S CACHE, baked against
his head. That is why SIX separate input changes -- surface pointer, parent,
every Object socket, all 3,636 authored points, both snap modes, and rest
geometry on our target -- produced identical output every time.

**Six inputs changed, one output constant, and I kept looking for a seventh
input.** The invariance was the finding from the second measurement onward
and I read it as failure five times before asking what could make an output
deaf to everything. This project's own rule already names it: a result that
survives a change to its own input was never computed.

### CLEARING THE BAKE MOVED IT ONTO OUR HEAD, AND BROKE IT

    before   Z 131.059 .. 154.646    31,570 curves
    after    Z 128.143 .. 178.434   180,926 curves
    our head Z 140.878 .. 178.437

The crown lands within **0.003 cm** of our skull's crown -- the roots were on
our head for the first time in three routes. And the strands are gone:
184,259 points across 180,926 curves is **1.018 points per curve**.

UE says so at a source line, and took the editor with it:

    Assertion failed: CurveNumVertices >= 2
    GroomBuilder.cpp:2403

**So the bake was not a cache of a reproducible computation. It WAS the
hair.** The node group that nominally interpolates does not regenerate its
own output; without the baked result there is nothing behind it. That is why
the demo .blend is 171 MB for 303 authored curves.

### MY PRECONDITION PASSED A GROOM THAT WAS NOT HAIR

The export gate checked the crown Z band -- the right question, asked alone.
It cleared a groom of one-point curves because that groom was in exactly the
right place. A Z band answers *where*; it cannot answer *whether this is a
strand*, and the second question is the one that takes the editor down.

`export_groom_object.py` now refuses below 2.0 points per curve, citing the
engine's assertion, and it asks that BEFORE the position check. Proven
against the exact artefact that crashed the editor: REFUSE at 1.018.

### WHAT THIS SETTLES

The demo's groom cannot be re-hosted on another head by any means available
from a script, because its geometry is not computed from its inputs -- it is
replayed from a bake made against one specific skull. Repointing, snapping,
moving the points and clearing the bake each do exactly what they say and
none of them can produce hair on our head, the last one because it removes
the only copy of the hair that exists.

**The attended experiment is now sharper than "click snap".** The question
for a UI session is whether the interpolation can be REBUILT -- rebaked --
against a new surface. If it can, everything downstream is already scripted.
If it cannot, this groom is a fixture of its author's file and the route to
custom hair is authoring from scratch with a working interpolation stack,
which is the one thing not yet tried.
