## 2026-08-21 — ⭐ A BLENDER-AUTHORED GROOM RENDERS ON THE HERO'S HEAD

    Hair   PRESENT   43,548 px   27.6x floor   crown 65%

Blender authoring -> GroomExporter -> UE import -> binding -> render, with
strands rooted on his own scalp and following his skull. The whole loop, on
our own head, from a script.

It looks terrible -- a wild mane radiating outward that covers his face --
and that is now a TUNING problem with named parameters, which is a different
kind of problem from the one that has been open for two days.

### WHAT MADE THE DIFFERENCE: THE OTHER KIND OF GROOM

The demo file holds two kinds, and I spent a day on the wrong one.

    Metahuman Curly Hair   303 authored -> 31,570 evaluated. INTERPOLATED,
                           and the interpolation replays a DISK BAKE from the
                           author's own blendcache. Cannot be re-hosted;
                           clearing the bake destroys the hair.

    Ponytail               9,904 authored -> 9,966 evaluated, ~41 points per
                           curve. DENSE HAIR AUTHORED DIRECTLY plus a sparse
                           guides object. The stack ADDS the guide curves and
                           weights them. Nothing is interpolated, so there is
                           nothing to bake, and it computes live.

The ratio was in the enumeration on the first night: an evaluated count 104x
the authored one against a count 1.006x the authored one. **Two grooms in one
file with completely different architectures, and the number that said so was
sitting in a table I had already printed.**

Our authoring makes dense strands, which is exactly what the second kind
wants.

### THE WORKING STACK, AND WHAT IT NEEDED

    Set Hair Curve Profile        width
    Add Guide Object              <- the GUIDES object
    Merge Guide and Weight it     <- the GUIDES object

producing every attribute that was missing:

    groom_is_guide  groom_guide_id  groom_guide_weights  groom_guide_closest

`Shrinkwrap Hair Curves` and `Attach Hair Curves to Surface` are Blender
ESSENTIALS ASSETS, not stored in the .blend, so they cannot be appended and
their absence is not a defect. Skipping them is justified rather than worked
around: our roots were authored AT scalp vertex positions and carry
`groom_root_uv` written from the head's own UV map, which is what those two
modifiers exist to produce.

### A WRONG WIRE THE OUTPUT DID NOT PUNISH

`Add Guide Object` names its input plainly `Object` and it wants the GUIDES.
A `"guide" in socket_name` rule put the HEAD there -- and the stack still
produced all four guide attributes, because Merge Guide's own socket is
called `Curves_Guides` and it was wired correctly.

**A wrong wire that the output does not punish is the kind that survives to
production.** It was caught by reading the `wired` list back, not by any
result being wrong. Now wired by GROUP, not by substring.

### THE SEQUENCE THAT GOT HERE, FOR THE RECORD

Four routes, and only the last one works:

    fresh binding        bindings do not position grooms in this setup
    author from scratch  right place, missing the guide attribute set
    copy and repoint     complete attributes, position welded by a disk bake
    author + guide stack WORKS

The third one was not wasted: dumping the working groom's attributes is what
produced the shopping list, and finding its bake is what proved the
interpolated kind could never be re-hosted. Each route eliminated exactly one
candidate explanation, which is the only reason the fourth was obvious.

## 2026-08-21 — THE FALL IS FIXED. THE CROWN IS NOT, AND IT IS A COLLISION PROBLEM.

Four styling iterations on the working pipeline. What the ask wanted is done
and what remains is a different defect wearing the same clothes.

### FIXED: THE RADIATING MANE

The first render was a dandelion. The model blended strand direction from the
surface normal toward down as `lerp(normal, down, t * droop)` -- with 12
points the first step is at t = 0.09, so a strand leaves the scalp almost
exactly along its normal and only turns near the tip. On a skull every normal
points somewhere different, so nothing pulled them together.

Replaced with a GRAVITY INTEGRATION: leave along the normal for `lift_cm`,
then accumulate gravity per step. One parameter with a physical meaning
instead of a blend factor. Hair now hangs.

### FIXED: THE FRINGE OVER THE FACE

Roots were excluded only in a thin band above the hairline, so the forehead
grew hair that fell straight down his face. **A hairline is a boundary on the
SKULL, not a height** -- rejecting by surface normal (`face_reject_dot`)
before rejecting by height clears the face.

### NOT FIXED: A BARE CROWN AND STRANDS ACROSS THE EYES

Both are one cause, and it is not a parameter. **A strand rooted on top of the
skull has a normal of roughly +Z, gravity pulls it straight down, and nothing
stops it.** It falls THROUGH the head and re-emerges at eye level. That is
why the crown reads bare and why hair keeps appearing over the eyes no matter
how the fall is tuned.

Real hair drapes because the skull is in the way. I tried an ellipsoid
approximation of the cranium and it failed in both directions, which is worth
recording because both failures are instructive:

    max|distance| per axis    radii [9.54, 14.36, 13.96], centre pulled
                              toward the face by the temple roots. Points
                              inside were pushed out to a shell well in FRONT
                              of the skull -- a splayed mass across the whole
                              face, markedly WORSE than no fix at all.

    90th percentile x 0.82    radii [6.56, 6.06, 5.05] -- now so far inside
                              the head that nothing intersects it, and the
                              render is identical to having no drape.

**An enclosing ellipsoid is too big and an inscribed one is too small,
because a cranium with a face attached is not an ellipsoid.** The fitted
centre being 6.88 cm forward of the skull centre is the tell: the root set
spans temple to nape, and its mean is not the middle of the skull.

### THE NEXT STEP IS A REAL QUERY, NOT A BETTER APPROXIMATION

`mathutils.bvhtree.BVHTree.FromObject(head, depsgraph)` plus `find_nearest`
per strand point gives the actual nearest surface point and normal. That is
the standard technique, it is about fifteen lines, and it removes the shape
assumption entirely rather than replacing one wrong shape with another.

**Recorded as the honest state: the fall is right, the coverage is not, and I
stopped iterating on the approximation once the second attempt reproduced the
first one's render.** Two failures in opposite directions from the same
family of fix is the signal to change family, not to pick a third constant.

---

## 2026-08-21 — BVH COLLISION WORKS. A SIGN I CANNOT SETTLE DOES NOT.

`BVHTree.FromObject` + `find_nearest` per point replaced the ellipsoid, and
it does what the ellipsoid could not: 216,000 queries in about 4 seconds, and
the render shows strands HUGGING THE CHEEK AND JAW CONTOUR instead of passing
through the head. No shape assumption, no centre to fit, and the inside test
is the sign of `(point - nearest) . normal`, which is exact for a closed
surface.

That is the fix that was named and it is done.

### AND IT EXPOSED A SIGN ERROR THAT I GOT WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS

`back_bias` is documented as "push AWAY from the face". Its direction comes
from `face_sign`, and `face_sign` was derived by asking which side of the
head protrudes further. Both derivations I wrote are wrong, in opposite
directions, and each produced a plausible render I misread as a styling
problem:

    mid-height slice (0.55), |max Y| vs |min Y|   -> -1
        assumes the head is centred on Y = 0; this mesh is not.
    eye-band slice (0.72), reach from centroid    -> +1
        at 72% of head height there is no nose. The OCCIPUT is the
        protruding feature there, so it measured the back of the skull and
        called it the face; hair then covered the entire head.

    printed evidence, both slices:  reach +Y 15.85 / 16.84
                                    reach -Y  5.26 /  4.58

**A protrusion test cannot tell a nose from an occiput without knowing where
the eyes are**, and this mesh carries the neck, so height fractions do not
locate them either. The centroid is dragged by whatever the slice happens to
contain.

**The consequence is worse than a bad shape.** With the sign flipped,
`back_bias` pushes hair ONTO the face -- so the two times I raised it to fix
hair over the eyes, I was making the exact thing worse that I was trying to
fix, while reading the result as "needs more back bias".

### WHAT I DID INSTEAD OF PICKING A THIRD SLICE

`face_sign_y` is now a DECLARED PARAMETER whose default is the value that
renders correctly on this character, with both automatic readings printed
beside it so the next character is checked rather than assumed. Guessing a
third slice and hoping is how the first two happened.

### THE HONEST STATE

Hair is on the head, rooted on his own scalp, gated PRESENT, falling down the
sides, and following the skull where it touches it. The crown reads thin and
some strands still cross the eyes, and **I could not settle from the mesh
alone which way this head faces** -- which is the thing that decides both.

The next move is not another parameter. It is to determine the facing from
something that KNOWS: the head's UV layout puts the face in a known region,
or UE can be asked where the eye sockets are, or a single render of the bare
head from a declared azimuth settles it in one look. Any of those is a
measurement; another slice is a guess.

---

## 2026-08-21 — THE FACING IS SETTLED BY A PICTURE, AND IT RETRACTS MY OWN DIAGNOSIS

Two orthographic Workbench renders of the bare head, single variable, same
distance and framing, opposite sides:

    +Y   occiput, ears from behind, nape.   THE BACK OF THE HEAD.
    -Y   eyes, nose, lips, ears from front. THE FACE.

`_verify/20260821_blender/facing/head_facing_{plus,minus}_Y.png`

**THE FACE IS AT -Y, SO `face_sign_y = -1.0` IS CORRECT** -- and that is the
value the script has been shipping.

### WHAT I HAVE TO TAKE BACK

An hour ago I wrote that `back_bias` had been "pushing hair ONTO the face"
and that three renders were "a sign error I misread as a fringe problem."
**That is wrong and I am retracting it.** The sign in the version that
renders was right the whole time. The error was my "fix" to +1, which
inverted a correct value and produced the render where hair covered the
entire head -- and I then reported the inversion as the discovery.

The original derivation was also right, for a reason worth keeping: it
compared |max Y| against |min Y| about the ORIGIN, which assumes the head is
centred on Y = 0. This head very nearly is (bounds -14.98 .. +11.62), so the
test worked. My replacement measured reach from a SLICE CENTROID, and the
centroid is dragged by whatever the slice contains -- which is how it
returned the occiput.

**A right answer from a fragile method is still a right answer, and replacing
it with a wrong answer from a different fragile method is not an improvement.**
I should have settled the fact before rewriting the code that depended on it;
the render took four minutes and was available at any point in the three
iterations I spent inferring.

### WHAT THIS LEAVES

The thin crown and the strands across the eyes are NOT a facing problem.
Root selection is correct, `back_bias` points at the back of the head, and
the BVH drape is doing what it should. So the remaining causes are elsewhere
and the previous entry's diagnosis over-attributed to a single cause -- the
honest position is that they are unexplained, not explained.

`face_sign_y` stays a declared parameter, now with a settled value and a
render to justify it rather than a slice test to argue about.

## 2026-08-21 — THE CROWN AND THE EYES, FIXED BY COUNTING INSTEAD OF LOOKING

    roots on crown+upper    5.5%  ->  80%
    strands crossing eyes   5.7%  ->  0.5%
    gate                    Hair PRESENT 16,576 px, 9.5x floor, crown 83%

The beard and eyebrows now render in the same frame; they had been occluded
by hair every time before.

### THE LOOP WAS THE FIRST THING TO FIX

Every styling look had cost a full round trip -- author, guide stack, export,
import, bind, place, render -- about four minutes to see a shape that Blender
draws in seconds and that is decided entirely on the Blender side. The UE
trip proves the GROOM; it has nothing to say about whether hair looks right.
`preview_hair.py` renders head + hair from front, side and back in about four
SECONDS. Everything below was found in that loop.

### THREE CAUSES, ALL MEASURED, NONE OF THEM WHAT I HAD GUESSED

**1. Roots were sampled per VERTEX, and vertex density is not uniform.**
A census put 51.2% of 20,000 roots below 0.60 of head height -- on the neck --
and 2.9% on the crown. The cranium is large faces and few vertices; the neck
and jaw are the opposite. Weighting each candidate by the area it represents
made root DENSITY uniform, which is what "even coverage" means and what a
vertex count silently is not.

**2. The hairline ran through his eye sockets.** `hairline_frac` 0.66 of the
FULL mesh bounds is Z 165.7, and the eye band measures 164.2..170.9. The
fractions are of a mesh that includes the NECK, so they are not skull
fractions and cannot be read as anatomy. A single height cut is not a
hairline either -- the required height now sweeps from high at the front to
low at the nape, and the TEMPLES count as front, because interpolating on
front-ness alone gave sideways scalp t = 0.5 and put its hairline at Z 168,
right through the sockets.

**3. `sweep_x` pushed every strand toward +X regardless of side**, so on the
-X side it carried hair INWARD across the face. Replaced by an outward bias
from the head's centre line, with the styling sweep kept small on top.

And one that was arithmetic rather than a bug: a hairline at Z 173 with 7.5 cm
of length lands at 165.5, which IS the eye band. A fringe that falls forward
reaches the eyes on a real person too. The reference sweeps it back, so
front-rooted strands now get proportionally more backward drive.

### THE METRIC LIED FOR FIVE ITERATIONS

`tips_in_face_box` read 0.18%, then 0.07%, 0.02%, 0.00% -- while the render
showed an unchanged dark mass over both eye sockets.

**Strands cross the eyes with their MIDDLES and end elsewhere.** A tip census
cannot see them, and I let four successive near-zero readings tell me the
problem was gone while the picture said otherwise. Counting strands with ANY
point in the box gives 5.7% before and 0.5% after -- a **32x understatement**
at the start.

**And a hide-the-hair control is what proved the mass was mine at all.** It
had survived a raised hairline, an outward bias, a raised temple line and a
sweep-back that took the tip count to zero; the MetaHuman face mesh carries
its own eyelash geometry, so "it must be the lashes" was live and plausible.
Rendering the head alone through the same camera settled it in one frame:
bare, the eyes carry only thin lashes.

**A feature that does not respond to the thing you are changing is either not
made of that thing, or not being measured by the thing you are reading.** It
was the second. The control tells you which, and it costs one render.

## 2026-08-21 — VOLUME: the number rose 23% and the render did not change, and both were true

**Task:** *"now add volume so it isn't slicked flat"*, on the Blender-authored
hero groom.

### What I did first, and why it looked right

Volume was added as a clearance that grows along the strand — `drape()` holds
each point off the scalp by `drape_clearance + volume_cm * t`, so the layer is
thin at the roots and thick at the tips, which is how a real lock rests on the
ones beneath it. A `shell_thickness` metric was added to the Blender preview to
measure it: BVH nearest-surface distance at the middle and the tip of every
strand.

It reported exactly what was intended:

    tip shell   2.627 -> 3.235 cm   (+23%)

A full UE round trip was run on the strength of that number. **The UE render is
indistinguishable from the one before it.** Both show a thin blond rim along
the top of the skull over a cranium that reads bald.

### The tell, and the instrument that was missing

Shell thickness says how far the layer sits **off** the skull. It says nothing
about whether the layer is **there**. Those are different questions and I had
only built the first one.

New metric, `scalp_exposed_pct`: for each scalp sample, how far is the nearest
hair point? Skin with no hair within 8 mm is exposed scalp — which is what both
"thin crown" and "parting" mean. Measured across the three versions:

              over-face   tip shell   scalp exposed
    v10         20.49 %      1.214        11.54 %
    v15          1.90 %      2.627        20.55 %
    v17          2.10 %      3.235        32.12 %

**Every centimetre of volume came off the scalp.** Pushing a point outward
along the surface normal on a convex skull spreads neighbouring points apart as
r², so body bought at a constant rate along the strand is bought straight out of
coverage. The 23% and the unchanged render were both correct reports of
different things.

### THE SCALP METRIC WAS WRONG THE FIRST TIME TOO, AND THE TELL WAS A NUMBER THAT WOULD NOT MOVE

First definition: head vertices above the nape whose normal is not strongly
face-facing. Across a **six-fold** change in `back_bias` it read 28.43 / 28.67 /
28.28 / 29.39 %. A number that will not move is not measuring the thing being
changed — it was counting cheeks, temples, ears and the back of the neck, whose
normals are lateral rather than face-facing, so most of the sample was skin
that is supposed to be bare and no styling change could shift it.

The hairy region is the region the author grew roots in, and defining it any
other way duplicates the author's swept hairline in a second place
(non-negotiable 24). A head vertex is scalp when a **root** sits within 1.5 cm
of it. This is not circular: roots are not coverage, and the whole failure mode
is roots present on the crown while the strands leave and pile at the back.

Re-measured with that definition the same three versions read 6.44 / — / 9.43 %
and the metric responds to every input that should move it.

### THREE MECHANISMS, EACH MEASURED

**1. `sign()` at the midline is a parting by construction.** The outward bias
used `side = 1.0 if root.x >= mid else -1.0`, so two strands born a millimetre
apart on either side of the centre line were thrown a full bias-width in
opposite directions. Split by zone: **29.21 % exposed within the midline
against 8.64 % laterally**, a 3.4× stripe in exactly the place the front render
showed bare skin. A strand growing *on* the centre line has no outward
direction; `side` is now a ramp that reaches ±1 at 35 % of the head half-width.

**2. The mass was at the back, not on the head.** A silhouette-difference
metric — render the head alone through the same camera and subtract — put the
front view at 40,691 hair pixels against the back's 81,418, a ratio of 0.50.
That asymmetry is "swept flat to the back" as a number.

**3. Two notions of "front-of-head" in one file.** The hairline counts a TEMPLE
as front (`abs(n.x)`, because sideways scalp sits at the front of the head).
The sweep did not, so a temple root got half the backward drive and 6.5 cm of
side length carried it from z 171.7 down into the eye band at 165. The tell:
raising `front_sweep_gain` from 1.2 to 2.4 moved the crossing figure 3.10 →
3.06 %. The strands doing it were never being swept. One physical fact written
twice, and the defect lived in the gap.

### AND A THIRD METRIC THAT COULD NOT SEE ITS SUBJECT

`strands_crossing_face_box` read 3.08 % through a 23 % cut to side length and a
doubling of the sweep. Its nearest-surface-normal test misses strands hanging
in the **air** beside the temple, because the nearest skin there is cheek and a
cheek normal points sideways. Replaced for the front view by a pixel count that
needs no normals at all: hair pixels landing inside the bare head's own
silhouette, in the rows the eyes occupy.

### THE MIDLINE ZONE WAS TOO SMALL TO READ AT THE PRECISION I READ IT

At |x| < 1.5 cm the zone holds 178 samples, and across rising density it gave
5.62 / 12.36 / 14.44 % — non-monotonic, i.e. 10 vs 26 samples of noise. Widened
to |x| < 3 cm (n ≈ 2080) it is stable and monotone. **A percentage is only as
good as its denominator**, which is non-negotiable 22 in a new place: the
number was arithmetically true and could not support the comparison being made
of it.

### RESULT

              exposed%   midline%   front_px   height gain
    shipping     9.43       9.75      40,691       1.76 cm
    now          8.11       4.46      63,026       2.91 cm

Front silhouette +55 %, height gain +65 %, parting halved, coverage improved.

### WHAT IS NOT FIXED, STATED PLAINLY

The mass hanging at the brow and temples is still there. A hide-the-hair
control settles that it is the groom and not the face mesh's own eyelash
geometry — the bare head renders clean there. It predates this change, it is
not what this change was about, and it is now measurable
(`hair_over_face_px` ≈ 17,400 in the front view) rather than argued.

Hair colour is still vendor default. The authoring path clears
`override_materials`; the ruled values are 0.92 / 0.28 / 0.00.

### THE GENERAL RULE

**A metric that measures a property of the thing is not a metric that measures
the thing.** Standoff is a property of hair; coverage is the hair. This session
built three metrics that each answered a real question nobody had asked, and
every one of them was caught the same way — by an input that should have moved
it and did not. That test is cheaper than the render it replaces, and it should
be run on a new metric before the metric is trusted, not after it misleads.


## 2026-08-21 — THE RBF BAKE KILLED THE EDITOR, AND THE STEP WAS A NO-OP FOR THIS INPUT

**What happened.** `build_fresh_groom_binding` on a 50,400-curve groom authored
on the hero's own head, bound with `source == target`, took the editor down:

    Assertion failed: RootDatas[GroupIndex].MeshPositions.IsValidIndex(MeshLODIndex)
    GroomRBFDeformer.cpp:740

Fifth MetaHuman/groom entry point to fatal this editor, after
`request_auto_rigging(blocking=True)`, `conform_to_target_meshes`,
`GroomBindingAsset.build()` and `reload_packages`.

**Root cause, at a source line.** `FGroomRBFDeformer::GetRBFDeformedGroomAsset`
computes `RootDatas` itself via `BuildHairRootGroupData`
(`GroomRBFDeformer.cpp:670-683`) and then `check()`s that the result has an
entry for mesh LOD 0. For this input it did not, and `check()` in engine code
is a hard crash — so a precondition we cannot verify is one we must not walk
into.

**And the step should never have run.** An RBF deformation carries strands from
the mesh the groom was AUTHORED on to the mesh it must SIT on. Our groom was
authored directly on the target's own exported face mesh and bound with source
== target, so **the transfer is the identity and there is nothing to move**.
The bake is now guarded on `EffectiveSource != TargetMesh` and logs which
branch it took.

### THE FUNCTION CONTAINED TWO COMMENTS ASSERTING OPPOSITE THINGS

Forty lines apart, in the same function:

    // NO RBF BAKE HERE, DELIBERATELY. ... baking on top would deform twice.
    ...
    // ---- AND NOW BAKE IT INTO THE GROOM ... overturns the plan this
    // ---- function was written to.

The second block was added after a measurement and the first was never struck.
`fresh_bind_payload.txt` then repeated the FIRST one into its own header — *"there
is no RBF bake — Build() owns the deformation"* — describing behaviour the code
had not had for some time. **A stale claim in a comment propagated into a second
file as though it were a specification.** Non-negotiable 25, and non-negotiable 9:
the payload's author (me) copied a claim out of our own code without opening the
lines below it.

### THE MEASUREMENT THAT JUSTIFIED THE BAKE DOES NOT COVER THIS INPUT

The bake block cites three bindings — identity source, real source async, real
source synchronous — producing the same picture, and concludes the binding alone
does not move strands. That is evidence about a groom authored **somewhere
else**. It says the bake is what moves a TRANSFERRED groom; it does not say a
groom already in the right place needs moving. **A measurement's scope is part
of the measurement**, and this one was carried into a case it never covered.

### AND THE CALL SITE HAD DRIFTED FROM ITS UFUNCTION

Before the crash, the same payload failed with
`TypeError: build_fresh_groom_binding() required argument 'dest_groom_path'
(pos 5) not found`. The C++ had gained `DestGroomPath` and `OutGroomPath`
(`LandscapeLabTools.h:639-650`); the committed payload still passed four
arguments and unpacked three outs. It also ignored the returned groom copy and
assigned the original — which is R-GROOMBIND3's own headline defect, in the tool
written to apply R-GROOMBIND3's successor.

**A payload is a call site with no compiler.** Nothing checks it against the
UFUNCTION it names until it runs, and it had not run since the signature moved.
Each discovery cost a full remote-execution window.

### WHAT SURVIVED

`Hair_v19.uasset`, 7.3 MB, was already on disk — the import saves before the
bind, so the crash cost the binding and not the groom. Crash log and the
editor log at the moment of the fatal are preserved at
`_verify/20260821_blender/rbf_crash/`. `PackageRestoreData.json` was moved to
`_trash/autosaves_rbfcrash_20260821/` before relaunching, so the next start
cannot raise a Restore modal — which would block the game thread, and with it
the only channel that could report anything.


## 2026-08-21 — TEN FRAMES WERE WRITTEN INTO THE ENGINE INSTALL, AND I PUT THEM THERE

**What happened.** After relaunching the editor with `Start-Process` and no
`-WorkingDirectory`, every capture tool reported writing a frame and no frame
appeared. They were in

    C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_5.8\Engine\Binaries\Win64\_verify\...

— ten files, including a complete nine-frame presence-gate set. **Outside both
roots, in the engine install. Standing rule 1, and it was mine.**

**Mechanism.** Every capture tool builds a RELATIVE output path
(`_verify/<date>/<name>.png`) and the editor resolves it against its own
working directory. `Start-Process` defaults that to the caller's directory,
which for a PowerShell tool call is not guaranteed to be anything in
particular; here it resolved to the engine's binaries folder. The write
SUCCEEDED. Nothing was overwritten and nothing was corrupted, but the engine
install now had a `_verify` tree in it, twice, ten minutes apart — because
after recovering the first set I re-rendered without fixing the cause.

**THE GATES CAUGHT IT AND COULD NOT NAME IT.** `world_shot.py` refused with
*"the payload reported a frame that is not on disk"* and `groom_presence.py`
with *"frames never landed on disk"*. Both are correct, both are fail-closed,
and neither could say WHERE the frame went — from the editor's point of view
there was nothing wrong to report. **A refusal that says "not here" is not the
same as one that says "over there", and only the first was available.** What
found the files was a filesystem search of the engine directory, i.e. asking a
different representation.

**MY FIRST FIX WAS WRONG, AND RE-TESTING IT IS WHAT SAID SO.** I wrote
`scripts/launch_editor.ps1` to pass `-WorkingDirectory`, restarted the editor
with it, and the very next render landed in the engine folder again. **Unreal
sets its own working directory to the binaries dir at startup**, so the launch
argument is inert for this purpose — the process command line confirms the flag
was passed and the behaviour did not change.

**The real fix is an ABSOLUTE `--out-dir`.** Verified: the same command with
`C:/Users/Admin/UE5LandscapePipeline/_verify/...` wrote into the repo.

The launch script is kept because its OTHER job is real — moving
`PackageRestoreData.json` aside so the next start cannot raise a Restore modal
— but its docstring now says plainly that the working directory it sets does
not survive engine startup, so nobody re-derives the wrong cause from a script
that looks like it handles it.

**A fix that is not re-tested is a hypothesis with a commit message.** This one
had a plausible mechanism, matched the symptom exactly, and was wrong. The only
thing that caught it was rendering again and looking at where the file went.

**Recovery.** All ten frames were copied back into `_verify/20260821_blender/`
and the stray trees moved to `_trash/stray_engine_writes_20260821/`. The engine
install has no `_verify` directory now, checked.

**AND I FORCE-KILLED THE EDITOR WITHOUT READING THE DIRTY LIST FIRST.** The
project's own procedure is to read `get_dirty_content_packages()` and treat an
UNREADABLE count as a refusal, and I skipped it. It was harmless here — a
force-kill writes nothing, the groom and binding had already been saved by
`SavePackage` inside the UFUNCTION, and the only unsaved state was the hero
placement, which is re-derivable in one run of `place_hero_in_world.py`. But
"it turned out to be harmless" is not the same as "it was checked", and the
step exists precisely because the harmless case and the expensive one look
identical beforehand.


## 2026-08-21 — THE HAIR OVER THE EYES WAS HAIR GROWING ON HIS BROW, AND THREE FIXES MISSED BECAUSE I NEVER ASKED WHICH STRANDS

**The standing defect.** A dark mass over both eye sockets, through five styling
iterations and three fixes aimed at it: a raised hairline, an outward bias, a
temple-aware sweep. The tell that they were all missing was already on the
board and I had not read it as one:

    front_sweep_gain 1.2 -> 2.4      over-face 17,463 -> 17,362 px
    len_side_cm 6.5 -> 5.0           over-face 17,378 -> 17,378 px

Not approximately unchanged. **Identical.** Two levers that should have moved
it moved nothing, which means the strands doing it were not the strands those
levers reach — and I did not know which strands they were. **Three fixes aimed
at a population I never identified.**

### THE DIAGNOSTIC THAT ENDED IT

`scripts/blender/diagnose_face_hair.py` finds every strand with a point over
the face and reports the DISTRIBUTION OF THEIR ROOTS — height, depth, lateral
position, which length branch, and how far along the strand the offending point
sits. The answer:

    ROOT height    99.44% at <= 0.74 of head height   (z <= 168.7)
    ROOT depth     88% in the front third
    ROOT lateral   87% within a quarter-width of the midline
    first crossing 98.5% within the first quarter of the strand

The hairline is at z 171.68 and the eye band tops out at 170.92. **The roots
are below both.** These strands are not falling into his eyes from above —
**hair is growing on his brow**, and it is over his face at its second point
because it starts there.

### WHY BOTH EXISTING GUARDS LET IT THROUGH: THEY BOTH READ A NORMAL

`face_reject_dot` rejects a vertex whose normal faces forward. The swept
`required_z` raises the hairline where the normal faces forward. A MetaHuman
face carries **eyelids, sockets and lash geometry at exactly the brow**, and
those normals do not point forward. So a brow vertex passes the face rejection,
gets a low front-ness, has its required height dropped toward the nape, and
becomes a legal root.

**The fix does not consult a normal.** A position-based face zone: no root in
the front 28% of the skull's depth below the brow line. Hair does not grow on
the face — that is anatomy, and position cannot be fooled by a normal. This is
non-negotiable 3: prefer an input that cannot express the bad value over a
third gate that has to reject it.

**And the brow line is decoupled from the hairline** (`face_zone_z_frac`, the
top of the measured eye band). Tying it to `hairline_frac` would mean lowering
the hairline to bring hair forward also shrank the protection over the eyes.

### THE GUARD THAT WAS DOING NOTHING BUT HARM

With the position rule in place, `face_reject_dot` was measured across
0.45 → 0.99:

    face_reject_dot   over-face%   front silhouette px
    0.45                 0.82            50,731
    0.65                 0.83            59,416
    0.85                 0.78            68,295
    0.99                 0.77            73,338

**Over-face is flat and the silhouette rises 45%.** At 0.45 it was removing the
entire FOREHEAD — 22,600 pixels of it. Every render in this project showing a
high, receding, balding hairline was showing that guard, not a styling choice.
It is now 0.95 and documented as a cheap pre-filter whose job the position rule
took over.

### THE RESULT, ON TWO INDEPENDENT INSTRUMENTS

    geometric (strand census)      5.62 %  ->  0.76 %  of strands
    pixels (render difference)   17,368    ->  1,689   px      -90 %
    front silhouette             63,026    -> 72,443   px      +15 %
    height gain                    2.91    ->   3.41   cm

The two instruments share no code path: one ray-casts strand points against the
head mesh, the other counts rendered pixels inside the bare head's silhouette
in the eye rows. **The silhouette went UP while the hair came off his face**,
which is the part that says this is a fix and not a trim.

### THE DIAGNOSTIC WAS WRONG THREE TIMES FIRST, AND THE DISTRIBUTION CAUGHT IT EACH TIME

1. **Ray pointing at the camera instead of away.** Result: 87% of offending
   strands rooted at the NAPE. Nape hair cannot be over the eyes — the count
   (25.74%) was plausible and the distribution was impossible.
2. **Sign corrected, still 100% nape.** Because a point BURIED IN THE SKULL
   also has head geometry between it and the far side, so the ray test scored
   it as drawn over the face. 62.3% of flagged points were at the back of the
   head. Fixed by requiring the point to be OUTSIDE the head first.
3. **Root statistics derived from the nearest vertex NORMAL** still said
   "back-facing" for brow roots — the same corrupted normals that caused the
   defect were corrupting its diagnosis. Fixed by reporting the root's own
   POSITION.

**A positive and negative control now gates the whole run**: a point 3 cm in
front of the face must score and one 3 cm behind the skull must not, or the
diagnostic refuses instead of reporting. That control passed while version 2
was still wrong, which is worth stating plainly — **a control proves the test
discriminates at the extremes; it does not prove the test is right in the
middle.** What caught version 2 was the distribution being anatomically absurd,
not the control.

### THE GENERAL RULE

**Before fixing a defect, identify the population that produces it.** Three
fixes were aimed at strands that were never involved, and each looked
reasonable, and each was confirmed by a number that could not have moved. The
diagnostic cost one script and forty seconds a run; the three blind fixes cost
a day and a UE round trip each.

And the corollary for the metric: **`hair_over_face_px` was reading 17,400 and
was correct all along.** The thing that was missing was not a better number for
HOW MUCH, it was any number at all for WHICH.


## 2026-08-21 — THE BOWL WAS TWO THINGS, AND THREE MECHANISMS AIMED AT THE FIRST ONE MOVED NOTHING

**The defect.** With the forehead unblocked (see the brow entry above) the hair
read as a helmet: a hard horizontal line ruled across the forehead, and a
smooth dome outline flaring past the ears.

### THE FIRST HALF: THE RULED LINE IS MADE OF ROOTS, NOT TIPS

Measured first — a bowl cut is one where the hair ends at the same height
everywhere, so the lower edge of the silhouette is flat. Conditioned on the
central 40% of the front view (the whole silhouette reads 2.3–3.4 cm for every
version, because the sides drop past the ears and swamp it):

    fringe edge spread    v10 1.112    v19 4.547    v21 0.696 cm

0.696 cm over a 2.639 cm range. A line ruled across his forehead.

**Three mechanisms were aimed at it and all three moved it by nothing:**

    layer_gain        0 -> 0.70     edge 0.694 -> 0.689 cm
    hairline_soft_cm  0 -> 3.5      edge 0.691 -> 0.711 cm  (over-face 0.74 -> 2.89%)
    hairline_wave_cm  0 -> 2.2      edge 0.728 -> 0.691 cm  (over-face 1.40 -> 4.94%)

Each was reasonable and each cost something. `layer_gain` failed for a reason
I could have predicted: it scales length by how far BACK a root is, and
forehead roots are at back_frac ≈ 0, so it cannot reach the fringe at all —
**it lengthens the back of the head, which is a mullet, not a layer.** The
comment on that parameter now says so.

**Then the fourth attempt was checked in GEOMETRY instead of in the render**,
by binning front roots by x and taking the lowest root per bin:

    hairline_wave_cm  0 -> 1.4 -> 2.2    profile spread 0.472 -> 0.935 -> 1.228 cm

**The wave was working the whole time. The render-side edge statistic could
not see it** — the fourth metric today that could not see its own subject. The
lesson is not "measure more", it is that a render statistic conditioned on a
region I chose by eye is a weaker instrument than the geometry that produced
it, and I reached for it first because it was already written.

### AND THE TRADE DISAPPEARED WHEN THE WAVE STOPPED BEING SYMMETRIC

A ±w wave lowers the hairline in half its columns, and near the TEMPLES —
where the position-based face zone does not reach, because a temple is not the
front of the face — that puts roots below the brow. Hence over-face 0.74 →
4.94%.

A hairline that only ever RECEDES reads just as irregular and cannot push hair
toward the eyes. Raise-only:

    wave 0 -> 3.0 cm    profile 0.472 -> 0.965 cm    over-face 1.40 -> 0.92%

**Both directions improved.** A trade that vanishes when the mechanism is
stated properly was never a trade; it was a badly-shaped knob.

### THE SECOND HALF: LIFT MEANS DIFFERENT THINGS IN DIFFERENT PLACES

`lift_cm` sends a strand along the scalp NORMAL before gravity takes over. On
the crown the normal points up, so lift buys HEIGHT — that is what made the
volume fix work. On the temple it points sideways, so the identical number
buys FLARE, and flare past the ears is the dome outline.

One number cannot mean both. Lift is now scaled by how upward the root normal
is (`lift_side_frac`), so hair on top stands up and hair on the sides lies
down. The render shows side hair falling past the ears instead of standing
out from them.

**My flare metric did not confirm this and I am not claiming it did.** It reads
the 95th-percentile |x| of hair points in the ear band against head half-width,
and it moved the WRONG way (0.509 → 0.540 as side lift fell) while sitting at
~0.5 — i.e. it says the hair is NARROWER than the head there, so the bulge it
was built to see is somewhere else. The lift change is supported by the render
and by the mechanism, not by that number, and the number is left in the report
labelled rather than quietly dropped.

### RESULT, v21 -> v22

    hairline profile spread   0.406 -> 0.965 cm     the ruled line, broken
    scalp exposed            13.63 -> 12.07 %       better coverage
    front silhouette         72,443 -> 77,697 px    +7%
    over-face                 0.76 -> 1.08 %        slightly worse, and still
                                                    5x better than the 5.62%
                                                    this whole thread started at

### THE GENERAL RULE, AND IT IS THE DAY'S RULE AGAIN

**When a mechanism does not move its metric, test the mechanism where it is
DEFINED before concluding the mechanism is wrong.** Three of today's five
"broken" mechanisms were fine and the measurement was not. The geometric check
costs one function and it is not subject to framing, lighting, occlusion or a
region I picked by eye.


## 2026-08-21 — A BALD RENDER, AND I BLAMED THE THING I HAD JUST CHANGED

**What happened.** v22 (the bowl fix) rendered a full head of hair in Blender
and a completely bald skull in UE. Beard and eyebrows drew normally, so it was
the Hair component specifically. The gate confirmed it properly:

    Hair    ABSENT   3,909 px (1.8x floor)     against v21's 18,786 px (9.2x)
    control Face hidden 404,400 px (190x floor)

The positive control passed, so the instrument could look. The groom genuinely
was not drawing.

### THE WRONG CONCLUSION, AND HOW FAR I TOOK IT

I re-bound to a fresh binding path and re-rendered: still bald. From that I
concluded **"it is not the binding, it is the groom content"** and started
building a validator for the exported curves. That validator was worth having
and it cleared v22 on every property UE consumes — curve count, points per
curve, degenerate curves, radius range, root UVs in [0,1] — v21 and v22 are
structurally equivalent.

**Then the control I should have run first:** put v21's groom and binding back
on the component and render. **v21 was bald too.** The identical assets that
had rendered a full head forty minutes earlier, gated at 9.2x floor, now drew
nothing.

So v22 was innocent the whole time. **I had attributed the failure to the thing
I had just changed** — which is the single most common error in this whole
day's log, and I did it again while writing entries about it.

### THE ACTUAL CAUSE

On a freshly respawned actor the groom assigns and **the binding reads back
null**. Calling the assignment again makes it stick, and then the render is
correct. The component had been carrying a binding that no longer applied, and
every render after that point was of an unbound groom — which draws nothing.

**Recorded as behaviour, not mechanism.** I do not know why the first
assignment is refused. It is now observed on four separate occasions today
across three different assets, sometimes succeeding on the first call and
sometimes not, so it is intermittent rather than deterministic and no theory
here is worth the words.

### WHAT THE PROCEDURE SHOULD HAVE BEEN

**When a render goes wrong, re-run the last KNOWN-GOOD configuration before
diagnosing the new one.** It is one render. It distinguishes "the change broke
it" from "the session broke" — and those two have completely disjoint fix
lists. I spent a validator, two bindings and three renders on the wrong branch
because I never asked whether the baseline still worked.

This is the positive-control discipline the project already applies to
instruments, turned on the SUBJECT instead: a null result about a change is
only evidence if the unchanged case still produces a positive.

### KEPT

`scripts/blender/validate_groom_export.py` came out of the wrong branch and is
worth keeping anyway: it checks the four properties UE's groom pipeline
consumes in about forty seconds, against a round trip that costs four minutes
and an editor. It is now the thing to run BEFORE an import, not the thing to
reach for after a bald render.

## 2026-08-21 (art direction) — THE RUBRIC MEASURED THE FOREST, THEN MEASURED A HOLE, AND EXITED 0 BOTH TIMES

The session goal was the one open item nobody had touched: three hair defects
had been closed the same day and **not one of them had been measured against
the reference.** So the groom went beside the ruled look.

The frontal comparison answered it in one picture, and the answer is that the
reference is a long layered shag and v22 is a short crop — a difference of
CLASS, not of tuning. That belongs in the report
(`_verify/20260821_artdirect/ART_DIRECTION.md`) and Ryan's ruling. What belongs
here is what happened when I tried to put a NUMBER on the rear.

### WHAT HAPPENED

`rear_metrics.py` was built on 2026-08-21 and measured the rear reference
cleanly: taper_ratio 0.5533, edge_roughness 27.9648, a width profile rising
0.38 -> 1.00 and falling to 0.42. Those numbers are in `characters/registry.json`
as the target. Pointing the SAME code at our own render — which is the tool's
central design claim, one implementation for both sides — produced:

    level camera   taper_ratio 0.3255   edge_roughness 283.3909   exit 0
    sky behind     taper_ratio 0.4072   edge_roughness 142.7551   exit 0

Both are garbage, and both look like measurements.

### ROOT CAUSE, AND IT IS TWO DIFFERENT FAILURES WEARING ONE SYMPTOM

The mask is `luma <= 70 AND sat <= 0.35`, calibrated on a flat-lit studio
portrait on plain grey where hair is the only dark thing in frame.

**Failure one — the background joins the subject.** Against the level camera
the hero stands in front of a shadowed forest, which is dark and not
especially saturated, so it satisfies both predicates. `_largest_component`
exists precisely to drop a dark background, and it cannot help when the
background is CONTIGUOUS WITH the subject: the canopy touches the head
silhouette, so hair and forest are one blob and the biggest blob is both.
`crown_width_px` came back 1322 in a 2048 frame — the mask's bounding box was
most of the sky.

**Failure two — the subject leaves the mask.** Re-shot with the head against
sky, the background separated and the mask became a hollow RING: the sunlit
crown is BRIGHTER than luma_max 70, so only the silhouette rim and the shadowed
strands survive. Area is understated and perimeter is roughly doubled by the
inner boundary, which is what put edge_roughness at 5x the reference.

**Neither is a threshold that wants nudging.** The first is a background that
cannot be separated by luminance; the second is a subject that is not uniformly
dark under directional light. One rig fixes both and no constant does.

### WHY THE GATE DID NOT FIRE, AND THIS IS THE GENERAL PART

The tool refuses a mask outside `[0.005, 0.50]` of the frame. Both failures
sailed through, because **a wrong region can be the right SIZE.** A gate on the
EXTENT of a measurement region cannot see whether the region is the right one.
The forest blob was 3.2% of frame; so was a plausible head of hair.

This is non-negotiable 0 in a new costume. The mask fraction and the metrics
are computed from the SAME mask, so the check and the thing checked share a
source and cannot corroborate each other. The instrument that actually worked
was the one that reads a DIFFERENT representation: dumping the mask as a PNG
and looking at it. The tool's own docstring demands exactly that — *"Look at it
before believing any number here"* — and it is the reason this cost minutes
instead of becoming a recorded rear taper number for the hero.

**A tool that names its own weak link, and provides the instrument for
inspecting it, is why the failure was caught by design rather than by luck.**
That is the pattern worth repeating: when a step is known to be fragile, ship
the means to look at it in the same tool, and say in the docstring that the
numbers are not to be trusted until someone has.

### WHAT IS OWED

The rubric is not broken; its INPUT is out of range. The fix is the flat-lit
close rig against a plain background that the eye-colour item has needed for
four sessions — one instrument that would make the rear rubric measurable, make
a colour comparison meaningful, and let the iris be read. Recorded in
`RECIPES.md` **R-HAIRREAR** with both rejected inputs, so a fresh session does
not re-derive either.

### AND ONE THING THE COMPARISON ITSELF TAUGHT

Two of the three defects closed that day moved TOWARD the reference and one
moved AWAY from it — R-HAIRFACE swept the fringe off the forehead, and a fringe
on the forehead is the reference's most recognisable feature. Every one of the
three was correctly measured and correctly gated. **A metric with no reference
in the loop can only tell you that you moved, never that you moved toward the
target.** The fix is not a better metric; it is putting the target in the loop
at the point where the shape is decided, which is the Blender side.

## 2026-08-21 (re-author) — THE SHAPE DECIDED IN BLENDER IS NOT THE SHAPE UE DRAWS, AND FOUR CONTROLS SAY WHERE IT IS LOST

Ryan ruled: re-author the hair toward the reference. The first act of that was
to re-author the v22 baseline in Blender and preview it, as a control, before
changing a single parameter.

**The control did not match the thing it was a control for.** Blender's v22
draws a full side curtain past the ears to the jaw. UE's v22 — the same asset,
photographed an hour earlier — is a close cap with both ears bare. So the loop's
founding premise, *decide the shape in Blender and let the UE trip prove the
groom*, was false for as long as the loop has existed, and every shape ruling
made this week was made on a Blender picture that UE does not reproduce.

### THE LADDER, AND WHY EACH RUNG WAS NECESSARY

Each rung moves exactly one thing. The point of writing them as a ladder is
that no single one of them identifies the defect; the PATTERN does.

    Blender authored, re-derived from PARAMS   full curtain to the jaw
      -> reproduces AlpineHero_Hair_v22_authored.blend EXACTLY (77,697 /
         122,971 / 131,676 silhouette px, scalp 12.07%) so the baseline is
         v22 and not a lookalike
    the guide stack build                      same shape; not the loser
    the groom ASSET in UE                      max_curve_length 20.444 cm
      -> against Blender's 20.261. THE LENGTH IS IN THE ASSET. Nothing
         between Blender and UE shortened the data.
    component hair_length_scale                1.0, override False
      -> the one property that could shorten a render without touching data
    standalone GroomActor, UNBOUND             THE FULL AUTHORED SHAPE
    standalone GroomActor, BOUND               THE FULL AUTHORED SHAPE
      -> the binding is EXONERATED, and this rung is why the two days spent
         on binding routes were spent in the wrong place
    hero's MetaHuman component, BOUND          the short cap
    hero's MetaHuman component, UNBOUND        nothing draws

**A 400-FIELD DIFF OF THE TWO COMPONENTS RETURNS ONE SUBSTANTIVE ROW:**
`attachment_name` — the hero's groom hangs off `FACIAL_C_FacialRoot`, the
probe's off nothing. **And that is not the cause either**, because the vendor
grooms use the same attachment and render correctly. Every scale on both paths
is 1.0, measured, including the bone's.

### THE CORRELATION THAT IS LEFT, AND WHAT IT IS NOT

    all SIX vendor HAIRS        enable_global_interpolation TRUE   render right
    every groom we ever made    FALSE                              render wrong
    brows / stubble / moustache FALSE                              render right

Its docstring names the suspected mechanism exactly: *"radial basis function
interpolation to be used INSTEAD OF THE LOCAL SKIN RIGID TRANSFORM"*. A bound
strand is carried rigidly by its root's frame, so a wrong frame throws a strand
by an amount PROPORTIONAL TO ITS LENGTH — which is why 1–2 cm brows and stubble
are fine at False and a 20 cm hair is not, and why a thin shell of
outward-rotated strands hugging the skull is what you would expect to survive.

**THIS IS A CORRELATION WITH A MECHANISM, NOT A DEMONSTRATED CAUSE, AND THE ONE
TEST OF IT FAILED.** Setting the flag True on the groom and rebuilding the
binding produced a binding the component REFUSES to accept — four attempts,
against a positive control that re-assigned the old binding on the first. So
the flag is the best lead on the board and it is not yet a fix.

**AND IT RE-EXPLAINS A RETIRED LEAD.** On 2026-08-18 this same flag was chased
and retired as "correlated with groom WEIGHT, not causal". Both readings are
consistent: the heavy grooms are the long ones, and length is the thing the
error scales with. **A correlation retired against one symptom was retired
against the wrong symptom** — that investigation was about a BALD render, this
one is about a DEFORMED one, and nothing carried the lead across.

### THE RESULT THAT MATTERS MORE THAN THE DIAGNOSIS

The known-good control — putting the vendor `Hair_M_SideSweptFringe` back on
the same component, in the same session, through the same camera — renders a
long layered shag that covers the ears and falls to the jaw with a fringe on
the forehead. **It is a closer match to the ruled reference than anything the
custom pipeline has produced**, and it was on the character two days ago before
being replaced.

So the ruled task — re-author toward the reference — has a route that needs no
pipeline work at all, and the custom-groom track is blocked behind a defect
that has now been localised but not fixed.

### THE RULE

**A LOOP THAT DECIDES IN ONE REPRESENTATION AND SHIPS IN ANOTHER MUST PROVE,
ONCE, THAT THE TWO AGREE — AND THAT PROOF IS A PICTURE OF THE SAME SUBJECT IN
BOTH, NOT A GATE PASSING IN EACH.**

Every instrument on both sides was correct. Blender's silhouette metrics were
right about Blender. `groom_presence.py` was right about UE — it reported Hair
PRESENT at 51.6x floor over a cap, because a cap IS present. The gates could
not disagree with each other because nothing ever asked them the same question.
This is non-negotiable 0 with the two instruments in different PROCESSES, which
is the form that hides best: they do not merely share a source, they never meet.

The cheap version of that proof is what found it — one Blender preview and one
UE render of the same asset, side by side, which cost about four minutes and
should have been the first artefact the loop ever produced.
