## 2026-08-21 (seating) — ONE GROOM, THREE SHAPES: THE PIPELINE DESTROYS THE HAIRCUT TWICE

Ryan ruled: fix the seating. This is what the fix attempt found, and it starts
with a correction to the entry above it.

### THE CORRECTION, AND IT MATTERED

The previous entry says the standalone-bound control **exonerates the binding**.
**That is too strong and the rung was weaker than it read.** A standalone
`GroomActor` has no skinned mesh, so a binding's transfer data is never
exercised — the control proves only that the binding does not corrupt the
ASSET. It cannot see binding-driven deformation, which is the thing under
investigation.

It also says the standalone renders "the full authored shape". **It renders
full LENGTH and a DIFFERENT SHAPE**, and putting the three pictures in one
frame is what showed it (`SHEET_three_shapes.png`):

    1  Blender raw curves          a curtain hanging DOWN both sides, fringe
                                   over the forehead
    2  UE standalone, post-stack   swept BACK and up, voluminous -- full
                                   length, different haircut
    3  UE bound on the hero        a short cap, ears bare

**Two unintended transformations, not one**, and the first happens before UE is
involved at all.

### WHAT THE FIX ATTEMPT ESTABLISHED

**Our binding builder is not the defect.** A VENDOR groom built through our own
`build_fresh_groom_binding` with an identity source renders correctly on the
hero — indistinguishable from the vendor's own binding, same camera, same
session. That is the control that clears an entire subsystem, and it is the
kind of control that only works because a known-good input exists.

**The guide stack is NECESSARY AND INSUFFICIENT.** Importing the raw authored
alembic — no stack — gives a groom that imports cleanly at exactly the authored
48,000 curves, binds without complaint, assigns with both groom and binding
read back, and **draws nothing at all**. With the stack it draws, collapsed.

    no guide stack     assignment verified, render BALD
    guide stack        renders, collapsed to a cap
    vendor groom       renders correctly through the SAME binding builder

So the stack supplies something UE's deformation requires — the surface
attachment and the guides — and supplies it in a form that also loses the
shape.

### THE METRIC THAT WAS TELLING ME THIS ON THE FIRST RUN

`preview_hair.py` on the guide-stack blend reported `height_gain_cm` **0.05**
against the authored blend's **3.52**, and `hair_over_face_px` 9,192 against
2,194. **I dismissed both as metric artefacts because `hair_px` barely moved.**
They were the finding, or at least the flag: the stack changes the geometry
enough to move the silhouette gain by 70x.

**And the metric is probably ALSO void**, which is why dismissing it was so
easy to justify: that blend contains a guide OBJECT, so hiding the hair object
does not produce a bare head, and the difference render's control is
contaminated. **A number that is both alarming and untrustworthy is the worst
kind, and the right response is to fix the control, not to explain the number
away.**

### THE DEEPER SHAPE OF IT

`preview_hair.py` takes its CENSUS from raw curve data and its SILHOUETTE from
a render, which evaluates modifiers. On a blend with a Geometry Nodes stack
those are **two different pieces of geometry**, and the tool reports them side
by side as though they describe one thing. Every scalp and root statistic this
week described the pre-stack curves; every silhouette described the post-stack
evaluation; and the alembic that shipped carried the post-stack evaluation.

**This is the same disease as the entry above, one layer down.** There, two
representations lived in different processes and never met. Here they live in
one tool, in one report, under one heading.

### THE RULE

**A TOOL THAT REPORTS ON MORE THAN ONE REPRESENTATION MUST LABEL EVERY NUMBER
WITH THE ONE IT CAME FROM.** Not in a docstring — in the report, beside the
value, where the person reading it is looking. `preview_hair.py` already
separates GATES from DESCRIPTIVE metrics, which was the right instinct applied
to the wrong axis: the dangerous split here is not trustworthy-versus-not, it
is raw-versus-evaluated.

### WHAT IS NOT DONE

**The seating is not fixed.** It is localised to two stages with a picture of
each, which is a much better place than the session started, and the next unit
is a bisect of the five-node stack — Set Hair Curve Profile / Add Guide Object
/ Shrinkwrap Hair Curves / Attach Hair Curves to Surface / Merge Guide and
Weight it. **Shrinkwrap and Attach are the two that can move geometry**, and
Attach is the one whose absence makes the groom draw nothing, so the bisect has
an obvious first cut: keep Attach, drop Shrinkwrap.

---

## 2026-08-21 (seating, continued) — THE AUTHORED HAIR RENDERS ON THE HERO, AND THE THING THAT FIXED IT IS NOT THE THING I WAS BISECTING

**The seating works.** `_verify/20260821_artdirect/TEST_v22_guides_every1_*.png` is
the Blender-authored groom, bound, on the hero's own MetaHuman component, with
its length and volume intact. Gated at the comparison framing: **Hair PRESENT,
29.6x floor, crown 91%, drift 0.6%**, reproduced across two passes.

### FIRST, THREE CORRECTIONS TO THE ENTRY ABOVE, ALL FROM ITS OWN TOOL

**1. THE GUIDE STACK DOES NOT MOVE THE GEOMETRY.** `build_guide_stack.py`
reports `evaluated_z` **[158.645, 181.894]** against the raw authored
[158.633, 181.971], and `crown_delta_cm` 3.457 against the authored height gain
3.52. The stack's evaluated output is the authored curves to within a
millimetre.

**2. SO "ONE GROOM, THREE SHAPES" IS WRONG, AND SO IS THE COMMIT NAMED AFTER
IT.** Panels 1 and 2 of that sheet were an ORTHOGRAPHIC Blender workbench
preview and a PERSPECTIVE UE render of the same geometry, and I read a shape
difference into a camera difference. There are TWO shapes, not three: the
authored one, and the collapsed one on the hero. **This is the project's own
recurring error — judging shape across two cameras — committed by me one entry
after writing the rule against it.**

**3. THE TWO NODES I NAMED FOR THE BISECT NEVER RAN.** The tool's report says
so, in a field called `skipped`, with a reason: `Shrinkwrap Hair Curves` and
`Attach Hair Curves to Surface` are Blender essentials assets that are **not in
the demo .blend** and are absent after append. The applied stack is three
nodes, not five. I had read the comment that says this at line 153 of the file
and written the bisect plan anyway.

**And I nearly destroyed the evidence for it:** the env-override I added for
the bisect wrote `rep["skipped"]`, which is that field's name, and overwrote it
on the first run. Renamed to `skip_requested`. **A new key that collides with
an existing one in the same report is a silent data loss, and it landed on the
one field that mattered.**

### WHAT ACTUALLY FIXED IT, AND IT IS A SHARP THRESHOLD NOT A GRADIENT

Single variable, same blend, same builder, same session, only `guide_every`
differing:

    guide_every 20     2,400 guides    BALD
    guide_every  4    12,000 guides    BALD
    guide_every  1    48,000 guides    FULL HAIR, gated, reproduced

**A gradient would mean density. A cliff at "every curve is a guide" means
CORRESPONDENCE.** When every curve is its own guide, each strand's nearest
guide is itself and its weights are trivially correct. Any subset requires
`Merge Guide and Weight it` to compute which guides drive which strands, and
for our groom it computes something the deformation cannot use.

**So this is a WORKAROUND, not a repair.** It costs 3x the curves (144,000
against 52,800) and it leaves the weighting defect in place. Saying that
plainly matters more than the win: a fix that works for a reason you have not
established will break the first time something moves.

### THE OTHER THING THAT CLEARED A WHOLE SUBSYSTEM

A VENDOR groom built through **our own** `build_fresh_groom_binding` renders
correctly on the hero — indistinguishable from the vendor's own binding. That
single control retired the binding builder as a suspect after two days of work
had gone into binding routes.

### AND A GROOM FROM A THIRD-PARTY PACK, WHICH IS THE GENERAL CASE

`SC_Hairstyle_Male_11` (94,408 curves), three configurations:

    its own binding GB_SC_...        BALD
    our IDENTITY binding             DRAWS -- seated on the JAW, scalp bare
    our SOURCE-TRANSFER binding      BALD
      (source = the pack's own SKM_MH_Groom_Head, target = our face)

**The jaw seating is the informative one.** An identity binding says "this
groom was authored on the target's own topology", and this one was not — it was
authored on `SKM_MH_Groom_Head`, so its raw coordinates land where they fall.
That is what `SOURCE_MESH` exists for, and supplying it correctly still
produced nothing, so the transfer path is unproven rather than wrong.

**The rule this hands forward:** a groom carries the head it was authored on,
and that head is discoverable — the pack's own binding declares it as BOTH its
source and its target. Read it from the binding rather than guessing.

### THE RULE

**A SHARP THRESHOLD AND A GRADIENT ARE DIFFERENT DIAGNOSES, AND ONE POINT
CANNOT TELL THEM APART.** Had `guide_every 1` been tried alone it would have
read as "denser guides are better" and the next session would have tuned
density. Three points showed a cliff, and a cliff names a different mechanism
entirely. **The second and third measurements were the cheap ones and they are
what turned a working configuration into a diagnosis.**

## NATTEN 0.17.5 CANNOT BE BUILT FOR BLACKWELL, AND THE REASON IS NOT THE TOOLCHAIN

**Date:** 2026-08-22. Target: sm_120 (RTX 5080 Laptop, compute capability
verified `(12, 0)` on hardware, not inferred from a model name).

### THE TOOLCHAIN VERDICT, WHICH IS THE PART THAT WORKED

Two Visual Studios were installed. **Build Tools 2022 won, and Community
2026 lost on a version ceiling rather than a missing workload** — it had
the C++ toolchain, it just carried MSVC 14.51:

    VS 18 Community    cl 19.51.36256   REJECTED
    Build Tools 2022   cl 19.44.35228   nvcc -arch=sm_120 COMPILES

CUDA 12.8's `crt/host_config.h` refuses `_MSC_VER >= 1950`, and 19.51 is
1951. The error names its own escape hatch (`-allow-unsupported-compiler`)
and that hatch was not taken, because a host compiler NVIDIA has not
qualified is a bad foundation for a twenty-minute template-heavy CUDA build.

**The cheap measurement that made this a verdict instead of a guess:** a
six-line `.cu` compiled at `-arch=sm_120` under each vcvars. Reading
`host_config.h` predicted the answer; compiling proved it, and also proved
the thing actually being asked — that this toolchain can emit sm_120 at all.

### THE ACTUAL WALL

`setup.py` never reaches the compiler. Its arch validator:

    arch = float(arch) * 10          # 8.6 => 86
    assert arch >= 30 and arch < 100, \
        f"Only SM30 and above are supported at this time, got {arch}."

`12.0 * 10 = 120`. Reproduced verbatim:

    Only SM30 and above are supported at this time, got 120.0.

**The upper bound is silent in the message.** It reports itself as a
*minimum* check — "SM30 and above" — while failing on a maximum. A message
that describes only half of its own condition sends you looking for a
floor you clear by four generations.

### TWO TRAPS UNDER THE FIRST ONE

**The pinned env var was the wrong variable.** The build spec pinned
`TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0`, which is the torch convention; natten 0.17.5
reads `NATTEN_CUDA_ARCH`. Had that been the only problem it would have
presented as the pin being silently ignored, not as an error.

**And unsetting it does not help.** With no arch specified natten derives
one from the live device — `major + minor * 0.1` — which on this card is
`12.0`, into the same assert. **There is no configuration of the
environment that gets this source tree past its own front door.**

### HOW DEEP IT GOES, WHICH IS THE PART THAT DECIDES THE FIX

The assert is one line and patching it is one edit, so the only question
worth asking is what is waiting behind it. The bundled CUTLASS answers:

    third_party/cutlass/include/cutlass/arch/   mma_sm50 ... mma_sm90.h
    grep -rl "sm120|Sm120|SM120"                (nothing)
    grep -rl "Sm100|SM100"                      (nothing)

Ceiling is sm90, with no Blackwell awareness anywhere in the tree. The
autogen kernels agree: `gemm/2d/` stops at `sm80`, and the fused path
(`fna/`) is CUTLASS-backed.

**So the one-line patch buys a compile, not a kernel.** Arch-guarded
CUTLASS kernels compile to nothing at `__CUDA_ARCH__ == 1200` and the
result is a natten that imports, reports 0.17.5, and dies at the first
real op with *the exact "no kernel image is available" that started this* —
a build that looks like a success everywhere except where it is used.

### THE RULE

**AN ASSERT IS A CHEAP LIE ABOUT HOW DEEP A GAP IS.** One line stood
between this tree and a compile, which made "delete the line" look like
the fix; the vendored dependency three directories down had never heard of
the target architecture, which made it a way to convert a loud build
failure into a quiet runtime one. **Before patching a version gate, go
read what the gate is protecting** — the guard is a claim about the code
behind it, and that claim is checkable in about two minutes.

Corollary, earned twice today: **the shi-labs wheel index falls through to
an sdist build in silence.** The retry produced not "index unreachable"
but `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch'` from a build-isolation
subprocess — a message about the *build* of a package you never intended
to build. Watch what pip actually resolved, not what it printed last.

Corollary, mechanical: **CUTLASS cannot be extracted into a deep path on
Windows.** `depthwise_fprop_activation_tile_access_iterator_direct_conv_
fixed_stride_dilation.h` blows MAX_PATH from a normal scratchpad
directory. Build third-party CUDA from a short root; `C:\nb` worked.

## NATTEN BUILDS ON BLACKWELL; IT IS WINDOWS THAT FIGHTS BACK

**Date:** 2026-08-22, continuing from the 0.17.5 wall above. Operator ruled
for the newer-natten + shim path. Target still sm_120, RTX 5080 Laptop.

### THE ARCH PROBLEM EVAPORATED AND EVERY REMAINING PROBLEM WAS PORTABILITY

natten **0.21.7** deletes the `arch < 100` assert that stopped 0.17.5 — its
validator checks only `arch >= 30`. The first build attempt printed

    Building NATTEN for the following archs: [120] (max: 120)
    --generate-code=arch=compute_120,code=[sm_120]

on its way to failing for reasons that had nothing to do with Blackwell.
**Every subsequent failure was a Windows bug, and the arch handling was
never wrong again after the version bump.** Two of them, both in flags:

**One.** `csrc/CMakeLists.txt` adds `-Xcompiler=-Wconversion` and
`-fno-strict-aliasing` unconditionally. With nvcc's
`-forward-unknown-to-host-compiler` these reach `cl`, which reads
`/Wconversion` as a malformed `/W<n>`:

    cl : Command line error D8021 : invalid numeric argument '/Wconversion'

All 88 units failed identically. The file already had a `NATTEN_IS_WINDOWS`
branch further down — the flags simply were not in it.

**Two.** At 60/88, `natten/helpers.h` uses the C++ alternative operator
token `not` inside a `TORCH_CHECK(not x.is_sparse(), ...)` macro that
expands at dozens of sites:

    error: identifier "not" is undefined

nvcc's EDG front-end in MSVC-compatibility mode does not enable alternative
tokens. `--pre-include iso646.h` fixes it by defining them as macros, so the
preprocessor rewrites `not` to `!` before the front-end ever sees the token.

**The trap inside the fix:** `-Xcompiler /FIiso646.h` is the obvious-looking
equivalent and does nothing, because `-Xcompiler` forwards only to the host
compiler pass and this error comes from nvcc's own front-end. *A CUDA
translation unit is compiled by two different compilers and a flag aimed at
the wrong one fails silently rather than loudly.*

### THE RULE

**A TWENTY-FIVE MINUTE BUILD IS A TERRIBLE PLACE TO TEST A ONE-LINE
HYPOTHESIS.** Both flag fixes were verified against a six-line `.cu` in
about four seconds each — reproduce the exact error without the flag, watch
it compile with it — before touching the real build. The second probe also
answered a question the build could not have answered cheaply: `cl` rejects
`not` too (C2065), so the host `.cpp` path needed checking. It turned out
`natten.cpp` is the only host source, does not include `helpers.h`, and is
clean — **so the right change there was no change at all**, which is a
conclusion only reachable by asking.

**Why this class of bug was waiting:** natten publishes **no Windows wheels
on PyPI** — sdist only, every version. Nobody upstream compiles this path.
Expect flag portability bugs, not algorithmic ones, and expect them in
whichever file the platform branch forgot.

### AN OUTPUT DIRECTORY THAT DELETES ITSELF

Unrelated to the build, found while reading `server.py` before trusting it
with a ten-minute generation. `SessionOutputRegistry.clear()` removes every
directory listed in `outputs/.aihair_session.json`, and it is reached from
**two** places: `POST /shutdown`, and `cleanup_pending()` at **server
startup** (`server.py:271`).

**So the outputs of a run are destroyed by the next server start, not just
by an explicit shutdown.** The manifest already listed `hero_hair_v1` from
an earlier failed attempt. The rule this hands forward: **copy results out
of `runtime\outputs\` before restarting or shutting down anything** —
treat that directory as scratch with a timer on it, never as storage.

### A GREEN PING FROM THE WRONG PROCESS

The build finished, the shim went in, the server was started, and
`GET /ping` returned `ok`. Everything said go. **The `ok` came from a
different server.**

A pre-natten server from an earlier attempt was still bound to 8765
(started 15:16). The freshly launched one could never take the port, sat
there importing torch, and printed nothing but its own launcher banner —
so its log looked like a slow start rather than a failure:

    port 8765 owned by PID 31844  started 15:16:09     <- the stale one
    my server              PID 19900  started 16:37:20 <- never bound

Had `/generate` been fired then, it would have run **the old code with no
shim and no sm_120 natten**, and whatever came back — success or failure —
would have been attributed to a build it never touched.

**THE RULE: A HEALTH CHECK PROVES SOMETHING IS LISTENING, NOT THAT YOUR
THING IS LISTENING.** After starting a service, verify the *identity* of
what answers — owning PID and start time against the moment you launched
it — not merely that the port answers. The check costs one command; the
alternative is a whole afternoon's conclusions hanging off the wrong
process. Same family as the earlier exit-0 that only proved a redirect
succeeded: **the cheap green signal is the one worth distrusting.**

Corollary: kill stale servers before starting a new one, and confirm the
port is actually free rather than assuming the previous session tidied up.

## 2026-08-22 — THE SUSPECT LIST WAS RANKED BY PLAUSIBILITY AND MEASURED IN THE OPPOSITE ORDER

An external analysis arrived with a ranked causal catalog for the bald DiffLocks
render, with probability mass attached: degenerate strands ~55%, guide
correspondence ~15%, quantization collapse ~10%, empty render resources ~8%,
stale-component measurement ~7%, root UVs ~2%. It was a good catalog. Four of
the six were already measured false by the time it was written, and the one
genuinely untested item it named — the per-group physics/simulation diff — came
back acquitted with a positive control inside the same reading.

That is not a criticism of the catalog. It is the reason to write down what a
ranked list is FOR: it orders the CHEAP DISCRIMINATORS, and its probabilities
are a statement about the author's information, not about the artefact. The
useful part of the document was its list of discriminators; the percentages were
the part that aged in one turn.

### THE ACQUITTAL, AND WHY IT IS AN ACQUITTAL AND NOT A SHRUG

The theory was mechanically sound: UE's documented contract says guide
interpolation runs when simulation is enabled or a skinned binding is attached,
which should exempt an unbound groom — but a per-GROUP `enable_simulation`
defaulting on would push the unbound groom through interpolation with whatever
guide weights it has. And the earlier "interpolation settings read identical"
check had covered the ASSET-level settings, not the per-GROUP ones. A real gap.

Four grooms, one call, same instrument:

    groom                        enable_simulation   curve/vertex decimation
    DiffLocks k28   BALD               False               1.0 / 1.0
    DiffLocks k12   BALD               False               1.0 / 1.0
    procedural      DRAWS              False               1.0 / 1.0
    vendor          DRAWS              True                0.8 / 0.5

**The field that DIFFERS between the two grooms that both render is the same
field that is IDENTICAL between one that renders and one that does not.** That
shape is what makes it evidence rather than a null: a reading in which every row
agreed would have been consistent with an accessor that returns a default. Here
one row moved, so the instrument demonstrably discriminates, and it still puts
the bald groom on the same side as a groom that draws.

### THE ARITHMETIC CORROBORATION FOR THE DEGENERACY ACQUITTAL

The strand-length histogram had already cleared degeneracy (min 2.6756 cm, zero
under 2 cm, unimodal 2.7–15 cm). A second, independent argument fell out of the
count itself:

    100,943   sqrt 317.715  (317^2 = 100489, 318^2 = 101124)
              /1024 = 98.577
              no small factors

It is not a grid, not a power of two, not a texel budget. A generator emitting
one strand per scalp texel produces a round number; 100,943 is what is LEFT after
a filter. DiffLocks filtered before writing. That reasons from a completely
different property than the histogram does, which is the whole point of asking a
second question rather than re-asking the first more carefully.

### THE GATE THAT CAME OUT OF IT — AND ITS BARS ARE SET BY A CONTROL

Checks 5-7 (segment collapse, strand collapse, root collision) are now permanent
in `validate_groom_export.py`, recipe **R-GROOMVALID**. The class is real and
cheap to catch; the next generative style will regenerate it.

But calibrating them against the groom that DRAWS inverted every intuition:

    metric                     DiffLocks (BALD)   procedural (DRAWS)
    min consecutive-point d      0.0806 cm          0.0092 cm
    distinct root positions     76,379 of 100,943   1,211 of 48,000
    largest root cluster            10                166

**The groom that renders has 2.5% distinct root positions.** Procedural
authoring grows clumps from guides, so its roots pile up by construction. A bar
tightened to look strict — "refuse many roots sharing a spot" — refuses the
known-good groom on its most characteristic property. Only the exactly-zero
cases refuse, because a zero-length segment has no tangent and a zero-length
strand has no direction; those are UNDEFINED rather than merely ugly.

**This is the third time in two days that a gate written for a real defect class
would have refused a working artefact if it had not been positive-controlled**
(`verify_export_bounds.py`, retired in place; the rear rubric's `mask_frac`;
this). The pattern is specific enough to name: **A GATE WRITTEN FROM A THEORY OF
THE DEFECT MUST BE CALIBRATED AGAINST THE ARTEFACT THAT WORKS, NOT AGAINST THE
THEORY.** The theory says what to measure. Only the working artefact says where
the bar goes.

### AND ONE ORDINARY BUG THAT WOULD HAVE INVERTED THE WHOLE READING

Hair points are stored in one flat buffer. The last point of curve *i* and the
first point of curve *i+1* are adjacent in it and are NOT a segment. A `diff`
over the whole buffer invents one large bogus segment per curve — 47,999 of them
on the procedural groom — and its magnitude dominates every statistic taken
afterwards, so `min_segment` reads plausible and the short-segment count reads
zero on a groom that has short segments. Masking `starts[1:] - 1` is the fix,
and the refusal test corroborates it independently: collapsing one 12-point
strand produces ELEVEN zero segments, not twelve.

## 2026-08-22 — READING THE FILE FOUND THREE REAL BUGS AND ACQUITTED THE SUSPECT

The first instrument in this investigation to read the ALEMBIC FILE rather than
the arrays on either side of it returned one substantive row out of a 60-field
schema diff:

    arb geom params, procedural (DRAWS)  ['groom_group_id','groom_group_name',
                                          'groom_root_uv']
    arb geom params, DiffLocks  (BALD)   ['groom_group_id','groom_group_name']

Everything else matched: kCubic, kNonPeriodic, kBezierBasis, kConstantTopology,
nVertices summing to P on both, widths at kVertexScope, uvs at kUniformScope.
Sixteen fields differ and fourteen are "this groom has more curves".

`validate_groom_export.py`'s own docstring says what a groom with no root UVs
does: *binds cleanly and renders nothing*. It looked decisive.

### THE SAME MISTAKE THREE TIMES, EACH ONE UNCOVERING THE NEXT

**1. The gate checked a name I chose.** `export_hero_groom.py` refused unless an
attribute called `groom_root_uv` existed — the attribute `land_difflocks.py`
creates, by the name I picked. The exporter does not read attributes by that
name; it reads the name held in a per-object pointer,
`obj.GroomProperty.att_groom_root_uv`, and skips the param in silence when the
pointer does not resolve (`AlembicGroomExporter.py:282`,
`ExporterOperators.py:42`, `AlembicGroomExporter.py:349`). Measured: that
pointer is `'groom_root_uv'` on the groom that draws — set by the add-on's own
operator, `GroomOperators.py:45` — and the EMPTY STRING on both DiffLocks
objects, which I built by hand with `bpy.data.hair_curves.new()`.

**2. Then the right name on the wrong copy.** Setting the pointer made it
resolve against `ob.data.attributes` and the export still wrote nothing.
`GetCurvesObjects` returns `obj.evaluated_get(depsgraph)`
(`ExporterOperators.py:26-28`) and the exporter reads the pointer off THAT copy
(`:231`). My corrected gate was still reading a different representation than
the consumer. `ob.update_tag()` carries it across.

**3. Then a real add-on bug the silence had been hiding.** With the pointer live
the export stopped skipping and crashed: `ExporterOperators.py:65-75` allocates
a flat `(2n,)` buffer and `np.copyto`s it into an `(n,2)` view without
reshaping, so `groom_root_uv` as FLOAT2 can never export.

**4. And the FLOAT_VECTOR branch it falls back to writes ZEROS.**
`ExporterOperators.py:53` sets `out_type = type(out_array)` — a type object —
and `:79-97` `match`es it against the STRING literals `"imath.V3fArray"` and
`"imath.V2fArray"`. A type never equals a string, no case matches, the `match`
falls through with no default, the function returns, and the array keeps the
zeros it was allocated with at `AlembicGroomExporter.py:244`. The same bug
zeroes FLOAT_COLOR and BYTE_COLOR.

**MEASURED CONSEQUENCE, AND IT IS BIGGER THAN DIFFLOCKS.** `cr_g75.blend` holds
real root UVs — u 0.003–0.997, v 0.097–0.990, 1,223 distinct — and
`cr_g75_ue.abc` ships 48,000 rows of `V2f(0, 0)`. **Every groom this project has
exported through this add-on has all-zero root UVs**, including every hero
candidate for the last week.

### AND THAT IS THE ACQUITTAL

**The groom that DRAWS has all-zero root UVs in its file.** So root UVs are not
what makes a groom render, and the thread that looked decisive is closed by its
own control. Prediction recorded before the confirming test — *still bald* — and
the corrected groom, with 1,758 genuine distinct UVs in the ABC, imported,
bound, and gated **Hair ABSENT 3,940 px, 1.9x floor**, reproduced over two
passes. Unchanged from the zero-UV version.

The advisor's step 4 (export a variant with `groom_root_uv` absent, predict
bald, acquit the method) is answered in a stronger form without being run: the
control groom effectively has no root-UV data and draws.

### WHY THE FIX SHIPS ANYWAY

It is not the render cause and it is still a real defect, and it lands on an
open item: **the third-party groom that seats on the JAW.** UE's binding
transfer consumes root UVs, and every binding this project has built has been
handed zeros. That is a live candidate for the seating failure, and it was
invisible because the value never left Blender.

Patched on the module object at export time. The vendor add-on on disk is not
touched — it lives outside both roots.

### THE RULE, STATED AT THE ALTITUDE THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT

Non-negotiable 5 says a check that consumes the value it is verifying verifies
nothing, and it was written about a value. This is the same defect about a
NAME and then about a COPY:

**A GATE MUST ASK THE QUESTION IN THE CONSUMER'S OWN TERMS — ITS NAME, ITS
REPRESENTATION, AND ITS VALUES.** Three gates in a row here got one of the three
right and read as PASS:

    checked          missed                        looked like
    my chosen name   the pointer the exporter uses  PASS
    the right name   the evaluated copy it reads    PASS
    presence         the values, which were zeros   PASS

The third is the one to watch for, because presence checks are the easiest to
write and they are satisfied by an array of zeros. The post-export check now
reads the values back out of the written file and refuses on fewer than two
distinct UVs.

### AND ONE ORDINARY SLIP WORTH KEEPING

`abc_api_probe.py` — the script whose entire job is to enumerate an API so
nothing is written from memory — died on its first run calling
`ar.getUsingVersion()`, an accessor I invented. Its guard wrapped the CALL, and
the attribute lookup happens before the guard is entered. **A wrapper that
exists to make guessing safe cannot itself be reached by a guess.** Now
`gattr(obj, "name")`.

## 2026-08-22 (later) — MY CONTROL DID NOT DRAW, AND AN ENGINE ASSERTION NAMED THE FIELD

Two findings, and the second only became readable once the first was admitted.

### 1. THE GROOM I HAD BEEN CALLING "THE ONE THAT DRAWS" IS BALD

`AlpineHero_Clay_R4` — the procedural groom used as the positive control in
every comparison in this investigation — gates **Hair ABSENT, 4,126 px, 1.9x
floor**, reproduced over two passes. Identical to DiffLocks.

The vendor groom, put back on the same component in the same session, gates
**Hair PRESENT, 39,239 px, 19.5x floor, crown 74%, drift 0.3%**. So the rig,
the capture path and the session are all sound; the control was wrong.

**Every acquittal that used it is VOID**, and they must be re-graded rather than
quietly kept:

    degeneracy      "the groom that draws is dirtier"     was BALD vs BALD
    root UVs        "the groom that draws has zeros too"  was BALD vs BALD
    points-per-cur  "k12 matches the drawing groom"       was BALD vs BALD

The per-group physics table inverts outright. Read with the corrected label:

    groom                    renders   enable_simulation   curve/vertex decim
    DiffLocks k28              BALD         False              1.0 / 1.0
    DiffLocks k12              BALD         False              1.0 / 1.0
    procedural Clay_R4         BALD         False              1.0 / 1.0
    vendor SideSweptFringe     DRAWS        True               0.8 / 0.5

I reported that as an acquittal with the words *"the field that differs between
the two grooms that both render is the same field that is identical between one
that renders and one that does not."* Both halves of that sentence were built on
the false label. It is a **perfect correlation**, and it is the advisor's #3.

**HOW IT HAPPENED, because that is the reusable part.** The label "procedural
(draws)" was inherited from an earlier session's board and carried forward into
probe after probe as a literal string in the PAIRS list. It was never measured
in this session. `LESSONS.md` 2026-08-21 already carries the rule —
*re-run the last known-good configuration before diagnosing the new one* — and
the reason it did not fire is that I thought I HAD a known-good configuration.
**A control is not a control because it is labelled one.** The label has to be
re-measured in the session that relies on it, and cheaply enough that it is
never skipped: one gate run, four minutes, against three days of work built on
top of it.

### 2. AN ENGINE ASSERTION NAMED THE MISSING FIELD

Setting `enable_simulation` True on the DiffLocks groom killed the editor:

    Assertion failed: !!(BulkData.Header.Flags &
                         FHairStrandsInterpolationBulkData::DataFlags_HasData)
    GroomResources.cpp:1919

That is `FHairStrandsInterpolationResource`'s constructor refusing to build a
GPU resource from interpolation bulk data that carries no data. Sixth
MetaHuman/groom entry point to fatal this editor, and the first one whose crash
is worth more than the operation would have been.

**The mechanism reads straight down the source:**

    GroomAsset.cpp:3835  NeedsInterpolationData() returns true ONLY if
                         IsSimulationEnable || IsGlobalInterpolationEnable ||
                         GetEnableSimulationCache || IsDeformationEnable
    GroomAsset.cpp:636   interpolation is built only under that flag
    GroomBuilder.cpp:1752-1758  BuildInterplationBulkData RETURNS EARLY when
                         PointCount or CurveCount is 0, leaving Flags at 0
    GroomResources.cpp:1919  the resource constructor check()s that flag

Our grooms have `enable_simulation` False and `enable_global_interpolation`
False, so `NeedsInterpolationData` is false, so **the interpolation bulk data was
never built** and the flag was never set. The vendor groom has simulation True,
so its interpolation data exists — which the crash proves independently, since
the vendor asset does not assert.

**And it explains why flipping the flag alone is not the fix.** The DDC key
includes `bNeedInterpolationData` (`GroomAsset.cpp:2494, 2607`), so the data is
built per-key at BUILD time. Setting the property afterwards changes the flag on
an asset whose bulk data was already built empty; the next resource creation
walks straight into the check. **The flag must be true when the asset is BUILT,
which means at import or at reimport — not as a post-hoc property write.**

### THE 2026-08-21 CORRELATION IS NOW A MECHANISM

That board entry reads:

    all SIX vendor HAIRS   enable_global_interpolation TRUE   right
    every groom we ever made                          FALSE   wrong
    brows/stubble (1-2 cm)                            FALSE   right

It was recorded as *"a correlation over five assets, not a mechanism"* and the
suspected mechanism was RBF-versus-rigid-transfer. That guess was wrong and the
correlation was right: `IsGlobalInterpolationEnable` is one of the three
disjuncts in `NeedsInterpolationData`. Set it and the interpolation data gets
built; leave it and there is nothing for the resource to bind.

**Both halves of that old entry now have one explanation**, including the part
that looked like noise — 1–2 cm brows and stubble render at False because a
groom that never deforms has less need of the interpolation path than a 20 cm
hair does.

### WHAT WAS NOT DAMAGED

The crash landed inside the property write. Nothing was saved: `git status`
shows no modified tracked file, and the groom packages on disk are the ones the
import wrote. Crash log preserved at
`_verify/20260822_interp/crash_enable_simulation.log`.

### AND THE CVAR PROBE THAT PRECEDED IT WAS UNINTERPRETABLE

Before any of this, the hair cvar table was rebuilt on names grepped out of the
5.8 engine source — 145 registered `r.HairStrands*` names — and **not one of the
four I had probed earlier exists**: `r.HairStrands.Cluster.Culling`,
`r.HairStrands.Streaming`, `r.HairStrands.Visibility` and
`r.HairStrands.Interpolation` are all absent. I had read their zeros as "off"
and recorded cluster culling as eliminated. It was never tested.

The new probe carries its own control — a deliberately impossible cvar name —
and it reads `float 0.0 / int 0 / bool false`, identical to a real cvar sitting
at its default of 0. **The instrument cannot distinguish absent from off, so
every zero it returns needs a source-side existence check beside it.** That is
non-negotiable 6 against a tool that had been trusted for a week.

### THE OWNER'S EYE SETTLED THE INSTRUMENT QUESTION

Three standalone GroomActors framed by hand in the live editor:

    STAGE_GROOM_1_clay_r4      RENDERS
    STAGE_GROOM_2_vendor       RENDERS
    STAGE_GROOM_0_difflocks    MISSING

So the DiffLocks defect is real and asset-intrinsic, verified standalone by eye.

**AND THE CONTROL WITHDRAWAL IS SCOPED, NOT TOTAL.** Clay is bald when BOUND on

**The interpolation-absence visibility theory is DEAD by that control.** Clay has

true and move to the BINDING ledger, where they may still matter; they are not
why a standalone groom is invisible. That theory lasted one turn, and what
killed it was a control being measured rather than inherited.

**NEW INSTRUMENT RULE, and it is the session's most reusable output:** no groom
render verdict is recorded from the SceneCapture gate until the gate passes its
own engulfment self-check. Standalone verdicts use a level-viewport
`HighResShot` plus the owner's eye. The gate returned ABSENT for the vendor
groom -- which the owner then watched rendering -- on a frame measuring mean

A full audit of all twelve exporter attribute pointers found the root-UV bug was
not one bug. It is a MECHANISM, and it had two instances:

    pointer                clay (renders)      DiffLocks (missing)
    att_groom_width        'radius'  -> WRITE   ''  -> SKIP SILENTLY
    att_groom_root_uv      'groom_root_uv'      ''  -> SKIP SILENTLY

Measured in the written files:

    cr_g75_ue.abc          widths  min 0.012  mean 0.0235  max 0.035  12 distinct
    difflocks_k12_ue.abc   widths  min 0.0    mean 0.0     max 0.0     1 distinct

**A groom with zero width draws zero pixels.** That is the first line of
`validate_groom_export.py`'s own docstring, written on 2026-08-21.

### AND THE SCHEMA DIFF HAD IT AND I READ PAST IT

The ABC diff listed `widths.len 576000 -> 1211316` and I bucketed it as
"count-driven, this groom has more curves". True, and it is a statement about
the ARRAY'S LENGTH. `groom_width` is not an arb geom param -- it feeds the
ICurves schema's own `widths` -- so `widths` shows PRESENT on both files and
only its length ever differs. **Presence and length were both correct while
every value was zero.**

This is the third time in two days that a presence check passed over a
zero-filled array, and the second time in this same investigation. The rule
already existed after root_uv and did not fire, because I applied it to the
field it was learned on instead of to the class.

### THE MECHANICAL BUCKETING IS WHAT FOUND THE REST

The first pass reported "16 fields differ, 14 are count-driven". That was
arithmetic done by eye over a printed table and it was wrong: it is 7 root_uv
rows, 8 count rows and 1 other. Re-bucketed mechanically
(`abc_diff_classify.py`), the leftover is **`name`** -- the ICurves object name.
Checked against the engine: `AlembicHairTranslator.cpp` reads attributes by the
`groom_` prefix and contains no object-name logic at all, so `name` is benign.

**Which means the ABC carries no structural difference beyond root_uv presence
and the width values.** That is a much stronger statement than "16 fields
differ", and it took a mechanical classifier to reach.

### THE STAGING FACTS, MEASURED RATHER THAN ADJUSTED

The first stage put three grooms at head height and they hung in midair. Each
groom's bounds BOTTOM sat ~318 cm above ground with the actor origin at 165.
**The groom asset carries the head's own ~155 cm offset in its local space**, so
spawning at head height adds it twice. Arithmetic, not a defect. Solo arms now
spawn at ground level and land with bounds centred at z 31186.6 = ground +
167.1, which is a head.

The blue object beside them is **`PlayerStart_LandscapeLab`**, class
`PlayerStart` -- the editor's blue capsule icon, 253 cm from the camera.
`HeroInWorld` was 299 cm away. Solo arms moved 2 m clear of both.

### TWO MORE INSTRUMENT FAULTS, BOTH THE SAME SHAPE

`create_render_target2d` defaults to a FLOAT format and `export_render_target`
then writes **OpenEXR under whatever filename you give it**. Five 7.6 MB files
named `.png` began `v/1 ... channels` and PIL refused them with "cannot identify
image file" -- which reads as a corrupt capture rather than a format mismatch.

`hidden_in_game` has a SETTER and no reflected GETTER on `GroomActor` in 5.8.
The reflected surface is the contract, and half of it existing is worse than
neither.

## 2026-08-22 (closure) — THE PROPERTY LAYER AND THE SOURCE LAYER AGREED WHILE THE FILE BETWEEN THEM CARRIED ZEROS

**The shipped artefact is an instrument. Read it.**

That is the whole lesson and it took nine days to reach, because every other
layer was checked and every other layer was fine.

### THE ARC, AND HOW LONG THE ANSWER SAT IN PLAIN SIGHT

    day 1   validate_groom_export.py line 1 of its docstring:
            "radius   zero width draws zero pixels"
    then    constraint 5 recorded "not width" -- from a PROPERTY-LAYER read
            (hair_width 0.01 on all four assets, which is the asset default and
            says nothing about the per-point array in the file)
    then    the Blender source layer checked out: radius present, 0.018, FLOAT
    2026-08-22  the FILE was read for the first time and the widths array is
                1,211,316 zeros

Both ends agreed. The middle was empty. **A property read and a source read are
not two representations of the artefact — they are two representations of the
INTENT.** Non-negotiable 0 asks for a different representation of the ground
truth, and the ground truth here was always the .abc on disk.

### THE MECHANISM, FOR THE RECORD

`att_groom_width` is a per-object pointer naming which Blender attribute feeds
`groom_width`. On the clay object, built through the add-on's own operator, it
reads `'radius'`. On every hand-built object it is the empty string.
`getAttribute` short-circuits at `ExporterOperators.py:42`,
`getAttributeArray` returns at `:51-52`, and `out_widths` keeps the zeros it was
allocated with at `AlembicGroomExporter.py:244`. The array ships present,
correct-length and correctly-typed.

**And that defeats the builder's fallback.** An ABSENT width attribute makes the
groom builder substitute a 1 cm default. A PRESENT width array of zeros is
obeyed. The silent skip produced the one input shaped to slip past the safety
net — worse than writing nothing.

### THIRD INSTANCE OF THE PRESENCE-PASSES-ZEROS CLASS IN TWO DAYS

    groom_root_uv   absent entirely      -> caught by a presence check
    groom_root_uv   present, all zero    -> presence check PASSED
    widths          present, right len,
                    all zero             -> presence check PASSED, cost a render

The rule was written after the second and did not fire on the third, because I
applied it to the FIELD it was learned on instead of to the CLASS. **A lesson
scoped to its instance is a lesson that will not fire.** Check 8 now reads
values on every resolved attribute, and the export path refuses a zero-width
ABC.

### FOUR PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS, FOUR CORRECT

    11_k12     widths all zero          PREDICT BALD    owner: BALD
    12_rootuv  root UVs fixed, widths 0 PREDICT BALD    owner: BALD
    13_full    widths 0.018, real UVs   PREDICT DRAWS   owner: DRAWS
    14_clay    the working control      PREDICT DRAWS   owner: DRAWS

Two of the four were predicted to FAIL and shot anyway. A prediction only ever
made about the arm you expect to win is not a prediction.

### AND IT SHIPPED

    DiffLocks bound on the hero   Hair PRESENT 46,080 px  21.7x floor  crown 79%
    after colouring 0.92 / 0.28   Hair PRESENT 88,840 px  42.7x floor  crown 85%
    vendor, same rig, same day    Hair PRESENT 39,239 px  19.5x floor  crown 74%

Above vendor magnitude, reproduced over two passes at drift 0.5% and 0.0%.

### TWO SUSPENDED VERDICTS RE-MEASURED, AND ONE WAS NEVER A MEASUREMENT

**Clay-bound now reads PRESENT, 29,967 px, 14.3x floor, crown 79%, drift 0.1%.**
The first re-measure attempt read ABSENT at 2.0x — and its bind had returned

That is could-not-look wearing a verdict, and the only thing that caught it was
reading the bind's own report before believing the gate.

**The earlier clay-bound ABSENT is NOT REPRODUCIBLE and its cause is NOT
ESTABLISHED.** That run's bind did report ok. I am not going to invent a

**The stage-11 guide cliff is inconsistent with today's result.** It held that a

path and carried zero widths, and `guide_every 1` changed which object the

### THE GATE IS CALIBRATED, NOT VALIDATED, AND THE DISTINCTION IS LOAD-BEARING

`solo_gate.py` agrees 4/4 with the owner's eyes. It also had its bar re-derived
from those same four points, so 4/4 shows the instrument can be MADE to agree —
not that it generalises. It earns trust the first time it calls an arm it has
not seen and the eye confirms it.

Three faults were fixed to get there, and the first two were mine:

    engulfment       the old arm returned ABSENT for a groom the owner watched
                     rendering, over a frame of mean 254.10 / std 3.90. Now a
                     REFUSAL at mean > 250 or std < 5.
    exposure theory  I pinned AEM_MANUAL at a computed bias to stop the
                     blow-out. Still white. Diffing against the rig that WORKS
                     showed it overrides NOTHING on exposure -- the real
                     difference was `always_persist_rendering_state`. **A theory
                     that explains the symptom is not a cause**, and the diff
                     cost one payload against three failed guesses.
    the floor        two identical captures give a STABILITY MASK; they cannot

**INSTRUMENT RULE, recorded:** no groom render verdict is taken from the
SceneCapture gate until the gate passes its own engulfment self-check.

## 2026-08-22 (delivery) — THE DECISION GATE SAID YES, SO NOTHING WAS REGENERATED

**Verdict: YES.** The already-landed groom draws once the fix is applied to it.
The panel path was never run.

### THE LINEAGE, UNBROKEN AND SINGLE-GENERATION

    difflocks_raw/hair_output_strands.npz   hash-pinned, the canonical strands
      -> land_difflocks.py                  similarity solve, scale 100.5884,
                                            snap mean 0.70 cm p90 1.37 max 3.24,
                                            roots on face 0.00%
      -> dl_full.blend  -> resample k12 -> dl_k12.blend
      -> export_hero_groom.py WITH THE FIX  difflocks_k12_full_ue.abc
                                            + .groomstats.json sidecar
      -> AlpineHero_DL_full  -> BND_DL_final  -> the hero

One diffusion sample throughout. A regen would have been a different sample
from the same image, voiding a registration that was proven by perturbation and
buying nothing — the operator ruled it out and the gate had already routed
around it.

### WHAT THE FIX DID TO THE VALIDATED LINEAGE

    same .abc lineage, pre-fix    Hair ABSENT   ~4,100 px    1.9x floor
    same lineage, widths fixed    Hair PRESENT  46,080 px   21.7x floor  crown 79%
    after colour 0.92 / 0.28      Hair PRESENT  89,360 px   41.9x floor  crown 85%
    vendor, same rig, same day    Hair PRESENT  59,115 px   28.5x floor  crown 77%

Reproduced at drift 0.0% and 1.1%. **The only thing that changed between ABSENT
and PRESENT was one exporter pointer.**

### THE FIX IS NOW IN THREE PLACES, AND THE THIRD IS THE ONE THAT GENERALISES

Blender export refuses a zero-width file; `validate_groom_export.py` check 8
refuses at source; and **ingest refuses an .abc that does not carry a sidecar
from the fixed exporter.**

The sidecar exists because neither end can see the defect:
`max_import_width` is **not a reflected property** on `GroomAsset` in 5.8 --
measured, it raises -- so UE cannot report the widths it imported; and PyAlembic
ships inside the Blender add-on built for **Python 3.13** (`imathnumpy.cp313`,
`boost_python313`) against a system Python of 3.12, so `ingest_groom.py` cannot
open the .abc either. That is an ABI mismatch, not a missing DLL, and no amount
of path fixing changes it.

**So the only process that can see the widths is the one that wrote them.** It
now records what it verified by REOPENING its own output, hashed, beside the
file. An .abc from outside the fixed path has no sidecar and is refused by
construction — non-negotiable 3's unreachable-state preference, taken as far as
it goes here. Proven both directions: the pre-fix file refuses at exit 2, the
fixed file passes with widths max 0.018 and 1,758 distinct root UVs.

### AND THE UE-SIDE GUARD FAILED HONESTLY, WHICH IS WHY IT IS NOT THE GATE

`groom_draw_guard.txt` refused all three test grooms with
*"max_import_width UNREADABLE -- could not look, which is not a pass"*,
including the two that draw. That is the correct behaviour for an unreadable
field and it is useless as a discriminator, so it was demoted rather than
tuned. A guard that cannot see the defect it was written for should say so and
step aside, not be adjusted until it produces agreeable verdicts.

### THE LENGTH NUMBER, MEASURED, FOR THE JUDGMENT

    groom                   curves    guides   max reach   mean strand
    DiffLocks (this cut)    100,943   10,094    15.05 cm      8.16 cm
    clay cr_g75              48,000    4,800    11.56 cm      9.12 cm
    vendor SideSweptFringe   37,520    1,034    27.10 cm         --

The brief's "~20 cm clay reach" is the **v22** authored groom (max_curve_length
20.444, recorded 2026-08-21), not cr_g75. Against the groom that actually looks
closest to the reference, this cut reaches **55%** of the vendor's length. That
is the named one-knob candidate and the number is on the sheet.

### THE THREE-PANEL CROPS ARE MEASURED, NOT EYEBALLED

A reference portrait is 1375x768 and a HighResShot is 4064x2546. Pasting them at
equal width compares a head against a landscape, which is how this project twice
produced a sheet that read as a hair difference and was a framing difference.

The reference crops come from a warm-subject mask restricted to the head band.
That mask FAILS on the game frames -- the autumn terrain is warm too, and it
returns the full frame -- so those crops are derived analytically instead
(camera 75 cm out, viewport FOV 90 deg, visible width 150 cm, a ~30 cm head is
20% of frame width, centred by construction) and then VERIFIED: mean |diff|
between the two arms inside the crop is **11.49** against **2.18** in a corner
control, 5.3x, so the head is demonstrably inside the box. Every crop is burned
into its own caption.

The rear reference crop is derived from the **neck** -- the only warm region
visible from behind -- expanded upward, and the caption says so.

## 2026-08-23 — A GAMUT LIMIT THAT WAS A SEARCH LIMIT

**What was attempted.** The operator gave a four-zone colour breakdown for the
hero's hair — shadow `#141517`, midtone `#2A2C31`, highlight `#52565D` — all
cool, B > G > R. Five measured cycles moved `hairMelanin`, `hairRedness`,
`WhiteAmount`, `hairDye` and `PaintColor`, every write verified by read-back
off a reloaded asset, and none reached negative R-B. It was recorded as a
GAMUT LIMIT: *"the MetaHuman hair master is a MELANIN model and melanin is warm
by construction"*, with the conclusion that a cool blue-grey needs a different
master or a grade.

**What happened.** The operator later asked for the colour to be *"a bit darker
and cooler"*. Enumerating the material's parameters off the asset before
touching anything showed the master carries **FOUR melanin layers, not one**:

    hairMelanin        0.92   hairRedness        0.00   dye [0.5,0.58,0.72]
    HighlightsMelanin  0.28   HighlightsRedness  0.25   dye [1,1,1]
    OmbreMelanin       0.28   OmbreRedness       0.25   dye [1,1,1]
    RegionMelanin      0.28   RegionRedness      0.25   dye [1,1,1]

The base layer was already dark and neutral — every one of the five cycles had
been tuning the layer that was already correct. The other three sat at a THIRD
of its melanin with redness 0.25 and a neutral white dye, and **those three own
the HIGHLIGHT, which is exactly the zone that measured warmest** at R-B +40.
Moving all four together took the midtone from R-B +17.9 to +10.7 and the
highlight from +40.2 to +34.1, both darker and cooler, in a single cycle.

**Root cause.** The search space was defined by which parameter names had been
typed before, not by which ones exist. And the enumeration was already in hand:
`hair_color_probe.txt` had printed all four families in the earlier session, and
its output was read as *a list of names* rather than as *a map of what had not
been tried*. Nothing was measured wrongly; the wrong quarter of the space was
measured thoroughly.

**The general rule.** **A NEGATIVE RESULT ABOUT A SYSTEM IS A CLAIM ABOUT THE
SEARCH UNTIL THE PARAMETER LIST CAME OFF THE ARTEFACT AND EVERY FAMILY IN IT
HAS BEEN MOVED.** "This cannot be done" is only as strong as the enumeration
behind it, and an enumeration you generated but did not act on is worse than
none — it makes the gap invisible, because the names were technically on the
board. When a tool prints a list of levers, mark which ones you have actually
pulled.

*This is non-negotiable 6 turned around.* That rule says a failed measurement
must report "I could not look" rather than a number. The mirror image, and the
one that bit here, is that **a successful measurement over an incomplete input
reports a confident conclusion about the wrong thing** — and it does not feel
like a failed measurement at any point, because every write landed and every
read-back agreed.

**A second, smaller failure in the same work, and it cost a restoration.** The
earlier cycle's FINAL state was recorded in a commit message as *"redness 0,
dye, White 0.25"* — the levers named, the dye's three numbers written nowhere.
When the DiffLocks cycles later overwrote the shared material instance, the
previous colour could not be restored, only *reproduced from its recorded
intent*, and the difference had to be stated rather than glossed. **A tuning
result whose numbers live only in prose is not a result you can return to.**
Every applied parameter set now writes a sidecar
(`_verify/20260823_colour2/params_*.json`).

**And a third: the shared mutable.** `MI_AlpineHero_CustomHair` is ONE material
instance used by whatever groom is mounted, and `cycle.py` rewrites it on every
run. Six DiffLocks cycles in one day each silently overwrote the operator's
ruled colour, and nothing reported a regression because every write succeeded.
Detected only by a read-only probe that reads groom, binding, length scale AND
its enable flag, and the material parameters TOGETHER — `read_hair_state.txt`.
**A settings surface owned by the tool that runs most often will be overwritten
by that tool; the state has to be re-read, not assumed to persist.**

Specification: `RECIPES.md` **R-HAIRCOLOUR** and its REJECTED section.

## 2026-08-23 — A LOCKED RECIPE DOES NOT STOP A TOOL THAT CARRIES ITS OWN COPY

**What was attempted.** The hero's hair colour was ruled by the operator and
locked as `RECIPES.md` R-HAIRCOLOUR, specifically *because* six DiffLocks cycles
had already overwritten it that day. The very next `cycle.py` run — the first
after the lock — overwrote it again, and its own report printed the evidence:
`hairMelanin 0.92, hairRedness 0.28` where the ruled values are 1.00 and 0.00.

**Root cause.** `cycle.py:101-102` declared `--melanin default=0.92` and
`--redness default=0.28` as literals. Those are a SECOND COPY of a value the
tool does not own, and `MI_AlpineHero_CustomHair` is one material instance shared
by whatever groom is mounted, so the most frequent writer of the colour is a tool
whose defaults were authored before the ruling existed.

**The general rule, and it is uncomfortable.** **WRITING THE RECIPE DID NOT
PROTECT THE VALUE.** A recipe is a record; it has no enforcement. The lock was
filed in RECIPES.md, LESSONS.md and a machine-readable sidecar, and the next run
clobbered the value anyway, because nothing in the code path reads any of those.
Non-negotiable 24 says two lists that must agree are one list badly stored — and
the second list here was a pair of argparse defaults, which is the least
conspicuous place a duplicate can hide. Fixed by deriving the defaults from the
sidecar the recipe names, with the fallback going to the RULED numbers rather
than the old literals, and a printed warning if the read fails: a silent
fallback to a stale default is how this happened seven times in one day.

**The test that would have caught it earlier:** after locking a value, run the
tool that most often touches it and read the value back. Locking and verifying
are different acts.

## 2026-08-23 — A SAVED ACTOR OUTRANKS AN IN-MEMORY MOUNT, AND STREAMING DECIDES WHEN

**What happened.** The v2 groom was mounted, verified from an independent
payload, and its full cycle ran green — export, import, bind, colour, gate
PRESENT 23,030 / 23,041 px at 10.8x floor, drift 0.0%. A later read of the same
component returned the VENDOR groom, the vendor's wardrobe materials, and no
custom material at all. Nothing had been asked to revert it.

**Root cause.** Earlier the same session the hero actor's external package was
SAVED with the vendor configuration, deliberately, to make the ruled length
scale durable. `/Game/Alpine8K` is World Partition; the actor can be unloaded
and re-instantiated from that saved package at streaming's discretion, and every
unsaved component edit dies with the instance. The frames were valid — they were
taken before the reload — but the state behind them was gone by the time it was
next read.

**The general rule.** **A COMPONENT EDIT IS A RENDER-STATE CHANGE ON A
PARTITIONED WORLD, NOT A CONFIGURATION CHANGE.** Its lifetime is bounded by
streaming, not by the editor session, so "I set it and verified it" carries no
guarantee about ten minutes later. Two consequences that are now procedure:
render immediately after mounting rather than mounting a set of candidates and
rendering them later; and when two candidates must be COMPARED, mount and render
each one back to back so the pair is single-variable in one window.

*And this is the third distinct lifetime found in the same component today* —
groom and binding live in the saved actor package, colour lives on a material
asset, and the length scale lives only in memory. The recipe now tabulates all
three, because the failure mode of each looks identical from a read-back: the
value is correct when you ask.

**A confound this created, stated rather than hidden.** The v1-vs-v2 comparison
frames rendered on the vendor's `MI_WI_*` wardrobe materials, because the
reverted component no longer carried the custom instance. The comparison remains
SINGLE-VARIABLE — both arms share that material and differ only in geometry —
but neither frame shows the ruled colour, and a reader must not take the colour
in them as the ruled colour.

## 2026-08-25 — THE TOWN IS 155 TOWNS, AND THE BAR WAS NEVER THE PROBLEM
> STATUS: SUPERSEDED — Slope-metric misapplication superseded: town shipped 838 streets on the 6.25-deg basin. Corrected downstream. [Pass 5 ruling, 2026-09-16]

**What was attempted.** Picking the city build back up. The 2026-08-24 placement
commit named one open item in its own message — *"gating each street segment
INDEPENDENTLY breaks CONNECTIVITY, so the outer streets are stubs. A town whose
streets do not join is not navigable. ... Not done."* — and proposed a fix in the
same breath: keep the largest connected component of the segment graph.

**Nothing had ever measured it.** The severity was carried as a qualitative
phrase, "the outer streets are stubs", for a day.

**What happened.** `scripts/measure_city_connectivity.py` (new, selftested in
four directions before first use) read the shipped plan:

    459 segments            155 disconnected pieces
    largest component        42 segments, 9.2%, 821 m of 8281 m
    the town CENTRE          in a 22-segment fragment, not the largest
    stranded                417 of 459 segments

**THE PROPOSED FIX WOULD HAVE DESTROYED THE TOWN.** "Keep the largest connected
component" on this data deletes 91% of the streets AND the town centre with
them. The fix was proposed from a mental model of a mostly-good network with
frayed edges; the network is rubble, and the centre is not in the biggest piece.
**A remedy designed against an unmeasured defect is a guess wearing a plan's
clothes** — and it was written by the same session that had the data in hand.

**Root cause, at a source line, and it is not the bar.**
`plan_city.py:143 street_slope_deg` takes the **MAX of six consecutive height
differences** along a segment and divides by one sixth of its length. That is a
ROUGHNESS statistic, not a grade: a single rough 2.5 m sub-interval anywhere
along the run condemns the whole segment. Measured over the full ungated
lattice of 1342 segments:

    shipped max-of-6        p50 10.54   p90 40.72   max 64.00 deg
    end-to-end grade        p50  3.84   p90 19.48   max 50.29 deg

The site was chosen and accepted at **mean slope 6.25 deg**. Against an 8 deg
street bar the shipped metric therefore rejects the MEDIAN segment of a basin
floor that was measured flat enough to build a town on — 883 of 1342 rejected.
The bar was ruled from physics and is right; the quantity it was applied to was
not the quantity it was ruled about.

**The general rule. A BAR IS RULED ABOUT A QUANTITY, AND THE METRIC MUST BE
THAT QUANTITY.** "8 degrees is about the limit for a cart" is a statement about
a street's GRADE — rise over run. It was enforced against local surface
roughness, which is a different physical thing that happens to carry the same
units and the same name in the code. Both numbers are slopes; only one is the
slope the ruling was about. This is the misleading-denominator class
(non-negotiable 22) moved from the denominator to the MEASURAND: the number was
arithmetically correct and answered a question nobody had ruled on.

**And the tell was on the board the whole time.** The plan's own reject tally
recorded `streets_rejected_slope: 883` against 459 kept. A gate refusing two
thirds of its input on ground already certified flat is a statement about the
gate. It was recorded, committed, and read as terrain being difficult.

**The repair, measured before it is built.** A street is a levelled strip, so it
wants the same pair of gates a building pad already has — a grade limit and an
earthmoving limit. Grade alone is insufficient and would accept a segment that
dives through a gully and climbs out level at the far side, which is why the
chord deviation is measured alongside it rather than after it fails:

    grade <= 8 deg AND max deviation from the end-to-end chord <= 1.8 m
      kept 973 of 1342    largest component 838 = 86.1%    centre INCLUDED

One coherent network holding the plaza, plus 67 outlying scraps to prune — which
is the shape the original fix assumed it was starting from.

**A second-order finding: `plan_city.py` called `main()` at module scope**, so
importing it to reuse its terrain sampler REWROTE THE PLAN as a side effect. The
alternative was a second copy of the heightmap sampler, which is non-negotiable
19 — one physical fact, defined once, read by every consumer. Guarded under
`if __name__ == "__main__"`, and the guard is proven inert the only way that
counts on a seeded generator: the plan re-runs **byte-identical**, sha256
`222d2b3f…` before and after, `git status city/` clean.

**Owed and named rather than skipped:** the specification altitude of this entry
has nowhere to go, because there is no `R-CITY` in `RECIPES.md`.
`recipes/city.json` says so itself in `_schema_status`. Until that recipe exists
a fresh session can repeat this by following the recipe, which is exactly the
completeness test the two-altitude rule sets.

## 2026-08-25 — THE CAMERA WAS 122 m INSIDE THE HILL, AND THE GUARD FOR THAT ALREADY EXISTED

**What was attempted.** An oblique render of the town, to judge whether the new
roofline reads as an alpine settlement. Camera placed 900 m south-west of the
basin centre at z 337 m, derived by adding 150 m to the basin floor elevation of
187 m.

**What happened.** The frame came back showing terrain with **trees hanging
downward** and a large pale gradient below. Ten minutes of render, useless.

**Root cause, measured rather than argued.** A trace at that exact XY reports
ground at **458.9 m**. The camera was **122 m below the surface**, looking out
through the inside of the hill — the hanging trees are rooted on the far side of
a ridge, seen from underneath through backfaces.

The arithmetic was the defect: **the basin floor's elevation is not the ground
elevation 900 m away from the basin.** That is the whole point of a basin. A
trace at the camera's own XY answers it in one call, and eight bearings x two
distances x two eye heights answered it in one payload afterwards — bearing 225
sits at 458.9 m, bearing 270 at 74.7 m, a **384 m spread** across candidate
positions at the same radius.

**AND THIS PROJECT ALREADY OWNS THIS FAILURE.** `CURRENT STATE` 2026-08-15
records "D1 DONE — four cameras were INSIDE the hill", and
`scripts/fix_camera_z.py` was written for exactly it.

**So why did the guard not fire? Because of its SCOPE.** `fix_camera_z.py`
lifts cameras declared in a RECIPE, and `sweep_cameras --resite` sites the sweep
stations. Both operate on persisted, named camera stations. This camera was an
ad-hoc argument to a render payload, so it passed through no camera-siting code
at all and no guard was in a position to see it.

**The general rule, and it is rule (e) applied to a guard rather than to a
lesson.** **A GUARD SCOPED TO THE DECLARED FORM OF A THING DOES NOT COVER THE
AD-HOC FORM OF THE SAME THING.** The dangerous case is precisely the ad-hoc one,
because it skips the machinery where the accumulated knowledge lives. Recipe
cameras are safe *because* they go through a tool; a hand-typed `--set LOC=[...]`
is the unguarded path, and it is the path a person reaches for when they want
one quick look.

**The cheap fix, not yet built:** the shot payload already asserts its camera
transform reads back correctly. It should also trace the ground under the
requested eye position and REFUSE when the camera is below it — the same
information, one extra trace, at the only place every camera necessarily passes
through. Recorded here rather than built, because the render queue was mid-flight
and a change to the payload under a running shot is its own trap.

**A second observation, measured while waiting.** A `HighResShot 2` at this
viewport takes **~10 minutes**, not the "over two minutes" recorded on
2026-08-24. The editor throttles hard when it is not the foreground window —
this project measured **17.8x** — and these renders were taken with the editor
backgrounded. Foreground the window before a render, or budget ten minutes.

## 2026-08-26 — A GUARD THAT COMPARED THE WRONG TWO THINGS, AND COST A THIRD OF A TOWN

**What was attempted.** Navmesh over the town, PlayerStart in it, encounters
planned around it — the ruled sequence for an autonomous session.

**What happened.** All three landed, and the reachability gate then found that
**19 of 60 street points in the town were unreachable from the town's own
plaza**. All 60 projected — navmesh existed under them — so they were
disconnected ISLANDS, not missing navmesh.

**Root cause, and it is a comparand.** `apply_navigation_config.py` enforced
ruling 19 as *navmesh agent slope must not exceed
`world.primary_movement_mode`*. The world is declared `mount` (35°). So the
navmesh was built for a horse.

But ruling 19's own stated purpose is to stop a navmesh **granting paths onto
ground the character slides off**. The thing that slides is the PAWN, and the
pawn is `climb` (70°). The guard was comparing the navmesh against a
WORLD-SCALE declaration — one that WORLD_VISION uses to size POI spacing
against mounted speed — instead of against the object whose behaviour it names.

Two different questions, one comparand. The measured cost was a basin town
built for an agent none of its consumers use: a basin whose rim climbs
186.7 → 333 m is *expected* to fragment at 35°.

**The general rule. A GUARD MUST COMPARE THE TWO THINGS WHOSE DISAGREEMENT
CAUSES THE FAILURE IT NAMES.** Reading the guard's own error message is the
test: it said "ground the character slides off", and it was not looking at the
character. A guard can be correct, tested, one-directional and load-bearing —
and still be pointed at the wrong pair.

**And the fix did not weaken it.** walk 44.765 ≤ climb 70 is still
one-directional and still refuses an agent steeper than the pawn. Proven in
four directions before it was trusted: `air` 90 REFUSED, `climb` 70 allowed at
equality, `walk` 44.765 allowed, `mount` 35 allowed.

**The ruled fix could not be implemented as ruled, and the lookup is why.** The
consult ruled "add a walk agent ALONGSIDE the mount agent". The engine refuses
that shape: `AgentMaxSlope` is not part of `FNavDataConfig` — SupportedAgents
entries carry radius/height/step only — and setting it per-actor reverts via
`ARecastNavMesh::PostLoad` when the voxel cache is on
(`RecastNavMesh.cpp:963-1015`), which this repo *already* records as a REJECTED
pattern. Two agents would have differed in radius/height/step and been
identical in the one property causing the fragmentation. Taken back for a
decision rather than implemented as something that cannot work.

**AND THE AGENT WAS NOT THE WHOLE STORY.** After the rebuild, reachability went
41/60 → 45/60. The outer districts stayed cut off. The hypothesis was tested and
mostly refuted, which is why it was tested rather than assumed.

## 2026-08-26 — PER-ELEMENT GATES DO NOT COMPOSE INTO WHOLE-TRAVERSABILITY. SECOND OCCURRENCE.

**First occurrence, same week:** `plan_city` gated each STREET SEGMENT
independently on slope. Every segment passed its own bar and the network came
out as 155 disconnected pieces with the town centre stranded in a 22-segment
fragment.

**Second occurrence, this session:** the town's EXTENT was drawn by
per-structure gates — cut/fill and pad slope, each building judged alone. Every
building passed its own bar and the town reaches onto ground that cannot be
walked to from its own plaza: 185 of 838 streets and 50 of 303 buildings
unreachable, measured against the built navmesh.

**The general rule. A GATE THAT PASSES EVERY ELEMENT SAYS NOTHING ABOUT THE
WHOLE.** Connectivity, reachability and continuity are properties of the SET,
and no amount of per-element correctness produces them. If the thing that
matters is a property of the whole, the gate must be computed on the whole.

**This is non-negotiable 4a's automatic escalation trigger**: a trap class that
recurs across two different tools is promoted to shared infrastructure on the
spot, without waiting for a third. Recorded here; the shared reachability module
is named as the next unit rather than patched into each planner, and
individually-patched connectivity checks are a REJECTED pattern from this entry
forward.

---

## 2026-08-26 — FOUR MEASUREMENTS THAT WERE ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT, NOT THE WORLD

Each was caught by a control, and each would have been written up as a finding.

**1. `project_point_to_navigation` takes FIVE arguments**, not four:
`(world, point, nav_data, filter_class, query_extent)`. Passing four put the
extent into `filter_class` and left `query_extent` at `[0,0,0]` — a zero-extent
projection, which misses nearly everywhere. Result: 0 of 40 street points, with
both negative controls also at 0. **The positive control is the only reason
this was not reported as "the town has no navmesh"** — the PlayerStart, known
to project since 2026-08-17, failed in the same run, so the verdict came back
COULD NOT LOOK. Non-negotiable 6, doing precisely its job.

**2. A LARGE QUERY EXTENT DOES NOT MERELY WIDEN THE SEARCH — IT CHANGES THE
ANSWER.** At a 120 m extent the plaza spawn reported projecting to a polygon
116.7 m away in Y, which reads as "the player spawns off-navmesh". A radial map
at 500 cm then showed the plaza centre projecting at **0.0 cm** lateral, and
every ring from 10 m to 200 m projecting. R-NAVBUILD already recorded the
too-tight direction (±20 m read 7/25 where ±120 m read 25/25); this is the same
lesson's other half. **A coverage number is a property of the query in BOTH
directions.**

**3. `get_path_length` needs endpoints ON the navmesh.** A point 42 m from the
spawn at the SPAWN's z returns `(ERROR, 0.0)`; the same point at its PROJECTED
z returns `(SUCCESS, 5702.7)`. Both ends are projected first now, and a point
that will not project is reported as a projection failure rather than as
unreachable — different findings that a single boolean would have merged.

**4. Querying a building's CENTRE for reachability** projects into the solid
volume the navmesh is carved around, so all 303 buildings read unreachable. A
fact about the query, not the town. Corrected to sample the DOORSTEP, just
outside the footprint: 253 of 303.

**The through-line:** every one of these produced a plausible, alarming,
publishable number. Not one was caught by inspection; all four were caught by a
control that could fail — and the two negative controls mattered as much as the
positive ones, because a query that returns "no" everywhere agrees with a
world that has nothing.
