## 2026-08-26 — THE DENOMINATOR AGAIN: A TARGET COMPUTED OVER GROUND THAT DOES NOT EXIST

The encounter planner set its target as `density × area of the box`. The box is
1.08 km² and the town spans 940 m of its 1040 — so most of it is settlement
(excluded) or cut off by the basin rim. The planner was asked for encounters in
ground that does not exist for the purpose, and then refused for failing to find
them.

Measured properly, applying exactly the tests a candidate must pass:

    prior 40 m    0.69% of the box available = 0.0074 km²
    prior 60 m    2.59%                      = 0.0281 km²
    prior 100 m   8.49%                      = 0.0919 km²

At the ruled 4.68/km² even the most generous prior yields **0.43 encounters**.

**And the correct reading is not "the density is too low".** WORLD_VISION:305
rules that encounter density scales with remoteness, and this basin is the least
remote place in the world. **The starting town's basin is SAFE BY DESIGN and the
density curve says so.** Widening needs navmesh beyond the town volume — not a
smaller settlement margin, which would put encounters inside bowshot to satisfy
a bar.

This is non-negotiable 22 wearing new clothes: the number was arithmetically
correct and answered a question nobody asked.

**A related restraint worth naming.** The planner's offline heightmap
connectivity model passed five encounters that the built navmesh then refused,
at two different agents. It was NOT tuned until it agreed. Tuning a model until
it matches the authority is fitting a model to an answer; the model stays
optimistic, is labelled a PREFILTER, and the collision-derived gate remains the
authority.

---

## 2026-08-26 — COVERAGE IS NOT CONNECTIVITY, AND THE BASIN IS SEALED

The encounter planner was blocked on one thing: there was no ground outside the
settlement that was also connected to the player. The named fix was navmesh
beyond the town volume. So a second 1040 m volume was declared to the east,
sharing its western edge with the first so the pair is contiguous, and built.

**The direction was measured, not picked.** The offline walkable-component
prefilter over a 5 km box closed at 440–780 m on bearings 165–285 and ran open
eastward. It was used for exactly what a prefilter is for — choosing where to
spend an expensive build — and its CLOSED verdicts ruled out the western half.

The build was clean by every bar it carries:

    chunk actors   10 (was 8)     size 35.18 MB (was 21.59)
    wall clock     36.0 s         bar 30 min
    peak commit    20.0 GB        bar 200 GB
    RegistrationFailed_AgentNotValid   ZERO

**And it changed nothing, because coverage is not connectivity.** A directed
probe along the extension, every 50 m to 1400 m:

    projects     True at ALL 28 points
    reachable    True to 300 m, False for the remaining 22

Twenty-eight points with navmesh under them, six of which a player can walk to.
The extension is real, navigable, correctly built ground that nobody can reach.

**This is the same distinction that has now cost this project three separate
readings, and it is worth stating as a rule rather than as an anecdote:
PROJECTION SAYS A POLYGON IS UNDERFOOT; ONLY A PATH QUERY SAYS YOU CAN GET
THERE.** A tool that reports coverage and calls it access will report success
over an island. The first occurrence was unit 8's original verification (25/25
projecting was read as a working navmesh); the second was the town's own outer
districts (all 60 ring points projected, 41 were reachable); this is the third,
and it is the one where the coverage was *deliberately added* and bought
nothing.

**AND THE PREFILTER WAS WRONG AGAIN, IN EXACTLY THE PREDICTED DIRECTION.** It
had claimed the plaza's component reached 2480 m on that bearing and covered
95.2% of a 5 km box. The built navmesh reaches 300 m. This was not a surprise
and was not treated as one: the model reads the heightmap, the navmesh is built
from collision, and the model had already passed ground the navmesh refused
twice. It is labelled PREFILTER, its OPEN verdicts are not trusted, and it was
NOT tuned to agree — fitting a model to the authority's answer destroys the only
thing the model is good for.

### THEN THE DENOMINATOR DECIDED THE DIAGNOSIS, AND IT NEARLY DECIDED IT WRONG

A 50 m probe localises a barrier to a 50 m band. That is a LOCATION, not a
cause, and three mechanisms fit it with three different fixes: a slope step the
agent will not climb (real terrain), a gap with no polygon (coverage, fixable),
or a thin strip discarded by `MinRegionArea` (config, fixable). They are
separable — a gap fails to PROJECT, and a discarded strip projects without a
local gradient over the bar.

At 5 m sampling the gradient at the flip read **35.71°**, under the 44.765°
agent bar, which says "not a slope problem" and points at the two fixable
mechanisms. At 0.5 m the same ground reads **51.34°**:

    d_m      elev_m   grad_deg   projects   reachable
    322.0    198.36      23.25       True        True    <- last reachable
    322.5    198.73      36.58       True       False
    323.5    199.73      51.34       True       False    <- over the bar
    324.0    200.35      51.33       True       False    <- over the bar

**A 1.25 m rise over 1 m.** Recast evaluates at `CellSize` ≈ 19 cm; a 5 m
average is 26 cells wide and hides a sub-metre step completely. **A GRADIENT
WITHOUT ITS DENOMINATOR IS NOT A SLOPE**, and the denominator that matters is
the one the CONSUMER evaluates at, not the one convenient to sample.

This is non-negotiable 22's shape — a statistic that is arithmetically true and
answers a question nobody asked — reaching a new place: not a misleading MASK
this time, but a misleading SCALE. Both are "state the denominator".

### AND MY FIRST ANSWER TO "IS THERE A PASS?" WAS A STATISTIC THAT MOVES

Six rays reported the FIRST unreachable sample along each ray as the island
boundary. That number is sampling-dependent and a single dropout destroys it:
bearing 0 read **244 m at 2 m spacing and 322 m at 0.5 m**, because the coarse
probe stopped early at an isolated unreachable sample. Genuine dropouts exist —
324.5 m reads reachable among unreachable neighbours.

**THE FIRST FLIP ALONG A RAY IS NOT THE BOUNDARY OF A REGION.** The 24-bearing
sweep scans the whole ray and takes the FURTHEST reachable point, which no
single dropout can move, and the six-bearing figures are marked superseded in
the artefact rather than deleted.

    24 rays at 15 deg, 4 m to 700 m
    furthest overall 504 m (bearing 90)   median 360 m   min 252 m

**There is no natural pass.** A pass would show as one bearing running far
beyond its neighbours with nothing over the bar before it; the profile is
uniform and the best bearing is 1.4x the median. All 24 cross ground above the
agent bar.

**But the sweep bought something a yes/no could not: the rim is not uniformly
thick.** Bearing 315 has 2 samples over the bar and 285 has 4, against 19 at
bearing 195. A question that was "should we cut a pass?" — unbounded, and
therefore easy to defer forever — is now "cut it at 315 or 285, where the least
earth moves". **A negative result is worth measuring properly when the
measurement also narrows the alternative.**

### THE CORRECTION THIS ENTRY OWES

The east-extension commit called the barrier "a local step, not a wall", from
50 m samples, and noted the elevations either side were gentle. **It is a wall,
all the way round.** The gentleness was real and irrelevant: a 1.25 m step in
otherwise gentle ground stops the agent exactly as a cliff does, because the
agent's bar is a LOCAL gradient and a step height, not an average.

## 2026-08-26 — A LESSON RECORDED AND NOT ENCODED FIRES AGAIN. THIRD TIME.

On 2026-08-25 a ten-minute render came back showing the UNDERSIDE of the
terrain with the trees hanging downward. The camera had been sited by adding
height to the BASIN's elevation while standing 900 m away, where the ground is
458.9 m — so it was placed 121.9 m underground.

**Division 1 of this file already carries that exact defect**, from 2026-08-01:
*"a close-up 127 m from a known instance — which came back looking at the
UNDERSIDE of the terrain, because I picked the camera position without checking
the ground height there."* It even names the tool that does the check and
records that it was bypassed to move quickly.

**AND THE TRANSFORM ASSERTION PASSED PERFECTLY BOTH TIMES.** The camera WAS
where it was asked to be. The request was wrong, not the placement, so no
read-back could have caught it — this is the class where verifying that the
value landed proves nothing about whether the value was right.

The 2026-08-25 session diagnosed it correctly and wrote it down as debt: "named
and NOT built". That is the failure this entry is actually about. **A lesson
whose fix is recorded rather than encoded is a lesson that will fire again**,
and CLAUDE.md's operating loop (e) says so directly: when the same mistake
recurs, the finding is not "be more careful" but *why the existing lesson did
not prevent it*.

**Why it did not fire:** `fix_camera_z.py` guards RECIPE cameras. An ad-hoc
`--set LOC` on the shot payload passes no guard at all — and the ad-hoc path is
the one a person reaches for when they want one frame quickly. The guard was
sitting on the road nobody was driving on.

**The fix is placement, not vigilance.** The guard now lives in the shot payload
itself, which is the one place every camera necessarily passes through, and it
refuses BEFORE the output directory is created:

    REFUSE: the camera is 121.9 m BELOW the ground at its own XY
            (camera z 33700.0, ground 45886.7)

An unreadable ground trace reports COULD NOT LOOK and does not pass — a camera
whose ground cannot be measured is not thereby above it.

**The general form, and it is non-negotiable 3 in a new setting:** prefer the
choke point over the correct tool. A guard on the tool a careful person would
use protects careful people; a guard on the path every call must take protects
the run.

## 2026-08-26 — A CONTROL THAT FAILS FOR THE WRONG REASON IS WORSE THAN NO CONTROL

`plan_city` carries four refusals and every one of them had only ever seen the
single town that passes it. `max_orphan_building_fraction` had never refused
anything in its life. So a prover was written — mutate one gate value per case,
run the planner against a copied recipe, assert it refuses.

**And then the prover needed its own positive control**, because a prover that
has only ever seen working gates is in exactly the state it was written to fix.
The control: a copy of `plan_city.py` with the orphan gate's condition made
unsatisfiable, and a requirement that the suite then report FAILED.

**IT REPORTED FAILED. AND IT WAS WRONG.**

    FAIL  POSITIVE CONTROL (unmutated)   the unmutated recipe was REFUSED
    FAIL  orphan fraction 0.0            refusal never names 'orphan'
    FAIL  building-to-street 1 m         refusal never names 'orphan'
    FAIL  min_buildings 10000            refusal never names 'building'

The verdict was the expected one. The reason was not. The broken copy had been
written to a scratch directory outside the repo, and `plan_city` derives its
repo root from its own file location — so the copy could resolve neither
`recipes/` nor its sibling `measure_city_connectivity` import, and **died before
reaching a single gate.** Every case "refused" because every case crashed.

**A dead planner and four working gates produce the same table.** Had the
control been run once, seen FAILED, and been ticked off, the prover would have
been recorded as positive-controlled while being incapable of detecting
anything at all — and every later "ALL CASES BEHAVED" would have inherited that
false credential.

**What caught it was the POSITIVE control failing too.** The broken-gate
hypothesis predicts that the unmutated recipe still PASSES — only the orphan
cases should move. It failed as well, and a hypothesis that does not predict
your result is not the explanation of your result. One `--planner` run outside
the harness showed the traceback in two lines.

**The corrected control DISCRIMINATES, and the difference is visible:**

    orphan fraction 0.0        FAIL   did not refuse, WROTE ITS PLAN
    building-to-street 1 m     FAIL   did not refuse, WROTE ITS PLAN
    min_buildings 10000        ok     still refuses
    min_street_segments        ok     still refuses
    POSITIVE CONTROL           ok     still passes

Exactly the two cases routed through the broken gate failed and nothing else
moved. **That is evidence. "Everything failed" was not**, and the two are told
apart only by looking at WHICH rows moved — never by the verdict line.

**The general rule, and it is non-negotiable 6 pointed at a control rather than
at a measurement:** a control must distinguish *the instrument detected the
defect* from *the instrument could not run*. Assert that the control's failures
land where the injected defect predicts, and treat a control that fails
everywhere as an instrument fault until proven otherwise.

**And the mechanism is worth carrying separately, because it will recur:**
`plan_city`, `bootstrap.py` and several others locate the repo from
`__file__`. That is correct and deliberate — it is why no script in this repo
carries a machine-specific path. **The consequence is that a COPY of such a
script is not a copy of its behaviour.** Anything that duplicates one for a
test must place it beside the original. The prover now writes its control copy
into `scripts/`, removes it in a `finally`, and asserts its absence afterwards.

## 2026-08-26 — A COMMITTED PLAN ITS OWN PRODUCER NOW REFUSES

`encounters/alpine_8k_all.json` has been sitting in the repo since this morning
carrying five encounters, with `target_count: 5`. The availability denominator
was corrected the same day — the target is computed over ground a candidate can
actually OCCUPY, not over the area box — and the corrected planner computes a
target of **0** and REFUSES.

**Nothing noticed, because nothing was looking.** A plan is a DERIVED RECORD and
this repo re-checks derived records everywhere except here. The artefact does
not look stale: it is well-formed, it names its recipe and its world, it has a
seed, and it sits at exactly the path a placer would read.

And it could not have been checked from the file, because **the plan carries its
inputs' PATHS and not their HASHES.** That is non-negotiable 20's live-pointer
problem exactly: "what IS the plan" is answerable only by re-running the
producer, and the producer's inputs may have moved since.

### THE TWO INSTRUMENTS DISAGREED, AND THE DISAGREEMENT IS THE POINT

    HISTORY     git: is any declared input committed LATER than the artefact?
    REPRODUCE   re-run the producer to a TEMP path and compare bytes

    city/alpine_basin_town_plan.json   STALE by HISTORY  ->  REPRODUCES
    encounters/alpine_8k_all.json      STALE by HISTORY  ->  PRODUCER REFUSES

The city plan is the discriminating row. Three of its four inputs were committed
after it — the planner, its recipe and the world recipe all moved — and the
output is **byte-identical**, `65ab655e` both ways. HISTORY alone would have
condemned a perfectly good plan; REPRODUCE alone costs a planner run per
artefact and cannot run at all for the in-editor ones.

**A commit that touches a producer is not a change to its output.** Timestamps
answer "could this have changed"; only re-derivation answers "did it".

### AND THE TOOL DIED AT EXACTLY THE MOMENT IT HAD SOMETHING TO REPORT

`UnicodeEncodeError: 'charmap' codec can't encode character '⛔'` — an emoji
in the DIFFERS and PRODUCER REFUSES markers, against this machine's cp1252
stdout. Every `ok` row printed cleanly; the first bad row killed the process
before the summary line.

**A tool that cannot print its own worst verdict reports success by omission**,
and it fails in the one direction where nobody is looking for a failure. The
error was visible only because the run was watched; piped into a log, the
output would have ended after the passes with a non-zero exit nobody reads.

The markers are ASCII now and the file asserts it carries no non-ASCII at all.
**The general rule: a diagnostic's OUTPUT PATH is part of the diagnostic.** Any
character that can fail to encode must not appear on the failure branch, because
that branch is the one that has to survive.

### WHAT WAS NOT DONE, DELIBERATELY

The stale plan was not regenerated, moved to `_trash/`, or edited. It is
dangerous only when something consumes it and no encounter placer exists yet, so
the honest act was to make it VISIBLE and leave the disposal to a ruling —
regenerate it, trash it, or keep it as the record of the pre-correction method.

**Sixteen further plans declare no inputs at all** and are reported UNSTAMPED:
listed, counted, and explicitly not counted as fresh, including in the success
line. Stamping every plan with the SHA-256 of its inputs is owed. Until then
those are unknown, and "unknown" is never "yes".

## 2026-08-26 — A PLANNER WHOSE ONLY OBSERVED BEHAVIOUR IS REFUSAL

`plan_encounters` has been correct all day and has never once written a plan
under its corrected method. The committed `encounters/alpine_8k_all.json`
predates the availability-denominator fix; since the fix the planner has only
ever REFUSED, which is the right answer for a basin that cannot hold an
encounter. **So the gates were well tested and the half that produces output had
never run.**

That is a familiar class here. `create_landscape_from_heightmap` and
`build_landscape_nanite` were each committed as code that compiled, was
reflected, and had never once produced its output; both were noted at the time
as "the success path is unexecuted". **A refusal is not evidence that the
acceptance path works, and a tool that only ever refuses looks identical to a
tool that can only refuse.**

`scripts/prove_encounter_plan.py` widens the area box to 3 km and relaxes the
reachable-proximity prior IN A COPY of the recipe:

    placed        66, target 66
    by archetype  scavenger 43, raider_camp 17, highland_beast 6
    determinism   byte-identical across two runs, 176a0e7b
    negative ctrl separation x60 -> REFUSED, wrote nothing

**And it re-verifies the plan with a different instrument than the one that made
it** (non-negotiable 8). The planner asserts its own invariants and then reports
success; a read-back that re-reads the field the writer wrote proves only that
the value landed. So every row is re-checked from the OUTPUT plus the RECIPE, by
code that did not place it:

    separation   tightest pair 10924 cm against a required 10500 -- and it is
                 the PER-PAIR requirement, raider_camp vs scavenger, not one
                 global radius
    settlement   0 of 66 rows inside the town's 1142 oriented rectangles,
                 rebuilt from the committed city plan
    spawn        nearest row 322 m out against a 150 m bar
    eligibility  every row above its archetype's minimum elevation, under the
                 44.77 deg walkable bar, party size in range

**THE SYNTHETIC WORLD IS LABELLED AND MUST STAY LABELLED.** It does not show the
real basin can hold encounters — it cannot, and the refusal there is correct. It
shows the placement, separation, archetype selection, gate arithmetic and write
path all work when a world permits them. Conflating the two would turn a
capability proof into a false claim about the world.

### AND A REFUSAL THAT NAMED THE WRONG BAR

The count gate is `need = max(floor, ceil(frac * target))` and the message
always attributed the refusal to the FRACTION. On the real basin, where the
target is 0, it printed:

    below 80% of target (need 3)

80% of 0 is 0, so the fraction was not binding at all — the floor was. The
reader is pointed at `min_fraction_of_target` when the knob that actually
refused is `min_encounters_floor`. **A refusal the operator cannot attribute is
half a refusal**, and this is the same family as non-negotiable 25: a claim
compiled into a message string that nothing re-checks.

The message now names the binding bar and prints all three numbers. **Both
branches are exercised**, which was not planned and is the better evidence: the
real basin takes the FLOOR branch, and the prover's negative control takes the
FRACTION branch (*"the binding bar is 80% of the target of 66"*).

## 2026-08-26 — THE TOWN VERIFIER REFUSED A CORRECT TOWN, AND ITS ALARM WAS A ROOF

Running `city_verify_payload.txt` against the committed plan — the "different
representation" check nobody had made since the roofs landed — returned:

    ok            false
    error         world count does not match the plan
    counted       1446
    by_kind       buildings 303, roofs 303, streets 838, landmark 1, spire 1
    planned       buildings 303, streets 838, landmark 1

**The world is right and the verifier is stale.** It summed three hardcoded
terms; roofs and a spire were added to the planner afterwards. The plan's own
`counts` block declares `roofs: 303` and `spire: 1` — the information was
present the whole time, in the file the verifier had open.

**Non-negotiable 24 exactly: two lists that must agree are one list, badly
stored.** The plan declares its contents; the verifier kept a second copy of
what those contents are. Adding a kind could be done in one place and forgotten
in another, and it was. The test the rule states — *if adding a thing can be
done in one place and forgotten in another, the structure is wrong, not the
author* — is met precisely.

**AND THE FIX IS NOT "ADD ROOFS TO THE LIST".** That reproduces the defect one
kind later. The verifier now derives what to expect **from the plan's own
geometry**: a section carrying `loc_cm` is a placement, a list of them is that
many actors, a single one is one. Nothing is named, so the next kind is covered
the day it is planned. `counts` is deliberately NOT the source either — it also
holds `streets_rejected_grade` and `streets_pruned_disconnected`, which were
never placed.

    ok            true
    planned       buildings 303, roofs 303, streets 838, landmark 1, spire 1
    mismatch      {}

### THE SECOND SYMPTOM WAS THE MORE DANGEROUS ONE

The same run reported `base_above_ground_cm max 883.1`. Read alone that is an
actor floating 8.8 m in the air — the exact defect this project has chased
before.

**It was a roof, and it was measuring the height of the building underneath
it.** A roof sits on its building and a spire on the landmark BY DESIGN, so
tracing their base down to the terrain measures what they stand on. Grounding is
now taken over ground-sitting kinds only, declared in the output:

    grounding_kinds   buildings, streets, landmark
    grounding_pool    1142 of 1446
    base_above_ground p50 -0.0   min -0.0   max 0.0 cm

**Max 0.0 cm across 60 fresh traces, 0 misses.** The alarming number and the
perfect one describe the same town; the difference is entirely which actors were
in the denominator. Non-negotiable 22 again, in a place nobody had thought to
look for it: **a grounding statistic is only meaningful conditioned on what is
supposed to be on the ground.**

### AND THE GATE WAS PROVEN TO REFUSE, ON THE SAME WORLD

A mutated COPY of the plan — one building removed and the whole `spire` section
deleted — against the unchanged world:

    REFUSE: world does not match the plan per kind:
            buildings planned 302, in world 303,
            spire planned None, in world 1

It names both, and the second is the property the rewrite bought: **a whole KIND
going missing is caught**, which a hardcoded three-term sum structurally could
not do for any kind it did not already know about. It also fails closed when the
plan declares no recognisable placement at all, reporting that it could not
determine what to expect rather than passing.

## 2026-08-26 — A PLAN NOW CARRIES ITS INPUTS' HASHES, AND ONE KEY SET DECLARES THEM

The stale-encounter finding earlier today left one thing owed: the plans could
not be checked FROM THE FILE. They named their inputs by PATH, so "is this plan
current" was answerable only by re-running the producer — whose own inputs may
have moved since. Non-negotiable 20's live pointer, in the artefacts this
project generates most.

`scripts/plan_stamp.py` writes `_input_sha256` at write time, after every gate.

**IT IS A MODULE BECAUSE THE KEY SET IS CHECKED IN MORE THAN ONE PLACE.** Two
producers stamp it and one checker verifies it; three copies of `INPUT_KEYS`
would be non-negotiable 24 with three ways to drift, and the rule's test is met
exactly — an input key could be added to the producer and forgotten in the
checker, and the checker would go on reporting MATCHES over an unhashed input.

**And it REFUSES rather than stamping around an input it cannot read.** A stamp
that silently omits what it could not hash verifies clean later against a plan
built from something else, which is worse than no stamp at all: it converts an
unknown into a false positive.

### THE TOWN DID NOT MOVE, AND THAT WAS DEMONSTRATED, NOT ASSERTED

Adding a key to a committed plan the placer reads is exactly the kind of change
that is "obviously harmless" right up until it is not. So the claim was made
falsifiable: regenerate to a temp path, **strip the stamp key, re-serialise
both, and require byte-identity**.

    committed     399997 bytes  sha 65ab655e
    regenerated   400412 bytes  sha 63e11d0d
    stamp stripped, both re-serialised:   47abfa61  ==  47abfa61

Same 303 buildings, 303 roofs, 838 streets, landmark, spire, same seed, same
rejection tallies. Then every consumer was re-run — the four offline provers,
and the live world against the new plan, which still reads `ok true`,
`mismatch {}`, grounding p50 -0.0 / max 0.0 cm.

### THREE INSTRUMENTS, AND THEY RANK — which is more useful than agreeing

    city plan   STALE by HISTORY     a suspicion
                STAMP MATCHES        a fact on disk
                REPRODUCES           decisive

**The stamp outranks HISTORY**, because a commit that touched a producer is not
a change to its output, whereas a changed hash IS a change to its input.
**It does not outrank REPRODUCE**, and the module's own docstring says so: a
stamp proves the INPUTS are unchanged, never that the OUTPUT is what those
inputs would produce today. A producer whose behaviour depends on something it
does not declare will still drift, and only re-derivation catches that.

Writing that ordering down is the point. Three green checks that are not ranked
invite the cheapest one to be quoted as though it were the strongest — which is
the failure non-negotiable 0 describes, in a new shape: not instruments sharing
a source, but instruments of different authority being read as equals.

### AND THE STAMP WAS PROVEN TO REFUSE BEFORE IT WAS TRUSTED

    POSITIVE CONTROL (unmutated)   -> MATCHES
    one input hash corrupted       -> DIFFERS, and it NAMES that input
    stamp removed                  -> UNSTAMPED, never "fresh"
    a stamped input deleted        -> UNREADABLE, not MATCHES
    stamping with a missing input  -> REFUSED

The last two are the ones worth having. `UNREADABLE` and `MATCHES` are easy to
collapse into one branch, and a stamp that reports MATCHES when it could not
read the file is the "unknown is never yes" failure with a hash on top.

**Sixteen plans remain UNSTAMPED and are declared so** — every `foliage/*.json`
and the reachable sidecar, produced by in-editor payloads or by `place_foliage`.
They are listed, counted, and excluded from the success line. Partial coverage
stated as partial is honest; partial coverage summarised as a pass is not.

## 2026-08-26 — A BINDING THAT WAS RECORDED AND NEVER ENFORCED, IN THE MODULE BUILT TO ENFORCE BINDINGS

`city/alpine_basin_town_reachable.json` opens with its own warning: *"a
reachability claim is true for ONE navmesh build... it records the agent it was
measured with."* Its `_bound_to` block records four things — the agent, the
PlayerStart, the query extent, and `nav_chunk_actors_resident`.

`reachability.py` enforced **one of the four.** The agent mismatch refuses. The
chunk count was read into the summary and never compared to anything.

**And it was live.** The east extension took the world from 8 navmesh chunk
actors to 10, AFTER the sidecar was last measured. The file went on declaring 8,
the module went on loading it without complaint, and every consumer got answers
about a navmesh that no longer existed.

**This is non-negotiable 25 landing on the module written specifically to stop
this class of error.** The 4a escalation that produced `reachability.py` was
justified by "a reachability claim is true for exactly ONE navmesh build, so the
sidecar records what it was measured against and the module REFUSES a caller
declaring a different one" — and the sentence was three-quarters aspiration. A
claim worth making in a docstring is a claim worth asserting.

### THE RE-MEASUREMENT IS THE MORE INTERESTING HALF

    streets    838 total, 653 reachable, 185 unreachable, 0 failed projection
    buildings  303 total, 253 reachable, 50 unreachable
    row by row 1141 rows, same positions, ZERO flipped

Exactly one field differs across the whole 175 KB file: `8 -> 10`.

**That is a second, independent confirmation that coverage is not
connectivity.** The directed probe reached the conclusion from one end —
28 points project, 6 are reachable. This reaches it from the other: adding
13.6 MB of navmesh and two chunk actors moved **not one of 1141 reachability
answers**. Two measurements, different shapes, same finding.

It also means the stale binding cost nothing THIS time, which is exactly why it
would have gone on being unenforced. A staleness that happens not to matter is
the most durable kind.

### THE ENFORCEMENT, AND ITS LIMIT STATED AT THE CHECK

    matching nav chunk count (10)    accepted
    a DIFFERENT nav chunk count      refused

**An OFFLINE caller cannot supply the live count** — it is an editor query. So
`expect_nav_chunks=None` means UNCHECKED, not verified, and that is written at
the check rather than left to be inferred from a default argument. A default
that silently means "skip this" is how the first version of this binding came to
be three-quarters unimplemented; naming it keeps the gap visible.

Offline consumers get the agent half and no more. An in-editor caller counting
`NavigationDataChunkActor`s gets a refusal instead of a stale answer.

## 2026-08-26 (later) — A NEGATIVE RESULT FROM A SEARCH IS A STATEMENT ABOUT THE SEARCH

**RETRACTION. The basin is not sealed. There is no rim, there is no wall, and
there was never anything to cut.** The operator had already ruled CUT THE RAMP
on the strength of the finding withdrawn here; the design step found the ruling
moot before any terrain was touched. That is the one thing that went right.

Every "unreachable" verdict in this project's rim work came from ONE
`get_path_length` call from the plaza. A path query has a finite search budget,
and a query that exhausts it returns FAIL — which, from a single call, is
indistinguishable from ground that cannot be walked to.

The discriminating test needed no terrain edit at all:

    A  plaza  -> 520 m    FAIL      (and it reports a partial length, 424 m)
    B  350 m  -> 520 m    SUCCESS   189 m
    C  plaza  -> 350 m    SUCCESS   373 m

**B and C both succeed while A fails.** The walk from the plaza to the far point
IS C followed by B. Reachability over a navmesh is transitive when every leg is
a real path, so a relay through an intermediate point settles it.

### SIX MEASUREMENTS ALREADY POINTED HERE AND I EXPLAINED EVERY ONE AWAY

    terrain 93.0% walkable at the agent bar, no continuous steep band at 1 m
    agent-radius erosion to 2.0 m does not disconnect it
    919 of 925 probe points PROJECT -- the navmesh exists out there
    nav_dz p50 12.4 cm reachable vs 13.4 cm "island" -- same surface, same datum
    offline model vs navmesh: 91.5% on PROJECTS, 48.9% on REACHABLE
    24 bearings: furthest reachable 252-504 m, median 360

**The last one is the tell I read backwards.** I wrote that a uniform profile
across 24 bearings meant a uniform WALL, and that "the best bearing is only 1.4x
the median" made a natural pass unlikely. It means the opposite: **a roughly
circular limit centred on the query START is the shape a BUDGET makes, and the
shape terrain does not make.** Real terrain barriers are irregular. I had the
evidence for the right conclusion and used it to strengthen the wrong one.

**And the model-vs-navmesh calibration said it outright.** A model that predicts
"is there navmesh here" at 91.5% and "can you get there" at 48.9% is telling you
that reachability is not a property of the surface. I wrote that number down,
labelled the model a PREFILTER, and moved on.

### THE TOWN IS NOT 78% REACHABLE EITHER

Re-testing each "unreachable" street from the NEAREST reachable row rather than
from the plaza:

    recovered via relay   136 of 185
    still unreachable      39
    failed projection      10
    positive control      10 of 10 known-reachable rows still pass
    negative control      a point 50 km away does not project

**653 -> at least 789 of 838. 77.9% -> 94.2%.** The remaining 39 may recover
with a longer relay chain; nobody has tried.

### WHY THE INSTRUMENT WAS BELIEVED

It was CONSISTENT. Every bearing agreed, every re-run agreed, the numbers were
stable across sampling intervals and across two navmesh builds. **Consistency is
exactly what a budget produces** — it is a property of the query, so it
reproduces perfectly. Non-negotiable 0 warns that agreement among instruments
sharing a source is one measurement; this is the same failure with ONE
instrument asked many times, which is not even that.

The corroboration I did have was real and I mis-scoped it. Projection and path
query are genuinely different calls — but they answer different questions, and
"projects everywhere, reachable nowhere" was treated as two instruments agreeing
that something was wrong with the ground, when it is one instrument saying the
ground is fine and another saying the search stopped.

### WHAT IT INVALIDATES

- the ramp ruling — moot, and no terrain was touched
- `city/alpine_basin_town_reachable.json` understates reachability, and every
  consumer inherits it
- the encounter planner's "the basin cannot hold encounters", which rests on
  that sidecar's availability figures
- the east extension's "navigable ground the player cannot walk to"

### AND A CONTROL THAT CRASHED AFTER PRODUCING ITS HEADLINE

The first run of the relay recheck died with `IndexError` — `loc_cm` is `[x, y]`
and I indexed `[2]` for a z — **in the negative-control block, after the "136
recovered" figure was already in the payload.** It reported `ok: false` with the
answer sitting right there.

A number that arrives without its control is not a result, and a run that
reports `ok: false` has not produced one no matter how complete the output
looks. Fixed and re-run; both controls then passed.

## 2026-08-27 — THE SAMPLE WAS THE LIMIT, NOT THE WORLD (unit 9 closes)

With the search-budget error corrected, the whole chain it had blocked came
apart in one sitting. Three separate defects, and every one of them was about
WHERE WE LOOKED rather than what was there.

### 1. A "GROUND" TRACE THAT DOES NOT EXCLUDE WHAT STANDS ON THE GROUND

The rewritten reachable-region payload traced the collidable ground before
projecting — correct in principle, and a genuinely better datum than the plan's
own heightmap-derived z. It excluded FOLIAGE from the trace and nothing else.

The result looked like a regression: 17 streets reachable in the old sidecar and
unreachable in the new one, reproducibly, all of them projecting. Measured from
both datums side by side:

    reachable from planned z    17 of 17
    reachable from ground z      0 of 17
    planned - ground         -1293 cm

**Twelve point nine metres.** The trace was landing on BUILDING ROOFS, and a
navmesh projection from roof height finds no reachable polygon.

`city_verify_payload.txt` already carried that exclusion, with a comment saying
exactly why — *"otherwise a building traces onto its neighbour's roof"* — and I
had read that comment earlier the same day. With city actors ignored: **136
gained, 0 lost**, a strict superset of the old measurement, which is what a
correct relay must be.

**A trace answers "what is above this point", not "where is the ground".** The
difference only shows up where something is standing there.

### 2. THE REACHABLE REGION SAMPLED ONLY THE TOWN, SO NOTHING OUTSIDE IT COULD EVER QUALIFY

The sidecar's rows are street midpoints and building doorsteps — every one
INSIDE the settlement. So `near_reachable` returned True only inside the town,
and the encounter rule *"OUTSIDE the settlement AND near reachable ground"* was
**unsatisfiable by construction.**

That is what produced "the basin cannot hold encounters", and I wrote it up as a
fact about the world — *"in this basin those are the SAME GROUND"* — with a
`WORLD_VISION` citation about remoteness to explain why it was correct and even
desirable. **The reasoning was elegant and the premise was an artefact of the
sample.** A satisfying explanation for a measurement is not evidence the
measurement is right; if anything it makes the measurement harder to doubt.

The fix is a LATTICE over the whole built navmesh — grid BFS, a cell joins when
a path exists from an already-reachable 4-neighbour:

    cells 1431 at 40 m over 2.163 km2   projecting 1423   REACHABLE 1261
    path queries 1557 -- about one per cell

**Every query is between ADJACENT cells**, so none approaches the search budget.
That is the same transitive-closure idea as the relay, done cheaply enough to
cover a whole region rather than a list of features.

Then: available 6191 of 8646 cells (71.61%) = 1.549 km², target 6, **placed 6**,
and all six VERIFIED reachable in the editor against the built navmesh.

### 3. THE VERIFIER CARRIED THE VERY DEFECT IT WAS CHECKING FOR

`city_encounter_verify_payload` reported all 6 encounters unreachable on its
first run. It asked one query from the spawn. It now tries direct, then relays
off the nearest measured lattice point, and only a failure of BOTH is
unreachable.

**All six come back via RELAY and none directly** — which is exactly what
"outside the settlement" should look like, and is a small independent
confirmation that the budget, not the ground, was the limit.

**AND THAT MADE ITS LENGTH FIELD A LIE.** A relay length is only the last leg,
from an anchor at most one lattice step away. `path_len_m` read 15.2–60.0 m for
encounters sited outside a 940 m town. Every row now records WHICH leg answered,
the summary counts them, and the length range is renamed
`path_len_m_DIRECT_ONLY` with relay rows excluded. **A number whose meaning
depends on a branch must carry the branch.**

### WHAT THE WORLD ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE NOW

The corrected relay sweep, 12 bearings to 1500 m:

    furthest 1050 m   median 600 m   min 350 m

and almost every ray stops **exactly on a NavBounds volume edge** — bearing 0 at
x −1598 against an east edge of −1588; bearing 90 at y 3308 against a north edge
of 3308; bearing 150 at x −2628 against a west edge of −2628. **The playable
world is bounded by where navmesh was BUILT, not by terrain.** That is a
completely different situation from a sealed basin, and an entirely fixable one.


---

## 2026-08-27 — THE WORLD BECOMES WALKABLE, AND WHAT CALIBRATION IS ACTUALLY FOR

Full navmesh coverage: 72 volumes from one recipe declaration, 64 chunk actors,
**36.53 km² of ground the player can reach** against 1.5 km² yesterday.

The ruling was fable's under the operator's standing delegation, and the useful
thing it did first was **find that the decision had already been taken**.
`PHASE2_PLAN:250` reads *"Unit 8 builds one chunk. The other 63 are a decision,
not a plan"*, and unit 8's own note rules the navigable region to be authored,
versioned recipe data. I had framed this as "how much navmesh does the content
need" and was told the prior question is different and already answered: **the
ruled boundary is the region edge, so every metre between the navmesh edge and
the region edge is an unruled invisible wall** — and this project had just spent
a week diagnosing one of those as a sealed basin.

### THE CALIBRATION EARNED ITS COST TWICE, AND NEITHER TIME WAS "IS IT SAFE"

    volumes    nav MB    wall s    peak GB    chunk actors
       2        35.18      36.0      20.0        10
       3        48.14      42.0      20.4        12
       9       116.01      46.0      20.6        16
      72       756.58     110.0      22.2        64

**FIRST: the two-volume figures were unrepresentative in a way I could not have
guessed.** They came from the only two tiles in the region that are basin-flat
AND had 2,541 trees cleared out of them. A full-density forest tile (6,782
trees) cost +12.96 MB and +6 s — and bought **+0.76 km² of reachable ground from
a 1.08 km² tile**, which is the number that actually matters and which no cost
figure would have produced.

**SECOND, AND IT CHANGED THE PLAN: THE BUILDER IS NOT INCREMENTAL.** 13 packages
created, 10 DELETED. It discards every chunk actor and regenerates. So per-tile
cost is not additive across runs, and the batching I had planned bounds RISK —
learning the curve as you go — rather than bounding peak memory, which is what I
had assumed it was for. Peak commit then turned out to be nearly flat (20.0 →
22.2 GB across a 36× increase in coverage) because the builder streams cells.

**The predictions from the 9-volume point held**: ~830 MB predicted against
756.58 actual, and every bar cleared with room. That is what a cost curve is
for — not reassurance, but the ability to say what the next order of magnitude
costs before paying for it.

### TWO INDEPENDENT CALCULATIONS OF THE SAME THING AGREED

The recipe's own tile-budget check computes 388,622 tiles for the union; the
engine's own warning reports `maxTiles` calculated at 401,843. **3.4% apart,
from completely different code**, and 38% of the 1,048,576 hard limit. The
engine recreated its `dtNavMesh` at 19 bits to hold them — handling the growth
rather than clamping, which is the failure mode the budget check exists to
prevent.

### AND THE GUARDS BUILT THIS WEEK ALL FIRED, ON REAL DRIFT

**The binding check refused to merge two navmesh builds.** Installing the new
region lattice made `reachability.py` say: *"the lattice was measured against 64
navmesh chunk actors and the town sidecar against 10 — different builds."* That
check was added the same morning after finding a sidecar declaring 8 chunks
against a world with 10, where the staleness happened to cost nothing. **A
staleness that happens not to matter is the most durable kind**, and this is
what it was insurance against.

**The stamps caught a cross-cutting change.** Adding 72 volumes to
`recipes/alpine_8k.json` moved an input of the town plan, four foliage plans and
the lattice; every one reported STAMP DIFFERS naming that file. All were
regenerated and compared field by field: **content that moved, NOTHING.** 303
buildings, 838 streets, 219,659 trees byte-identical. The stamp did exactly the
job it was written for — it did not tell me something was wrong, it told me
what to re-derive and then let me prove nothing had.

### THE ENCOUNTER GATE REFUSED TWICE, AND THE SECOND REFUSAL WAS THE LESSON

At the shipped 60 m proximity radius, 7 of 440 encounters projected but were not
reachable. Tightening to 30 m gave 3 of 320 — and **one survivor sits 8.1 m from
a reachable lattice cell.**

An 8 m miss is not a resolution problem. Those are genuine small pockets, ground
beside the reachable region across a gap the agent will not cross, and **no
radius separates them from legitimate ground without discarding most of the
region.** Proximity to a sampled lattice is a PREFILTER; the path query is the
authority, and tightening the prefilter further would have been fitting it to
the answer — the exact thing this project refused to do to the offline
walkability model.

**So the navmesh's verdict feeds FORWARD instead.** The plan stays
byte-reproducible at `encounters/<region>_all.json`; the adopted set at
`_verified.json` is the plan minus what the navmesh refused, hash-stamped
against BOTH sources. Editing the plan in place would have destroyed the
property `check_plan_freshness --reproduce` exists to test. **A placer reads the
verified file; a plan stays a plan.**

**One radius rule worth keeping:** a proximity radius must be well INSIDE the
resolution of the measurement it queries, never equal to it. 60 m against a 60 m
lattice admits a candidate a full cell from anything measured.

### WHAT WAS NOT DONE, AND WHY

**Nothing was placed.** 317 verified encounter sites exist and nothing spawns
them. Writing a placer is unblocked; running it is not, because placing
wilderness content sits behind `WORLD_VISION` item 4's POI tripwire, which
reserves reconfirmation to the operator. Generation is delegated; placement is
not, and the difference was stated in the ruling rather than discovered later.

## 2026-08-27 — THE AUDIT CAUGHT ME WRITING ASPIRATIONAL DOCUMENTATION

Unit 10's first half — `AEncounterMarker` and `UEncounterDirectorSubsystem` —
went to the auditor before first compilation. Seven findings, three major, and
**the sharpest was about my own prose rather than my code.**

The director's header said the subsystem *"owns the spawn and despawn of
encounter pawns"*, that *"the pawn is spawned at bIsSpatiallyLoaded = false"*,
and carried a bold rule that *"SPAWNING REFUSES WHEN NAVMESH PROJECTION FAILS"*.

**It spawned nothing. It despawned nothing. It owned no pawns.** Two counters
tallied refusals of spawns that could never have happened. There is no enemy
pawn class yet — that is unit 12 — and I had written the header for the class I
intended rather than the class I wrote.

This is non-negotiable 25 in its purest form, and the mechanism is worth naming:
**a header written before the implementation describes the design; a header left
unedited after a smaller implementation describes a lie.** The gap was never a
decision. Nothing re-checks a comment, so the moment the scope narrowed the
prose became false and stayed false silently. The header now leads with what the
class does NOT do, and says where the missing half lives.

### THE TWO LOGIC DEFECTS BOTH CAME FROM THE SAME WRONG MODEL

I wrote the director as if a marker were a stable object. It is not — markers are
spatially loaded BY DESIGN, which is the entire point of the class.

**Discovery was single-shot and wrong in both directions.** Rescanning only when
`Markers.Num() == 0` meant a world with genuinely zero markers walked a full
`TActorIterator` over 2,500+ external actors every half-second forever; and once
ONE marker was found the list never returned to empty — stale weak pointers
still count toward `Num()` — so **every marker that streamed in later was
invisible to the director permanently.** The comment promising "the next
evaluation retries once the chunk arrives" was false for the same reason.

**Active state keyed on the actor pointer lost identity across exactly the event
the design exists to survive.** A `TWeakObjectPtr` hashes on object index and
serial number, so a marker streamed out and back is a DIFFERENT key. Stale
entries were removed nowhere, so the set grew without bound — and the
per-evaluation recount of active encounters, which I had written as a
correctness measure, was *masking* the leak: the reported number stayed sane
while the set diverged from it with no instrument watching.

The durable identity was already on the marker: `(PlanId, PlanRowIndex)`, the
plan row it came from, which I had put there for traceability and then not used
for the one thing that needed it. **An encounter is a plan row, not an actor** —
so a site whose marker streams out now stays active deliberately, because its
cell coming and going is not the player leaving it.

### WHAT THE AUDIT DID NOT FIND, AND WHY THAT MATTERS TOO

Zero compile or link defects. Every API name — the subsystem base and its
override signatures, `bIsSpatiallyLoaded` as a constructor write, the three-arg
`ProjectPointToNavigation`, the stat macro, `SetHidden` in a constructor — was
checked at engine source and confirmed. **The design was buildable and the
reasoning was wrong**, which is the split this project keeps rediscovering:
getting the number right from a wrong premise produces confident, wrong output.

It built clean first try in 16.4 s and verified on a cold boot: both classes
reflected, 7 of 7 and 6 of 6 properties reading back, `is_spatially_loaded`
true, the hysteresis invariant asserted on the shipped defaults, and a negative
control confirming a class that should not resolve does not.

**Still unproven, and stated rather than implied:** no marker actor exists in any
level, the director has never ticked against a real marker, and unit 10's
acceptance test has not run. A reflected name is not a working feature.


---

## 2026-08-27 — AN INSTRUMENT CAN OUTLIVE THE WORLD IT WAS BUILT FOR

Unit 5's acceptance clause is *"walk 1 km without falling through and without a
step-height stall"*, and `walk_character.py` implements it by driving a STRAIGHT
LINE from the PlayerStart with no steering. It passed on 2026-08-15 at 1000.1 m.

Today it stalled at **27.3 m**, and then at **57.5 m** on a second heading.

**Nothing about the world got worse. A town was built on the spawn.** The
PlayerStart now sits in a plaza ringed by 303 buildings, and measured over 72
headings: **65 are blocked within 100 m, and the best runs 156 m.** A 1 km
straight walk from this spawn is impossible in every direction.

R-WALKTEST already carried the sentence that explains it — *"a straight-line
walker with no steering stops there forever; that is the test's property, not
the world's"* — written when every heading from the spawn was open ground. **The
sentence stayed true and its consequence inverted**, because the world moved
underneath it. That is a different failure from a stale claim: nothing in the
record was wrong, and the instrument still silently stopped measuring what it
was built to measure.

**The narrow thing the walks DO prove is worth keeping:** `is_falling` 0.1% over
2,312 samples across both runs. The ground holds. Traversability at scale is
proven better elsewhere — 36.5 km² reachable by path query — so the walk test's
remaining job is local, not global, and it should be described that way.

### AND A PREFILTER WAS WRONG, THEN CALIBRATED, WHICH IS THE PART TO KEEP

`find_walk_heading.py` picks a heading offline so a PIE run is not spent
guessing. Its first version read the heightmap and the city plan, called yaw 260
clear for 238 m, and the character stalled at 57.5.

**Its own docstring had predicted that failure** — it could not see foliage, and
~3,700 trees stand in the gaps between structures. Trees are query-collidable BY
DESIGN (R-TREECOLLIDE made them so and a PIE trace proved it), so a trunk stops
a straight-line walker exactly as a wall does.

219,659 tree positions were already on disk in `foliage/*.json`, so seeing them
cost a file read rather than an editor query. It now predicts both measured
stalls, and predicts them CONSERVATIVELY:

    yaw   model says             character measured
     30   22 m (building at 24)      27.3 m
    260   42 m (tree at 44)          57.5 m

**Conservative is the right direction for a tool used to CHOOSE a test.** A
prefilter that overshoots sends you to run an expensive test that fails; one
that undershoots merely costs you a slightly better option.

`--no-foliage` is kept so the improvement stays MEASURABLE rather than asserted:
47 of 72 headings blocked without trees, 65 of 72 with them. A tool that quietly
got better cannot be checked later.

**And the docstring and the printed footer were both updated**, because "It
cannot see foliage" became false the moment it could. Stale prose in a tool's
own self-description is the defect this project keeps finding in other people's
files, and it takes about a minute to introduce.

### THE THIRD THING, AND IT IS OPERATIONAL

**I orphaned a tick driver.** A 120 s tool timeout killed `walk_character`'s
driver process while its `register_slate_post_tick_callback` kept running inside
the editor — logging to nobody for 410 s, and after PIE ended it was ticking
against a dead world. The tool's cleanup runs on ITS completion paths, which a
killed driver never reaches.

Stopped externally by ending PIE; the callback count went 47 → 47 over 25 s,
which is how I know it stopped rather than assuming. **A tool that installs an
ENGINE callback needs an external stop, not only an internal one** — because the
thing most likely to kill it is not its own code path.


---

## 2026-08-27 — I ADDED A FIELD TO ONE OF TWO TRACE DUMPS, AND THE ONE I MISSED WAS THE RECOVERY PATH

`walk_character.py` gained a residency series: how many landscape proxies and
foliage actors World Partition keeps resident around a moving pawn. The series
is written into the trace file at the end of the run.

**There are TWO places that write that file.** `PAYLOAD_STOP` is the ordinary
teardown. `PAYLOAD_FORCE_STOP` is the one that runs when `PAYLOAD_STOP`'s reply
does not come back — and that reply has been lost on three separate completed
walks, which is precisely why the forced path exists.

I added the new fields to the ordinary one. The auditor found the other.

**The severity is the wrong way round from how it looks.** A missing field on
the happy path is an inconvenience; you re-run. This was a missing field on the
path that runs *when the run cannot be reported*, i.e. on the only occasion the
file is the sole surviving copy. The defect was invisible in every successful
run and would have appeared exactly once, on the run that could least afford it.

### ROOT CAUSE: TWO LITERALS FOR ONE REQUIREMENT

The dump was written out twice, as two `_json.dump({...})` literals inside two
payload template strings. Nothing connected them. Non-negotiable 24 names this
shape exactly — *two lists that must agree are one list, badly stored* — and its
test is the one that applies here: **if adding a thing can be done in one place
and forgotten in another, the structure is wrong, not the author.**

The fix is not "add the fields to the second literal", which reproduces the
defect the next time a field is added. The dump is now ONE declaration,
`_TRACE_DUMP`, projected into both payloads by `_trace_dump(indent)` and
substituted at import, with two assertions:

    no payload may still carry an unsubstituted placeholder
    every payload must still contain the dump

**A PAYLOAD IS A CALL SITE WITH NO COMPILER.** That sentence is already in this
file, from the 2026-08-21 groom-binding drift where a payload passed four
arguments to a five-argument UFUNCTION. The import-time assertions are the
compiler this call site does not have, and they are the part that makes the
single declaration load-bearing rather than decorative — a shared constant that
nothing checks is still two copies once someone re-inlines one.

### WHAT CAUGHT IT, AND WHAT DID NOT

Not the syntax check, not the placeholder audit I wrote myself, and not the
key-set comparison I ran after the fact — that last one compared the two dumps
and printed AGREE, because by then I had already patched the second literal by
hand. **A check written after a fix confirms the fix; it cannot find the
defect.** The auditor read both payloads against each other before either ran.

This is the audit gate doing the job the constitution claims for it: *reach for
review when the cost of being wrong is not recoverable by git.* A lost trace
from a PIE run is not in git and never was.

### THE GENERAL RULE

**A TEARDOWN THAT WRITES A SUBSET IS A SILENT PARTIAL LOSS.** Whenever a tool
has an ordinary exit and an emergency exit that both persist state, the
emergency one must persist the SAME state — by construction, not by care —
because it runs on the occasion when nothing else will.

## 2026-08-27 — THE WALK TEST STILL WORKS PERFECTLY. THE WORLD MOVED UNDER IT.

Unit 10 owes a PIE residency figure at mounted speed. The tool for it is
`walk_character.py`, which walked 1000.1 m cleanly on 2026-08-15 and has been
stamped PROVEN since. It ran twice today and STALLED both times, at 29.2 m and
58.4 m.

**Nothing about the tool regressed. The spawn moved into a town.**

On 2026-08-26 the `PlayerStart` moved from a forest clearing 8,245 m out to the
basin town, at yaw 35 *facing the landmark* — deliberately, because the landmark
is the first thing a player should see. The landmark is an 11 × 11 × 34 m solid
volume 29 m away, and `walk_character` drives the pawn in a straight line with
no steering.

So the first run walked into it and stood there for 291 seconds. **The stall
report was the instrument being right**, and for about a minute I read it as the
instrument being broken.

### THE PREMISE THAT EXPIRED WITHOUT ANYONE EDITING IT

R-WALKTEST's procedure says *"a straight line on a declared heading from the
spawn point, and says so"*, and it was careful about the one limitation it knew
of — that this is not the inter-massif corridor. It could not be careful about a
limitation that did not exist when it was written: **the spawn was in a forest,
where the only obstacles are foliage the walker brushes past.**

A recipe stamped PROVEN records that a procedure worked *against the world it
was proven on*. Nothing re-checks that premise when the world changes, and the
town landed a full day before this ran. This is the same shape as R13's
CALIBRATION CLASS — a number that is not wrong, but belongs to conditions that
have moved — except here it is a PROCEDURE rather than a figure, and procedures
do not usually carry their calibration class.

### THE SECOND HEADING WAS CHOSEN BY MEASUREMENT AND STILL FAILED

Rather than guess again, `scripts/find_clear_heading.py` marches every bearing
against the 1,446 planned footprints, inflated by the pawn's 34 cm capsule so
contact happens at a wall rather than at a centre:

    from the PlayerStart, to 1200 m
      including street slabs   0 of 360 bearings clear, first blocker at 57 m
      excluding street slabs   9 of 360 (2.5%)
      widest clear arc         3.0 deg, centred on bearing 259

Bearing 259 was taken from that, and the pawn contacted a building at 58.4 m
anyway. **A 3° arc is 2.6 m wide at 50 m**, and an unsteered walker drifts more
than that. The tool reports the arc's CENTRE and warns in its own output that a
clear bearing with blocked neighbours is a gap between two buildings — which is
exactly what 3° is. The warning was right and 3° was never enough.

**The finding worth carrying is the first row: with street slabs counted, ZERO
of 360 bearings are clear.** The town does not merely obstruct a straight walk
out of it; it forecloses one.

### WHAT I DID NOT DO, AND WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN WHAT I DID

Residency WAS sampled on both runs: 3–4 landscape proxies, 10–11 foliage actors.
That is a real number from a real PIE session and it is **residency at rest,
inside a town** — the pawn spent 291 s and 175 s of those runs stationary.

Reporting it as "streaming at mounted speed" would have closed the owed item on
the board today. It is arithmetically true and it answers a question nobody
asked — non-negotiable 22, the misleading denominator. The owed figure is
residency UNDER MOTION, and it is still not obtained.

**The instrument half did land and is proven.** `--speed-cm-s` is gated twice:
the property must read back within 0.5 *and* the trace's own achieved speed must
reach 0.9 of commanded. The second gate returned **p50 1800, max 1800, = 1.00**.
Only the first would have been the read-back-the-field-you-wrote error — a pawn
capped by acceleration or root motion reads 1800 on the component while
travelling at 600, and the artefact would certify streaming at a speed nothing
ever moved at.

### THE RULE

**A PROVEN PROCEDURE CARRIES THE WORLD IT WAS PROVEN ON.** When a world-shaping
change lands — a settlement, a spawn move, a terrain adoption — the tools whose
premises that change touches have not been re-proven, and their stamps do not
know it. The cheap version of this is not re-proving everything; it is asking,
at the moment of the change, *which instrument's assumptions did I just
invalidate.* Moving the PlayerStart into a town invalidated the straight-line
walker, and the entry that recorded the move did not mention it.

travelling at 600, and the artefact would certify streaming at a speed nothing
ever moved at.

### THE RULE

**A PROVEN PROCEDURE CARRIES THE WORLD IT WAS PROVEN ON.** When a world-shaping
change lands — a settlement, a spawn move, a terrain adoption — the tools whose
premises that change touches have not been re-proven, and their stamps do not
know it. The cheap version of this is not re-proving everything; it is asking,
at the moment of the change, *which instrument's assumptions did I just
invalidate.* Moving the PlayerStart into a town invalidated the straight-line
walker, and the entry that recorded the move did not mention it.

## 2026-08-27b — THE EDITOR AGREED WITH ME FOUR TIMES WHILE THE DISK DID NOT

Four separate operations today reported success, read back correctly, and wrote
nothing:

    disabling three DirectionalLights   components read back   0 dirty
    spawning 317 EncounterMarkers       counted_in_world 317   0 dirty, 0 files
    destroying a duplicate actor        registry says gone     file still there
    re-placing 1,446 city actors        ok true                1,447 orphans left

**In every one the editor was RIGHT and the disk was STALE**, and no check that
reads the editor could see the difference. World Partition streams from the
packages, so PIE and a cold boot get the old state.

### THE COUNTER I WAS TRUSTING DOES NOT COUNT WHAT I NEEDED

`get_dirty_content_packages()` returned **0** through all four. It reports
packages pending a WRITE. It does not report:

- a component property set through a live actor (`actor.modify()` is not enough
  when the change is on the COMPONENT)
- an actor spawned into an OFPA world
- a package pending DELETION

That last one is the dangerous one. After destroying 1,446 city actors and
placing 1,446 replacements, disk held **4,713 packages against 3,266 live
actors**. A cold boot would have loaded all 4,713 and drawn the town — and all
317 encounter markers — **twice**. Nothing in the editor said so.

**The only instrument that saw it was `save_level.py`**, which enumerates the
world's own package list rather than the dirty set, and it named all 1,447 as
OWNED. That tool was written in August for a different reason and it is the one
that caught this.

### THE PROMOTION, AND WHY THE FOURTH INSTANCE AND NOT THE FIFTH

Non-negotiable 4a promotes a trap class to shared infrastructure on the SECOND
tool, without waiting for a third. This class had already reached three
(foliage collision 2026-08-16, navmesh SetConfig 2026-08-17) and was patched
locally each time. `scripts/save_tagged_actors.py` is the shared implementation:
select by TAG or CLASS, `set_dirty_flag`, `save_loaded_assets(...,
only_if_is_dirty=False)`.

**Its verdict comes from `git status`, not from the editor's reply**, and it
REFUSES if the editor says saved and no file moved — the exact defect, occurring
inside the tool that exists to prevent it. An unreadable git is COULD NOT LOOK
and also refuses, because an empty set would read as "nothing changed" and fail
in the wrong direction.

`save_foliage_actors.py` remains the earlier single-purpose copy. Declared, not
accepted.

### AND I RE-DERIVED A PROVEN TRANSPORT AND LOST A ROUND TO IT

The first version of `save_tagged_actors` opened its own remote-exec connection
and staged its payload as `.txt`. It got an EMPTY reply with no error:
`MODE_EXEC_FILE` hands the path to the engine's `ExecuteFile`, which wants a
real `.py`. `ue_exec.py` has staged as `.py` since it was written. **Step (a) is
a search, not a recall** — and the toolbox listing I ran at the start of this
session had `ue_exec.py` in it.

## 2026-08-27b — THERE WERE FOUR SUNS, AND THE ANSWER WAS IN OUR OWN COMMENT

The editor warned that multiple directional lights were competing. I expected
two. There were four: the recipe's sun at 130,000 lux and three `HeroStage_*`
rig lights adding **43,750 lux from three directions at 6500 K**, all four
claiming atmosphere sun index 0 at priority 0.

They are R-HEROCAP's flat-lit face-comparison rig, built in `/Game/Alpine8K`
rather than a scratch level, and swept into the world by the city placement's
save on 2026-08-24. **Every render proof since then was taken under an undefined
sun**, including unit 11's Rock/Grass separation render from earlier the same
day.

### THE FIRST THING I DID WAS GUESS AN ACCESSOR

`DirectionalLight.directional_light_component` raises. It IS in the 5.8 stub —
as an **EditorOnly READ-ONLY reference** — which is exactly why the wrong name
looks right until it runs. The correct one is `light_component`, and
`apply_lighting.py:246-248` already says so in a comment written for a previous
occurrence of this:

    "light_component on EVERY light actor -- there is no
     directional_light_component / sky_light_component."

Non-negotiable 23, in a file this project wrote, against a comment left
specifically to prevent it. `Package.is_dirty` and `Package.mark_package_dirty`
do not exist either; the pair that does is
`EditorAssetSubsystem.set_dirty_flag` / `save_loaded_assets`.

### WHAT MADE THE FIX SAFE WAS REFUSING TO USE THE LABEL

`build_capture_stage.py` tears its own rig down by label prefix, which is right
for a rig rebuilding itself. This was a different operation — saved, committed
actors in the game world — and standing rule 8 applies: this project has two
landscapes whose proxies carried identical labels.

The signature used is **AGREEMENT WITH THE RECIPE**: intensity within 1 lux and
pitch within 0.5° of `lighting.sun`. It REFUSES unless exactly one light
matches, and both directions were proven before it was allowed to act — a recipe
whose sun matches nothing REFUSED and changed nothing; a recipe rewritten to
describe `HeroStage_Key` kept THAT light and called the real sun foreign. The
second control is what proves it is a property test and not a name test.

## 2026-08-27b — A PASS FROM A TEST WITH NO POWER, AND THEN A FLOOR THAT MEASURED THE WRONG THING

Unit 10's acceptance is that nav data is resident before the marker on it. The
first version of the test flew the streaming source between the marker cloud's
corners at a fixed 838 m altitude and reported **PASS** with **one** marker
resident at every step.

Zero offenders out of one observation is not evidence that streaming orders
correctly. It is evidence that almost nothing streamed — World Partition is
distance-based in 3D and flying high silently shrank what was in range.

**Then the floor I added to catch that was also wrong.** It gated on how many
markers were resident AT ONCE and called a clean run INCONCLUSIVE at 1. But 317
markers over 66 km² sit ~460 m apart and the loading range is smaller, so **one
resident at a time is correct behaviour**. The evidence accumulates in (marker,
step) PAIRS across the traverse, not in concurrency.

The underlying rule survived both corrections and is worth stating plainly:
**a clean result from a test that observed almost nothing is not a pass.** Only
the denominator moved. Non-negotiable 6 — "I looked and it's absent" versus "I
couldn't look" — and an underpowered pass is the second wearing the first's
clothes.

Two smaller things from the same tool. `editor_request_end_play` is a REQUEST,
so reading `get_game_world()` in the same payload asks whether it finished
before it had the chance; both earlier runs printed STILL IN PLAY over a
teardown that worked. And `ue_exec.run` returns THREE values, not two.

## 2026-08-27b — THE VERIFIER AND THE OPERATOR'S EYE WERE BOTH RIGHT ABOUT THE STREETS

`city_verify_payload` reported `base_above_ground max 0.0 cm`. The operator's
eye-level screenshot showed daylight under the street slabs. Both were correct,
and the reconciliation is geometric: **the verifier traces under each actor's
ORIGIN, and a slab is not a point.**

A flat 15 m × 7 m box on ground sloping 2–8° touches at its centre and lifts at
its ends. Measured over all 838 streets: centre gap p50 0.3 cm, worst corner gap
**p50 67.9, max 442.0**. This is the misleading-denominator class (non-negotiable
22) in geometric form — the number was true about the point it measured and
answered a question nobody asked.

### THE INSTRUMENT I BUILT TO MEASURE THE FIX COULD NOT SEE IT

My first corner-gap payload computed each corner's slab height from the PLAN's
centre Z — i.e. it assumed the slab was flat. **That quantity is invariant under
rotating the slab.** It returned byte-identical numbers before and after the fix
and would have reported the fix as having done nothing.

An instrument whose reading cannot move when the thing it measures moves is not
measuring that thing. It now reads the PLACED ACTORS' transforms and carries a
positive control on its own input: if no slab has a tilt, any improvement is
coming from somewhere else.

### THE CONVENTION WAS SETTLED BY MEASUREMENT BECAUSE REASONING HAS LOST HERE THREE TIMES

The plane fit's values were right — scored analytically against one set of
ground traces, (+pitch, +roll) gave p50 14.1 against FLAT's 45.9. The placed
world still read 60.0, so the error was in how the ENGINE applies
`Rotator(ROLL, PITCH, YAW)`.

Rather than reason about which axis a positive pitch raises in a left-handed
Z-up space — the exact reasoning that has produced three separate roll/pitch
defects in this project — all four sign combinations were applied to the placed
actors and re-traced over all 838 streets:

    p+ r-   p50  10.9   over 50 cm 107   <- adopted
    p+ r+   p50  60.0   over 50 cm 484
    p- r-   p50  85.6   over 50 cm 597
    p- r+   p50 130.6   over 50 cm 757
    flat    p50  67.9   over 50 cm 558

**Roll is negated at the ENGINE BOUNDARY, not in the plan.** The plan stores the
ground plane's slope, which is a physical fact; the placer converts it to the
renderer's convention. Pass boundaries organise work; they do not partition
truth.

The offline heightmap model predicted p50 9.2 and engine collision measured
10.9 — two representations agreeing, which is what makes the fix believable.

## 2026-08-27b — A CHECKER'S FIRST RUN PROVED ITS OWN RULE WRONG, TWICE

Ruling 5 permits prose keys in planner recipes under three conditions, and
`check_prose_keys.py` was written to enforce them because a schema rule nothing
checks is a claim compiled into text (non-negotiable 25).

Its first run reported four violations. **None was a defect.**

Three were `_`-prefixed keys holding non-strings: `site._selection_bars` (a
documentation block whose leaves include `cell_m: 8.0`), `meshes._cube_extent_cm`
(100.0, recorded so a reader knows why the scale arithmetic looks as it does)
and `area._area_km2`. Those are recorded MEASUREMENTS inside documentation —
exactly what the keys are for — and nothing reads them. **My type check was a
PROXY for the real invariant and a bad one:** what makes a prose key dangerous
is not its type, it is whether a consumer reads it.

The fourth was `adopt_verified_encounters.py:115`, which **WRITES**
`out["_what"] = ...`. An instrument that cannot tell a write from a read reports
authorship as a violation.

And rule 1 — that every prose key is `_`-prefixed — turns out not to be
machine-checkable from the JSON at all: telling prose from data WITHOUT the
prefix is precisely the judgement the prefix exists to remove. The checker now
enforces rule 2, reports the measurements as information, and says which rule it
cannot decide. The write case is a permanent self-test row.

**Worth noting what did NOT catch the type-check error: the check I ran
afterwards.** By then I had already reasoned it through. A check written after a
fix confirms the fix; it cannot find the defect.

## 2026-08-27c — SEATING EACH SLAB CORRECTLY IS WHAT MAKES THE JOINS WRONG

The eye-level plaza frame closed a proof owed from the previous session: the
street slabs lie flat on the grass and tilt with the ground, with no daylight
under the edges. The fix had been established by measurement — worst corner gap
p50 67.9 → 10.9 cm — and had never been seen.

**The same crop shows the 932 overlapping street pairs**, and the relationship
between the two findings is the lesson. Each slab is pitched to ITS OWN local
ground plane. Adjacent slabs have different local planes. So consecutive
segments meet at a lip, and **the better each slab's individual seating, the
more visible the discontinuity between neighbours.**

This is the per-element-gate class again, in geometry rather than in gates:
*per-element correctness does not compose into whole-network correctness.* The
project has now hit it three times — street segment slopes gated individually
while the network fragmented; building pads gated individually while the town's
extent turned out unreachable; and now slab seating computed individually while
the surface they form is discontinuous.

The fix is the same shape every time: emit the NETWORK as the unit, with shared
edge heights between adjacent segments, rather than emitting elements and hoping
they agree.

### AND ONE DEFECT THE FRAME FOUND THAT NO RE-PLAN WILL FIX

A conifer stands 3–4 m directly in front of the PlayerStart. Press Play and the
first thing the player sees is a trunk.

**It is not a bug in the tree clear.** The clear removes foliage inside
per-structure oriented rectangles plus a margin, and the plaza is DEFINED as
ground with no structures on it — so nothing in the plaza was ever a candidate
for removal. Re-running the clear against kit footprints, which is on the
board, will not touch it either, for the same reason.

**A clear scoped to structures cannot clear a space defined by the absence of
structures.** The plaza needs its own radius, declared separately.

    6.04 CPU-s/s   rendering, delivered the frame late
    1.02 CPU-s/s   busy, answered on the next attempt
    0.01 CPU-s/s   wedged, no modal, no progress

## 2026-08-27d — A CLEAR SCOPED TO STRUCTURES CANNOT CLEAR A SPACE DEFINED BY THEIR ABSENCE

The eye-level frame showed a conifer 3–4 m in front of the PlayerStart. The
town's foliage clear had run, twice, and reported success both times.

**It was correct both times.** The clear tests instances against BUILDINGS,
STREETS and the LANDMARK as oriented rectangles plus a margin. The plaza is
DEFINED in the plan as ground with no buildings on it — `rejected.in_plaza`
counts the ones it refused to put there. So nothing inside the plaza was ever a
candidate for removal, and no margin, however generous, would have reached it:
a margin grows outward from a structure, and the plaza's defining property is
that it has none.

**The general shape: a rule scoped to the presence of a thing has a blind spot
exactly where that thing is absent, and the blind spot is invisible to the rule
itself.** Every count the clear reported was true.

### AND THE RECIPE'S OWN WARNING SAID NOT TO FIX IT THIS WAY

`recipes/city.json` carries, in capitals, *"IT FOLLOWS THE TOWN SHAPE, NOT A
RADIUS"*, with the reasoning: clearing the settlement as a disc leaves a
perfectly circular bald patch, the same error the city plan already made once
when its boundary "came out a PERFECT CIRCLE ... the circle was drawing the edge
and the terrain was not".

That warning is right and it does not transfer. It is about the town EXTENT,
whose true shape is the terrain's. **The plaza IS a declared circle** —
`plan.plaza_radius_m`, a designed open centre. Clearing it as a disc matches its
own geometry instead of imposing one.

**The distinction is worth more than the fix.** A warning written against one
shape can read as a ban on that shape everywhere, and the next reader has no way
to know which it meant. Both readings now sit side by side in the recipe, so the
exception is documented where the rule is.

### THE MARGIN IS ADDED TO THE PLAN'S RADIUS, NOT DECLARED BESIDE IT

The obvious implementation is a `plaza_clear_radius_m` field. That would be a
SECOND number for the plaza's size, and the two would diverge the first time
anyone resized the plaza — non-negotiable 19, a physical fact defined twice.

So the recipe declares a MARGIN and the disc is `plan.plaza_radius_cm + margin`.
Which exposed a real gap: **the plan did not record its own plaza radius.** The
planner used the value to reject buildings and never emitted it. Added; every
other key in the regenerated plan is identical, so nothing needed re-placing.

The payload REFUSES if the plan lacks the field rather than defaulting. A
guessed radius would cut a differently-sized hole and report success — the
failure mode with no symptom.

## 2026-08-27d — 7,949 DIRECTORIES, ZERO FILES, AND THE FOLDER NAMES WERE THE FINDING

The kit was reported added at a specific path. The path existed. It held 7,949
directories and **not one file — not even the `.uproject`**.

### RULING OUT THE EXPLANATION I WAS HANDED

The brief warned about OneDrive Files On-Demand leaving `.uasset` files as cloud
placeholders. That is a real hazard and it was not this one, and the thing that
settled it was a CONTROL rather than more inspection of the failing case:
**`ProjectTitan` sits in the same reparse-pointed OneDrive folder with 3,086
files.** Hydration works there.

Also ruled out: disk (193 GB free); placeholder invisibility (`-Force` sees zero
file entries, and the offline-attribute count is zero *because there are no
entries to carry it*, which is a different statement from "no files are
offline"); and wrong-project targeting (only four `.uproject` files exist on the
machine, newest 2026-08-10, and nothing anywhere was created or modified in the
last 14 hours).

The directory was created **2026-08-10 17:20** — eighteen days before the
session that supposedly created it.

### THE PART THAT MADE THE DEAD END USEFUL

**Directory names survive when file payloads do not**, and 7,949 of them are an
inventory. They identify the pack beyond doubt
(`Content/Maps/DataLayers/MedievalVillage_P_WP`) and, more usefully, they
describe its CONTENTS:

    MedievalModularWall 1x2MA 1x2MB 15x2M 2x2MD 2x2MG 2x2MH 3x2M
    MedievalModularCornerWall1x2M
    MedievalModularDoor 1x2M 15x2M 2x2MA 2x2MB 3x2M
    MedievalModularGable4, Gable4M

**It is a MODULAR WALL KIT, not a set of house meshes** — 2 m tall segments in
1, 1.5, 2 and 3 m widths.

That invalidates the coverage gate I was asked to run. The gate compares
whole-building meshes against 303 footprints at ±20%; a modular kit has no
building meshes, and a footprint is BUILT to size rather than matched. Footprint
coverage would be near-total by tiling, and the binding constraint moves to
height: 2 m modules against the recipe's 3.2 m `storey_m`.

**A blocked unit can still return the thing the unit was for.** The gate existed
to tell the operator whether the town must re-form; the inventory says the
question itself is different, which is more useful than the number would have
been.

**And the instrument is declared:** this is read from DIRECTORY NAMES, not
measured geometry. The `2x2M` convention is a strong read of a naming scheme and
not a measurement of a mesh, and nothing here has been verified against one.
Saying which of those it is costs a sentence and is the difference between
evidence and a number someone will quote back as measured.
