## 2026-08-27d — A TRACE ANSWERED IN 25 SECONDS WHAT A RENDER COSTS 1,470 FOR

"The player must not spawn facing a trunk" reads like a question for a picture.
It is not: it is a question about whether geometry stands in a cone, and a fan
of line traces answers it as a number.

    61 rays, +/-45 deg, 30 m, eye height, on the PlayerStart's own yaw
      CLEAR         48 of 61
      blocked       13, ALL the same actor
      that actor    City_Landmark, confirmed by label and tags
      FOLIAGE HITS  ZERO

25 seconds, against ~840 s for a render on this world plus the ~630 s
remote-exec wedge that follows every capture. And it is re-runnable after any
foliage change, which a render is not, because judging a render is a judgement.

**The trace's polarity is the opposite of every other trace in this project**,
and that is the part worth remembering. The city grounding traces deliberately
EXCLUDE foliage and city actors because they ask where the LANDSCAPE is. This
asks what is standing in FRONT of the player, so foliage must be included — and
the landscape must not count as an obstruction, so terrain hits are tallied
separately rather than inflating the blocked count.

Two more controls, both cheap: the payload refuses unless there is exactly ONE
`PlayerStart` (UE picks among several unpredictably, so a cone measured at one
of them is not the cone the player gets), and the blocking actor was IDENTIFIED
by label rather than inferred from its distance matching the landmark's.

## 2026-08-29 — A RULING WAS HELD FOR A DAY ON A COST THAT DID NOT EXIST

The kit's wall modules are 2.00 m tall and `buildings.storey_m` was 3.2, so no
planned building height was a whole number of courses. The 2026-08-28 write-up
put the fix to the operator like this: changing `storey_m` to 2.00 *"visibly
shortens the town: 2/3/4-storey buildings go from 6.4 / 9.6 / 12.8 m to
4 / 6 / 8 m"* — a 33% cut across 303 buildings. Three readings were written out
and none was chosen, correctly, because a 33% height cut is exactly the kind of
thing that belongs with the operator.

**The premise was wrong, and reading four lines of the planner settled it.**
`plan_city.py:392-395` does not multiply a floor height by a storey count. It
computes a CONTINUOUS height from the falloff and then snaps it:

    h       = (hc + (he - hc) * f) * 100      # continuous, 14.0 -> 6.5 m
    storeys = max(1, int(round(h / (storey_m * 100))))
    h       = storeys * storey_m * 100

**The planner holds the HEIGHT and derives the COUNT.** So `storey_m` is a
quantisation step, and changing it re-quantises the same heights onto a finer
grid. Measured over the whole town: mean height 9.99 -> 9.91 m, a fall of
**0.8%**, with the max snap error against the recipe's own declared falloff
**halving** from 1.59 to 1.00 m and a fourth distinct height appearing. The
change is not a compromise; it is strictly closer to what `height_m` declares.

**THE GENERAL SHAPE: A PARAMETER'S NAME IS A CLAIM ABOUT ITS ROLE, AND THE ROLE
LIVES IN THE CODE.** `storey_m` reads like "how tall is one storey", which
carries an implicit model — that storeys are the fixed thing. The consumer says
otherwise in four lines. This is the same class as `ReductionSettings[0]` being
LOD 0 and `CullDistance` 0 meaning disabled: the number was never in dispute,
the MEANING was, and the meaning is only ever settled at the call site.

**AND THE CONTROL IS WHAT MADE THE PREDICTION SAFE TO ACT ON.** Before touching
anything, the continuous height was reconstructed from each building's distance
from the plaza and re-snapped at 3.2 — it reproduced the shipped plan EXACTLY,
0 mismatches of 303. Only then was the 2.0 prediction worth quoting. A model
that reproduces the present is allowed to predict; one that has not been asked
is arithmetic.

After the change, the things that must not have moved were checked rather than
assumed: building XY, footprint, yaw and pad_z identical on 303 of 303; streets,
landmark, spire and counts identical; roofs moved in z only, because they sit on
walls. That control is what licensed the reachability waiver below — reachability
depends on FOOTPRINTS, and the footprints are byte-identical.

## 2026-08-29 — A REFUSAL THAT SAYS "RECORD WHY" AND GIVES YOU NOWHERE TO RECORD IT

`check_plan_freshness` has always ended a stale verdict with *"Re-run the
producer, or record why the artefact is kept."* **There was no mechanism to
record it.** So when the `storey_m` ruling moved `recipes/city.json` and the
reachability sidecar — produced by an in-editor payload, unreachable offline —
went STAMP DIFFERS, the only ways to a green suite were:

1. fake the stamp (falsifying provenance; `stamp_plan` already REFUSES to
   invent one, so this would have meant working around our own guard), or
2. declare the whole exit code 3 as an expected FINDING in the offline suite —
   which the suite's own comment warns about in as many words: *"a finding code
   left declared after the finding is fixed EXCUSES the next genuine staleness
   in the same tool"*. One stale plan today would have bought permanent
   blindness to all nineteen.

**A tool that names the right remedy and does not implement it pushes its users
toward the two wrong ones.** The mechanism is now `_stamp_waiver` on the plan:
which inputs are accepted as moved, why, when recorded, and what retires it.

It is narrow on purpose. It must name EVERY differing input — one unnamed input
and the plan is stale as before; it must carry a non-empty reason, because a
waiver with no reason is not a waiver but a silenced alarm; it never applies to
UNREADABLE, which is *"I could not look"*; and it prints its reason in full on
every run so it cannot rot quietly.

**A WAIVER IS A GATE TURNED OFF, SO IT GETS WHAT EVERY GATE HERE GETS: PROOF
THAT IT REFUSES.** `--self-test` now runs five waiver cases beside the five
stamp cases — grant, unnamed second input, wrong input, no reason, no waiver —
and the four refusals are the point. The grant on its own would have proved
nothing.

## 2026-08-29 — A GROUND TRACE THAT IGNORES NOTHING MEASURES THE CANOPY

The kit's 15 modules were stood up in `/Game/Alpine8K` for a look test. They
came out **27 metres in the air** — measured, 2717.7 to 2815.4 cm of float
across the row, not eyeballed from the render.

The placement traced ONE point, from z+40000 straight down, with an **empty
ignore list**. The row stood in forest, and the conifers here are 17–33 m tall.
The trace hit a tree.

**THIS PROJECT ALREADY OWNS THIS LESSON AND I STILL WALKED INTO IT.** On
2026-08-27 seventeen streets traced 12.9 m high onto BUILDING ROOFS, and the
rule written down then was *"a 'ground' trace that excludes only foliage
measures the ROOF — exclude `LandscapeLab.City` too."* Mine excluded neither.
The recorded rule is phrased as an ADDITION to an existing exclusion, so it
reads as advice for someone who already has an ignore list. It does not say the
thing that would have caught this: **a ground trace begins with an ignore list,
and an empty one is a defect, not a default.**

Two things made it survive as long as it did:

**The trace succeeded.** It returned a hit, at a plausible Z, in a world whose
ground genuinely is around that height elsewhere. Nothing refused. A trace that
hits the wrong thing is indistinguishable from one that hits the right thing
unless you ask what it hit.

**And the frame looked FINE at a glance** — modules standing in a forest,
lit, materially correct. It was only on the crop, with sky and trees visible
UNDER the base, that the float was obvious. The whole-frame view had the
modules against a mountain, where "how high is that" has no reference.

**The fix is not a bigger ignore list, it is a different question.** The reseat
traced PER MODULE and ignored foliage, the city and the eval actors — but what
actually made it trustworthy was standing the row on the PLAZA, which is
declared ground with no structures and was cleared of trees. **Prefer an input
that cannot express the catastrophic value over a gate that rejects it**
(non-negotiable 3): there is no canopy over the plaza to hit.

Result after the reseat: ground span 93.8 cm over 56 m, read-back error 0.0 cm,
and the crop shows the module's base meeting grass with no daylight under it.

**The kit itself was never in doubt.** Materials bound on 15 of 15, master
compiled with 0 errors, and the pixels showed plaster and timber. The defect was
in the look test, and separating those two is the only reason the intake verdict
survived the bad frame.

## 2026-08-29 — THE CAPTURE WATCHER HAS NOW BEEN WRONG FOUR TIMES OUT OF FOUR

`city_shot_payload.txt` exited 1 and reported `ok: false`. The frame existed —
`HighresScreenshot00098.png`, 5,019 KB, written after the payload gave up.
R-CITYSHOT already records three of these across two sessions and says plainly
*"the watcher has never once been right about whether a frame exists"*. This is
the fourth, and the first taken as a routine expectation rather than a surprise:
the shot was dispatched and then a POLL FOR A NEW FILE ON DISK was run beside
it, so the payload's verdict was never load-bearing.

Both frames landed around 840 s. Both were followed by the documented wedge —
editor at 0.02–0.05 CPU-seconds per wall-second with `Responding=False`, then
recovery to 6.55 after roughly the recorded 630 s.

**A tool whose verdict you have learned to ignore is not a tool, it is a
delay.** The right repair is to make the watcher poll the directory it already
knows about instead of waiting on a fixed budget — its own `_before` set is
computed at the top of the payload and then never used for this. Recorded in
BACKLOG rather than fixed mid-unit.

## 2026-08-30 — A BUDGET POLICES THE BINDING THREAD, AND GPU-ONLY IS A TRAP

`recipes/perf_budgets.json` was written with `per_zone_ms` alone — a GPU budget.
That is the number everyone reaches for, it is what "frame cost" colloquially
means, and on this world it is **the wrong one**.

The first baseline, 300 frames at each of four stations:

    zone          GPU p90   Render p90   Game p90
    plaza            8.84         8.45       9.67
    main_street      5.73         8.21      10.26
    treeline         7.44         8.43      10.80
    vista            9.24         8.68      10.20

**The game thread is highest at all four.** A GPU-only budget would have sat at
12 ms while the actual constraint ran at 10.8 and climbing, and the check would
have printed `ok` the whole way. Not a wrong number — a number about the wrong
thing, which is the harder failure to notice because nothing looks broken.

**THE RULE, and it is now project law: every performance zone declares a budget
for EVERY thread that could bind it, and the checker enforces all of them.**
`per_zone_game_ms` was added because the measurement demanded it, and
`check_perf.judge()` reads both — because a declared budget nothing reads is an
inert field, and this repo found two of those on 2026-08-29 alone
(`landmark.spire_mesh`, and five decorative gate booleans in `city.json`).

**Any future zone gets both numbers.** A zone added with only a GPU budget is
half a zone.

### WHY IT WAS CAUGHT AT ALL

Only because the recipe was filled from a measurement instead of from
judgement. `_order_is_deliberate` in that file says **MEASURED FIRST, THEN
DECLARED**, and the reason it says so is `max_orphan_building_fraction` — a bar
set at 0.05 against a measured 3.6%, chosen to pass the number it first saw.
Had the budgets been written before the flythrough ran, the GPU-only shape
would have looked complete and shipped.

### AND IT CORROBORATES A PREDICTION FROM A DIFFERENT INSTRUMENT

`PHASE2_PLAN.md`'s bottom line, written 2026-08-15, says: *"the binding budget
is the game thread, not the GPU, and it cannot be closed today"*. That was
reasoned from struct sizes, engine defaults and an AI-perception estimate. This
is 1,200 captured frames from a CSV profiler. **Two routes that share no source
reached the same answer**, which is the standard non-negotiable 0 asks for and
the reason this finding is worth more than either measurement alone.

### THE LIMIT, STATED

Editor viewport. The editor's own overhead is inside every game-thread figure
and cannot be separated out, so these numbers are an **upper bound** on a cooked
build's game thread, not a prediction of it. A cooked budget is a different
recipe and must not be derived from these by arithmetic.

## 2026-08-30 — THREE DEFECTS THAT ONLY THE FIRST REAL RUN COULD FIND

`perf_flythrough.py` was written, reviewed, compiled clean, and was wrong in
three ways that reading it would never have surfaced.

**1. It reimplemented the tool it was supposed to drive.** The first draft
carried its own camera payload, its own CSV wait, its own reduction — before I
noticed `measure_frame_cost.py` already accepts
`--camera x,y,z,pitch,yaw,roll` and already owns all of it. That is step (a)
failing in miniature: *the toolbox is ground truth, and memory of the toolbox
is a derived record*. The rule exists because of `scripts/open_level.py` on
2026-08-05, and it did not fire because I was writing a NEW tool and never
asked whether the OLD one already did the job.

**2. `argparse` ate a negative coordinate.** Every station is at negative world
X, and `--camera -210800.0,...` makes argparse read the leading `-` as an
option. All four stations exited 2 on a usage error. **This project wrote the
rule down on 2026-08-17** — *use `--flag=value` so argparse does not eat a
negative coordinate* — after the DNA-edit work paid for it. Recorded, and still
walked into.

**3. My wrapper captured `stderr` and never printed it.** `subprocess.run(...,
capture_output=True)` and then only `stdout` was echoed, so four stations
reported a bare "exit 2" with the reason sitting in a variable nobody read.
**A wrapper that hides its child's error message turns a one-line fix into a
diagnosis.** Anything that shells out prints the child's stderr on failure.

The through-line: all three were invisible to inspection and immediate on
execution. A tool is not written until it has run against the real thing once.

## 2026-08-30 — GENERATED TEXTURES LOSE TILEABILITY BY DEFAULT, SO INTAKE GATES IT

The operator generated five albedo maps for the C0 texture swap. **All five
failed the tiling check**, and it was not close:

    Poly Haven, KNOWN-TILING (the donor's own maps)   0.76 - 1.92x   7/7 PASS
    the generated set                                2.55 - 7.90x   5/5 REFUSE
    bar                                                      2.00x

The measure is the half-offset seam test with **the image's own interior as the
control**. That control is the whole design: "how different are two adjacent
columns" is meaningless in the abstract — small on plaster, large on planks —
so a fixed threshold would pass every smooth texture and fail every detailed
one regardless of whether it tiled.

**FIVE OF FIVE FAILING IS THE SHAPE THIS PROJECT TREATS AS INSTRUMENT FAULT
UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE.** `prove_city_gates` paid for that rule when a broken
positive control made five gates look like they refused. So before the finding
was believed, the donor zip's own Poly Haven maps — *known* to tile — were run
through the same code as a real-world positive control. They passed 7/7 with no
overlap against the generated set, and the bar sits in the gap between them.
**Only then was it a finding rather than a suspicion.**

**THE GENERAL FACT: image-generation and image-to-image models do not produce
seamless tiles unless specifically made to.** They compose a picture, and a
picture has edges that were never asked to meet. Nothing about the images looks
wrong — they are good textures — and the defect is invisible until the surface
is tiled across a wall, at which point it is a hard line every metre.

### THE RULING AND THE STANDARD

Ruled: **repair, don't reject.** `scripts/repair_tileable.py` — offset by half
on both axes, blend the centre content out to the borders, restore — then
**re-run the gate on the repaired file**. Output is `<name>_tiled.<ext>` beside
the original; **the operator's authored files are never overwritten**.

    beam_wood      2.92x -> 1.35x        roof_tiles     7.89x -> 1.52x
    plaster_wall   2.55x -> 1.20x        wall_planks_a  6.01x -> 1.07x
    wall_planks_b  7.90x -> 1.37x
    all five now inside the Poly Haven range; ZERO need regeneration

**Gate + repair is now standard intake for every operator-generated tile, and
that includes Phase C1's concept-derived materials.** A generated texture is
assumed non-tiling until measured.

### THE REPAIR HAS A REAL LIMIT, AND ITS OWN SELF-TEST FOUND IT

The first self-test built a synthetic with a hard step at exactly x = w/2 —
and the repair moved it 74.57x to 69.70x, i.e. nowhere. **That is not a bug.**
The method substitutes centre content at the borders, so it assumes the centre
is continuous; a step at w/2 is moved ONTO the border by the half-offset,
breaking B exactly where the blend depends on it.

**A texture with a discontinuity through its middle is a different defect and
needs regenerating, not healing.** The self-test now uses a representative
specimen — continuous interior, mismatched edges from non-integer periods,
which is what a generated tile actually looks like — and there the repair takes
13.19x to 0.96x.

**Both times the specimen was wrong and the instrument was right**, here and in
the ramp check that called a one-period sine "52.9% baked lighting". The
correct move each time was to fix the specimen, never to widen the bar:
loosening a threshold until the sample passes is how a gate stops meaning
anything.

## 2026-08-30 — C0: FOUR INSTRUMENTS DISAGREED WITH THE TRUTH, AND THE CONTROLS FOUND ALL FOUR

The C0 texture swap is a warm-up: take one donor house, replace five of its
seven albedos with the operator's generated set, and get it standing beside its
own unmodified copy. It is deliberately small. **Four separate instruments
still reported something false, and in every case what caught it was a check
whose expected answer was known in advance.**

### 1. PIL DESTROYED THE INPUT, AND THE RED CONTROL SAID SO BEFORE ANY VERDICT

The normal-map convention had to be established. ambientCG ships `_NormalDX`
AND `_NormalGL` for the same surface beside one `_Displacement` — five
surfaces, ten labelled files — so the convention test could be run against
ground truth the vendor had already written down.

Every one of the ten came back at **correlation 0.000**.

That is not the sign test failing. Those displacement maps are `I;16`, and
`Image.open(p).convert("L")` returns **ALL 255** for Ground037, whose real
range is 18770..59293. The height field was a constant, so every correlation
against it was zero.

**The red channel is what made this legible.** The test correlates red against
the column gradient, which has the SAME expected sign under both conventions —
so red is not a verdict, it is a control. A zero there cannot be read as "the
green channel says GL"; it can only be read as *the instrument is not working*.
Without it, ten rows of 0.000 would have been ten rows of a coin flip.

**THE FIX WENT WHERE THE KNOWLEDGE ALREADY LIVED.** `texture_16bit.py` already
owns `DEFECT_MODES` and its line 38 already says truncation "is what PIL's own
`I;16 -> L`" does — it simply had no reader, only a file-staging function. A
private `load_float` in the calling script would have been a second copy of a
fact that module exists to hold, which is the individually-patched-fix pattern
non-negotiable 4a makes REJECTED in its own right. It is added there, and its
selftest reproduces the destruction rather than describing it: max error
0.000e+00 against PIL's `convert("L")` returning std 0.0000.

### 2. THEN THE TEST LABELLED ALL TEN FILES BACKWARDS, AND THE VENDOR WON

With the read fixed, correlations came back strong — 0.53 to 0.90, red control
positive on every row — and the labels were **inverted on all ten**.

A red control that strong rules out a broken height field and a flipped row
axis. What was left was my predicted sign, and re-deriving it settled it: image
rows increase DOWNWARD, so `y_up = -row` and `-dH/dy_up = +dH/drow`, which
makes **OpenGL the positive convention and DirectX the negative one** — the
opposite of what the tool asserted, and the opposite of what the intake skill
states.

**Ten labels across five surfaces outrank a remembered rule.** CLAUDE.md's
resolution protocol says it in one line: *if a lookup contradicts an
assumption, the lookup wins — say so.*

And it is worth being clear about what was NOT happening here. Flipping the
sign is not tuning a threshold to make a sample pass, which this same unit
refused to do twice with the tiling gate. **The sign is binary, and the vendor
already knew the answer before the test ran.** There was nothing to fit.

### 3. THE SETTER RETURNED FALSE ON ALL 21 WRITES AND ALL 21 LANDED

`set_material_instance_texture_parameter_value` returned **False for every
parameter on every one of the seven instances** — 21 writes — while the
read-back off the instance returned the correct texture every single time.

This is the 2026-08-16 hero-bake trap reproduced at scale: six instances
created, `"bound": []` on all of them, and the tool reported failure over work
that had succeeded. **The return value is not evidence in either direction.**
The read-back is the gate, and this run would have been thrown away without
it.

### 4. THE SAMPLER AUDIT COULD NOT SEE A SINGLE SAMPLER, AND SAID SO AS A PASS

`audit_material_samplers.py` run against the new master printed
**"0 sampler(s) audited, 0 mismatch(es)"** and exited 0 — over a material
carrying three samplers. The filter was

    type(_e).__name__ != "MaterialExpressionTextureSample"

an exact class-name match, blind to every subclass — and the entire
`TextureSampleParameter` family are subclasses. Every material this project
has ever audited happens to use plain `TextureSample` nodes, so **the blind
spot existed for months and was never exercised.** A gate that has only seen
input it can see has not been tested.

**The enumerator was only half the defect.** The verdict cheerfully printed
zero-of-zero as clean, which is non-negotiable 6 exactly: a failed measurement
must report *"I could not measure this"*, never the number the broken
measurement produced. Fixing the blindness without fixing the verdict would
have left the NEXT blind spot equally silent, so both are fixed in one commit,
and "0 audited on a non-empty graph" now refuses with exit 5.

`audit_material_connectivity.py` carried the same exact-match filter. Its
VERDICT was never affected — reachability does not care what class a node is —
but its listing read "no textures in this graph". Swept in the same commit per
non-negotiable 4, with `M_AutoLandscape` as the regression control: 37
samplers, 0 mismatches, the recorded figure exactly.

### AND TWO SMALLER ONES WORTH NOT REPEATING

**DELETE-AND-CREATE WORKS EXACTLY ONCE.** The material builder deleted the
master and re-created it, and passed. On the SECOND run `create_asset`
returned None: the seven instances minted by the first run still referenced
the master, so the delete could not complete and the name stayed taken. A tool
that succeeds once and then reports "could not create" over a perfectly good
asset is worse than one that never worked, because the message points away
from the cause. **Reuse-and-clear is idempotent by construction** and is what
pipeline rule 3 asks for anyway.

**A WRAPPER MIS-PARSE READS EXACTLY LIKE AN EDITOR FAILURE.** The host driver
scanned stdout for a `__LL__` line that `ue_exec` has already consumed and
pretty-printed (`ue_exec.py:155`), so it announced "NO RESULT FROM THE EDITOR
— that is 'could not look'" over a run that had completely succeeded. The
honest-sounding refusal was itself the bug.

### THE ONE THAT DID NOT GO WRONG, AND WHY IT MATTERS

The operator ruled that materials bind **by what each slot references, not by
slot number**. The mesh then proved the ruling: its slot ORDER is not the
wiring order — index 1 is `Material_007` and index 2 is `Material_009`. An
index-keyed bind would have put rock wall on the plank slots and reported ten
successes. **The ruling was made before anyone had looked at the index order,
and it was right.**

## 2026-08-30 — FIVE TIMES IN ONE NIGHT I REBUILT SOMETHING THE REPO ALREADY HAD

Not five different mistakes. **One mistake, five times**, and the operating
loop already names it: *step (a) is a SEARCH, not a RECALL.*

    EditorStaticMeshLibrary.get_number_triangles   does not exist
        -> get_num_triangles(lod) is on StaticMesh          stub :414175
    DirectionalLight.directional_light_component   does not exist
        -> .light_component, on EVERY light actor    apply_lighting.py:246
    StaticMesh.get_num_uv_channels                 does not exist
        -> class method on EditorStaticMeshLibrary          stub :368004
    my own FbxImportUI options block               incomplete
        -> import_static_mesh.py:235-247 had it right
    my own Start-Process editor launch             incomplete
        -> launch_editor.ps1 moves PackageRestoreData.json aside

**The last one is the worst and it is worth dwelling on.** I force-killed an
editor to free VRAM, then launched a new one by hand. A force-kill WRITES
`PackageRestoreData.json`, so the new editor came up on a *"Restore
auto-saved packages?"* modal and sat there for **seven minutes** answering
`Responding=True` to Windows while answering nothing at all on the remote
execution port.

That is a nasty failure signature: the process is alive, the OS says it is
healthy, and the only symptom is silence on a socket. I read it as "shaders
still compiling" for two of those seven minutes, which is a plausible story
that fits the evidence and is wrong. `launch_editor.ps1` moves that file aside
as its *first action*, and its inline comment says why.

### WHY THE COMMENT DID NOT FIRE, WHICH IS THE ACTUAL DEFECT

In three of the five cases the answer was in a comment *in this repo*, and in
two it was in the generated stub. Every one was one `grep` away. What they
share is that **I already believed I knew the answer**, so no lookup ever got
scheduled — the search step is skipped precisely when confidence is highest,
which is exactly when it is least reliable.

The rule that fires on "I don't remember a tool for this" does not fire on
"I remember the tool". That gap is the defect, and it is the same one
non-negotiable 15 describes for derived records: **memory of the toolbox is a
DERIVED RECORD; the directory is ground truth.**

### THE COST, HONESTLY

Four round trips of ~25 s each, plus seven minutes on the modal. Roughly nine
minutes of wall clock, no data lost, nothing shipped wrong. **Cheap this time,
and the cheapness is not the point** — the same reflex applied to a destructive
operation instead of an accessor lookup is how a night's work disappears.

### WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY HAVE CAUGHT IT

Not "be more careful". The concrete trigger: **before any editor-touching
payload, `ls scripts/` for the verb and `grep` the stub for the accessor** —
mechanically, before writing the call, not after it fails. The failures all
looked different (an attribute error, a silent import of nothing, a modal) so
no single symptom could have taught the lesson; only the shared cause does.

## 2026-08-30 — A LICENCE TERM WHOSE VIOLATION CANNOT BE DETECTED AFTERWARDS

The C0 donor turned out to be **"Medieval House" by Darek Dubiniec**, Fab
Standard License, in the operator's own library — so it is **shippable**, and
last night's "fit for a warm-up, not clearable for shipped content" caveat is
withdrawn. Recording the licence closed the row.

**But the listing also says "Allows usage with AI: No", and that term has a
property almost nothing else in this project has.**

Every other rule here is enforceable after the fact. A wrong sampler shows up
in a compile error. A dangling reference draws as a checkerboard. An unsaved
asset vanishes on restart — which is exactly how this week's worst defect was
caught. Each leaves an artefact that a later session can inspect, and git can
undo the ones that matter.

**A generation model leaves none.** Feed it a restricted mesh and the output
carries no hash of its inputs, no manifest, no trace. There is nothing to
inspect afterwards, no way to prove what produced it, and no way to un-ship it
once it is in a build. The violation is **undetectable and irreversible**, so
the only moment a check can work is *before the model runs*.

### THAT CHANGES WHERE THE RULE HAS TO LIVE

A note in `ASSETS.md` would be enforced by whoever remembers to read
`ASSETS.md`. This project already knows what that is worth: R-CITYSHOT
specified `ShowFlag.Volumes 0` in prose for three days while the one payload
every render passes through never issued it.

So the rule lives in `recipes/ai_restrictions.json`, `ai_input_guard.py` reads
it and **refuses**, both generation scripts call it under `set -e` ahead of the
model load, and `check_ai_restrictions.py` asserts the document still agrees
with the register. Two of those are in the offline suite, so the guard is
exercised on every run rather than when someone edits the register.

### FAIL CLOSED — the one place in this project where that is right

Everywhere else, a gate that cannot measure must say *"I could not measure"* and
hand the judgement back. Here it must additionally **decline to proceed**,
because the costs are asymmetric: a false refusal costs a re-run and a
question; a false pass costs something that cannot be detected, undone, or even
proven to have happened.

### TWO NEAR-MISSES IN THE SAME HOUR, BOTH OF THE SAME SHAPE

**A `0` that might be a default.** The Fab library DB has an `is_ai_forbidden`
column, and for the Medieval Village kit it reads `0` — which looks like "AI
permitted" and would have been a genuinely useful clearance. The row has an
empty description, no tags, no formats and 0 reviews: the `0` is
indistinguishable from a field that was never populated. Recorded as an
observation, **not** as a finding (NN21).

**An absent record that is not an answer.** `medieval_houses_10` does not
appear in the launcher's listing DB, which invites "so it is not owned". But
that DB caches only what was downloaded *through the launcher* — the C0 donor
is absent from it too, and it **is** owned. Absence there says nothing about
the web library. Reported UNKNOWN, and restricted precautionarily because an
unknown licence from an author whose other work forbids AI input is not a
coin-flip worth taking.

Both are the same error waiting to happen: **treating the absence of a signal
as the presence of its negation.**

## 2026-08-30 — COUPLED PARAMETERS MUST BE SOLVED JOINTLY, AND SOLVING THEM SEPARATELY MAKES IT WORSE

The C0 grade had to pull two measured quantities to two targets: **saturation**
and **warmth (R−B)**. Three attempts, and the failure mode is worth the space
because **the second attempt was further from target than the first**.

    attempt                                   wall_planks_b sat (target 0.4248)
    1. k = target / current                              0.3103
    2. bisect each gain SEPARATELY                       0.2739   <- WORSE
    3. solve the PAIR, alternating                       0.4248

**Attempt 1** failed because the metric is not linear in the gain. `sat` is
`(max−min)/max` averaged over pixels; scaling `(colour − luma)` by *k* does not
scale that by *k*, because the max and min channels move by different amounts
and their ratio is non-linear. A ratio of means is not the mean of ratios.

**Attempt 2 is the interesting one.** Bisecting on the measured metric fixed
the non-linearity — and made the answer worse, because it fixed the wrong
problem. The warmth damp pulls red and blue toward their mean, and **that
removes saturation too**. So `k_sat`, solved with `k_warm = 1`, was then applied
to an image the warmth damp had already desaturated. Two couplings, each solved
as though the other did not exist, and the errors compounded in the same
direction.

**THE GENERAL FACT: when two controls both move both outputs, solving them
independently is not an approximation — it is a systematic error, and it can be
larger than the naive fix it replaced.** The separate solves each looked
rigorous. Each converged. Each hit its own target exactly, in isolation. The
combination missed by 35%.

**Attempt 3** alternates the two bisections for six rounds so each gain sees
the other's effect. Residual: sat +0.0000, warmth −0.0153, both reported rather
than hidden.

### THE DIAGNOSTIC THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT IMMEDIATELY

**Measure the final transform, not the intermediate one.** Each separate solve
verified `grade(a, k, 1.0)` — a transform that is never actually applied. The
thing shipped was `grade(a, k_sat, k_warm)`, and nothing measured *that* until
the output was written. A solve that validates a function you do not call is
not a solve.

### ⚠ FORWARD POINTER: ATMOSPHERE TUNING HAS EXACTLY THIS STRUCTURE

Ruled 2026-08-30, recorded before the work starts rather than after it fails.
`recipes/alpine_8k.json` carries **sun** (elevation, intensity, temperature),
**fog** (density, start distance, height falloff) and **exposure**
(compensation_ev) — and every one of them moves every observable:

* raising sun intensity brightens the frame **and** changes what the fog
  scatters;
* fog density lifts the shadows **and** lowers apparent contrast **and** shifts
  measured mean luma, which is what exposure is solved against;
* exposure compensation moves mean luma **and** therefore the very
  denominator any of the others would be tuned against.

The existing `compensation_ev: -1.923` was solved for ONE of these with the
others fixed, and its own note already records that **three denominators were
tried and they disagreed by 0.13 EV**. That is this same defect, already
observed in the atmosphere domain and not yet named as such.

**So: expect joint solves there.** Tune the triple together against the frame
that is actually rendered, alternate to convergence, and report residuals per
quantity. Do not solve sun with fog held, then fog with sun held, and expect
the pair to land — that is attempt 2, in a domain where the couplings are
stronger and the render is 14 minutes instead of 3 seconds.

## 2026-08-30 — `--timeout` IS A DISCOVERY WINDOW, AND THE GUARD THAT SAYS SO WAS SUPPRESSED BY MY OWN PIPE

**What was attempted.** Fire the concept iter1 shot through
`scripts/ue_exec.py scripts/city_shot_payload.txt`. Knowing the capture takes
~14 minutes, I passed `--timeout 1200` to "give it room".

**What happened.** The shot did not fire for 20 minutes. No
`__LANDSCAPELAB_CONFIRM__`, no `ShowFlag`, no `HighResShot` in the log; the
payload was staged to `Saved/LLPython/city_shot_payload.py` and the client sat
at 0.09 CPU.

**Root cause, at the source line.** `ue_exec.py:174-180`. `--timeout` is the
**discovery window**, not an execution budget, and it is **spent in full**
before the payload is sent. The docstring's own advice is 12-25. A render's
duration has nothing to do with it — the payload runs inside the editor and is
not governed by this flag at all.

**This is a recorded lesson repeating.** The comment at that line says it
plainly: the rule "existed in LESSONS.md and did not fire" on 2026-08-16, when
a caller passed 120-180 and paid minutes per call. So a NOTE was added that
prints at the point of use, which is the correct fix.

**AND THE FIX WORKED. I JUST COULD NOT SEE IT.** The NOTE printed. I had run
the command backgrounded and piped through `tail -30`, and a pipe buffers until
it closes — so the warning sat undelivered in a pipe for twenty minutes while I
read the output file as "empty" three times and inferred a wedge from it.

**The general rule, and it is not about timeouts.**

> **A guard that prints at the point of use is defeated by any pipe that
> buffers.** `| tail`, `| head`, `| grep` on a long-running or backgrounded
> command withhold exactly the early diagnostics that were designed to fire
> before the cost is paid. **Do not filter the output of a command whose
> warnings are the reason it is safe to run.** Let it print, and read it.

This is non-negotiable 0's shape one layer out: I had two instruments (the
empty output file and the quiet log) that shared a single cause — my own pipe —
and I read their agreement as evidence about the editor.

**Second-order cost.** From that false premise I built a foreground/throttle
hypothesis, put a before/after CPU table in front of Ryan, and proposed
promoting it into R-CITYSHOT. The iter1 column of that table was the
foregrounded viewport redrawing, not a blocked render — it measured nothing.
**A hypothesis is only as good as the weakest instrument feeding it, and I did
not check the instrument before offering the conclusion.**

**What did survive, and is worth keeping.** The iter0 observation stands on its
own evidence: the periodic `LogEOSSDK` lines appear every ~5.5 min, and during
iter0's 14-minute block there were NONE, while during iter1's non-block they
appear on schedule (19:37:26, 19:43:10, 19:49:31). That absence is a real
measurement of a blocked game thread, taken with an instrument independent of
my pipe. The mechanism it points at — `_time.sleep()` in the payload's watcher
running ON the game thread, so the tiled `HighResShot` cannot tick to
completion until the watcher gives up — remains the best explanation of why
five frames have landed ~1 s after their watcher declared them absent. It is
still UNPROVEN, and the clean test is the shot now queued.

## 2026-08-30 — THE REPLACEMENT WATCHER HUNG ON ITS FIRST SELF-TEST, WHICH IS THE BEST THING THAT HAPPENED TO IT

**What was attempted.** Fix the shot watcher. The diagnosis was solid and
Ryan approved it: `city_shot_payload.txt` slept on the **game thread**, and
`HighResShot` completes over subsequent engine **ticks**, so the frame could
not be written until the watcher gave up. Move the wait to the host, where
sleeping costs the editor nothing. `scripts/shoot.py` is that host-side poller.

**What happened.** `shoot.py --self-test` did not finish. It ran past 120 s on
a test whose longest case has a 15 s deadline.

**Root cause, at the line.** `poll_for_frame`'s inner settle loop was:

    size = -1
    while True:
        cur = os.path.getsize(path)
        if cur == size and cur > 10000:
            return path
        size = cur
        time.sleep(settle_s)

A file that settles **below** the size floor satisfies `cur == size` forever
and `cur > 10000` never. There is no other exit, and **the loop does not look
at `deadline_s` at all** — the deadline the caller passed governs only the
OUTER loop. So a truncated, empty or non-frame `.png` in the screenshot
directory hangs the poller indefinitely.

**Fixed** by bounding the settle loop with the same deadline, and by folding a
settled-but-too-small file into `before` so the next sweep looks past it
instead of re-picking the same dud. `MIN_FRAME_BYTES` is now one declaration
used by both the poller and the caller's warning.

### THE POINT IS NOT THE BUG. IT IS THAT THE BUG WAS THE SAME SHAPE AS THE ONE BEING FIXED.

The tool being replaced **was wrong six times out of six while looking, in its
own terms, like it worked**. It reported `ok:false` over frames that existed,
and every session read the verdict and moved on.

Its replacement, written by someone who had just spent an afternoon
root-causing exactly that failure, shipped with **a loop that could never
terminate on a case it would meet in production** — the screenshot directory
is precisely where a truncated capture lands. Had it gone in unproven, the
next session would have found a "hung" poller and had every reason to blame
the editor again, because that is what the last six occurrences looked like.

**Understanding a failure class does not immunise the code you write to fix
it.** The self-test caught it in ninety seconds, before a single real shot.

### THE RULE

> **A replacement instrument is not more trustworthy than the one it replaces
> until it has proven itself in three directions.** It must FIND the thing
> (positive control), REFUSE the things that are not it, and REFUSE TO CLAIM
> EARLY. And every bounded wait must be bounded on EVERY path out — a
> deadline that governs the outer loop and not the inner one is not a
> deadline, it is a comment.

Seven cases now run in the offline suite. The positive control is first and is
listed first deliberately: `check_plan_freshness.py` is at this moment failing
its own positive control while all nine of its mutation cases pass, and that
is the state this rule exists to prevent shipping.

## 2026-08-30 — THE STAMP INSTRUMENT WAS RIGHT ALL ALONG. ITS POSITIVE CONTROL WAS A LIVE ARTEFACT.

**The alarming version, which is what it looked like:** `check_plan_freshness.py
--self-test` reported `POSITIVE CONTROL (unmutated) -> DIFFERS, want MATCHES`
while all nine of its mutation cases passed. An instrument that cannot certify
itself was assumed to poison every STALE verdict it had ever issued.

**The actual diagnosis: the instrument was correct and the FIXTURE was wrong.**

The positive control loaded the **live** `city/alpine_basin_town_plan.json`,
called `plan_stamp.verify` on it, and asserted `MATCHES`. Measured:

    plan last stamped   53feeec2  2026-08-29  storey_m 3.2 -> 2.0 by ruling
    inputs then moved   abe88eae  2026-08-30  RULING 4 -- roof servability

    verify() -> DIFFERS, naming exactly:
      recipes/city.json     ed61d0b7b400 -> 85f1e7abcc8b
      scripts/plan_city.py  72118abd4195 -> c70ad130b051

Both files genuinely changed, one commit after the plan was stamped, for a
recorded and operator-approved reason. **`verify` reported the truth.** The
assertion `MATCHES` was the thing that was wrong.

### THE SHAPE OF IT — NON-NEGOTIABLE 0, AGAIN

**The positive control and the artefact under test were the same object.** The
question "does this instrument work?" was being answered by "is the town plan
fresh?" — which is the question the instrument exists to ask. They were never
two measurements.

So an approved change, correctly detected by a correctly-working tool,
**destroyed that tool's ability to certify itself**, and the failure presented
as "the stamp checker is broken". A fixture that can go stale is not a control.

### AND THE SAME COUPLING EXISTED ONE LEVEL UP

`--self-test` printed PASSED and then **fell through to the corpus audit**, so
it exited 3 whenever any live plan was stale. The offline suite entry named
"the input-stamp instrument refuses" was therefore reporting the state of the
CORPUS under the name of the INSTRUMENT. Two entries already exist for the two
questions; `--self-test` is now standalone and returns 0 on its own merits.

### A SECOND DEFECT THE FIRST ONE HID

Every mutation case used the stale live plan as its base. `verify` returned
DIFFERS for that document **whether or not the mutation was applied**, so the
verdict half of "one input hash corrupted -> DIFFERS" was **vacuous**. Only the
`named` assertion was still doing work. *A refusal that would have happened
anyway is not evidence that a gate refuses.*

All stamp cases now run against a synthetic fixture that is MATCHES by
construction, so each mutation is measured against a known-good baseline. Two
cases were added: that the verifier names **only** the corrupted input (a
verifier that names everything would have passed the old case while being
useless), and that a stamped input **edited on disk** is caught — which is the
direction the instrument actually meets in production, as opposed to a
corrupted record.

### THE RE-AUDIT

Run with the now-certified instrument, banked at
`_verify/20260830_stamp/reaudit_20260830.txt`:

    18 artefacts   STAMP MATCHES
     2 artefacts   STAMP DIFFERS
                     city/alpine_basin_town_plan.json      -- ruling 4, GATED
                     city/alpine_basin_town_reachable.json -- WAIVED, declared

**No verdict changed.** `plan_stamp.verify` was never modified, so nothing it
ever reported was produced by a broken instrument. It was UNCERTIFIED, not
wrong — and those are different findings with very different consequences.

### THE RULE

> **A positive control must be inert.** It has to be something that cannot
> change for reasons unrelated to the instrument — a synthetic fixture built
> and checked in the same breath. The moment a control is a live artefact,
> every legitimate change to that artefact reads as an instrument failure, and
> the instrument goes dark exactly when the repo is most active.
>
> And a **self-test must not run the corpus.** "Does this tool work?" and "is
> the data good?" are different questions; wiring them together means neither
> can be answered when the other is unhappy.

## 2026-08-30 — A PERFECT SCORE ON THE WRONG AXIS, AND THREE FIXES THAT SILENTLY DID NOTHING

**What was attempted.** Import the first forged asset -- the church -- into the
editor, scale it to the ruled height, and stand it beside a kit mesh.

**What happened, and how nearly it shipped.** The payload reported:

    church_top_cm      1341.3   <- the ruled number, hit exactly
    church_over_chalet 2.5      <- ruling 1, a perfect score
    church_base_cm     0.0      <- sitting on the ground
    church_footprint   2591 x 3107 cm

Three of those four are the numbers anyone would check, and all three were
right. **The church was lying on its side.** The FBX round trip rotates -90
about X, so UE's Y held Blender's Z; the scale step then stretched the
church's DEPTH to 1341.3 cm. The scale is computed FROM the axis it is applied
to, so hitting the target proves nothing about which axis got it.

**Only the footprint gave it away** -- a 26 x 31 m church 13 m tall -- and only
because it was measured rather than assumed.

### THE THREE DEAD ENDS, NAMED SO THEY ARE NOT RETRIED

1. **FBX export axis flags.** `axis_forward="X", axis_up="Z"` produced
   **byte-identical UE extents**. UE applies its own Y-up to Z-up conversion
   regardless of what the file declares. The flags are not the lever.

2. **`bpy.ops.object.transform_apply` in background mode — THE DANGEROUS ONE.**
   `obj.rotation_euler = (-pi/2, 0, 0)` followed by `transform_apply` ran
   without error, and the report recorded `export_rotation: applied_deg
   [-90, 0, 0]`. **The exported file was unchanged.** An operator that depends
   on context is a REQUEST, not a transform.

   > **This is "the read-back is the gate" in another costume.** The project
   > already knows not to trust that a camera moved because the call returned,
   > and not to trust that an asset saved because the editor says it exists.
   > Here a transform was logged as applied by the same code that requested
   > it — the log recorded the INTENT and was read as the OUTCOME. Fixed by
   > writing vertex coordinates directly and ASSERTING the extents changed
   > before export: the exporter now proves it sent.

3. **`replace_existing=True` on the import task.** The FBX was re-exported
   three times with different content -- mtime and sha256 both changed -- and
   UE returned identical bounds each time, reporting success over the STALE
   asset. Same family as an editor-side check that cannot tell `loaded` from
   `saved`. Fixed by deleting the destination first, guarded to
   `/Game/Scratch/` so a typo cannot remove anything real.

### THE RULE

> **Prove BOTH ENDS of a transfer.** The exporter must prove it sent what it
> claims (assert the geometry changed), and the importer must prove it
> received what was sent (compare per-axis extents to the source bbox and
> refuse on mismatch). One end is not enough: each of the three failures above
> was invisible from the other side, and two of them REPORTED SUCCESS.

And the specific corollary: **a target hit is not evidence when the target is
computed from the same quantity it is applied to.** Scaling to a height will
always achieve that height, on whatever axis it was handed.

## 2026-08-30 — A GATE THAT MEASURED THE WRONG QUANTITY, AND A FIXTURE THAT NEVER BUILT THE CONDITION IT NAMED

Three failures in one instrument, in the order they were found. The first was
ruled on by the operator; the second and third were found only because the
first forced me to look at the fixture.

### 1. THE HEIGHT GATE REFUSED AN HONEST SET

`check_generation_input.py --set` gained a consistency check on the premise
that **azimuth does not change height**, so a bbox-height jump between views
means the generator moved the camera or changed scale — the reconstruction
hazard `GENERATION_VIEW_SPEC.md` names. Implemented at ±8%, it refused
`wood_stack_az090` at 8.6% and blocked the forge.

Measured on that set:

    ground line (bbox bottom)  889, 890, 880, 889   spread  1.1%
    top edge                   229, 182, 233, 234   spread 22.5%
    bbox height                661, 709, 648, 656   spread  9.3%

**Root cause: bbox height is not the quantity the rule is about.** It is a sum
of two independent terms — the ground line (moves only when the camera moves)
and the top edge (moves whenever the silhouette changes, which is what azimuth
is *for*). The top edge varied 22.5% on a set whose camera was provably fixed
to 1.1%. Any tolerance on the sum must therefore either admit real camera
moves or refuse honest rotations; there is no value that separates them,
because the noise term is larger than the signal term.

The ground line alone does separate them. Ruled (option 1, operator): the
ground line at ±3% is the GATE; height at ±15% is reported always and cites
only alongside a ground-line failure, retained to catch a generator that
rescaled the object while holding the ground line.

**The general rule: a gate's tolerance cannot fix a gate's QUANTITY.** When a
check refuses something you believe is correct, the first question is not
"what tolerance?" but "does this number contain anything other than the effect
I am detecting?" A proxy that sums signal and expected variation is not a
loose instrument, it is the wrong instrument, and widening it only trades
false positives for false negatives. This is non-negotiable 0's shape at the
level of a single measurement.

### 2. THE NEGATIVE CONTROL DID NOT SIMULATE DISTANCE

The self-test's refusal fixture claimed to be "a rotation shot from further
away". It built one by resizing the WHOLE FRAME to 0.75x and pasting it onto a
background canvas.

That is not what moving a camera does, and the fixture proved it: the paste
left a rectangular seam, `subject_mask` locked onto **the seam** rather than
the subject, and the fake measured a ground delta of **0.6%** — well inside
any tolerance. The control was never exercising the condition it was named
for. It has since been rebuilt to composite only the subject's masked pixels,
scaled about the frame centre as a projection actually behaves, and now
measures a ground line at y=792 against the master's y=890, **11.0% off**.

**Root cause: the fixture was verified by its own name, not by its output.**
Nobody had ever asked what ground delta the "further away" image actually had
— only whether the test printed a pass.

### 3. THE ASSERTION GREPPED FOR PROSE

The test decided refusal with `any("bbox HEIGHT" in f for f in fail)`. When
the gate moved to the ground line, the failure message stopped containing that
string. **The test did not fail — it reported a pass**, because absence of the
searched-for string was indistinguishable from absence of a problem in the
direction it was written.

**Root cause: an assertion coupled to a human-readable message is asserting on
prose.** The message is the part most likely to be reworded, and rewording it
silently inverts the test. Where a message must be matched, the match belongs
to a stable token that the code and the test both reference, and the failure
direction must be checked — a control that can only go green when it matches
is a control that goes green when it stops matching for any reason at all.

### WHAT THESE SHARE

All three are the same defect at different altitudes: **something was trusted
because of what it was called.** The gate was called a consistency check and
measured inconsistency plus expected variation; the fixture was called
"further away" and moved nothing; the assertion was called a refusal check and
searched for a sentence. The stamp instrument two entries above failed this
way too, and the fix is identical — make the control produce a MEASURED number
and look at that number, not at the pass line underneath it.

## 2026-08-30 — THE FORGE'S SECOND ASSET, AND A READER THREAD THAT DIED WITHOUT STOPPING ANYTHING

The wood stack forged clean on the first attempt once the ground-line ruling
unblocked stage 1: 133.3 s end to end, exit 0, every stage 1–9 green. Two
things happened underneath it that the exit code did not mention.

### THE DECODE FAILURE THAT NOBODY NOTICED BECAUSE IT PICKED THE RIGHT STREAM

The run printed a `UnicodeDecodeError` traceback from `Thread-4
(_readerthread)` and then carried on to a successful forge.

`forge.py::_run` called `subprocess.run(..., text=True)` with no `encoding`.
`text=True` alone decodes with the **locale** codec, which is cp1252 on this
machine. TRELLIS's sampler loops emit tqdm progress bars; U+258F `▏` is
`E2 96 8F`, and **0x8F is undefined in cp1252**. The reader thread raised and
died.

Measured, on that exact byte sequence:

    text=True alone      rc 0, stdout is None, __FORGE_GEN__ NOT found
    + encoding="utf-8"   rc 0, stdout 423 chars, __FORGE_GEN__ found

**It survived on which stream tqdm happens to use.** tqdm writes to stderr by
default, so the stderr reader died and stdout arrived intact. Had the bar gone
to stdout, stage 3's gate — `"__FORGE_GEN__" not in (p.stdout or "")` — would
have returned 3, *"could not look"*, over a perfectly good 56-second GPU run.
And there is a second edge already live: stage 3's error path prints
`p.stderr`, which was **already None**, so a genuine stage-3 failure would
have been reported with no diagnostic whatsoever.

**Root cause is one missing argument, but the lesson is the failure SHAPE: an
exception in a thread does not fail the process.** It printed a traceback into
a log nobody was gating on, set a return value to None, and let a check that
reads `(p.stdout or "")` convert that None into a confident false verdict. The
`or ""` idiom — written to be defensive — is what laundered a crash into an
empty string. Defensive defaults hide the difference between *nothing was
there* and *we could not read it*, and those two need opposite responses.

The fix is `encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"` on the helper. The general
rule: **when a child process's output is evidence, decode it explicitly.** The
locale codec is a property of the machine that happens to be running, not of
the data, and it is chosen silently.

This class is not confined to the forge — 20+ `text=True` call sites across
`scripts/` have no `encoding`. Only the forge one is PROVEN to have fired;
the sweep is backlogged rather than done blind, because changing 20 decoders
at once with no failing case for 19 of them is how a fix becomes the next
defect.

### GENUS 392, AND A VRAM MARGIN OF 1.2%

    church      190,562 v   60,000 tris ceiling   genus  61   VRAM 10,082 MiB
    wood_stack  1,400,074 v 15,000 tris ceiling   genus 392   VRAM 14,870 MiB

The wood stack is **7.3x the church's vertex count against a quarter of its
triangle budget**, and its genus is 6.4x higher. Some of that is honest — a
stacked cord of firewood genuinely is full of tunnels, and gaps between round
logs are real handles, not artefacts. That is precisely why it cannot be read
as a defect *or* dismissed: `tri_within_budget` is a TRIANGLE claim, the
decimator reported `392 -> 392` exactly as designed, and nothing in the forge
distinguishes a legitimate tunnel from reconstruction noise.

**The VRAM number is the one that should be uncomfortable.** Peak 14,870 MiB
against 15,045 MiB free — **175 MiB of headroom, 1.2%**. VRAM fit is one of
the four ratified ABSOLUTE acceptance floors, and this run passed it by a
margin thinner than measurement noise, with nothing in the output calling
attention to that. A pass at 1.2% margin and a pass at 40% margin print
identically, which makes the floor look satisfied when it was very nearly
breached. Reporting headroom as a number, and warning under a threshold, is
backlogged.

## 2026-08-30 — STAGE 8 NEVER WROTE ITS ROW, AND STAGE 10 WOULD HAVE DELETED THE CHURCH

Both found by reading the forge's own output against the files it claims to
touch, after the wood stack forged to exit 0. Neither was caught by any gate,
and the run reported complete success.

### STAGE 8 PRINTED ITS HEADER AND WROTE NOTHING

`FORGE_LOG.md` gained its cost line. `ASSETS.md` gained nothing. The code:

    row = _assets_row(spec, fin, gen, cls, max_tris)
    print("[8/9] ASSETS.md row and [9/9] FORGE_LOG cost line")
    report["assets_row"] = row          # <- stashed in the report
    _append_forge_log(log_line)         # <- stage 9 writes. stage 8 does not.

The row was computed, put in `forge_report.json`, and never written to the
register. Two things hid it:

**The church's row was written BY HAND** in the session that built the forge,
so the register looked correct and the defect had no first victim. The wood
stack was the first asset to go through stage 8 without a human also doing
stage 8's job.

**`ASSETS.md`'s own preamble says "`scripts/forge.py` writes the row".** That
sentence has been false for as long as it has existed, and it is the exact
class non-negotiable 9 names: *a claim in our own artefact, trusted because it
is ours.* The register's rule is "no asset without a row", and the tool
nominated to enforce it never did.

There was also a silent format drift, only visible once the row was actually
written: `_assets_row` emitted SEVEN fields in a different order than the six
columns the table declares. **Nothing forced them into agreement because the
output had no destination.** Dead output cannot be wrong, so it drifts freely
and then is wrong the instant it is connected.

The fix writes into the table, REPLACING any row for the same asset — a
register is one row per asset, unlike `FORGE_LOG.md`, which is a run log and
correctly appends per run. Proven in three directions on a copy: adds when
absent, reports `already current` on re-run, replaces without duplicating when
the row changes, and leaves the church's row byte-identical.

### STAGE 10 EMITTED A COMMAND THAT WOULD HAVE DESTROYED THE CHURCH

`forge.py` prints the stage-10 command for whatever asset just forged. The
payload had:

    DEST = "/Game/Scratch/ForgeChurch"
    NAME = "SM_Church_Forge"

hardcoded, while `SRC`, `TARGET_CM` and `EXP_*` were templated. The payload
**deletes `DEST + "/" + NAME` before importing**, deliberately, because
`replace_existing=True` was proven untrustworthy on the same day.

So the line printed at the end of the wood-stack forge — presented as the next
step to run — would have deleted the forged church asset and re-imported the
wood stack under the church's path and name. **The church `.fbx` is the
artefact of record and is not reproducible**; the forge is not bit-deterministic,
so re-running it yields a different mesh.

**Root cause: partial parameterisation.** Templating `SRC` made the payload
*look* general, and the four `--set` arguments in the emitted command made it
read as fully driven from the recipe. Pipeline rule 2 says every scene
parameter comes from recipe JSON — `SRC`, `TARGET_CM` and `EXP_*` obeyed it,
and the two that select *what gets overwritten* did not. **The dangerous
parameters were the ones left behind**, which is the wrong half to forget and
is not a coincidence: the templated values are the ones that visibly differ
per asset, while a destination silently keeps working for the asset it was
written for.

Templating them fixes the destruction. It does NOT make stage 10 general: the
payload still emits `church_top_cm` and `church_over_chalet` and scores ruling
1's 2.5x chalet ratio. For the wood stack the scale would apply and read back
correctly while those keys are misnamed and that ratio is meaningless, so
`forge.py` now says exactly that for any non-church asset rather than letting
the numbers be read as if they generalised. Generalising the measurement is
backlogged; stage 10 has NOT been run for the wood stack.

### THE COMMON SHAPE, AGAIN

Every defect in this session is an artefact trusted for its NAME rather than
its behaviour: a gate named for consistency that measured silhouette variation,
a fixture named "further away" that moved nothing, an assertion that searched
for a sentence, a stage named "ASSETS.md row" that wrote none, and a payload
parameter list that looked complete because the visible half was. **The check
that finds all five is the same one: open the thing it claims to have touched
and measure.**

## 2026-08-30 — GENERALISING THE PAYLOAD MOVED `/Game/...` ONTO A COMMAND LINE, AND GIT BASH REWROTE IT

Stage 10's first run for the wood stack was REFUSED by its own guard:

    REFUSE to delete outside /Game/Scratch/:
    C:/Program Files/Git/Game/Scratch/ForgeWoodStack

**Root cause: MSYS2 argument conversion in Git Bash.** An argument that looks
like an absolute POSIX path is rewritten to a Windows path against the Git
installation root before the process ever sees it. Measured directly:

    python -c "print(sys.argv[1:])" --set DEST=/Game/Scratch/ForgeWoodStack
      -> ['--set', 'DEST=C:/Program Files/Git/Game/Scratch/ForgeWoodStack']

    MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 python -c ... (identical command)
      -> ['--set', 'DEST=/Game/Scratch/ForgeWoodStack']

`LEVEL` was mangled the same way; `RATIO_AGAINST` was empty and unaffected.

### THE PART WORTH KEEPING: THE FIX FOR ONE DEFECT CREATED THE EXPOSURE

The church's stage 10 ran clean the day before, and it could not have hit
this, because `DEST` and `LEVEL` were **hardcoded inside the payload** — they
were never arguments, so no shell ever touched them. Making the payload
general is what moved those two values onto a command line, and a command
line is a place where things get rewritten.

**A value that was safe as a literal is not automatically safe as a
parameter.** The parameterisation was correct and I would do it again; what I
did not do was ask what the new transport does to the values. Every
generalisation swaps a literal for a channel, and the channel has its own
semantics.

### AND THE GUARD THAT CAUGHT IT WAS WRITTEN FOR SOMETHING ELSE

`if not DEST.startswith("/Game/Scratch/")` was written against a **typo**, so
that a mistyped destination could not delete anything real. It caught a shell
rewriting the argument — a mechanism nobody had in mind when it was written.

That is the second time in two sessions a guard has caught a hazard it was not
aimed at: the "exactly one CURRENT STATE block" assertion caught a script that
was about to truncate CLAUDE.md. **Both worked for the same reason — they
assert on the VALUE at the point of use, not on the correctness of the step
that produced it.** A check placed at the point of use does not need to
anticipate the mechanism, and that is what makes it worth more than its
author's imagination.

The corollary is uncomfortable and should be said: had the guard been written
as "refuse if DEST is empty" — an equally reasonable-sounding defence — it
would have passed a path pointing into `C:/Program Files/Git/`, and the delete
would have been attempted there.

### THE FIX

Run the stage-10 command from PowerShell, which is this project's primary
shell and does no such conversion, or set `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` when running it
from Git Bash. The emitted `stage10_command.txt` now carries that warning in a
header comment, because the command is written to be copy-pasted and the
person pasting it will not have read this entry.

## 2026-08-30 — `CloseMainWindow()` IGNORED FOR 3 MINUTES WHILE THE EDITOR STAYED FULLY RESPONSIVE

Second occurrence. Standing rule 11's motivating case records it going
unhonoured for 20 s; this time it was still running after **180 s**, and the
new fact is what the editor was doing in the meantime.

    CloseMainWindow() issued to PID 12324
    +60 s   still running
    +180 s  still running, 5.46 GB resident
    then    ue_exec round trip SUCCEEDS in 12.3 s, correct level reported

**It is not shutting down slowly. It is ignoring the request and working
normally** — the game thread ticks, remote execution answers, the loaded level
is reported correctly. Previous sessions could reasonably have read the delay
as a slow teardown; it is not one.

That distinction matters because the two states want opposite handling. A slow
teardown should be waited out. An ignored request will never complete, so
waiting is unbounded — the same shape as the watcher that slept on the game
thread waiting for a frame that could not land until it stopped sleeping.

**The check that separates them is a round trip, not a timer.** A process that
still answers is not mid-exit. Polling `tasklist` can only ever say "still
there", which is true in both cases and decisive in neither.

Not force-killed. A kill during package writes is how a `.uasset` gets
truncated, and the editor has an imported mesh and a saved level in it. The
editor is left RUNNING and that is recorded in CURRENT STATE, because rule 11
says the next session must wait for ZERO editors before launching one — and a
session that reads "no editor running" and launches a second one gets the
wrong-level failure class rule 11 exists to prevent.

## 2026-08-30 — RULING 1 WAS SCORED AGAINST A CHALET WITH ITS ROOF BURIED 2 METRES IN ITS WALLS

The church was built to 1341.3 cm as 2.5x a chalet silhouette of 536.5 cm.
**The silhouette was wrong.** Measured in the editor:

    roof alone, pivot at z=0   base -201.49   top +136.53   height 338.02
    as built    roof at 400 -> base 198.51, SUNK 201.49 INTO THE WALLS
                silhouette 536.5
    corrected   roof at 601.49 -> base 400.0 = wall top
                silhouette 738.0

`SM_House02_Roof`'s pivot sits 201.49 cm above its base. Both
`concept_build_payload.txt` and `forge_scale_payload.txt` placed the roof with
`Vector(x, y, WALL_TOP)` — putting the PIVOT on the wall top and dropping the
roof through the walls. `400 - 201.49 + 338.02 = 536.5`, exactly the number
every ratio has been scored against.

**Ruling 1 did not hold by real geometry.** The church measured 1.817x the
true silhouette against a ruled 2.50x. Re-scored and re-run: target
2.5 x 738.0 = 1845.0 cm, read back 1845.0, error 0.00, ratio 2.500. It holds
now. The church grew by 503.7 cm — 38%.

### THE NUMBER WAS RIGHT AND THE THING IT MEASURED WAS WRONG

`chalet_silhouette_cm` was never miscomputed. `max(roof_top, wall_top)` is the
correct formula, the bounds reads were accurate, and the same 536.5 came back
on the concept loop, the church run and the wood stack run — **three
independent agreements, all wrong together**, because they shared the
placement. That is non-negotiable 0 at work: instruments sharing a source are
ONE measurement, and repeatability is not accuracy.

Nothing downstream could catch it. The ratio check compared the church to the
silhouette and both came from the same misassembly, so the check confirmed a
relationship between two numbers that were consistently wrong.

### WHAT ACTUALLY FOUND IT: A FRAME THAT LOOKED ODD

Not a gate. The stage-10 frame showed a thin arch straddling the wall box
instead of a roof sitting on it, and that was written up as a cosmetic
observation to be parked. **It was the only symptom the defect ever produced**,
and it was nearly filed as a rendering curiosity.

The rule this implies is narrow and worth stating: **when a measurement's
scene looks wrong, the measurement is suspect even when it is stable and even
when it agrees with itself across runs.** Stability was the reason it looked
trustworthy. A picture is a different instrument from a bounds read, and
non-negotiable 8 says to verify with a different instrument than the one that
made the claim — the picture WAS that instrument, and it was disagreeing.

### THE MESH WAS NOT THE PROBLEM, AND WAS NEARLY BLAMED

The roof still renders as a ragged, holey gable shell, which is what made it
look like a wrong or ruined asset. It is not:

    nanite_enabled true    nanite_fallback_percent 1.0
    nanite 1,417,280 tris  fallback LOD0 8,902 tris   MI_Roof   1 UV channel
    bounds z -201.49 .. +136.53

**A 1% Nanite fallback of a detailed thatch roof is exactly that shredded
shell.** The frames are showing the fallback, not the asset. Bounds are
identical either way, so the silhouette is sound and only the APPEARANCE is
degraded — but note the trap: two completely different diagnoses ("broken
asset" and "fallback rendering") produce the same picture, so the picture
could raise the alarm and could not settle it. The asset query did.

Chasing the mesh would have been the wrong repair, and the pivot would have
survived it.

## 2026-08-30 — THE DEFECT CLASS: **A NAME THAT KEEPS WORKING FOR THE ASSET IT WAS WRITTEN FOR**

Ruled a named class 2026-08-30, after it appeared three times in one session.
Recording it by name so it can be recognised rather than re-derived.

**Definition.** A hardcoded identifier — a path, a destination, a level, a key
— that was correct for the FIRST subject and stays syntactically valid for
every subject after it. It does not error. It silently addresses the first
subject's resources while claiming to act on the current one.

**The three instances, all in one payload:**

    DEST    "/Game/Scratch/ForgeChurch"   the stage-10 command emitted after
            the WOOD STACK forge pointed at the church, and the payload
            DELETES DEST/NAME before importing
    NAME    "SM_Church_Forge"             same line, same delete
    LEVEL   "/Game/Scratch/ForgeScale"    `new_level` OVERWRITES, so staging a
            second asset destroys the first's staged scene

**Why it evades review.** The value is correct in the file where it is
written, correct in every test that uses the original subject, and correct in
the code review that reads it beside that subject. It only becomes wrong when
a second subject exists — and by then nobody re-reads the constant, because it
has been working.

**Why partial parameterisation makes it worse, not better.** `SRC`,
`TARGET_CM` and `EXP_*` were templated, which made the emitted command LOOK
fully recipe-driven: five `--set` arguments and a payload path. The two values
that were not templated were the ones selecting **what gets destroyed**. The
templated values are the ones that visibly differ per subject; a destination
silently keeps working, so it is exactly the kind that gets left behind.

**The counter-practice.** When generalising, enumerate every constant in the
file and ask *which subject is this correct for?* — not *does this look
wrong?* And prefer a derivation (`_dest_path(asset)`, `_level_path(asset)`)
over a literal, because a derivation cannot be correct for only one subject.

Related: [[stage-10-guards]] and the guard design rule below.

## 2026-08-30 — THE STUCK EDITOR CLOSED IN 10 s ONCE THE TREE WENT QUIET. IT WAS BUSY, NOT DEAF.

Follow-up to the entry above, and it corrects its conclusion.

The operator ruled a protocol for the editor that ignored `CloseMainWindow()`
for 180 s: run a dirty-package census, and **if clean AND the Content tree's
newest write is older than 120 s, a force-kill is authorized** — the
truncation risk quantified instead of feared.

Applied it. Both conditions held:

    dirty packages            0   (content and map queried separately)
    newest Content write      552.6 s ago  (Scratch/Forge_lineup.umap)
    force-kill                AUTHORIZED

**Then the graceful close was retried first, and it worked in 10 seconds.**

So the request was never being ignored in the sense the previous entry
implied. **The editor was BUSY** — the first close was issued moments after a
stage-10 import, several level saves and four HighResShots, with Nanite builds
and shader compilation still draining. It answered `ue_exec` throughout
because remote execution is serviced on the game thread between those tasks,
which is exactly what made it look healthy and idle. It was healthy and NOT
idle, and I read "responds to a round trip" as "has nothing to do".

**The round-trip test told me the process was alive. It did not tell me the
process was free**, and I drew the second conclusion from the first.

### THE PROTOCOL IS RIGHT FOR A REASON BEYOND THE ONE IT WAS WRITTEN FOR

The two conditions that authorize the kill — nothing dirty, nothing written
for 120 s — are a measurement of **the editor having finished its work**. That
is also precisely the condition under which it will honour a close. So the
census is not only a safety check before killing; it is the readiness check
that makes killing unnecessary.

Hence the ordering that should be kept: **census, then quiet-window, then
RETRY the graceful close, and only then kill.** Retrying is nearly free and,
on the one occasion it has been tried, it removed the need for the kill
entirely. A kill authorized is not a kill required.

### WHAT TO MEASURE NEXT TIME, INSTEAD OF INFERRING

A busy editor and a deaf editor are indistinguishable from outside: same
process, same memory, same successful round trip. The Content tree's mtime is
what separated them, and it is a HOST-side observation — not something the
editor was asked to self-report. Different instrument, per non-negotiable 8;
the editor could not have told me it was too busy to answer, because answering
was the thing it was still managing to do.

## 2026-08-30 — THE CONCEPT LOOP RE-RUN: THE RATIOS WERE NEVER WRONG, THE REFERENCE WAS 27% SHORT

Closure of the buried-roof entry. Both iterations rebuilt in a verified editor.

    chalet SILHOUETTE   536.5  ->  738.0 cm
    church nave         804.8  -> 1107.0 cm   (1.50x -- UNCHANGED)
    church spire       1341.3  -> 1845.0 cm   (2.50x -- UNCHANGED)

**Every ratio the loop checks was correct before and after.**
`nave_over_silhouette` read 1.50 and `spire_over_silhouette` 2.50 on both
sides of the fix, and the delta list flagged neither. The loop was faithfully
building the ruled proportions against a reference 27% short.

That is the whole shape of the defect and it is worth stating as a rule: **a
ratio check cannot detect an error in the quantity it is a ratio OF.** Both
terms moved together, so the quotient was invariant. Anything expressed as
"X times Y" is blind to Y, by construction, and the more such checks agree the
more convincing the wrong answer looks.

### THE INDEPENDENT AGREEMENT, AND WHAT IT IS ACTUALLY WORTH

The re-run's spire lands at 1845.0 cm. The forge's stage 10 — a separate
payload, its own chalet assembly, no shared output — placed the forged church
at 1845.0 cm earlier the same day.

Both were 1341.3 before the fix and both are 1845.0 after it. **Two paths
sharing a defect agree; two paths sharing a correction also agree.** The
agreement is worth something only because the fix was applied to each payload
separately and neither reads the other's result — it is consistency, not
proof, and it would have looked exactly this convincing while both were wrong,
because for most of today it did.

### WHAT DID NOT MOVE, WHICH IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE CHECK

    iter0  framing 4 chalets outside 60 deg  + fov at 1.00
    iter1  framing 1 chalet  outside 67 deg

Byte-identical to the pre-fix run. Correct, and checked deliberately: those
deltas are HORIZONTAL bearings and the fix is purely vertical. **A fix that
moved them would have meant it reached something it had no business
touching.** Verifying that the unrelated numbers did NOT change is the cheaper
half of verifying a fix, and the half more often skipped.

### AND ONE PROPAGATION THAT TURNED OUT NOT TO EXIST

`city/alpine_basin_town_plan.json` carries `ridge_height_cm` values in the same
range, one of them near 536.5, across 303 buildings. Checked instead of
assumed: `plan_city.py:504` computes `round(w_o * 0.5, 1)` — half each roof's
own width, per building — and never reads the chalet silhouette. Coincidence.
The plan is unaffected.

The instinct to trace a bad constant outward was right; the conclusion had to
come from the producing line, not from the number looking familiar.

## 2026-08-31 — `--help` IS A RUN if the script never parses arguments

**What was attempted:** probing `scripts/draw_city_plan.py`'s CLI with
`--help` during the side-project spike, the same probe that is harmless on
every argparse script in the repo.

**What happened:** the script has NO argument parser — module level code runs
unconditionally on invocation and ignores `sys.argv`. `--help` executed a
full default run and OVERWROTE `_verify/20260824_city/PLAN_topdown.png`, a
committed evidence artefact. Recovered with `git restore` (rule 3 is why the
file was recoverable at all).

**Root cause:** `draw_city_plan.py` line 1 onward: imports then straight-line
execution; no `argparse`, no `if __name__ == "__main__"` guard around the
work. Any invocation is a run with defaults, and its default output path
points INTO a dated evidence folder.

**The rule it implies:** `--help` is only a read-only probe on a script
PROVEN to parse arguments. Before invoking an unfamiliar script for any
reason, grep it for `argparse|sys.argv|__main__` — a two-second read that
distinguishes "CLI" from "payload that runs on touch". The deeper defect is a
generator whose DEFAULT output overwrites dated evidence; evidence folders
should be write-once by convention.

## 2026-08-31 — the audit gate refused an audit REQUEST, and that is the gate working

Submitted brief_loop.py for pre-execution audit without the two ROOTS
declared at the top. The auditor BLOCKED without reviewing a line: its
scope-safety checks are judged against DECLARED roots, and inferring them
from cwd would make the auditor the author of the boundary it enforces —
non-negotiable 0's instrument-sharing defect. environment.md already says
the roots go in every audit request; the miss was mine. Rule: the roots
are part of the request's SHAPE, validated before content, same as any
other gate.

## 2026-09-01 — concept2level audit: "repo-relative" held for the parent, not the children

The orchestrator passed repo-relative --recipe paths to editor-stage
subprocesses whose cwd is scripts/ — and every invoked script resolves
--recipe against ITS OWN cwd (open/abspath); none joins REPO. The parent
computed the absolute path for its own reads and then handed children the
relative one. Class: an argument contract that holds in one process and
silently breaks across a cwd boundary; the failure would have been a
refusal AFTER a full editor close+relaunch cycle — fail-closed but
expensive. Fixed by passing the absolute path everywhere.
