    14  WAIVED -- foliage plans for dead worlds, frozen evidence

**THE MISTAKE: I wrote 18 waivers before checking whether any producer would
simply reproduce the plan.** Two of the three reproducible plans came back
byte-identical in payload — only the stamp was stale. A waiver there turns off
a gate that had nothing to complain about, and it would have sat in the repo
as a permanent excuse for a file that needed a five-second re-run.

    city/alpine_basin_town_plan_roofbias.json   payload identical
    encounters/alpine_8k_all.json               payload identical
    encounters/alpine_8k_verified.json          payload identical
    city/alpine_basin_town_plan.json            303 -> 348 buildings. REAL.

**RULE: before waiving a stale plan, RUN ITS PRODUCER TO A TEMP PATH and
compare the PAYLOAD, not the file.** `check_plan_freshness --reproduce`
already does this and prints one whole-file hash; that hash cannot tell "the
rows changed" from "only the stamp moved", and those need opposite responses.
The cheap probe is 30 lines and it is what turned a blanket waiver into three
honest restamps.

### THE ONE THAT IS REALLY DIVERGENT, AND WHY IT IS KEPT

Re-running `plan_city.py` produces **348 buildings and 348 roofs against the
plan's 303**, pad_z spread 4465.0 -> 11475.9 cm, because `abe88eae` (2026-08-30,
RULING 4) made roof servability a planner constraint AFTER the plan was
produced. That output already exists as `alpine_basin_town_plan_roofbias.json`
and has never been adopted — CLAUDE.md's CURRENT SPEC still records 303.
Adopting it is a TOWN decision gated on the Medieval Village kit, not a
freshness decision, and the gate must not rebuild the town as a side effect of
a foliage unit.

**A waiver never applies to `--reproduce`, by law** (`check_plan_freshness.py`:
"A plan that will not reproduce STAYS RED"). So this line stays red and now
carries a `_divergence_note {why, retires_when}` — the instrument the tool
names for exactly this, which records the reason without changing the verdict.
**Waiving and silencing are different acts and the tool is right to separate
them.**

### DEFECT 1 — I TYPED A HASH INTO THE PROSE, THEN CHANGED THE FILE IT NAMED

The first waivers hardcoded `"place_foliage.py c2c160f9168b -> f5ffe94d8f12"`
into `why`. I then edited `place_foliage.py`, the real hash became
`9d6a5439bc7a`, and **the waiver's stated reason cited a value it was not
granted against.** `granted_for` stayed correct because it is COMPUTED from
the same comparison the gate makes.

That is rule 9 inside my own artefact: a derived claim copied into a new
document without re-opening the source. Fixed by deriving every hash in the
text from the same `sbad` rows that produce the binding, so the prose cannot
drift from the thing it describes. **If a number appears in both the reason
and the machine-checked field, only one of them can be typed.**

### DEFECT 2 — A WAIVER INSERTED INTO A REPRODUCIBLE PLAN BREAKS `--reproduce`

`sha12_content` hashes the WHOLE FILE with line endings normalised. A freshly
produced plan has no `_stamp_waiver`, so **inserting one guarantees DIFFERS**
for any plan whose producer can be reproduced. The waiver defeats the very
check it cannot legally satisfy. This is invisible on the default run — which
returned exit 0 and told me I was done — and only appears under `--reproduce`,
which is what the offline suite actually runs.

**RULE: a `_stamp_waiver` belongs only on a plan that CANNOT be reproduced.**
If the producer runs, restamp it. If it runs and genuinely diverges, the
instrument is `_divergence_note`, not a waiver.

### DEFECT 3 — ORDER: EVERY EDIT TO A STAMPED INPUT MUST LAND BEFORE THE WAIVERS

I waived, then edited `place_foliage.py` and `recipes/alpine_8k.json`, and the
`granted_for` bindings expired instantly — correctly, that is what they are
for. It also expired the four LIVE 8K foliage plans E1 had just stamped, which
had to be re-placed a second time (219,659 instances, byte-identical, only
`_input_sha256` moved).

**A recipe is a SHARED input and editing one is never a local change.** Finish
every edit to every stamped input FIRST, then stamp and waive once.

### THE INVENTORY WAS NOT WHAT I FIRST REPORTED

I told Ryan four plans were stale and the failure was mine. The gate said
**18**, and a good deal of the drift predates this session:

    recipes/city.json    ed61d0b7b400 -> 85f1e7abcc8b   abe88eae, 2026-08-30
    scripts/plan_city.py 72118abd4195 -> c70ad130b051   abe88eae, 2026-08-30

`git merge-base --is-ancestor abe88eae 12e0e417` returns true, and the town
plan's stamp records the 2026-08-29 `city.json` (`53feeec2`). **The city plans
were already stale when this session started.** My change added to a standing
failure and I attributed the whole thing to myself without resolving a single
differing input to its commit.

**RULE: before attributing a gate failure, resolve each differing input to the
commit that produced it.** Iterating `git log --format=%h -- <path>` and
hashing each blob turns "recorded X, actual Y" into a commit and a subject
line in seconds. I had the hashes in front of me the whole time.

**AND A FAILED ATTEMPT AT THAT, WORTH RECORDING.** I first tried to count how
many plans were already stale at session start by hashing `git show
<commit>:<path>` blobs. It reported 33 of 34 — implausible, and wrong: git
stores LF while the stamps were taken over working files with CRLF, so nearly
every text input mismatched. **That is the exact trap `reproduce()` documents
in its own comment** and I walked into it one function away. The number was
discarded rather than reported. The claim that survives rests on commit
ancestry, which needs no hashing at all. **When an archaeology result looks
too strong, suspect the representation before believing the finding.**

### THE BENCHMARK PLANS SHOULD NOT BE FRESH

Fourteen waivers are foliage plans for the pre-8K world and four `_verify/`
benchmark spikes. Their world recipes moved because those terrains were
RE-CARVED after the plans were produced (`608fa558`, "Coast recarved: ocean
floor 96 -> 16.7 m"). They genuinely do not match today's terrain — **and that
is correct**, because they record what was placed WHEN THE BENCHMARK WAS
MEASURED. Regenerating them to satisfy a gate would mutate `_verify/`
evidence, which CLAUDE.md holds is "cited, never obeyed".

**General form: a freshness gate assumes every plan is REGENERABLE. Evidence
is not.** The gate has no concept of a deliberately frozen artefact, so a
waiver is standing in for it — and a waiver is a gate turned off, which is the
wrong instrument for "this is correct as it is". BACKLOG carries a `_frozen`
verdict as the real fix.

### THE PLAN GRAPH SELF-REFERENCES

`encounters/alpine_8k_verified.json` stamps `encounters/alpine_8k_all.json` as
an input, so touching `_all` moves a hash `_verified` records and creates a NEW
differing input mid-operation. Handled by working in dependency order.
**Editing a plan to satisfy a gate can break a different plan's stamp** — the
write is not inert just because the payload is.

Waivers are inserted TEXTUALLY after the opening brace, because these files run
from a 2 MB single-line compact foliage plan to a 23,035-line pretty-printed
city plan and `json.dump` would reformat all of them into an unreviewable diff.
Read back by re-parsing both blobs and comparing the parsed documents: **15 of
15 identical to HEAD apart from `_stamp_waiver`**, 1 insertion and 1 deletion
each; and the 3 restamped plans identical apart from `_input_sha256`.

## 2026-09-08n — CORRECTION to 2026-09-08m: the city plan ALREADY declared its divergence, and I added a SECOND one

### WHAT I GOT WRONG

2026-09-08m reports that I measured `plan_city.py` reproducing 348 buildings
against the plan's 303 and treated it as a finding. **It was already written
down, in the plan's own `_divergence_note`, by an earlier session** — and that
note is better than the one I wrote:

    KNOWN-DIVERGENT AND DELIBERATELY KEPT. recipes/city.json moved when
    buildings.storey_m was ruled 3.2 -> 2.0 ... re-planning also moves the
    building count 303 -> 348. The re-placement is GATED to the kit-driven
    re-plan unit (ruling 4, R4a/b/c) because roof SEATING must land in the
    same pass -- re-planning now would place 348 buildings whose roofs still
    do not sit on their walls. The live town is the 303-building placement
    and it matches THIS file, which is why the file is kept.

It names the mechanism I did not have: the re-plan is gated because **roof
seating must land in the same pass**, not merely because the town is gated on
a kit. My measurement was correct and redundant.

**This is standing rule 9 turned the wrong way round.** The rule says do not
trust a claim inherited from our own artefacts without opening the source. It
does not say ignore the artefact — and the plan's own declared metadata is the
FIRST thing to read when diagnosing that plan. I opened the recipe, the
producer, and the git history of both, and never opened the file I was
diagnosing.

**RULE: before diagnosing a stale plan, read the plan's OWN `_stamp_waiver`,
`_divergence_note` and `_` prose keys.** They are written by the sessions that
already met this problem. It cost a redundant reproduction run and a duplicate
key.

### THE DUPLICATE KEY, WHICH IS THE REAL DEFECT

My applier inserted `_divergence_note` at the FRONT of the file without
checking whether one existed. **JSON permits duplicate keys and Python keeps
the LAST**, so:

  * my note was silently discarded — the gate printed the OLD one, which is
    how I noticed at all,
  * the committed file carried TWO `_divergence_note` keys, and nothing in the
    suite flags that,
  * every reader using `json.load` would see one note; anyone reading the raw
    file would see two, disagreeing.

Committed in `a91d57a5` and corrected in the commit that follows it. The
detection was luck: I read the gate's printed note, saw wording I had not
written, and checked. **Had my text been similar to the existing note I would
never have noticed.**

Fixed by checking the parsed document for the key before inserting, and by
counting raw key occurrences with a regex afterwards rather than trusting
`json.load`, which cannot see the duplicate it just collapsed.

**GENERAL FORM: a textual insert into JSON must check the PARSED document for
the key and re-count on the RAW text.** `json.load` is a lossy reader for this
purpose — it silently resolves exactly the defect the insert can create. That
is non-negotiable 0 again: the instrument that would report the problem shares
its failure mode with the operation that caused it.

### AND IT CONFIRMS THE INVENTORY CLAIM

The city plan carried a `_divergence_note` before this session, and a
divergent plan **stays red by law** regardless of the note. So
`check_plan_freshness --reproduce` — the check the offline suite runs — was
already RED at session start, on this plan, for a reason that has nothing to
do with me. That is now established from the artefact itself rather than from
commit ancestry alone.

## 2026-09-08p — GROUND COVER IS `system: grass`: its cull is a GRASS TYPE property, not a plan's `cull_cm`, and it is now READ BACK

### THE CORRECTION

2026-09-08k and 2026-09-08m argue the ground-cover cull as though Meadow and
Blueberry were placed like the trees — "culling Meadow at 18.6 m opens a 237 m
gap". The DECISION is unaffected and Ryan's ruling stands. **The mechanism I
described was wrong.**

    Meadow      system=grass    Blueberry   system=grass
    Conifer/ConiferPine/SpruceSub/SpruceSapling   (no system key)

`place_foliage.plan()` skips them before `_cull_cm_for` is ever reached:

    if sp.get("system") == "grass":
        continue                        scripts/place_foliage.py

So **there is no `foliage/alpine_8k_Meadow.json`, no instances, and no
`cull_cm`** — the `GROUND_COVER` branch in `_cull_cm_for` is unreachable for
the two species it names. It is not dead weight (it guards a hand-run or a
future non-grass ground cover) but it is not what governs the world today.
`check_derived_culls.py` reports all six because it reads the RECIPE, not the
plans, which is why the six-row table looked uniform when the pipeline is not.

### WHAT ACTUALLY CARRIES THE NUMBER

    recipes/alpine_8k.json  species.cull_distance_m
      -> make_landscape_material.py  GrassVariety.end_cull_distance
        -> /Game/Foliage/GT_alpine_8k_<species>   (LandscapeGrassType)

The landscape material's grass output spawns these per frame near the camera;
there are no persistent transforms, no weight_share, and no instance budget to
charge them against.

### READ BACK FROM THE SAVED ASSETS — rule 12

`read_grass_type.py` shares no code with the builder (non-negotiable 0) and
asks the saved asset:

    GT_alpine_8k_Meadow      4 varieties, cull 5000 cm each, densities -> 120.0
    GT_alpine_8k_Blueberry   6 varieties, cull 4500 cm each, every variety
                             carrying its MI_*_nowind override

50 m and 45 m — **exactly the authored values the ruling preserves.** Declared,
applied, and read back from a second instrument, so the ruling is now a
controlled parameter rather than prose.

### THE LESSON

**A species-level field can be consumed by two entirely different pipelines,
and the recipe does not say which.** `cull_distance_m` means a plan's `cull_cm`
for a foliage species and a grass type's `end_cull_distance` for a grass
species; the discriminator is a `system` key that four of the six species do
not carry at all. I derived, argued and ruled on a number for three sessions
without checking which pipeline consumed it.

**RULE: before reasoning about a recipe field, find its CONSUMER.** `grep -rn
<field> scripts/` costs seconds and would have surfaced `import_heightmap.py`
and `make_landscape_material.py` — neither of which is the foliage planner —
on the first day.

Nothing was mis-set: the world holds the ruled values. What was wrong was my
account of WHY, and an account that is wrong about the mechanism will
eventually be applied to a case where the mechanism matters.

## 2026-09-08q — I "FIXED" A QUOTING BUG BY MAKING IT PARSE, WHICH MOVED IT PAST THE CHEAP CHECK INTO THE EXPENSIVE ONE

### WHAT HAPPENED

`tree_lod_probe.py` takes its mesh list through `ue_exec --set MESHES=<json>`.
Run 1 was refused by `ue_exec`'s pre-flight syntax check, in about a second:

    SyntaxError: invalid syntax
    MESHES = [[Conifer, /Game/Meshes/Trees/SM_PVE_Norway_Spruce_01_A], ...]
    (checked AFTER --set substitution, which is what the editor receives)

**I read that as "the template must carry its own quoting"** and changed
`MESHES = __MESHES__` to `MESHES = _json.loads(r"""__MESHES__""")`.

Run 2 passed pre-flight — a raw triple-quoted string is valid Python whatever
is inside it — reached the editor, and died there after **240 seconds**:

    json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 3 (char 2)
    r"""[[Conifer, /Game/Meshes/Trees/SM_PVE_Norway_Spruce_01_A], ...]"""

### THE ACTUAL ROOT CAUSE, WHICH IS ONE LAYER LOWER

**PowerShell strips the embedded `"` characters when passing an argument to a
native executable.** The file on disk held valid JSON; what arrived at
`ue_exec` had no quotes at all. Both runs were the SAME defect. My change did
not address it — it only changed which layer noticed.

    on disk        [["Conifer", "/Game/Meshes/Trees/SM_PVE_Norway_Spruce_01_A"], ...]
    after -Raw     same
    at ue_exec     [[Conifer, /Game/Meshes/Trees/SM_PVE_Norway_Spruce_01_A], ...]

This is the msys-game-path hook's lesson wearing different clothes: **the
shell layer rewrites arguments, and the rewrite is invisible at the call
site.** That hook guards `/Game/...` paths in Git Bash; nothing guards
quote-stripping in PowerShell.

### THE PART THAT IS WORTH MORE THAN THE FIX

**Wrapping a bad value in quotes converted a COMPILE-TIME failure into a
RUNTIME failure, and that is strictly worse.** The pre-flight check exists
precisely so a malformed payload costs a second instead of a round trip; its
own message says so — "the editor would only tell you this 25 s from now". I
disabled that protection by accident while believing I was fixing the thing it
had detected.

**RULE: when a cheap check refuses a payload, fix the VALUE, never the
wrapper.** If a change makes a refused payload parse without changing what it
means, it has defeated the check rather than satisfied it. The tell is that
the "fix" touches syntax and not content.

Cost: 240 s, because `--timeout` is a DISCOVERY WINDOW and is spent IN FULL —
`ue_exec` prints that on every run and I passed 240 for a query that answers
in seconds. **12-25 is right**, as its own note says.

### THE FIX: DELETE THE CHANNEL, DO NOT ESCAPE IT

Any escaping scheme is one more thing that must be remembered per shell, and
standing rule 3 already records what that class of rule is worth — the
commit-message rule went to a FILE precisely because "remember which
characters the shell eats" is the weakest kind of rule.

So the payload no longer takes a mesh list. It derives the repo root from
`unreal.Paths.project_dir()` (the repo is its parent), reads
`recipes/alpine_8k.json` itself, and filters the placed species with the same
predicate `place_foliage.plan()` uses — skip `system == "grass"`, skip
anything with a `role`. **Nothing crosses the shell boundary, so nothing can
be rewritten in transit**, and the probe now reads the same source of truth
the placement does rather than a list I assembled by hand.

## 2026-09-08r — ELEVEN SMOKE FRAMES TO GET A TREE ONTO FLAT MAGENTA, AND EVERY ONE FAILED DIFFERENTLY

E2 needs one thing that sounds trivial: a mesh rendered against a flat key
colour. It took eleven frames, and the reason it took eleven is worth more
than the rig. **Nine of the eleven reported SUCCESS at the API level.** The
payload said `ok: true`, the material said the colour was set, the console
command returned, and the frame came back wrong anyway.

    1  sky background      backdrop invisible: rotator roll/pitch
    2  sky + editor sprites ShowFlag.Sprites did not remove them
    3  dark navy, no sprites game view worked; material was translucent
    4  sky again           EmissiveMeshMaterial is ADDITIVE
    5  sky again           opaque material is two_sided FALSE -> culled
    6  pure black          cube renders, LevelColoration Color unused
    7  pure black          built material, but `viewmode unlit` shows BaseColor
    8  pure black          same; asset cached, never rebuilt
    9  pure black          delete_asset silently failed -> stale asset reused
    10 (7, 0, 8)           right hue, crushed by exposure
    11 (211, 0, 199)       CORRECT

### THE ONE THAT MATTERS: A READ-BACK THAT READS ITSELF

    _mid.set_vector_parameter_value("Color", magenta)
    _rb = _mid.get_vector_parameter_value("Color")     # returns magenta

**This passes for a parameter the material does not have.** A
MaterialInstanceDynamic stores overrides in its own table, and the getter
reads that table -- not the material graph. So the check "set it and read it
back" cannot distinguish a real parameter from a typo, and I used it as
evidence for four frames.

Rule 12 says a parameter that is not read back is prose. **2026-09-08r adds
the corollary: a read-back that shares storage with the write is also prose.**
That is non-negotiable 0 in its purest form -- the instrument and the claim
had one source. The instrument that actually settled it asks the MATERIAL
(`MaterialEditingLibrary.get_vector_parameter_names`) and, finally, the PIXEL.

### THE ENGINE MATERIALS ARE A TRAP, AND THE PARAMETER IS NOT THE DISCRIMINATOR

Three engine materials all expose a `Color` vector parameter. None works as a
key backdrop, for three DIFFERENT reasons:

    EmissiveMeshMaterial          BLEND_ADDITIVE     invisible over sky
    DebugMeshMaterial             BLEND_TRANSLUCENT  shaded to navy
    LevelColorationUnlitMaterial  OPAQUE, but its graph ignores Color -> black

**Check the BLEND MODE and the shading model, not whether the parameter
exists.** `material_param_probe.py` now asks all four questions at once.

### `viewmode unlit` AND AN UNLIT MATERIAL ARE OPPOSITES

`viewmode unlit` visualises **BaseColor**. A material whose shading model is
`MSM_UNLIT` has **no BaseColor** -- its output is EmissiveColor. So an unlit
material under the unlit view mode renders **pure black**, and it reads
exactly like "the colour is not being applied".

Two different materials rendered black for this one reason and I changed the
material twice before suspecting the view mode.

### A SILENT `delete_asset` TURNS A CONSTANT INTO A CACHE

`EditorAssetLibrary.delete_asset(KEY_MAT)` returned without deleting --
`does_asset_exist` was still true immediately after. With a `create if absent`
branch, that meant **the first, faulty material was reused forever**: I raised
the emissive gain and got a byte-identical black frame, which is the signature
of a change that never reached the thing it was meant to change.

**RULE: when a builder can run twice, make the artefact a function of THIS
run's inputs.** Load-or-create, then rebuild the graph unconditionally. A
branch that skips the build on an existing asset is a cache with no
invalidation, and it hides exactly the experiment you are running.

### EMISSIVE 1.0 IS NOT BRIGHT, AND THE DECLARED KEY IS NOT THE RENDERED KEY

Emissive magenta at gain 1 and gain 40 both render near black: it goes through
exposure and the filmic tonemapper like anything else. Gain 5000 saturates.
**Overshooting is free** -- the channel clips at the key colour -- so the gain
is set far past saturation rather than tuned to a number that would drift with
the level's lighting.

And even saturated, the backdrop measures **(211, 0, 199)**, not (255, 0, 255).
Keying on the declared colour classifies the BACKGROUND as subject: at
threshold 60 the distance from (255,0,255) to (211,0,199) is 71. The capture
reported "subject 37.8% of frame" over a frame whose subject is 28.5%.

**RULE: measure the key from the artefact, never declare it.** The driver
samples four corners, requires them to agree, and passes the MEASURED colour
to the checker.

### THE EDITOR DRAWS ITSELF INTO YOUR MEASUREMENT

The first frames carried a CameraActor billboard and the viewport axis widget.
Editor billboards are drawn WITHOUT a depth test, so the backdrop cannot
occlude them, and `ShowFlag.Sprites 0` did not remove them either.
`LevelEditorSubsystem.editor_set_game_view(True)` does -- and it has a GETTER,
so it can be read back rather than hoped for.

They would have been identical in every LOD's frame, which is what makes this
dangerous: a constant additive error in every mask, invisible in a comparison.

### A PARSER FAULT WEARING THE COSTUME OF AN EDITOR FAULT

With the rig working, the first full run reported:

    "ConiferPine: scene setup failed: ..."
    "SpruceSub: scene setup failed: ..."
    "SpruceSapling: scene setup failed: ..."

**All three payloads had succeeded.** Printed inside my own failure message
was the evidence: `ok: true`, `backdrop_built: true`, `game_view_readback:
true`, `force_lod_ok: true`, both actors listed. The driver could not READ the
result:

    json.loads(out[i:])          # "Extra data" -- ue_exec prints a duration
                                 # line AFTER the payload's JSON
    json.JSONDecoder().raw_decode(out[i:])   # parses the prefix, ignores it

Every candidate offset failed, `blob` stayed None, and the driver blamed the
editor for its own inability to parse. **A failure message that quotes the
successful result it could not read is the tell**, and it is only visible
because the fallback printed the raw tail rather than a tidy summary.

**RULE: when a driver reports that a child failed, check that the driver could
READ the child.** Fold the raw output into the failure, always -- a summary
that says "setup failed" and nothing else would have sent me back into the
editor to debug a scene that was already correct.

### AND THE ROTATOR, FOR THE FOURTH TIME

`unreal.Rotator` takes **ROLL first**. `Rotator(-90, 0, 0)` rolls; it does not
pitch. `shoot.py`'s own `--rot` help says the project has done this three
times. I made it four, on a backdrop whose facing then could not be seen
because the material I was using happened to be two-sided.

**Use KEYWORD arguments for Rotator.** They are order-independent, so the trap
cannot fire. That is a fix to the CLASS, not to the instance.

## 2026-09-08s — E2: THE SILHOUETTES HOLD. I PREDICTED A COLLAPSE AND THE MEASUREMENT SAID NO.

### THE PREDICTION, AND WHY IT WAS WRONG

From the LOD probe I wrote: "Six triangles cannot carry a conifer silhouette",
and named ConiferPine LOD3 (27,824 -> 32 tris) and SpruceSub LOD4 (20,695 ->
6) as candidate failures. **Measured, both hold.**

    species        last LOD  coverage  IoU    verdict at its CURRENT switch
    ConiferPine     32 tris     0.993   0.921  geometry holds
    SpruceSub        6 tris     1.001   0.948  geometry holds
    SpruceSapling  326 tris     1.141   0.825  geometry holds

**A 6-triangle LOD is not a collapsed mesh; it is an ALPHA-MASKED BILLBOARD.**
Its silhouette comes from the texture's alpha, not from its geometry, so
triangle count says nothing about the shape it presents. I reasoned from
triangle count to silhouette and the two are not connected.

The candidate was worth raising and cheap to test. **The error was writing it
as "cannot" rather than "predict".**

### WHAT ACTUALLY FAILS: TONE, NOT SHAPE

**Every failing row in the entire audit failed on LUMA. Not one failed on
coverage or IoU.** luma_delta_weber runs 0.029 to 0.605 against a 0.03
threshold, and rises monotonically with LOD index on all three species.

That matches a suspicion already on record. `measure_lod_materials.py` exists
because "trunks beyond ~50 m go uniformly pale", and it established that every
LOD carries LOD0's materials across the same sections -- so a colour pop is
"NOT caused by a lost section; look at the material's own distance behaviour".
This audit is the second instrument agreeing with that.

**It is recorded as a CANDIDATE, not a verdict.** `luma_delta_weber`
normalises by mean luma, and these captures are lit by the level's own sun at
2.5 km with the subject largely backlit and dim. A small denominator inflates
the ratio. Re-measure under controlled lighting before acting.

### DEFECT 1 — A PERFECT SCORE THAT MEANT "NO MEASUREMENT"

The first judged run returned, for every LOD of every species:

    coverage_ratio 1.000   silhouette_iou 1.000   edge_error_px NaN

Identical silhouettes for meshes 900x apart in triangle count, over PNGs I had
already proven differ by sha256. The cause:

    if im.mode == "RGBA":  mask = alpha > 127      # lod_silhouette_check
    else:                  mask = distance from key > 60

**HighResShot writes RGBA with alpha = 255 everywhere.** So the mask was the
ENTIRE FRAME for every image, the key colour was never used, and coverage and
IoU were comparing the frame to itself. The whole magenta rig -- eleven smoke
frames of it -- was bypassed by a branch taken on the file's mode.

`edge_error_px: NaN` was the tell and I nearly read past it: there is no edge
to measure when the mask has no boundary.

**RULE: a metric pinned at its perfect value across every row is not a pass,
it is a disconnected instrument.** 1.000 on 13 of 13 should be as alarming as
0.000. Fixed by filing captures as RGB, which forces the key-colour path, plus
a guard that strips alpha at judge time so an old capture cannot revive it.

### DEFECT 2 — A VACUOUS PASS, PRESENTED AS A RESULT

Before that, the driver reported for all three species:

    "last LOD does not fail at its current switch."

It had read the checker's output as `{"lod0": ..., "lod3": ...}`. The checker
returns `{"thresholds": ..., "lods": [ ... ]}` -- a LIST. Every lookup gave
`{}`, `startswith("FAIL")` was false on an empty string, and the code fell
through to the reassuring branch.

**A missing measurement took the same path as a good one.** Now an empty
result yields "NOT JUDGED: the checker returned no comparison rows", because
absence of evidence must never render as evidence of absence.

### DEFECT 3 — POOLING TWO DIFFERENT FINDINGS INTO ONE VERDICT

With the mask fixed, the combined verdict indicted all three MESHES -- because
`verdict` is a single string that fails if ANY threshold fails, and luma
failed everywhere. That would have proposed mesh work on chains whose measured
shape is fine.

**Silhouette and tone are different findings with different fixes and
different confidence.** The sidecar now carries a geometric verdict (coverage
and IoU, which is what an audit named "silhouette" is for) and a separate
`tonal_candidate` block carrying the luma numbers, the corroborating prior
record, and the dim-lighting caveat.

### THE ANSWER TO THE RULING'S QUESTION

No ScreenSize proposal is written for any species. The rule was: fails at its
current switch and passes at the silhouette size => the switch is wrong. **No
species fails geometrically at its current switch**, so the switches are
defensible on silhouette grounds and the antecedent never holds.

SpruceSub's LOD0 at 1.000 and LOD1 at 0.990 is reported only, per ruling: LOD0
is displaced almost immediately and is close to unreachable in play.

Conifer is excluded and the reason is in the sidecar: Nanite, 1 LOD, screen
size 2.0. `r.ForceLOD` does not govern it and there is no discrete switch to
audit.

## 2026-09-08t — E3: THE PERF LAW'S RED IS THE EDITOR'S 60 Hz CAP. The game thread was measuring the harness.

### THE MEASUREMENT

Four ratified stations, standalone `-game` at 3840x2160 read back from engine
metadata, 25.0 s window each after a 60 s settle.

    zone         GPU p90  std/ed   Game p90  std/ed   FrameTime p50  std/ed
    plaza          8.33 / 7.84       3.98 / 14.00        9.32 / 16.67
    main_street    5.95 / 5.56       4.05 / 13.90        6.95 / 16.67
    treeline       5.58 / 7.05       3.96 / 13.98        6.58 / 16.67
    vista          6.99 / 8.33       3.85 / 14.15        7.96 / 16.67

**The editor's FrameTime p50 is 16.67 ms at every station.** That is a 60 Hz
cap, not a cost. Its GameThreadTime tracks the cap (13.90-14.15) rather than
the content -- which is precisely what REGISTER recorded as "pinned at
13.9-14.15 ms on all four zones regardless of content" and filed as an
oddity. It is not an oddity; it is the cap.

With the editor gone the game thread drops to **3.85-4.05 ms**, while the GPU
stays within a few percent of the editor's figure. **The GPU was measuring the
scene all along; the game thread was measuring the harness.**

`check_perf.py` is RED on plaza Game 14.00 against a 12.00 budget. Standalone
plaza is 3.98. Every zone is under both its GPU and its game budget in
standalone.

**NOTHING IS RE-RATIFIED.** `recipes/perf_budgets.json` is untouched. The
budgets were ratified against an editor baseline, and whether they should be
restated against a standalone one is an operator decision with a real
argument on both sides -- the editor number is not *wrong*, it is a
measurement of a different thing, and a budget policing the editor still
catches editor-side regressions.

### THE CAMERA COULD NOT BE VERIFIED DIRECTLY, SO IT WAS VERIFIED SIDEWAYS

`getall PlayerController Location` prints nothing: `Location` is not a
UPROPERTY on the controller. I removed the check rather than keep one that
always passes. The available evidence is cross-station variation:

    GPU p90 across the four stations: 5.58 .. 8.33 ms, a 49% spread

One fixed view cannot produce that. The camera moved. **The GAME thread is
nearly flat across stations in standalone too (3.85-4.05), and that is NOT
the failure signature** -- if BugItGo had done nothing, the GPU would be flat
as well. It says the game thread is not driven by what is on screen here.

### THREE VOID RUNS BEFORE ONE VALID ONE, AND ALL THREE LOOKED FINE

**Void 1 -- 720p wearing a 4K label.** `-ResX/-ResY` on the command line
LOSES to config (`LogConfig: Set CVar [[r.setres:1280x720]]`). My read-back
regexed `ResX=(\d+)` and matched THE COMMAND LINE, which the log echoes
verbatim. The instrument confirmed the label by reading back my own argument.
The camera check had the identical fault: it searched the log for "BugItGo"
and found the echoed command line, so it would have passed with the command
deleted.

**I wrote LESSONS 2026-09-08r this session -- "a read-back sharing a source
with the write is prose" -- and then broke it twice in the next script.** The
rule was in the file. Writing a lesson down does not install it.

Fixed: `r.setRes` in ExecCmds (runs after config), resolution read from the
CsvProfiler's `systemresolution` metadata, and `config_setres_seen` recorded
beside it so the override is visible rather than assumed.

**Void 2 -- a partial file caught mid-write.** I polled for the CSV to exist
with size > 0. The profiler writes INCREMENTALLY, so that caught a partial
file ~8 s in, and terminating the process truncated the capture. Those 8 s
were the level load, carrying a 4,626 ms GameThread hitch INSIDE the window.
It presented as a completed measurement with plausible numbers.

Fixed: dwell a fixed wall time (60 s settle + 25 s window + 20 s margin) and
take the TAIL. No assumption about flush behaviour or about when loading
finished. The frame budget is now effectively unbounded because the DWELL
bounds the capture -- a frame count that expires mid-run ends the capture
wherever it happens to be, which is what produced 823 frames of startup.

**Void 3 -- a NameError on a constant I had deleted.** It failed before
launching the engine, which is the cheap direction to fail in.

### THE COMPARISON IS NOT LIKE-FOR-LIKE AND SAYS SO

The editor baseline records `viewport_size: null` for all four zones -- it
never captured the resolution it ran at. A GPU figure is resolution-bound, so
the GPU columns are INDICATIVE only. The game-thread comparison does not
depend on resolution and is the load-bearing one.

**That gap is itself the rule-12 failure this session keeps meeting**: the
older instrument declared a viewport and never read one back, so its GPU
numbers cannot be placed beside anyone else's.

## 2026-09-08u — E4: the dolly does NOT stay sunlit, and the capture reported OK at 17 frames of 90

### THE RESULT

3.0 s from near_ground along its own forward vector, 419.99 cm of travel,
90 frames at 3840x2160, player instrument, no exposure changes.

    frame_0000   ground half 41.1% above 0.20 linear luma
    frame_0089   ground half 17.7%
    change       -57%

**The path does not stay out of canopy shadow.** Both frames are partly lit —
this is DAPPLED shadow striping the meadow, not a solid edge — but the walk
ends in a markedly more shadowed patch than it starts in. Confirmed by eye
against both frames, not read off the number alone.

**I predicted the opposite.** From the near_ground still I reasoned that
4.2 m was too short to leave the lit foreground. That was a guess off one
image and it was wrong, in the same way the E2 "six triangles cannot carry a
silhouette" guess was wrong: a plausible inference from a picture, stated as
though measured. **The dolly was still worth capturing — the check is what
E4 asked for — but the prediction should have been labelled a prediction.**

E4 says DO NOT SCORE, so the sidecar judges the two frames it was asked about
and stops. No heading was re-chosen and no threshold was moved to make it
pass. If a sunlit path is wanted, choosing one is a decision, not a fix.

### THE DEFECT THAT WOULD HAVE ANSWERED THE QUESTION AGAINST THE WRONG IMAGE

`bench_capture` printed **"dolly 17 frames"** and **OK**, and wrote its
sidecar, while 73 more frames were still being written.

    if a.dolly:
        return ok and len(fresh(glob(outroot/dolly/*.png))) > 0

`> 0` is evidence that rendering BEGAN, not that it finished. MRQ writes
frames lazily and keeps flushing after the window title clears, so the run
completed on the first frame to land. **A shadow check run on its say-so
would have read frame_0016 as "the last frame of the walk" and answered the
question against an image from a third of the way along.** Nothing would have
errored.

I only caught it because the frame count kept climbing while I read the
output: 17, then 26, 36, 51, 66, 80, 90.

**RULE: a completion test must assert the EXPECTED COUNT, never "more than
zero".** The count was knowable — the sequence declares seconds x fps — so it
is now derived from `benchmark.json dolly` rather than from the presence of
output. Before the check ran I confirmed independently: 90 files, range
0..89, none missing, count stable across three 10 s polls.

### ONE FLAG, FOUR PLACES, FOUR DIFFERENT PLAUSIBLE FAILURES

`--dolly-only` had to reach four independent consumers of `stations`, and I
found them one at a time, each with its own symptom:

    the JOBS                13 min silent wait on files never scheduled
    the completion check    refused on a transient remote failure at a
                            station this run never captures
    the residency pre-check same, one layer earlier
    the JUDGING             KeyError AFTER a successful 107 s render, so a
                            completed capture reported as a failure

None of the four symptoms pointed at the flag. **The lesson is not "check
four places" — it is that `stations` was computed once at the top and then
consulted by four consumers that each assumed it described THIS run.** A run
should derive what it judges from what it captured. Adding a flag that
changes the run changed none of them.

### THE STALL DIAGNOSED FROM THE LOG, NOT BY WAITING

The first failure looked exactly like a slow render. The editor log settled
it in seconds: sequence build at 04:42:45, residency query at 04:47:00, then
**nothing at all**. An IDLE editor, not a busy one.

That is R-EDITOR-CLOSE's distinction — "answers a round trip" is not "is
free" — turned the other way round: a silent log after a trigger means the
trigger did not take. Waiting longer would have produced the same silence at
the 1800 s timeout.

### CLOSE

R-EDITOR-CLOSE: census 0 dirty, quiet 2,433 s, **retry closed it in 39.1 s**.
Four applications, four times the kill was authorized by both conditions and
four times it was not needed.

## 2026-09-08v — THE CENSUS: three ways a wrong answer looked exactly like a right one

Four reference projects, five maps censused, one real survey. The findings
about the SAMPLE PROJECTS are in `research/census/`. These are the three
findings about MEASUREMENT, and each cost real work before it was caught.

### 1. A ZERO IS ONLY TRUSTWORTHY IF THE LOOKUP REACHED A PLACE WHERE THE THING COULD HAVE BEEN

    Electric Dreams   pcg_graphs     0 -> 72     foliage_types  0 -> 62
    Dark Ruins        pcg_graphs     0 -> 54

`_assets_of` hardcoded the package `/Script/Engine`. `UPCGGraph` lives in
`/Script/PCG` and `UFoliageType` in `/Script/Foliage`, so the query asked a
package where the class does not exist, got an empty list, **threw nothing**,
and returned a clean zero.

**The PCG reference project reported zero PCG graphs.** I read that, saw
`current_world` was correct and every neighbouring section sensible, and moved
on. `foliage_types: 0` survived THREE censuses the same way.

Worse than a dead accessor, which at least leaves an `_error`. This left
nothing at all — no exception, no record, no trace.

**RULE: "nothing found" and "looked in the wrong place" are indistinguishable
in a result and opposite in meaning.** Every census now carries
`asset_lookup_trace` — which package each class hit and how many it found —
so a zero is decidable in the artefact instead of by re-running. Dark Ruins'
`foliage_types` is still 0 and now PROVEN: the trace reads `/Script/Foliage:0`.

### 2. A COUNT OF ONE IS NOT A MEASUREMENT OF ONE

I reported City Sample's `world_partition` as a captured target, twice, on the
strength of the section showing **1 entry**:

    "world_partition": { "/Game/Map/...": {
        "_error": "'World' object has no attribute 'get_world_partition'" } }

An error record counts as an entry. In a section summary it is indistinguishable
from a result — and the payload's own header warned about exactly this: *"a
null with `_error` is a name to fix, not a finding"*.

**RULE: when summarising a collection, count what the entries ARE, not how
many there are.** The rollup now carries a STATUS on every number —
MEASURED / MEASURED_ZERO / UNVERIFIED / NOT_CAPTURED / ZERO_UNAUDITED —
because this census produced all five and a bare count flattens them.

### 3. "IS THERE A FILE?" WHEN THE QUESTION IS "IS THERE A FILE FROM THIS RUN?"

**Four instances in one session**, each with a different disguise:

    capture_truth   globbed `<station>*.png`, found the PREVIOUS run's frame
                    and never checked shoot.py's exit code
    the LOD driver  matched "lod0" by substring, so `sorted()[-1]` picked an
                    older file
    wait_for        returned on mere EXISTENCE, so a "re-run" reported the
                    prior run's census -- and I nearly filed "the fix did not
                    work" over a run that never happened
    the survey      the superseded -ExecCmds frames used the EXACT filenames
                    the new survey writes, so a file COUNT said "5 filed"
                    while the mtimes said 90 minutes stale

**RULE: freshness is a property of the ARTEFACT, not of the directory.** An
mtime anchored before the work started answers it; a filename never does.

**And the fourth fix is the one that should have been the first.** Instead of
remembering to check a fifth time, the stale set was MOVED OUT so the output
directory was empty and any file appearing in it could only be from this run.
Freshness by construction beats freshness by vigilance — three of the four
were patched with vigilance and the pattern kept recurring.

### THE SHAPE UNDERNEATH ALL THREE

A structurally valid result, computed without error, describing something
other than what was asked. It appeared this session as `coverage 1.000` from
an all-true alpha mask, a 60 Hz cap read as a game-thread cost, a
shot-differentiation metric that ranked the known-bad set ABOVE the good one,
and all three above.

None was caught by the instrument that produced it. Each was caught by asking
a different question of a different source — the engine header, the package
the class lives in, the file's mtime, the picture itself.

## 2026-09-09a — E4 CLOSED on yaw -67.5, and the baseline disagreed with the capture in DIRECTION

Ryan ruled -67.5 from the probe table. The dolly was rebuilt, captured once at
the player instrument and verified — first and last frames both sunlit, no
score taken. E4 is done. Three things are worth keeping.

### THE MEASUREMENT

    heading      -67.5 (ruled)     E4's original, for comparison: -12.8
    first/last   0.7545 / 0.6063   0.411 / 0.177
    change       -19.6%            -57%
    floor        0.5961            (not measured then)
    verdict      stays sunlit      does NOT stay sunlit

Thresholds SUNLIT_MIN 0.15 and DROP_MAX 0.50; the walk clears both by a wide
margin. The walk profile is smooth — .755 .751 .709 .596 .606 — a gentle
decline that flattens, not a cliff and not a dip that recovers.

### THE BASELINE PREDICTED A RISE AND THE CAPTURE FELL

The whole point of recording the heading's shade profile beside the capture is
attribution, and the first thing it did was disagree:

    probe (editor stills)   0.646 -> 0.739 -> 0.714    RISING  (+0.068)
    dolly (PIE via MRQ)     0.755 -> 0.709 -> 0.606    FALLING (-0.148)

Not noise, and not the +/-0.03 session drift: the start is 0.11 BRIGHTER in
the capture and the end 0.11 DARKER. A systematic divergence that varies along
the walk.

**Most likely cause, and it is already an open question.** The probe is
`shoot.py` HighResShot in the EDITOR world; the dolly is PIE through MRQ.
Those are different worlds, and Q12 records `7 InstancedFoliageActors absent
from PIE while in range`. Missing canopy in PIE means missing dapple, and how
much it matters depends on where the camera stands relative to those actors —
which is exactly a difference that varies along a walk. This is a HYPOTHESIS
with a named mechanism, not a conclusion; nothing here measured which actors
were absent during this render.

**The rule it implies: a baseline is only a baseline for the instrument that
took it.** Both numbers are correct measurements of different things, and
either one alone would have looked authoritative. Non-negotiable 0 says
instruments sharing a source are one measurement; the converse bit here —
these two do NOT share a source, so agreement was never owed, and I should
have said so when wiring the baseline in rather than after reading it.

The verdict does not depend on the disagreement: both frames are far above
SUNLIT_MIN under the instrument that actually captured them.

### A PREDICTION I MADE AND THEN HAD TO WITHDRAW

I said all three candidate headings should report the same lit fraction at
t=0.0 because they leave from the same point, and that I would discard the
table if they disagreed. They disagreed — 0.521, 0.646, 0.664 — and the table
was fine. Same point, different YAW, therefore three different FRAMES: lit
fraction depends on what the camera sees, not only on where it stands. Had I
held to the stated check I would have thrown away a correct measurement.

**A check invented on the spot, stated with a consequence attached, is not
free.** It sounded like rigour and was a confusion between camera position and
camera view.

### AND THE BUILD LOG WAS THE WRONG GATE

The editor came up on a cold DDC. Waiting for build silence would have waited
forever: the rate fell 2129 -> ~65 lines/30 s and PLATEAUED while the whole
world's external-actor DDC ground on. The gate that worked was re-shooting the
same frame five minutes later and comparing — 0.1890 vs 0.1917, delta +0.0027.

But the verdict was narrower than I reported it. Five minutes of stability is
not stability; two headings re-measured 30 minutes apart moved +0.025 and
+0.022 as DDC finished. Ranking survived, absolutes did not. **Say what window
a settle test covered, because "SETTLED" reads as unqualified.**

### OPERATIONAL, NOT ANALYTICAL

`scripts/bench_make_dolly.py` does not exist — it is
`scripts/payloads/bench_make_dolly.py`, run through `ue_exec`. I recalled the
wrong path and a two-second `ls` corrected it. Step (a) again, and the search
did its job this time.

Two background tasks were killed mid-run by the harness (cause unknown; one
of them I had launched with `timeout: 2400000`, above the documented 600000
maximum, which was wrong of me whether or not it caused the kill). The MRQ
render SURVIVED its driver's death, because PIE runs inside the editor
process, and completed all 90 frames cleanly. **A dead driver is not a dead
render**, and the evidence for that was the editor log advancing onto shader
compilation while the output directory sat empty.

I also called that same silence a stall on a run that was ONE MINUTE OLD,
reaching for R-BENCHDOLLY's own "reading a stalled run as a slow render"
entry. The remedy that recipe prescribes is to read the editor log — I read it
and misdated the run instead of checking elapsed time first.

## 2026-09-09b — BRIEF 2 START: the fog half-height has been base-e against a base-2 engine since v1.4

Brief 2 Task 2 tells you to VERIFY `fog_budget.py`'s `UNIT` constant against
`HeightFogCommon.ush` before writing anything to a recipe. Doing that found
the incoming tool correct and TWO OF OURS WRONG.

### WHAT IS TRUE

The exponential height fog density profile is **base 2**:

    HeightFogCommon.ush:225   FogDensity * pow(2.0f, -F * (z - z0))
    HeightFogCommon.ush:301   RayOriginTerms = ... * exp2(-Exponent)
    HeightFogCommon.ush:394   ExpFogFactor   = exp2(-LineIntegral)
    SceneCore.cpp:404-405     Density/1000 AND HeightFalloff/1000

So density halves when `(F/1000) * dz_cm = 1` exactly:

    FogHeightFalloff = 1000 / half_height_cm = 10 / half_height_m

with no `ln(2)` anywhere.

### WHAT WE HAD

    apply_lighting.py:323        1000 * 0.6931.. / (half_m * 100)
    atmosphere_solve.py:286      1000 * math.log(2) / (half_m * 100)
    atmosphere_solve.fog_opacity math.exp() in BOTH exponentials

A falloff 0.693× too small, therefore a half-height **1.4427× too large**.
The shipped recipe asks for 202.0 m and the engine has been rendering
**291.4 m** since v1.4. Nothing crashed, nothing looked obviously broken,
and the recipe's own number was not what the world did.

### THE ROOT CAUSE IS A COMMENT

`HeightFogCommon.ush:206` says, immediately above the code:

    // The exponential fog density function is d = GlobalDensity * exp(-HeightFalloff * z)

The code on the next lines uses `exp2`. **Both our tools implemented the
comment.** This is non-negotiable 9's motivating case with Epic's source in
the role of the docstring: an unverified claim propagated into our knowledge
base, in a place that is supposed to be checkable. It reached three artefacts
— two tools and `recipes/schema.md`, whose "the old `height_falloff: 0.12`
therefore meant a 57.8 m half-height" is that same wrong formula (correct:
**83.3 m**). Fixing the copies without the seed would have left it to
re-infect.

**RULE: a comment in engine source is a claim, not the contract. The
reflected surface and the executed code are the contract** — which is
`docs/ue58-api-protocol.md`'s rule, extended from the Python API to HLSL.

### HOW IT SURVIVED SO LONG

Because it was SELF-CONSISTENT. `atmosphere_solve.fog_opacity` used base-e
exponentials with a base-e falloff, so asking it "what half-height does this
falloff give" returned the authored number. The model agreed with itself and
never with the engine. **An instrument that validates against its own
convention cannot detect a convention error** — non-negotiable 0 again: the
falloff function and the opacity function shared a source, so they were one
measurement, not two.

What broke it open was a SECOND, INDEPENDENTLY WRITTEN implementation
arriving in the brief. After the fix the two agree to 5 decimals at 1, 4 and
8 km; before it they could not have.

### CONSEQUENCES, STATED PLAINLY

* Any fog opacity this project has quoted is suspect, including the
  2026-08-09 BACKLOG figure "8 km opacity 0.3889 at a 300 m camera",
  which was used to argue the fog was defensible alpine air.
* Re-applying the recipe unchanged now renders TIGHTER fog than before
  (202 m rather than 291.4 m). That is a visible change produced by a bug
  fix, not by a taste decision, and it lands before Task 2 replaces the
  values anyway.
* Had the fix not preceded Task 2, the derived half-height of 517.5 m would
  have been written through the broken converter and rendered at 746.6 m —
  a derived value silently corrupted on the way to the engine, which is the
  most expensive shape of this defect and the reason the brief says VERIFY
  FIRST.

### AND THE BRIEF'S OWN INPUTS NEEDED THE SAME TREATMENT

`BRIEF.md` §3 assumes a valley datum of 120 m and a camera at 130 m. The
measured values are **186.74 m** (the plaza, from
`bench_stations_derived.json`, and the town's `site_centre_cm` is the same XY
as the near_ground station) and 188.49 m. The derivation is robust to it —
the camera sits essentially AT the datum in both cases — so `fog_budget`
returns 0.00416 / 0.019324 against the brief's predicted 0.0042 / 0.019. The
agreement is real; it just had to be earned rather than assumed.

## 2026-09-09c — TASK 0: a binary test with two paths into it, and two bench_capture bugs stacked

Brief 2 Task 0 asks one question — is the flat band at the elevated stations
unrendered world? — and offers a clean binary: paint the SkyAtmosphere's
ground albedo magenta, count magenta pixels, non-zero means void. The answer
came out NOT VOID. Getting there needed the test rebuilt, and uncovered two
bugs in our own capture tool.

### THE TEST AS SPECIFIED COULD HAVE RETURNED A FALSE ZERO

`void_mask.py` thresholds on absolute colour (`r-g > 0.25`, `b-g > 0.25`,
`r > 0.2`, `b > 0.2`). The visible planet surface is shaded at
`SkyAtmosphere.usf:826` by `... * NdotL0 * GroundAlbedo.rgb / PI`, and this
recipe's sun is at **12 deg elevation** — so NdotL0 ~ 0.21, then /PI, then
tonemapped at -1.923 EV. Magenta can land below those floors on a frame that
IS void.

That matters more than a normal measurement error because **Brief 2 gates
every later atmosphere number on this reading**: a void band scores as "fog"
in every other measurement, so a false zero would silently corrupt Tasks 1-6.

The fix was to capture a BASELINE at the original albedo and compare, which
needs no brightness floor at all. **A test whose NEGATIVE result is
load-bearing must be shown capable of producing a positive.** The baseline is
what shows that: 71.7% and 80.7% of pixels moved toward magenta, so the
albedo demonstrably reached the render.

### AND THE PROPERTY DRIVES TWO PATHS, SO COLOUR ALONE CANNOT DECIDE

`multi_scattering_factor` is 1.0, and `SkyAtmosphereComponent.h:64` says the
albedo "will tint the atmosphere when the sun light will bounce on it". So
GroundAlbedo drives BOTH the visible planet surface (the `if (Ground && tMax
== tBottom)` ray-march branch at :815, which is NOT gated on multi-scattering
despite the header's wording) AND a global atmospheric tint. Both respond to
the same knob. "Count magenta pixels" cannot separate them.

**What separates them is SPATIAL STRUCTURE, not colour.** A surface is a
bounded region with an edge; a bounce is everywhere and smooth. The per-row
profile settles it: a smooth gradient, strongest in the sky, p99 <= 0.07 in
every one of 16 bands at both stations, and no step anywhere. A planet
surface would jump sharply, its green going 170 -> 0.

RULE: when one property feeds two rendering paths, discriminate on a
dimension the two paths do not share. Here that is geometry, not hue.

### TWO BENCH_CAPTURE BUGS, THE FIRST MASKING THE SECOND

**(1) A set in the sidecar killed the run AFTER a completed render.**
`json.dump` raised "Object of type set is not JSON serializable" at the last
step, so two 4K stills existed on disk with NO sidecar — no cvar read-backs,
no residency, no provenance. The frames survive that; the EVIDENCE does not,
and a 20-minute render has to be repeated to recover it. Now coerced to
sorted lists, and the coercion is REPORTED rather than silent.

**(2) `res` was rebound to a set of actor names, refusing every still.**

    line  635   res = bm["declared_camera"]["res"]        # [3840, 2160]
    line 1039   res = set(ln["resident_actors"])          # ~250 labels
    line 1217   bad = [... if v["png_size_from_file"] != res]

So the final gate compared each PNG's pixel size against a set of actor
labels and could never match. Measured: two 4K stills, the engine's own
`resolution lines [[3840, 2160]]` in the same run, and then
`REFUSE: ['mid_slope','vista'] rendered at a resolution other than
{'Alpine8K_HLODLayer_...'}`.

**It had been invisible because bug (1) crashed the run before the gate was
reached.** Fixing the first exposed the second. Both live in the same dozen
lines, and both were introduced by reaching for a short generic name in a
long function — `res`, `exp` — where an outer binding already owned it.

The refusal was LOUD and its message carried the evidence of its own defect:
a resolution comparison printing HLOD layer names. A silent version of this
would have been far worse; the message is what made it a two-minute
diagnosis.

### WHAT TASK 0 DID NOT SETTLE, STATED SO IT IS NOT READ AS MORE THAN IT IS

Ruling out void is not showing the band IS fog. BRIEF §0.3's objection stands
on its own evidence and Task 1 now owns it. The skyline-IoU half of Task 0's
acceptance is NOT done — it needs a near_ground player/truth pair, two more
~20-minute captures — and the missing-massif observation that motivated the
void reading is a separate signal from the elevated-station band.

## 2026-09-09d — THE TRUTH OVERRIDE WAS NEVER CONNECTED, and a conclusion built on that is retired

### (a) MainGrid vs MainPartition

`residency.truth.grid` was `"MainGrid"`. This world's hash is
`UWorldPartitionRuntimeHashSet`, whose default partition
`WorldPartitionRuntimeHashSet.cpp:269` names **`MainPartition`**.
`wp.Runtime.OverrideRuntimeLoadingRange` is an EXACT FName lookup with no
wildcard (`WorldPartitionSubsystem.cpp:563-571`), so `-grid=MainGrid` matched
nothing. **The 12 km truth range has always been a no-op.**

Corrected 2026-09-09, and with it:

    near_ground  PASS  expected 808  resident 3477  missing 0
    mid_slope    PASS  expected 20   resident 3420  missing 0

the first residency PASS this project has recorded, against 1415 and 258
resident under the 256 m derived range.

**RETIRED: the 2026-09-06 conclusion that "PIE cannot be force-loaded".**
That finding is recorded in `capture_truth`'s own docstring as the reason the
truth instrument was moved to the editor — "three levers were tried; all
three were measured; none moved residency off 16/1024". The measurement was
honest and the inference was sound given what was known. It was wrong because
ONE OF THE THREE LEVERS WAS NEVER CONNECTED, and a null result from a
disconnected lever is not evidence about the lever.

The tell was available at the time and in the same file: the `derived` block
had already discovered `MainPartition` from the live world and written its
provenance down, citing the very header that names it. Two blocks of one JSON
document disagreed about the name of the same grid, and nothing compared
them. **When two declarations in one artefact name the same engine object
differently, that is a defect even if both were derived honestly** — and it
is cheap to catch, because they are in the same file.

Cost: a whole instrument was rebuilt around the wrong conclusion. The editor
route then hit its own wall — `HighResShot` will not complete above ~960x540
against a force-loaded world — so the project ended up with no working truth
capture at all, from one stale FName.

### (b) CROSS-INSTRUMENT COMPARISON IS STRUCK AS A GATE BASIS

I ran Task 0's skyline-IoU acceptance against the 2026-09-07 truth frame and
reported **FAIL at 0.887**. Against a same-day MRQ truth frame it is **PASS
at 0.970**.

    truth frame              sky_iou   missing-world   reverse floor
    2026-09-07 editor/HRS    0.88713      0.01619         0.00703   FAIL
    2026-09-09 same-day MRQ  0.96989      0.00500         0.00101   PASS

The first comparison put an MRQ player frame against an editor/HighResShot
truth frame from two days earlier and called the difference residency. The
reverse-direction term is the giveaway and it was in the output the whole
time: `player_land_truth_sky` should be ~0 — the player cannot show MORE
world than the fully-loaded frame — and it read 0.70%. That number was the
instrument difference, measured, printed, and read past.

**RULE: a gate may not be decided by comparing frames from two different
instruments.** Same instrument, same pipeline, same session — or it is not a
residency measurement, it is an instrument measurement wearing that label. I
had even written the caveat into the artefact ("two dates apart, which is why
the 0.70% reverse direction is treated as a floor") and still let the verdict
stand on it. **Stating a caveat is not the same as acting on it**; the
correct move was to withhold the verdict, not to annotate it.

### (c) THE mid_slope BAND, DECOMPOSED

    mid_slope non-sky featureless   PLAYER 0.4001   TRUTH 0.2207
    near_ground non-sky featureless PLAYER 0.0067   TRUTH 0.0059

At full residency the band falls by 45% but does not vanish:

    ~18 points  PROXY FLATNESS -- what the player instrument renders at
                distance instead of the real geometry.  BRIEF 3 owns this.
    ~22 points  RESIDUAL, present with every cell loaded and no distance
                culling. Not streaming, not proxies. TASKS 1-2 own this.

This is the number that stops the band being argued about as one thing. It is
neither "all fog" nor "all void": Task 0 ruled out void, and this splits what
remains into a streaming/LOD half and an atmosphere half, each with an owner.

### (d) AND Q12 IS PROBABLY NOT A BUG

`InstancedFoliageActor_25600_-10_11_1` was deterministically absent across
four captures and is resident at a 12 km range, missing 0. The Q12 actors
were absent because the loading range was 256 m — the EXPECTATION was built
for a radius the streamer was never asked to cover. The gate was comparing
against the wrong world, not detecting a broken one.

## 2026-09-09e — THE SKY CLASSIFIER IS CALIBRATED AGAINST THE STATE THE BRIEF IS TRYING TO CHANGE

Brief 2 Tasks 4 and 5 desaturate and warm the sky on purpose — more Mie
whitens it, a warmer white balance pushes it away from blue. `SKY_BAND` decides
what counts as sky by colour:

    {min_blue_minus_red: 0.06, require_monotonic_bgr: true}

A pixel is sky if it is blue enough and its channels run B >= G >= R. So the
brief's own direction walks the sky out of the classifier. Measured across the
same three stations:

    mid_slope sky fraction   Task 2 0.3462 -> Task 4 0.1676 -> Task 5 0.0000
    vista     sky fraction   Task 3 0.4240 -> Task 4 0.3660 -> Task 5 0.2468

**At Task 5 mid_slope reports 0.0000 sky and 0.7907 non-sky.** The entire sky
is classified as not-sky. Nothing is wrong with the frame.

### WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A WRONG NUMBER

FOUR Brief 2 measurements stand on that mask: `featureless_split`'s sky/non-sky
split, `fog_vs_sky`'s horizon-sky median, `sky_saturation`'s zenith and horizon
bands, and `skyline_iou`. They degrade together and they degrade SILENTLY.

And the failure is CORRELATED WITH THE THING BEING MEASURED. Sky reclassified
as non-sky inflates the "featureless non-sky band" figure that BRIEF §0.3
exists to explain — so the more the brief succeeds at desaturating the sky, the
larger the defect it is trying to diagnose appears to be. An instrument that
gets worse in exactly the direction the work is heading will confirm whatever
the work does.

### THE RULE

**A classifier that keys on the property under test is not an instrument.**
`featureless_split`'s docstring already argues the harder half of this — the
band is DECLARED in benchmark.json rather than sampled from the frame under
test, precisely so a blown white frame cannot define white as sky. That
reasoning stopped one failure mode and not this one: a declared threshold is
still a COLOUR threshold, and colour is what Brief 2 is changing.

The scene-depth pass built for Task 2's re-measure already separates sky from
world GEOMETRICALLY — sky is what sits at or beyond the encoding ceiling — and
does not care what colour the sky is. That is the replacement.

### AND THE SAME SHAPE, TWICE MORE, IN ONE SESSION

  * `haze_metrics` binned by IMAGE ROWS and called it distance. Struck for
    near_ground: rows are not depth.
  * `highlight_tint` presumes a NEUTRAL sunlit surface. The sunlit meadow is
    green grass under a warm sun, so B/luma sits at 0.19-0.24 at ANY white
    balance, and the 0.9-1.1 acceptance may be unreachable at that station
    whatever the grade does.

Three metrics in one brief whose assumptions the world does not satisfy. The
common root: each was specified from what a frame LOOKS like rather than from
what the quantity IS, and each fails on the station where the appearance and
the quantity part company.

### TASK 5's RULE ALSO CONTRADICTS ITS OWN CITATION

BRIEF §3: "white_temp = the sun's temperature + ~1000 K (ED: sun 6500 K
uncorrected / WB 5600 ...)". 5600 is 900 BELOW 6500. The prose says +1000 and
the cited sample says -900.

`Scene.h:1505` settles it: WhiteTemp is the temperature "which the scene
considers as white light", so declaring 8800 K white against a 7800 K sun
renders the sun WARM. Applied, highlight_tint moved AWAY from neutral
(R 1.3005 -> 1.3748, B 0.2431 -> 0.1895) and shadow_tint_B fell out of the band
Task 3 had just reached (1.4456 -> 0.9829).

Left applied and unfixed, because changing the rule is Ryan's. **The citation
was checkable the whole time and reading it would have predicted the sign
before a capture was spent.**

## 2026-09-10 — APPLIED BUT NOT SAVED: EVERY MEASUREMENT OUTLIVED THE WORLD IT MEASURED
> STATUS: HISTORY — Brief-2 narrative: lighting applied but never saved, so the world read back pre-Brief-2; WHAT HAPPENED is honest record

### WHAT HAPPENED

The overnight close after Task 5 (commit 0a04be1c) hit the R-EDITOR-CLOSE
dirty-modal deadlock, and the machine then died. The four lighting packages
the Brief-2 tasks had mutated — Lighting_alpine_8k_Fog, _SkyLight, _SkyAtmo,
_PostProcess — were dirty and NEVER SAVED. `PackageRestoreData.json` names
all four (preserved with autosaves in `_trash/autosaves_launch_20260910161826/`).

On relaunch the world read back PRE-BRIEF-2 on every axis: fog
0.0015/0.03431/150000 cm against the recipe's derived 0.00416/0.019324/0;
sky light 1.8 against 1.0; Mie 0.003996 against 0.01; WhiteTemp 6500
against the grade block. The recipe, the _verify measurements and the
commits all carried Tasks 1–5; the world carried none of them.

### ROOT CAUSE, AT A LINE

`apply_lighting.py:30-32` (before today): "Does not save the level — saving
is the operator's call, and an unsaved lighting pass is trivially reverted
by reloading." The property advertised as a convenience IS the defect: for
five sessions the pass was never meant to be revertible, and no step in the
task loop (apply → read back → capture → measure → commit) ever owned the
save. Rule 12 was satisfied to the letter — applied AND read back — and the
read-back proved only the IN-MEMORY state. Nothing proved persistence,
because nothing attempted it.

### THE RULE

**Recipe-derived actors that are applied but not saved make every
measurement outlive the world it measured.** A capture's provenance chain is
recipe → applied actor → saved package; break the last link and the artefact
refers to a world that stops existing at the next editor exit. Apply, read
back, SAVE THE TOUCHED PACKAGES, and commit them — one unit, owned by the
applying tool, not by session hygiene. `apply_lighting.py` now does this
(RULED BY RYAN 2026-09-10); the spec altitude is RECIPES R-LIGHTSAVE.

Related: save_tagged_actors.py documents the sibling trap (applied but not
even DIRTY, 0-dirty saves that write nothing) — the save must be
only_if_is_dirty=False and the verdict must come from the filesystem.

### AUDIT LOG 2026-09-10 — apply_lighting.py R-LIGHTSAVE

First audit: FIX. Set-difference save verdict was blind to pre-dirty files
(a failed-commit re-run would mask its own exit-5) and the no-change branch
asserted on-disk existence it never checked. Braces, bindings, commit
containment, API names all clean. F1 (existence check, exit 5 on missing)
and F2 (pending-commit routing via fs_after) corrected by the main agent;
re-audit verified both: exit 0 now requires clean dirty-state + files exist
+ git-clean. PASS — cleared for first execution.

## 2026-09-10b — THE DEPTH SKY MASK: THE COLOUR BAND WAS NEVER VALID AT mid_slope

Ryan ruled the replacement 2026-09-10; the re-judge of Tasks 1-5 ran
offline against the 2026-09-09 depth passes (no re-render; vista has no
depth pass yet and its rows say NO DEPTH rather than a colour number).

### WHAT THE RE-JUDGE MEASURED

Geometric sky at mid_slope is STABLE across the whole brief -- 0.7281,
0.7444, 0.7443, 0.7475, 0.7582 for Tasks 1-5 -- while the colour mask
read 0.3460, 0.2549, 0.2529, 0.1676, 0.0000. The "featureless non-sky
band" at mid_slope, the number Q15 exists to explain, collapses from
0.79 (colour, Task 5) to 0.0325 (depth): MOST OF THE BAND WAS SKY,
counted as band by the instrument. near_ground moved little (colour
0.15-0.17 vs depth 0.12-0.13). dE fails under either mask, so Task 1's
"the band is not fog" conclusion survives the instrument change.

### THE SHARPER LESSON

The plan assumed the colour mask was valid BEFORE the desaturation and
eroded during it. FALSE at mid_slope: at Task 2 -- blue-sky era -- colour
said 0.2549 where depth says 0.7444. Horizon sky seen through haze sits
below the b-r >= 0.06 threshold at that station in EVERY era. The
2026-09-09e lesson ("a classifier that keys on the property under test is
not an instrument") was right and INCOMPLETE: the classifier was also
keying on a property the STATION suppresses. Validity of a mask is a
per-station fact, and nothing measured it until a second instrument
existed to disagree. Non-negotiable 0's shape: the colour mask and the
eye both looked at the same pixels; the depth pass is the different
source.

### INSTRUMENT EVIDENCE

Two independent depth captures of mid_slope (target_depth and
target_depth_task4) agree 1.0000 tile-for-tile with identical sky
fractions -- two captures, one geometry. The wrong-resolution pairing
(1920-wide send-back frame vs 4K depth) REFUSES with ValueError. The
audit (FIX -> fixed) added: the refusal check exits nonzero when it
cannot run or does not refuse, and beauty globs exclude *SceneDepth* and
*_diff.png so a missing beauty can never silently promote the depth pass
(bench_capture, both call sites).

Spec altitude: RECIPES R-DEPTHBIN (now written -- R-FOG had referenced it
before it existed). Artefact: _verify/bench/2026-09-10/sky_rejudge_depth.json.

## 2026-09-10c — LESSON 12.10 RECURRED, AND THE GAP WAS THE GUARD'S SCOPE

The first clouds apply failed with `Could not load Python file '<engine
dir>/<the whole script>'` — byte-for-byte the 12.10 failure. Root cause
identical (PythonScriptPlugin.cpp:813-898: ExecuteFile mode FindFirsts
the substring dot-p-y across the whole command; :872 accepts it as a
pathname when whitespace follows). The offending text was the NEW
_task6 recipe note: "cloud_mi_probe" with its extension, followed by a
space. The morning run of the same script had succeeded because the
payload's only prior occurrence ("capture" dot-p-y ":273") is followed
by a colon, which :872 rejects — one character of punctuation was the
difference between working and not.

### WHY THE EXISTING LESSON DID NOT PREVENT IT (operating loop e)

12.10's rule was ratified and a guard was built — and the guard was
OPT-IN PER TOOL. make_landscape_material, make_mesh_lods, push_heightmap
and save_level adopted it; apply_lighting never did. And the offending
string did not come from payload authorship at all: it came from RECIPE
PROSE, interpolated into the payload at run time. A rule addressed to
"payload authors" cannot fire on a recipe note written days later by
someone documenting provenance — which is exactly what _task6 was.

### THE FIX IS AT THE CHOKE POINT

apply_lighting._run now guards the COMPOSED source (the only place that
sees template + interpolated recipe together) via the shared
_guard_payload; the payload template and the recipe's lighting prose are
swept of the extension. ue_exec is immune BY CONSTRUCTION — it stages
payloads as real .py files and sends the path. The general rule,
sharpened: **a content guard must sit where the content is COMPOSED, not
where it is authored** — an interpolation site widens the set of authors
to everyone who can write a string that reaches it.

## 2026-09-10d — R-EDITOR-CLOSE, FOURTH OCCURRENCE: IT DEADLOCKS AT 0-DIRTY TOO

The dirty-modal theory (2026-09-09) explained that night's deadlock: dirty
packages raise a save prompt, the modal blocks the game thread, nothing can
click it. Tonight falsifies it as the ONLY mechanism. Measured:

    census        0 dirty, verdict CLEAN (the R-LIGHTSAVE runs had saved
                  and committed everything)
    quiet         2,132 s since the newest Content write
    close 1       CloseMainWindow returned True; window destroyed;
                  process ALIVE 120 s later
    remote exec   dead from close 1 onward ("no editor nodes answered")
    close 2       returned False -- there was no main window left
    extended wait 9+ minutes; CPU 0.1 s per 10 s at 12,015 MB RSS: wedged
                  idle, not tearing down

So the close path can wedge AFTER window destruction with nothing dirty and
nothing to prompt about. The kill (authorised by the ORIGINAL step 4:
census clean AND quiet, both closes tried) was clean: PackageRestoreData
written EMPTY (RestoreEnabled false), no post-kill Content writes, zero
processes, port free.

THE RULE HOLDS, THE THEORY NARROWS. Clean-census/quiet/retry/kill produced
the correct outcome in all four occurrences; what changes is the story we
tell about WHY it hangs -- "a modal" covers one case of a shutdown path
that can also wedge on its own. Do not spend another session diagnosing
the hang from outside: the gate measures everything the kill decision
needs, and a wedged-idle process with an empty restore file loses nothing.

### 2026-09-10e — THE REFUSAL PRINTER CRASHED ON THE PATH THAT REFUSES

bench_capture's residency-refusal detail loop indexed r["job"], but
DERIVED-mode rows key by "station" — so every refused derived run since
derived mode existed crashed with KeyError AT THE REFUSAL, truncating
exactly the per-station detail the refusal exists to print. Yesterday's
capture_task5.log ends at that line; the truncation read as a terse
refusal, not a crash, so nothing noticed. The exit code became Python's
1 instead of the documented 6. Fixed (get with both keys + a derived
fallback line); the artefacts were never affected — frames and sidecar
land before this loop. Verification-practice direction 3, again: the
error path is the least-exercised path and needs the test the happy
path gets.

### AUDIT LOG 2026-09-10b — greycard/HLOD changeset

FIX, 7 findings, 0 scope. Recurring shapes worth naming: a one-sided
refusal passes the oversized case (exact-shape checks, both directions);
a guarded read that returns an error STRING bool()s to a confident true;
a find-or-create that skips its cited pattern's rebuild-on-reuse step
leaves the instrument's albedo unverified. All applied by the main agent
(F1 exact shape, F2 per-station projection guard, F3 band cited to the
Brief 2b ruling, F4 BaseColor read-back-or-refuse on reuse, F5 string-
error handling, F6 Run line, F7 exclusion selftest + occlusion variance
ceiling from the QUESTION). Nothing auditor-corrected.

## 2026-09-10f — THE RESIDENCY EXPECTATION WAS 2D AGAINST A 3D SPHERE
> STATUS: HISTORY — records the 2D-vs-3D residency bug and its 3D fix

At 768 m the vista station left the SAME 12 InstancedFoliageActors
missing at 180 AND 300 warm-up frames -- identical sets, so not a
streaming tail. Probed in the editor world: all non-empty (1-59
instances), spatially loaded, main grid. Their cells sit 650-1100 m out
HORIZONTALLY -- and the vista camera sits ~600 m ABOVE the valley.

The engine queries a genuine 3D sphere: WorldPartitionRuntimeHashSet.cpp
:608-611 builds FStaticSpatialIndex::FSphere(Center, Radius) against 3D
cell bounds (a separate SpatialIndex2D exists and is queried Z-blind at
:648). bench_expected_set's 2D-XY hit test -- whose own comment argued
"a Z term would drop valid cells on the slopes" -- was therefore
demanding content the engine geometrically never streams from an
elevated source. The same defect SHAPE the 2026-09-09 ruling fixed
(typed expectations demanding out-of-range content), one dimension over;
at 256 m its magnitude was 4-of-15 at vista and it read as noise. The
range change did not create it, it AMPLIFIED it past ignoring.

Fixed: the hit test is 3D closest-point (LOC_Z was already passed in).
Direction argument for the subset verdict: a 3D expectation can only
SHRINK the expected set; 2D-indexed cells that load anyway land in
resident-not-expected, which the verdict allows. The near_ground
straggler (1 actor, both eras) is the same geometry: its cell rides a
ridge ~500 m above the low camera.

The general rule: AN EXPECTATION MUST MIRROR THE ENGINE'S OWN QUERY
SHAPE, and a comment that reasons about what the engine "would" drop is
a hypothesis until a frame has tested it -- this one shipped untested in
the direction the author found intuitive.

## 2026-09-11 — THE GRADE CHAIN IS NOT VON KRIES, MEASURED
> STATUS: SUPERSEDED — 3550 K superseded: RECIPES.md:17964 SUPERSEDED-BY B3.13 (3481.9), then A-6 (3438.6 K). [Pass 5 ruling, 2026-09-16]

Brief 3 Task 1 stepped WhiteTemp toward the grey card's neutral with the
Planck two-channel mired slope (9454 K), the textbook von-Kries move.
Measured on the card, target class:

    5200 K   ln(residual ratio) 0.5301
    4026 K   0.1719   (56.1 mired applied -> 68% of theoretical removed)
    3751 K   0.1031   (18.2 mired applied -> 38% of theoretical removed)

Two findings. First, the chain under-corrects the slope -- the
atmosphere spectrum, the sun disc/sky mix on a tilted card, and the
filmic tonemap all sit between WhiteTemp and the pixel, and none is a
blackbody diagonal transform. Second, the EFFICIENCY ITSELF FELL between
steps, so even a measured-efficiency extrapolation is optimistic near
neutral -- the tonemap is most compressive exactly where the residual
is smallest (the same compression the exposure _solve_caveat documents).
BRIEF 3.7's "one step gets within 3%" assumed a von-Kries chain; the
assumption was worth one sentence to test and two capture cycles to
falsify. Ryan ruled a final step to the extrapolated ~3550 K; R-GRADE
locks at the measured outcome either way, residual recorded. The
general rule: A CORRECTION FORMULA'S CONVERGENCE RATE IS ITSELF A
MEASURED QUANTITY -- budget steps by the measured rate, not the
formula's promise.

### ERRATUM to 2026-09-11 (von Kries entry): step-2 efficiency is 40.0%,
not 38% -- audit-recomputed as removed 0.0688 / theoretical 0.1721. The
step-1 68% figure and every qualitative claim stand; the 3550 K ruling
derives from the residual RATIOS (0.324, 0.600), not the efficiencies,
and is unaffected. This erratum is appended rather than editing the
entry (append-only file).
