## 2026-09-11b — AN ASPECT AXIS BOUND TO A MAP EDGE, NOT TO THE SUN

derive_layer_weights' snow line was `base - 125*cos(aspect)` with the
comment "0 = map +Y (north)". The brief's own formula says
`cos(aspect - north)` "at the recipe's sun azimuth" -- and the physical
driver is which flank the SUN MISSES, not which way the map's Y axis
points. Nothing in the level binds +Y to the shaded direction: with
sun.azimuth_deg 285 (the light's TRAVEL yaw, so the sun sits at 105),
the shaded flank faces ~(0.26, -0.97) -- almost exactly -Y, i.e. the
code was biasing snow onto the LIT flanks.

The selftest passed throughout, and correctly: it asserted N > S against
an independent geometric predicate and would have caught any sign flip
INSIDE the formula. What it could not catch was the formula's FRAME
being unbound to the world -- a selftest verifies the arithmetic it is
given, never the premise the arithmetic is about.

Fixed by derivation, not by a constant: shaded_aspect_rad(azimuth)
converts the light's travel yaw into the aspect frame, main() reads
lighting.sun.azimuth_deg, and the sidecar records both. The selftest
gained a direction the old one structurally could not have: FLIP THE
SUN AND THE SNOWY FLANK MUST FLIP. Also folded in from the same audit:
the snow floor now comes from the recipe's Snow band instead of a
duplicated local constant (pipeline rule 2), and `flow` is declared
RESERVED rather than loaded, passed and claimed in the sidecar while
nothing read it (rule 10).

THE RULE: a derived mask's FRAME is an input like any other. If a
formula says "north", something in the recipe must say which way north
is -- or the formula must compute it from something that does.


## 2026-09-11c — AN INSTRUMENT THAT LEFT ITS CLASS, AND THE TELL THAT CAUGHT IT

Asked to confirm from a render that the derived snow sits on the flank
the sun misses, I tried to measure aspect from the captured passes. The
vista frame carries a beauty pass and a scene-depth pass, so the obvious
move is to reconstruct world positions from the depth, take normals from
them, and bin snow by aspect octant. I built that. It ran. It produced
numbers.

The numbers were garbage, and the thing that said so was not a failed
assertion -- it was a SENSITIVITY CHECK I had added almost as an
afterthought. `SceneDepth` in UE is view-space Z, but I was not certain,
so I computed the whole thing twice: once reading the pass as depth
along the view axis, once as radial distance. If the octant verdict
survived both, the ambiguity did not matter.

It did not survive. The shaded-octant population went from **41 px** to
**517,913 px** -- four orders of magnitude -- on a choice that changes
each sample's range by at most 15%.

ROOT CAUSE, at a number rather than a feeling. `scripts/haze_metrics.py:68`:
the pass is 8-bit and LOG-encoded, `encoded = log2(max(depth_cm,1)) / 20`.
One 8-bit step is therefore a FACTOR of `2^(20/255) = 1.0559` -- 5.6% of
the distance, whatever the distance is. 5.6 m at 100 m. 56 m at 1 km.
112 m at 2 km. A normal is a DIFFERENCE of neighbouring positions, so
that quantisation is not a small error on the normal, it IS the normal.
The reprojection of the weightmap through the same camera came out in
vertical streaks for the same reason, which is what a 5.6% radial
quantisation looks like when you draw it.

The instrument was not broken. It was CORRECT, and it was calibrated for
a different specimen: R-DEPTHBIN built that pass to sort pixels into
distance bins of 100/300/1000/3000/8000 m, where 5.6% is irrelevant. I
carried it to a geometry question and it silently left its class. This
is verification-practice's first rule -- state the instrument's PREMISE
and check it transfers -- and the premise here was never written down as
a premise, only as an encoding.

WHAT I DID NOT DO: report the numbers with a caveat. A failed
measurement reports that it FAILED, never the number the broken
measurement produced. Both probes were discarded, and the vista frame
was reported as unable to answer the question.

THE REPLACEMENT uses the pass ONLY as a sky/not-sky bit -- a silhouette
needs no depth precision -- and compares that silhouette against a
ray-march of the heightmap. `scripts/heightmap_orientation_check.py`,
R-ORIENT.

THE RULE: an encoding is a premise. When a pass is quantised
MULTIPLICATIVELY, write its per-LSB error next to its decoder, in the
units a caller will care about, because the caller who misuses it will
not be the one who wrote it.

AND THE SECOND-ORDER RULE, which is the one I want to keep: the check
that caught this was not a test, it was computing the answer twice under
two readings of an ambiguity I had NOT resolved. When you are unsure of
a datum, do not pick the likely one and move on -- carry both and see
whether the conclusion cares. If it does, you have found the thing you
were unsure about, before it found you.

## 2026-09-11d — THE CONFIRMATION SHOT THAT RENDERED PERFECTLY AND PROVED NOTHING

Ryan ruled a top-down frame at `(0, 0, 900000)` cm to read snow against
the lit and shaded flanks directly in screen space, and then to R-lock.

The shot succeeded by every signal a capture tool reports. Frame on disk
in 4 seconds. `max_loc_err_cm 0.0`, `max_rot_err_deg 0.0`. The whole
8129 m world inside the frame, its square edge landing within 8% of
where the forward projection put it. Nothing to report as a failure.

And its terrain luma std was **0.0334** over 16,524,225 projected
texels. At 9 km the aerial perspective flattens this world below what
8-bit quantisation carries; there is no binning that recovers a signal
already gone. The frame cannot answer the question in EITHER direction
-- it is not evidence against the layers, it is not evidence for them.

R-CITYSHOT step 6 is what fired: "check the frame is tonally
non-trivial BEFORE reading anything into it". Written after a different
failure, it caught this one, which is the only real test of a recipe
step. The whole-frame std was 0.0206.

THE FIX WAS TO DERIVE THE CAMERA INSTEAD OF ACCEPTING ONE. Altitude
from CLEARANCE over the terrain (1000 m) rather than from covering the
world; centre chosen by maximising the SCARCER flank class, because a
window rich in one flank and empty of the other cannot compare them.
That returned `(29800, 73500, 169641.7)` cm with 365,717 shaded and
364,936 lit band texels -- balanced to 0.2%, which no hand-placed
camera would have hit -- and terrain luma std 0.2134, 6.4x the ruled
camera's. On that frame the measurement ran: at the same altitude and
the same flank class, snow renders brighter than bare in 5 of 5 bins.

I kept BOTH frames. The ruled camera's artefact is the evidence that
the ruled camera cannot answer, and deleting it would leave the
deviation looking like a preference.

TWO RULES.

A camera is a MEASUREMENT PARAMETER and derives like any other. "Put it
high enough to see everything" optimises for coverage; the measurement
needed contrast and balanced populations, and those pull the other way.

And the one that generalises past cameras: **a shot whose every
read-back is exact can still be worthless, because read-backs verify
that the instrument was AIMED, never that it can SEE.** Every field in
that sidecar was a true measurement of the request. None of them was a
measurement of the frame.


## 2026-09-11e — I HAND-ROLLED A MEASUREMENT THAT HAD A TOOL, AND THE NUMBER REACHED A RULING

Asked whether the top-down frame's whiteness was albedo or exposure, I
noticed the 18% grey card sitting in the vista frame and measured it:
loaded `_verify/bench/greycard_regions.json`, took the rect, averaged
the linear luma inside it, got **0.33964**, and reported a terrain/card
ratio of 1.36. The reasoning was right and the conclusion it supported
was right.

The number was not. `scripts/greycard.py --measure --station vista`
returns **card_luma 0.30195 and verdict FAIL** — the vista card sits on
a SHADED flank (it is near the vista camera, which stands on the flank
the snow is on), so it is lit by sky alone: `wb_ratio_B` 1.354 and
`card_luma_std` 0.0669 against near_ground's 1.000 and 0.0157. The tool
has an acceptance. My rect average had none, so there was nothing for it
to fail.

That number then propagated. I reported it; the next ruling said
"compensation_ev corrected by log2(measured/0.18) (currently ~-0.9
stops)" — and -0.9163 EV is exactly `log2(0.33964/0.18)`. The correction
from the VALID card is **-1.5943 EV**. A measurement that skipped its
own gate set a parameter in a ruling, and the only reason it did not
ship is that the same tool got run properly one step later.

ROOT CAUSE is the operating loop's step (a), and specifically its
motivating case, which this repeats almost exactly. The rule reads:
"STEP (a) IS A SEARCH, NOT A RECALL. `scripts/` gets LISTED before any
ad-hoc payload touches the editor." I did list `scripts/` this session —
twice — and I had `greycard.py` in front of me when I read its header to
find the regions file. I used the tool's DATA and skipped the tool.

THE GAP IN THE LESSON, which is the part worth keeping. Step (a) is
written about PROCEDURES — "do not invent a way to do a thing that has a
recipe". It did not fire here because I was not inventing a procedure, I
was reading a file. But `greycard_regions.json` is not data, it is the
INTERMEDIATE STATE of an instrument, and taking an instrument's
intermediate state and finishing the computation by hand discards
everything the instrument does after that point — which, for any
instrument worth having, is the acceptance.

THE RULE: **an instrument's output includes its VERDICT, and a number
lifted from its intermediates is not its output.** If a tool of record
exists, run it; if you only want part of it, you still want the part
that says whether the number is admissible.

AND THE SECOND-ORDER ONE: this is why a measured number that travels to
Ryan must carry the tool that produced it. Had I written "greycard
--measure says 0.33964" the discrepancy would have been visible the
moment the tool was run for real, because it never says that.

## 2026-09-11f — THE TONEMAP UNDER-DELIVERS CORRECTIONS BY A THIRD, IN EVERY DOMAIN

Applying the ruled exposure step: `compensation_ev` -1.923 -> -3.5173, a
requested -1.5943 EV. The card moved 0.54349 -> 0.26489, which is
**-1.0369 EV delivered: 65.0% efficiency.** The target band [0.162,
0.198] was missed, residual +0.5574 EV.

This was predicted, and predicted in writing — `exposure._solve_caveat`
in the recipe has said since 2026-08-14 that the method "CANNOT CONVERGE
BY CONSTRUCTION" because the decoded PNG is post-tonemap while the
target is a pre-tonemap scene value, and it measured a 0.137 EV step
yielding -5.4% where linear arithmetic said -9.1%. It was marked OPEN and
nothing had been done with it.

What is new is that **the same shortfall now has a number in a second,
unrelated domain.** The white-balance chain measured 68% then 40% per
step (LESSONS 2026-09-11), and that was written up as a property of the
von-Kries-style correction — "the chain is not von Kries". It is now
clear that was the wrong attribution, or at least an incomplete one:
white balance and exposure share exactly one thing, the filmic curve
they are both measured through, and both under-deliver by roughly a
third. The tonemap is the common cause.

That reframes a finding I recorded three days ago. I am not retracting
the von-Kries measurement — the numbers stand — but its EXPLANATION was
scoped too narrowly, because it had one domain and no control. Two
domains is not proof either; it is the second point on a line.

THE RULE: **when a correction is measured through a non-linear display
transform, its step efficiency is a property of the TRANSFORM, and you
will meet the same number again in an unrelated parameter.** Budget
steps. Do not expect a formula to land in one.

AND THE METHODOLOGICAL ONE: a finding explained by a mechanism specific
to its own domain should be held loosely until it has been looked for
somewhere that mechanism does not apply. I had a single domain and wrote
a domain-specific cause.


## 2026-09-11g — A STATION DERIVED FOR ONE MEASUREMENT DOES NOT SERVE ANOTHER, TWICE IN ONE SESSION

Brief 3 Task 3 asks for tile-repeat scores in two depth bins, 30-100 m
and 100-300 m, from the three bench stations. Every cell came back NO
VERDICT or NO BAND, and the reasons were not about tiling:

    near_ground   sees ground at 30-100 m, but under grass, blueberry
                  and their shadows -- not the "GROUND ONLY" crop
                  tiling_score's own docstring requires
    mid_slope     nearest ground is 581 m; it sees nothing in either bin
    vista         101 rows in 30-100 m; its 100-300 m crop is no cleaner

The three stations were derived on 2026-09-05 for Brief 1's angular
budget -- tree subtense, canopy coverage, the detail-threshold ladder.
They are excellent at that. Nothing about that derivation asked for an
unoccluded patch of ground at a controlled distance, so nothing about
them provides one.

THIS IS THE SECOND TIME TODAY. The ruled top-down camera at
(0, 0, 900000) cm rendered perfectly and could not answer its question
either (LESSONS 2026-09-11d), and the fix there was to DERIVE a camera
from what the measurement needed -- clearance for contrast, centre for
balanced flank populations. The fix here is the same and I have not done
it: Task 3 needs a purpose-derived ground-only station.

THE RULE: **a measurement station is part of the instrument.** Reusing
one across measurements is the same error as reusing a tolerance or a
denominator across specimens -- it carries a premise ("this station
shows what I need to see") that was established for a different
question. Bench stations are stable ON PURPOSE, so that frames compare
across sessions; that stability is exactly what makes them the wrong
default for a new measure.

AND THE ONE I KEEP PAYING FOR: when a tool's docstring states its
premise -- "a crop of the frame that is GROUND ONLY" -- that sentence is
a precondition to CHECK, not context to read past. I had it in front of
me when I wrote the caller.

## 2026-09-11h — TWO CONFIDENT FAILS THAT WERE THE SEARCH WINDOW'S EDGE

`surface_report` scored the tile repeat by handing `tiling_score` an
expected on-screen period and reading back its Michelson figure. It
returned 0.7154 at near_ground and 0.2784 at vista, against CSF
thresholds of 0.1000 and 0.0393. Two clean FAILs, a plausible story
(the new 5.03 m tile repeats visibly), and I nearly wrote it up.

The number that stopped it was `period_found_px`, which I had printed
only for completeness:

    near_ground   found 205.4 px   expected 341.9   window [205.1, 478.7]
    vista         found  60.0 px   expected  99.7   window [ 59.8, 139.5]

`score` searches a +-40% ring around the expected period and returns the
strongest point IN the ring. Both maxima sat ON the ring's inner edge --
205.4 against a 205.1 floor, 60.0 against 59.8. **A maximum on the
boundary of its own search window is the boundary, not a feature.**
There was no periodic structure at the tile's period to find.

So where did 0.7154 come from? `michelson = 2 * hi.std() * sqrt(peak) /
L.mean()`. With `peak` 0.0521 the sqrt term only scales by 0.23, and the
crop's own high-frequency contrast -- foliage, blueberry, hard shadows
at a 12 deg sun -- carried the rest. The statistic was reporting how
BUSY the crop is, and a busy crop is not a tiled one.

ROOT CAUSE: I read a composite statistic without its component. `peak`
was in the same returned dict the whole time, 0.0521 against ~1.0 for a
genuinely tiled crop and ~0.01 for noise -- it said "no repeat" plainly.

THE SHAPE IS ALREADY IN R-LAYERS REJECTED. The p90 gradient that
returned EXACTLY sqrt(2)/2 for two different blends was pinned by
quantisation; this peak was pinned by a search window. Both are
statistics reporting their own limit and being read as the world.

THE RULE: **a bounded search returns its bound when it finds nothing.
Before believing an extremum, check whether it is sitting on the fence
you built for it.** The guard is cheap -- compare the found location
against the window's ends -- and it is now in `surface_report`, which
reports NO VERDICT rather than a FAIL it cannot support.


## 2026-09-11i — THE SCENE-LINEAR PASS IS NOT LINEAR, AND THE TONEMAP WAS NOT THE WHOLE STORY
> STATUS: HISTORY — records the power-law slope and exposure solve

The ruling was well-founded and its expected conclusion was wrong, which
is worth separating carefully.

WELL-FOUNDED: every card reading this project had ever taken was
post-tonemap, and two independent correction chains had under-delivered
by about a third (exposure 65.0%, white balance 68% then 40%). Moving the
measurement to a scene-linear EXR is exactly the right response, and the
engine setting was verified at the source rather than recalled --
`MoviePipelineColorSetting::bDisableToneCurve`, "If true the Filmic Tone
Curve will not be applied... Force Disabled if Open Color IO is enabled."
Note it lives on the COLOR SETTING, not on the deferred pass node where
the ruling supposed it would be.

WRONG: "expect exact". With the curve disabled and read back true, I
asked for a step of **exactly -1.000 EV** and the card moved
**-0.7266 EV**. A second step of -0.4453 EV delivered -0.3276. Two
different step sizes, one answer: the chain is a POWER LAW with log-log
slope **0.731**, not a multiply. The frame maximum agreed with the card
to within 0.02 EV, so it is the whole image, not the card region.

DISABLING THE CURVE IS NOT A NO-OP, AND THAT IS THE INTERESTING PART. At
one fixed exposure, the same station rendered with and without the flag
gave card 0.26489 vs 0.24480 -- an 8% change. So the flag does something,
and what it does is far too small to explain a 27% shortfall. Something
else after exposure is compressive: the grade's own `color_contrast` 0.95
is a power around a pivot and accounts for part of it, and the remainder
is unattributed. **The tonemap was A cause, not THE cause**, and the
earlier write-up (LESSONS 2026-09-11f) attributed the whole shortfall to
it on two data points that shared a confound.

A DIAGNOSTIC I GOT WRONG, AND CAUGHT. To test whether the EXR was really
linear I sRGB-decoded the PNG from the same render and compared: they
matched to within 1%, and I first read that as proof the tone curve was
still on. It proves nothing of the kind. **The PNG writer sRGB-encodes
whatever buffer it is handed**, so decoding it reproduces the EXR whether
the curve ran or not. The test had no power in either direction and I had
already started reasoning from it. What actually settled the question was
the A/B at fixed exposure above -- two renders differing in one flag.

THE FIX WAS TO MEASURE THE TRANSFER FUNCTION AND INVERT IT, rather than
iterate against a model that does not hold. From the measured slope, the
step needed from -3.9626 was -0.1611 EV (giving -4.1237) and the
independent extrapolation from the -4.9626 probe gave -4.1298 -- agreeing
to 0.006 EV, which is the model corroborating itself on data it was not
fitted to. Applied -4.1268: the card landed at **0.180072** against a
target of 0.18, a residual of -0.0006 EV.

THE RULE: **when a correction under-delivers, characterise the transfer
before taking another step.** Two points and a straight line in log-log
cost one extra capture and turned an iteration into a solve. And the
corollary, which is the part I keep having to learn: a mechanism that
EXPLAINS a shortfall is not the same as a mechanism that ACCOUNTS for it.
The tonemap explained the sign and the rough size, and it was responsible
for 8 points of 27.

## 2026-09-11j — THE DISPLAY-REFERRED CARD WAS FLATTERING THE GRADE, AND R-GRADE WAS LOCKED ON IT
> STATUS: HISTORY — records the 3550->3481.9 K re-derivation

R-GRADE was LOCKED at 3550 K on 2026-09-11 because the card read
**R/G 1.0230, B/G 1.0000** -- both comfortably inside the ruled
0.97-1.03. I reported it as landed.

On the scene-linear pass, at the same 3550 K and the same station, the
same card reads **R/G 1.0549, B/G 1.0014**. R is OUTSIDE the band. The
grade had not converged; the instrument had compressed the error.

This is the same compression that ate the exposure steps, seen from the
other side. A tone curve that turns a requested -1.000 EV into -0.727
will also turn a 5.5% channel excess into a 2.3% one, and 2.3% sits
inside a band that 5.5% does not. **The acceptance band was being applied
to a measurement the curve had already shrunk.**

THE CORRECTION, one step, by the same Planck two-channel method as
before: r = (R/G)/(B/G) = 1.0534, delta = ln(r)/9454 = +5.51 mired,
281.69 -> 287.20 mired, 3550 -> 3481.9 K. Measured after: **R/G 1.0307,
B/G 1.0286**, so the excess RATIO went 1.0534 -> 1.0020. The temperature
axis converged in exactly one step, as the ruling predicted it would once
the curve was out of the loop.

What remains is not temperature. R and B are now within 0.2% of each
other and BOTH about 3% above G -- a green-magenta offset, which is the
`white_tint` axis that R-GRADE already flags as a separate single step
and the recipe declares at 0. It is left at 0 rather than guessed: UE's
WhiteTint has no documented mapping to a channel multiplier, so deriving
that step needs a measured slope the way the temperature step has one.

THE RULE: **a locked value inherits the class of the instrument that
locked it.** R-GRADE's 3550 was not wrong arithmetic -- it was a correct
reading of a compressed signal. When an instrument is replaced by a
better one, every acceptance it ever passed is re-opened, not just the
ones that failed.


## 2026-09-11k — TWO STATION LISTS, AND MRQ RENDERS A MISSING SEQUENCE IN SILENCE

Adding `ground` to `bench_capture.STATIONS` produced three consecutive
runs that polled an idle engine log for 8 minutes each and wrote no
frames, no error and exit 0.

ROOT CAUSE: `scripts/payloads/bench_make_stills.py` carries its OWN
`STATIONS = ["near_ground", "mid_slope", "vista"]`. MRQ renders
SEQUENCES, not cameras, and `bench_capture` points each job at
`/Game/Bench/Bench_Still_<station>`. I extended one list and not the
other, so the job for `ground` named a sequence that does not exist --
and **MRQ rendered it without complaint**. A job with a null sequence is
not an error to MRQ; it is a job with nothing in it.

This is NN24 exactly -- "two lists that must agree are one list, badly
stored" -- and the material-builder skill already carries the same
lesson from the preflight/assertion split. The test it states is the one
that would have caught this: *if adding a thing can be done in one place
and forgotten in another, the structure is wrong, not the author.*

FIXED by making the payload take the list from its caller, so there is
one declaration. But note what the fix does NOT do: it does not make MRQ
complain. **A missing sequence is still silent**, so the durable
protection is the one list, not a check.

DIAGNOSTIC COST, and why it ran to three attempts: I twice read "no
output" as evidence of a stall when it was my own `| tail` buffering the
pipe, and the engine log's MRQ line count was cumulative across the
session so it looked like activity. The run that actually diagnosed it
was the plain foreground one with no pipeline. **Two of my three
"observations" were properties of how I was looking.**

## 2026-09-11l — THE DERIVED STATION PREDICTED 405 ROWS AND THE RENDER GAVE 55

`derive_ground_station` searched 220 meadow sites and 1,760 views and
returned Bench_ground with predicted band heights of **405 and 375 rows**
at full resolution, against a 160-row floor -- both clearing it by more
than 2x, with zero canopy in the lower half and meadow weight 1.0.

The rendered frame gives **55 rows and 0**. Depth percentiles from the
engine's own pass: p50 **9.04 m**, p75 16.24 m, and 85% of the frame
inside 30 m. Zero sky, so the camera is looking into rising ground as
intended -- and the rise puts everything CLOSE, not far.

THREE CAUSES, and the third is the one I should have seen:

1. **The scoring resolution lied.** The search counted a row as in-band
   when >50% of its pixels were, on a 256x144 grid, then multiplied by
   15 to reach full resolution. At that grid one row IS 15 full-res rows,
   so the quantisation is the entire margin.
2. **The raymarch models terrain and TREES, not GRASS.** Meadow is
   scattered at 120 instances per 10 m^2 and is precisely what fills a
   standing-height view over meadow. The station was selected for having
   no trees in the lower half; the grass was never in the model.
3. **A uniform rise COMPRESSES distance, it does not spread it** -- and
   I wrote that down myself, in the selftest fixture comment, while
   fixing the fixture: "even a gentle uniform slope is degenerate here --
   every distance sits at the same angle atan(s)". Only a CONCAVE profile
   spreads them. The fixture required concavity; **the search did not**.
   I encoded the insight in the test and not in the thing being tested.

THE RULE: **a search scores what its model can see, and its model is not
the renderer.** The selftest proved the scorer ranked a concave site
above a flat one -- which it did, correctly -- and that was never
evidence that the winning site would render the way the scorer thought.
Every one of these derivations needs its prediction CHECKED AGAINST THE
FRAME before the station is used, and the check is cheap: one capture and
a depth histogram.

AND THE SHARPER ONE: when a fixture needs a property to work, ask whether
the SEARCH requires that property too. The fixture's concavity was a
workaround for a degenerate case, and a degenerate case a fixture has to
dodge is a case the search will happily select.


## 2026-09-11m — Q12: THE 0.731 POWER LAW, LEFT OPEN ON PURPOSE
> STATUS: HISTORY — Q12 left OPEN on purpose in 2026-09-11m; later narrowed and closed

RULED BY RYAN 2026-09-11: the exposure message that arrived mid-session
was **not from the research desk** and is discarded. **Pre-exposure is
not to be touched.** The 0.731 response is logged as an open question and
the measured-slope solve stands as the exposure instrument.

THE MEASUREMENT, restated so the question is precise. With
`MoviePipelineColorSetting.bDisableToneCurve` set and READ BACK true, and
OCIO read back false:

    requested EXACTLY -1.0000 EV  ->  delivered -0.7266 EV
    requested         -0.4453 EV  ->  delivered -0.3276 EV
    slope 0.731 in log-log, stable across both step sizes; the frame
    MAXIMUM tracks the card to within 0.02 EV, so it is the whole
    image and not the card region

And disabling the curve is NOT a no-op: at one fixed exposure the same
station read card 0.26489 with it on and 0.24480 with it off. **8 points
of a 27% shortfall.** Something else after exposure is compressive.

### OPEN

    Q12 with the filmic tone curve disabled, the render still responds to
        exposure as a POWER LAW of slope 0.731 rather than a multiply.
        Candidates, in the order they are worth testing:
          (a) SCENE PRE-EXPOSURE. r.EyeAdaptation.PreExposureOverride and
              r.EyeAdaptation.CachedLightingPreExposure both exist in 5.8
              (verified in PostProcessEyeAdaptation.cpp). NOT TO BE
              TOUCHED by ruling -- listed because it is the leading
              candidate, not as an action.
          (b) MRQ's TONE-CURVE-DISABLED RESIDUAL STAGES. bDisableToneCurve
              removes the film curve, not the whole colour chain; expand
              gamut and blue correction sit in the same block and are not
              covered by the flag.
          (c) LOCAL EXPOSURE (r.LocalExposure*). If the project's
              local-exposure settings are NON-DEFAULT, that is the
              finding -- read back ONCE, which this session did.
        The grade's own color_contrast 0.95 is a power around a pivot and
        accounts for part of the remainder by construction.

WHY IT IS SAFE TO LEAVE OPEN. The exposure instrument does not depend on
knowing the cause: the slope is MEASURED per pair of captures and
inverted, and it predicted the landing point to 0.04% (card 0.180072
against a 0.18 target) from an extrapolation the model was not fitted to.
An unexplained transfer function that is measured and stable is a usable
instrument; it is only dangerous when it is assumed.

THE RULE, and it is the one I got wrong twice this week: **a mechanism
that EXPLAINS a shortfall is not a mechanism that ACCOUNTS for it.** I
attributed the whole under-delivery to the tonemap on two data points
that shared a confound, wrote it up as settled, and had to withdraw it
when a controlled A/B put the tonemap's share at 8 points of 27. The
honest form is a named question with ranked candidates, not a story that
fits.

⛔ AND THE FIRST ATTEMPT AT THIS READ WAS WORTHLESS. I read
`r.LocalExposure.*` through `get_console_variable_float_value` and got
0.0 for every one, which looked like "all zeroed, non-default, that's the

(Scene.h:2037). The tell was `r.TonemapperFilm` in the same batch also
reading 0.0 when its default is 1 -- a value I had no reason to expect,
sitting next to values I did. **A reader that cannot distinguish "zero"
from "absent" reports absence as a measurement**, which is
non-negotiable 6 wearing a number. The volume read distinguishes them by
the `bOverride_` companion.

CANDIDATE (a), PRE-EXPOSURE, ALSO LOOKS OUT -- and the ruling's

     per project to cover used exposure range. Default 4 maps to ~[-8; 12]
     of usable exposure range, which should mostly cover physically based
     lighting range without any lighting response clipping."

So **[-8, 12] is the exposure range the default PRODUCES**, not a safe
range for the parameter. This world's `compensation_ev` is -4.1268 and
